Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Could either side have won World War II without relying heavily on aircraft carriers?
Answer: You’d have to look at this country by country. This may be a controversial answer, but I think that, on the whole, carrier air was not actually as vital as is usually thought. I look forward to an interesting discussion. Carriers are, of course, simply floating airfields and their use case is therefore in places where no terrestrial airfield is available. In WW2 the Pacific theatre with its vast expanses of ocean was the obvious candidate. In the European, Mediterranean, North African, and India-Burma theatres, land based air could, in most cases provide the necessary coverage. Before we get started, an important point to discuss is opportunity cost: what you have to give up to buy what you want in terms of other things. Aircraft carriers are quite expensive to build and operate. What else could you have had for the same money? Roughly speaking you could have twelve Gato-class submarines for the cost of one Essex-class carrier (and I believe that’s without the cost of the air wing). US Carriers in the Pacific Let’s look at the individual countries: Germany: having carriers wouldn’t have made any significant difference to Germany and they never seriously pursued the option, abandoning the Graf Zeppelin half-built. The opportunity cost analysis was unfavourable. Italy: exactly the same can be said of Italy. Having carriers wouldn’t have made any difference to Italy as they could generally rely on land-based air in the land-locked Mediterranean theatre. Russia: the Russians didn’t have any carriers at all, and they handily won their war. They fought in no theatre where carriers would have been relevant. Great Britain: the British had carriers, but the fleet carriers played a surprisingly minor role in the vital Battle of the Atlantic. Once VLR aircraft were based in Iceland, there was probably no very acute need even for escort carriers. Fleet carriers were key to the Battles of Taranto and Matapan, as well as in the reinforcement of Malta, and it was a fleet carrier that put paid to the Bismarck. USA: Turning to the Pacific, the US obviously made the most use of carriers, but I’m not sure that they were absolutely needed to win the war. I say this because US submarines were already achieving that objective on their own quite happily. As you can see from the graphic below, that US submarines sank two and a half times more tonnage that US carrier air. Could Japan simply have been left to wither on the vine? Of course, the key question is whether US submarines could have operated effectively from distant bases. The Gato and Balao-class could operate from Pearl, Brisbane or Freemantle and still cruise as far as the Sea of Japan. The question is probably whether the US could have supplied Pearl and Australia with land-based aircraft, fuel, etc. without the use of carriers? Possibly not. If US submarines could have neutralised the Japanese Navy and destroyed her supply lines, the island hopping campaign, and its necessary carrier support, is moot. Japan: was in the same position, needing carriers to support its expansion to its defensive perimeter in order to establish bases for land-based air cover. However, the Japanese carriers were of no use at all in protecting the vital fuel convoy routes from US submarines. This was an asymmetrical situation to that of the US. I would conclude that the war in Europe could have been won by either side without relying heavily on aircraft carriers. The situation in the Pacific was more nuanced. I would say that there was a reliance on carriers for certain tasks, but that these magnificent beasts weren’t quite the war winning weapons that they might appear in the public eye.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Are most people aware that it was actually Britain that invented concentration camps (during the Boer War) and not Germany?
Answer: To avoid arguments over terminology, it is my understanding that the questioner is attempting to draw a comparison between the British Boer War camps and the German extermination camps, or Todeslager, of WW2. Wrong on two counts. The first modern concentration camps were created during the Cuban War of Independence (1895–1898) when the Spanish Army, under General Valeriano Weyler, established a policy of reconcentrado, which involved moving rural Cuban civilians into detention camps. During the Philippine-American War (1899–1902), the US Army established concentration camps, again referred to as reconcentrado, for Filipino civilians. In both these cases, harsh conditions, led to high mortality rates due to disease, malnutrition, and poor sanitation. The concentration camps established during the Second Boer War (1899–1902) were therefore part of a common counterinsurgency approach and were not a British invention. Secondly, there is no parallel, apart from the name, between the Boer War concentration camps and Germany’s WW2 extermination camps. The intention behind the British camps was literally to concentrate the population in order to deny supplies to the Boers. The intention behind the German camps was explicitly to kill people. This is not to say that people didn’t die in the British camps. Inadequate shelter, poor diet, bad hygiene and overcrowding led to widespread disease and somewhere in the region of 22,000 civilians died in the camps. The difference is that when the conditions in the camps became known in Britain there was a huge uproar and public outrage. There was no such public objection to the German Todeslager. The government was forced to set up the Fawcett Commission and Millicent Fawcett was blunt in expressing her opinion that much of the catastrophe was owed to a simple failure to observe elementary rules of hygiene. The administration of the camps was placed in civilian hands, improvements were made and the annual death rate fell from 7% to 2%. It is worth bearing in mind that over 14,000 British soldiers, roughly 3-4%, died of disease during a conflict where only 8,000 died in combat. 1900 was not 2024. The British camps in South Africa were a disgrace but the difference in intent is clear. Deaths in the British camps were accidental, deaths in the German camps were systematic murder.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for using carrots as a cover story for German radar during World War II?
Answer: Not a cover story for German radar, but for British airborne intercept radar. ‘Cat's Eyes' Cunningham. John Cunningham, CBE, DSO (three awards), DFC (two awards), Silver Star - pretty impressive - was nicknamed 'Cat's Eyes' by the British press to explain his successes and to avoid communicating the existence of the new AI (Airborne Intercept) radar to the enemy. Cunningham flew Blenheim and then Beaufighter night fighters with 604 Squadron RAF which was the among first to be issued with AI Mk. IV (the first production AI radar) which could detect large enemy aircraft at a range of around four miles after being vectored on to the target by GCI (Ground Controlled Interception) operators. On the 14th November 1940, Cunningham made the second ever kill using AI radar, a Junkers Ju 88 over Chichester in West Sussex. Beaufighter night fighter with AI radar After twelve victories (he was an ace after five), the Air Ministry decided to publicise Cunningham’s achievements in order to improve public morale during the Blitz by showing that the RAF was fighting back against the German night bombing campaign. The RAF did not want the enemy to learn that RAF night fighters had working airborne interception radar as German night fighters would not be equipped with such devices until much later. In order to hide the existence of the radar, the RAF explained Cunningham's successes by saying that his eyesight was so exceptional it allowed him to see in the dark with the same visual ability as a domestic cat and that a diet rich in carrots provided him with vitamin A which allowed him to maintain excellent night vision. F/Lt. John ‘Cats Eyes’ Cunningham

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many convicts from Britain were sent to Australia and during what time period did this occur?
Answer: Originally, between the 1600s and 1776, convicts were transported to the North American colonies as an alternative to imposing the death penalty under the Bloody Code. The convicts, some 50,000 to 120,000, became indentured servants and were free to either remain or return to Great Britain, at their own cost, at the end of their sentences. However, many of the colonies were none too keen on accepting convicts and transportation diminished after 1670 and was largely suspended on the outbreak of the American Revolution, although some transportation to North America seems to have continued until at least 1784 (c.f. Thomas Barrett), with Parliament ruling that: the transportation of convicts to his Majesty's colonies and plantations in America... is found to be attended with various inconveniences, particularly by depriving this kingdom of many subjects whose labour might be useful to the community, and who, by proper care and correction, might be reclaimed from their evil course However, the pressure on prisons and hulks became too great and the 1784 and 1785 Transportation Acts re-introduced transportation and a new penal colony in New South Wales was established by Order in Council in December 1786. his Majesty hath declared and appointed... that the eastern coast of New South Wales, and the islands thereunto adjacent, should be the place or places beyond the seas to which certain felons, and other offenders, should be conveyed and transported The initial tranche of convicts arrived with the First Fleet of eleven ships, including the convict transports Alexander, Charlotte, Friendship, Lady Penryhn, Prince of Wales, and Scarborough which arrived in Botany Bay on the 20th of January 1788, carrying 548 male and 188 female convicts. Arrival of the First Fleet Convict transportation peaked in 1833 when 7,000 convicts arrived in Australia, but transportation continued until as late as 1868 when the passing of the Penal Servitude Act of 1857 replaced the practice with domestic imprisonment. The last convicts arrived in the convict transport Hougoumont docking at the port of Fremantle - Western Australia became a penal colony in 1849 - on the 9th of January 1868 with 269 convicts on board. The convict transport Hougomont It is estimated that over 162,000 men and women were subject to transportation during the period that it was in use in Australia. Convicts were predominantly from England and Wales, most from the rapidly growing industrial cities of England, but there was a large contingent of Irish (24%) and a smaller number of Scots (5%). About 20% were female and a small proportion were political, including Irish home rule insurgents, the Tolpuddle Martyrs, anti-industrialising Luddites, Canadian rebels and Chartists. By the mid-1830s only 6% of convicts were locked up. The vast majority worked for the government or free settlers and, with good behaviour, could earn a ticket of leave, conditional pardon or and even an absolute pardon. While under such orders convicts could earn their own living. Former convicts Thomas Tomlinson, Davey Evans, and Paddy Paternoster in 1898 Thomas Tomlinson born 1834. Horse breaker and pipe maker. Convicted of larceny of fixtures at Manchester Assizes (second conviction) and sentenced to 7 years on the 10th of June 1858. Transported from Portsmouth prison to Western Australia on the Clyde arriving at Freemantle on the 29th of May 1863. Convict 7274. Ticket of Leave granted on 23rd of June 1863, Conditional Pardon granted on 21st of March 1864. Dealer in skins. Died Claremont, Western Australia, 10th of March, 1908.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In WW1, when troops were in no man's land, what happened to let's say German soldiers who made unauthorized retreats back to their own trench? Were they shot like in "enemy at the gates"?
Answer: The reference to Enemy at the Gates refers to the Russians in WW2 where NKVD blocking detachments operating under Order No.227, Not a step back, did occasionally shoot panic mongers and cowards. Form within the limits of each army three to five well-armed defensive squads (up to 200 persons in each), and put them directly behind unstable divisions and require them in case of panic and scattered withdrawals of elements of the divisions to shoot in place panic-mongers and cowards and thus help the honest soldiers of the division execute their duty to the Motherland. Order No.227 Para 2.b Even then only around 4% of deserters were shot (in the first three months around 1,000 men); the rest were rounded up as stragglers and either returned to unit or, in the case of some 423,000 men, sent to a penal battalion. In WW1, No Man’s land was the area between the two trench lines and was typically between one and three hundred yards wide, although in some cases it could be as little as thirty yards. The only reason for troops being in No Man’s land was either because they were mounting an offensive patrol or a wiring party or because the were engaged in an all-out assault on the enemy’s lines. In the case of patrols and wiring parties, they were always intended to return to their own lines. As they were usually conducted at night, it was not particularly unusual for men to become separated and to have to return to their own lines alone. There was a danger of being shot by trigger-happy sentries and men on patrols often considered returning to their own trenches the most dangerous part of the operation. During a full-blown assault there would be a great deal of movement back and forwards with runners (messengers), stretcher bearers, walking wounded making their way back to a dressing station, linesmen, etc. If the attack failed then the remains of whole units would return to their own lines. Going over the top In the British Army, there were regimental police who manned posts to collect and organise stragglers, but there is scant or no evidence of field executions conducted out of hand in official documentation. The historians Gary Sheffield and Richard Holmes both comment on this, although they accept that unsupported anecdotal evidence exists and neither are prepared to discount the idea that it possibly occurred in isolated incidents. It might come as a bit of a surprise to realise that the German Army in WW1 was the least likely of all the combatants to shoot their own men. There is a recurring story that some German machine gunners were found chained to their guns, but this seems very likely to be apocryphal and probably a misunderstanding of the carrying harnesses that the Germans used. German soldier with (unused) carry harness

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for Britain not invading France at Waterloo and choosing to fight on Belgian soil instead? Did Napoleon have less support in Belgium?
Answer: The Battle of Waterloo took place on the 18th of June 1815 and was part of the War of the Seventh Coalition which followed Napoleon’s return from exile in February 1815 and his subsequent campaign known as the Hundred Days. The seventh Coalition (Britain, Prussia, Russia, Austria, and several smaller countries) had decided that France was to be invaded around the 1st of July, a date chosen to allow all of the coalition members time to mobilise and to get their troops in place - particularly the Russians who had a lot of ground to cross to get to the borders of France. This strategy was eminently sensible and was designed to prevent Napoleon from exercising his well known operational skills and defeating his enemies in detail (one by one). The idea was that the Allies would march on Paris from different directions and in great strength, crushing the smaller French armies with their superior numbers. In brief, Wellington and Blucher with about 112,000 Anglo-Dutch troops and some 117,000 Prussians would attack France from the Low Countries. Schwarzenberg and 210,000 Austrians would attack from the Black Forest, and an army of 50,000 Austrians and 25,000 Piedmontese under the command of General Frimont would threaten Lyons and the Rivièra. A Spanish-Portuguese army would attack from the south, and Barclay de Tolly's 150,000 Russians would form a reserve on the central Rhine. Wellington at Waterloo When Wellington arrived to take to the command of the Allied Army in early April 1815 he found mainly the original Subsidiary Army commanded by the Prince of Orange, which had been stationed in the Low Countries since the end of the previous war in 1814. The British campaign in the Low Countries in 1813–1814 in support of the Dutch revolt against the French is one of the lesser-known campaigns of the Napoleonic Wars. Sir John Fortescue wrote that it was impossible to understand the Waterloo campaign without a knowledge of it. Desiring a friendly client state across the narrow seas, Britain had encouraged the unification of the old Dutch Republic with what is now Belgium but which had previously been the Austrian Netherlands before being annexed to France, together with the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. This shotgun marriage had created the Dutch-dominated United Kingdom of the Netherlands, with William VI of Orange becoming King William I. The Prince of Orange at Quatre Bras Therefore, when Wellington arrived his army amounted to a small force of British and Hanoverians, stationed there in 1814 to assist with the formation of the new country and to guarantee its borders. I have got an infamous army, very weak and ill equipped and a very inexperienced Staff. Wellington, 8th of May 1815 Wellington assumed command and reorganised the army, merging the British, Hanoverian, and King’s German Legion forces with those of the Netherlands. The army was reinforced over the next three months with troops from Great Britain, The Netherlands, Hanover, Brunswick and Nassau. In this way, the Wellington’s force grew from perhaps 15,000 men in April to around 112,000 in June. On his way to assume command, Wellington and Gneisenau met in Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle) on what is now the Belgian border and agreed that the Prussian Army of the Lower Rhine and the Anglo-Allied Army would cooperate in invading France from the Low Countries (the Prussians would have to cross the Low Countries to take the most direct route to Paris). I hope that this makes it clear why both the Anglo-Allied and Prussian armies were concentrating in the Low Countries (Belgium). On the 3rd of May, Wellington and Blücher met at Tirlemont and agreed to concentrate some 220,000 Anglo-Allied and Prussian troops between Liège and Courtrai, along the line Quatre-Bras to Sombreffe whilst they waited for the Russian and Austrian armies to get into position. By early June, Wellington and Blucher had agreed to attack on the 27th of June and their forces were concentrated about nine miles from the French border in a position designed to mask Brussels whilst they waited to start their offensive. However, as is well known, Napoleon, realising that his only viable option was to defeat the allied armies in detail, attacked first in a last desperate throw of the dice, crossing the border in the 15th of June. Therefore, the reason that Britain fought on Belgian soil was simply that Napoleon pre-empted the Allied invasion of France by twelve days. Napoleon at Ligny As regards support for Napoleon in Belgium, this was not a factor in Wellington’s strategy. However, there were understandable concerns at the time regarding the reliability of the Dutch-Belgian units because quite a few of them had previously served under Napoleon prior to 1814. In the event, these concerns proved unfounded and the Dutch-Belgian troops performed very well at Quatre Bras and Waterloo. Yes, I know that Belgium didn’t actually come into existence until 1831, but I’m trying not to confuse people too much. The question refers to Belgium and we will assume the Belgium, the Low Countries, and The Netherlands are all synonymous for our purposes here.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain make a promise to protect Poland during World War II but fail to intervene due to an agreement with Russia?
Answer: Yes, No, and No. Britain had no agreement with Russia in 1939. There had briefly been a possibility of a four-power agreement between Britain, France, Poland, and Russia earlier in 1939 when the major concern was that Romania that would be the next target of German aggression. This possibility was quashed by the Poles themselves as well by as objections from the Romanian, Finnish, Yugoslav, Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese governments. Georges Bonnet, the French Foreign Minister, then proposed a tri-partite scheme, between Britain, France and Poland. At this point, which seems obviously wrong with hindsight, Poland was seen as better ally against Germany than Russia. The British Chiefs of Staff met to discuss a draft report of the Joint Planning Committee on the question of the military implications of an Anglo-French guarantee to Poland and Romania. This assumed the Russians remained a friendly neutral to the extent of being willing to supply war material to Poland and Romania. The Chiefs of Staff considered the Polish Army of fifty divisions modern and well equipped but that Poland's anti-aircraft defences were inadequate, her factories vulnerable, and her transport horse-based (as was that of the Germans). In the case of a German attack on the East and a holding operation in the West, they argued that Poland and Romania would eventually fall, but that as many German troops would be required to hold Poland and Romania and to guard against possible Soviet attack, as would be required to conquer it in the first place. The Chiefs of Staff were clear that no direct aid could be offered to either Poland or Romania for reasons that can readily be appreciated by glancing at a map. The Russians, on the 18th of April, sent a counter-proposal for a full-blown military pact. The pact was to cover cases of aggression against one of the signatories or against any East European state from the Black to the Baltic Seas. A comprehensive military convention was to be signed simultaneously with the political agreement. This was initially rejected on the grounds of the danger of stinging Germany into aggressive action and the likelihood of objections from other European countries but, by the end of May, an alliance with the Russians seemed to be on the cards. It was never to be due to mutual distrust and the Russian insistence that it be allowed to move troops through Poland and Romania if necessary. On August the 23rd, 1939, the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact was signed between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. This non-aggression pact included secret protocols dividing Eastern Europe into spheres. German and Russian troops carve up Poland between them Therefore, (a) Britain did make a pact with Poland, (b) Britain didn’t fail to intervene, declaring war on Germany two days after the German invasion of Poland and continuing that war for six years, and (c) Britain had no agreement of any kind with Russia.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: When did they begin to train RAF pilots in Canada during WW2?
Answer: Britain, not having ideal weather to train pilots, started the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan in 1939. BCATP was part of the Empire Air Training Scheme (EATS) which also saw pilots trained in Australia, Rhodesia, and the United States. Churchill visits the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan school at RCAF Uplands, (Ottawa) Ontario, in December 1941 The first BCATP course started on April the 29th, 1940 and ended on the 5th of November 1940 when thirty-four pilots gained their wings. By the end of the war, over 50,000 pilots and another 120,000 aircrew had trained in Canada. The courses not only trained pilots but also navigators (often washed out pilots), air gunners, bomb aimers, and wireless operators. The scheme called for the training of nearly 50,000 aircrew each year, for as long as necessary: 22,000 aircrew from Great Britain, 13,000 from Canada, 11,000 from Australia and 3,300 from New Zealand. Murray Peden, a Canadian as it happens, describes the training process very well in his book A Thousand Shall Fall. I personally found it very sobering to read how many candidates died during training. Learning to fly high-performance aircraft in the 1940s was still a demanding and dangerous business. A friend and neighbour of mine, Robert Smith, now deceased, trained in Canada under the scheme and he always remembered how welcoming the Canadians were to homesick British lads. For anyone interested in the scheme, I thoroughly recommend Peden’s book: and those interested in RAF training in the United States can do no better than Jack Currie’s Wings over Georgia:

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the meaning of WW2 Kriegspiel?
Answer: Kriegspiel is the German term for war game and is also the name of an umpire based simulation or game created by a Captain in the Prussian Army, Georg von Reisswitz, although the original concept was created by his father in around 1812. Reisswitz developed his system with the intention of using it as a tool for training army officers and, after he had demonstrated it to the King, the game was officially adopted in 1824. Although termed a “game”, simulation is probably a better word for it and the Kriegspiel sought to simulate tactical battles realistically using formalised rules and two minute time segments. It also introduced the concept of red and blue forces which we still use. The original Kriegspiel went through many iterations and survives to this day. However, in the inter-war period, the Germans developed a number of different games to simulate and test and rehearse plans at every level in the chain of command. This was partly because the Germans were severely limited by the Versailles Treaty in both number and type (no tanks for instance) and thus simulations were the only way of trying out new concepts at scale. Before and during WW2, the Kriegsspiel was broadened to include not only the traditional war game but also the planning game (Planspiel), staff exercise (Stabsuebung), exercise ride (Uebungsreise), terrain evaluation (Gelaendebesprechung), command staff exercise (Rahmenuebung), special exercise (Sonderuebung), and sand-table exercise (Sandkastenuebung). The aim was to make commanders at all levels thoroughly familiar with the situation and also with the difficulties they would have to overcome with respect to both enemy and terrain. The Germans also used war games to test combat principles. In these games one side used the doctrine and tactics of the potential enemy. The “friendly” commanders were changed several times, in order to bring the decisions of several persons to bear on principles to be tested. The Germans often used war games as teaching tools for the study of the past campaigns and operations and also for the testing and improvement of certain doctrine developed and used in the past… Another purpose of a war game was training in techniques and procedures of writing and issuing orders. At the highest levels there were Commander’s Rides (Fuehrerreisen) evaluating the potential for major operations and campaigns in World War II where the participants were exclusively generals—group, division, and infantry or artillery commanders. At the other extreme, junior officers and NCOs were engaged with Plannin games (Planuebungen) which looked at tactical problems. The Germans differentiated between educational (Belehrungspiel) and testing (Erprobungspiel) war games. The purpose of the educational war game was to educate officers in the use of doctrine whilst the purpose of a testing war game was to explore strategic or tactical thinking or to develop new concepts of troop leadership. Similar games were also played in the Kriegsmarine. For his crossing of the Meuse, Guderian issued exactly the same orders he had prepared during the preparatory planning game, changing only the date and time of attack. Therefore the meaning of WW2 Kriegspiel encompasses a wide range of simulations that the Germans developed prior to and during WW2 in order to test and evaluate everything from grand strategy to tactical issues and played by everyone from Field Marshals to Sergeants.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain protect Portugal during the Napoleonic Wars even though they were not allies?
Answer: Yes, Britain did indeed seek to aid Portugal during the Napoleonic Wars. However, it is not correct to say that the two countries were not allies. Apart from from the period when Portugal and Spain were dynastically unified, between 1580 and 1640, Britain and Portugal have been allied since the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty was signed between Edward III of England and Ferdinand and Queen Eleanor of Portugal in June 1373. At over 650 years old, this makes the treaty the world’s oldest diplomatic alliance. There shall be between the respective kings and their successors, their realms, lands, dominions, provinces, vassals, and subjects whomsoever, faithfully obeying, true, faithful, constant, mutual, and perpetual friendships, unions, alliances, and leagues of sincere affection; and that, as true and faithful princes, they shall henceforth reciprocally be friends to friends and enemies to enemies, and shall assist, maintain, and uphold each other mutually, by sea and by land, against all men that may live or die of whatever degree, station, rank, or condition they may be, and against their lands, realms, and dominions. The original treaty and celebrating the 650th anniversary of its signing in 2023 When Churchill announced Portugal’s agreement to the establishment of British air and naval bases in the Portuguese Azores in 1943, he later recorded: “I have an announcement", I said, “to make to the House arising out of the treaty signed between this country and Portugal in the year 1373 between His Majesty King Edward III and King Ferdinand and Queen Eleanor of Portugal." I spoke in a level voice, and made a pause to allow the House to take in the date, 1373. As this soaked in there was something like a gasp. I do not suppose any such continuity of relations between two Powers has ever been, or will ever be, set forth in the ordinary day-to-day work of British diplomacy. The Royal Navy’s use of the port of Lisbon, Portugal's trade with Britain, and her open refusal to join the Continental System, Napoleon’s ill-fated attempt to blockade all trade between Britain and the Continent, were all marks of the cooperation and friendship between Britain and Portugal, marks that Napoleon could not tolerate. France and Spain invaded Portugal in November 1807 and in August 1808 the first fifteen thousand British troops, including a contingent of the King’s German Legion, landed in Portugal under the command of Sir Arthur Wellesley (later the Duke of Wellington) to drive the French out of Portugal. The Battle of Vimeiro on 21st August 1808 put an end to the first French invasion of Portugal The British involvement in Portugal and Spain, generally known as the Peninsular War, lasted until the abdication of Napoleon in 1814. As Sir William Napier wrote: Those veterans had won nineteen pitched battles and innumerable combats; had made or sustained ten sieges and taken four great fortresses; had twice expelled the French from Portugal, once from Spain; had penetrated France, and killed wounded or captured two hundred thousand enemies — leaving of their own number forty thousand dead, whose bones whiten the plains and mountains of the Peninsula. It is worth noting that amongst his extraordinary list of honours, the Duke of Wellington was made Marshal-General of the Portuguese Army, Count of Vimeira, Marquess of Torres Vedras, and Duke of Victoria.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it true the Gen. MacArthur awarded himself the first purple heart in 1942? I cant imagine he was wounded in his desertion of the Philippines?
Answer: It is certainly true that MacArthur received the first Purple Heart, whether he awarded it to himself I could not say. MacArthur, as US Army Chief of Staff, was responsible for the introduction of the Purple Heart as a successor to both the original (but defunct) Badge of Military Merit and the practice of issuing wound chevrons copied from the French and British in WW1. Two gold US Army wound chevrons worn on the right sleeve. The chevrons on the left sleeve are war service chevrons representing six months overseas service each The Badge of Military Merit had been introduced by George Washington in 1782 but was hardly ever issued. This was a general purpose award and the Purple Heart was also originally also intended not just for wounds but for meritorious service until December 1942. Original Badge of Military Merit and Purple Heart Whether MacArthur deserved the award for meritorious service or not, he did qualify for two wound chevrons, and thus two Purple Hearts, as a result of being lightly gassed twice during WW1. MacArthur received his Purple Hearts on the day that the medal was authorised by Presidential Executive Order on the 22nd of February 1932, the bicentenary of George Washington’s birth. Some sources state that MacArthur has his medal engraved with the number #1. MacArthur’s medals including his Purple Heart and oak leaf for second award (4th row)

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the original name of Britain's Navy before it was renamed "The Royal Navy"?
Answer: “Britain” can be a rather ambiguous term. The Kingdom of Great Britain was created by the merger of England (including Wales) and Scotland as ratified by the Acts of Union in 1707. Before that date, there was an English Royal Navy and a Scottish Royal Navy. However, before that date the English Royal Navy was known as the Royal Navy from the time of the Restoration of Charles II in 1660; this was also when ships belonging to the Navy started to gain the prefix His Majesty’s Ship. Before that, during the Commonwealth, from 1649 to 1660, when there was no King and therefore, pretty obviously, no Royal Navy, the navy was known as the Commonwealth or Parliamentary Navy. Before that in 1546, and dating back to the reign of Henry VIII, it was officially termed the Navy Royal. This was not so much about ships, but marked the point when the administration of the Navy started to be formalised in the shape of the Admiralty and Marine Affairs Office. Before that, there was a Lord High Admiral dating back to 1385, originally called the High Admiral of England, Ireland and Aquitaine, but no really permanent establishment. Whilst the Monarch often owned a few ships in his own name, most ships were requisitioned or hired as the need arose. A 1381 Act in the reign of Richard II provided that “to increase the navy of England, no goods or merchandises shall be either exported or imported, but only in ships belonging to the King's subjects”but this probably just meant the total number commercial vessels, rather than being a reference to any kind of organised navy. When Henry VII came to the throne in 1485 the navy, in the sense that we’d think of it today, probably only consisted of six or seven ships. Henry Grace à Dieu, the largest warship in Europe and, possibly, the world in 1514

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many ships did Spain lose during the Battle of Trafalgar?
Answer: Ten, but that, as you will see, is not a straightforward question to answer. The Franco-Spanish fleet started with thirty-three ships of the line (2,632 guns), five frigates and two brigs, opposing a British fleet of twenty-seven ships of the line (2,152 guns), four frigates, a schooner and a cutter. Frigates and smaller ships traditionally took no part in major fleet actions and are excluded from this analysis. This gave the Franco-Spanish fleet an advantage of 22% in both ships and guns, with both forces averaging 80 guns per ship. The French component of the Franco-Spanish fleet was eighteen ships of the line (1,356 guns). Nine of these surrendered during the battle. Of these, one, Achille, subsequently blew up, four, Berwick, Redoutable, Fouguex, and Aigle foundered after the battle, one, Intrépide, was scuttled by the British after the battle and two, Algésiras and Bucentaure, were recaptured. Only one, Swiftsure, remained in British hands. However, of the nine French ships that escaped the battle, one, Indomptable was wrecked on the 24th of October, and four, Scipion, Formidable, Duguay-Trouin, and Mont Blanc were captured on the 4th of November. Battle of Trafalgar The Spanish component of the Franco-Spanish fleet was fifteen ships of the line (1,276 guns). Nine of these surrendered during the battle. Of these three, San Agustin, Monarca, and Argonauta were either burnt or scuttled by the British, and one, Nuestra Señora de la Santísima Trinida, foundered. Two, Neptuno and Santa Ana were recaptured, but the Neptuno then foundered. Three, Bahama, San Ildefonso, and San Juan Nepomuceno remained in British hands. Of the six that escaped the battle, one, Rayo, surrendered two days later but then foundered, and one, San Francisco de Asis, was wrecked two days after the battle. During the Age of Sail, ships did not very often sink after battles and the reason for the peculiar number that foundered or were wrecked is the violent storm that blew up immediately after the battle, hampering repair attempts and causing many of the badly damaged prizes to break their tows. In the end, only eleven Franco-Spanish ships escaped to Cádiz, and, of these, only five were considered seaworthy. These were the French Héros, Neptune, Pluton, Indomptable, and Argonaute, and the Spanish San Leandro, San Justo, Montañés, Principe de Asturias, Rayo, and San Francisco de Asis. Two of these Rayo and San Francisco de Asis were lost after the Cosmao and MacDonnell sortie on the 23rd and 26th respectively. As mentioned, a further four French ships, Scipion, Formidable, Duguay-Trouin, and Mont Blanc, evaded capture until the 4th of November. Therefore, the Spanish part of the fleet started with fifteen ships of the line and ended with five, San Leandro, San Justo, Montañés, Principe de Asturias, and the recaptured Santa Ana, whilst the French started with eighteen ships and also ended up with five, Héros, Neptune, Pluton, Argonaute, and the recaptured Algésiras, overall a 70% loss rate. The frigate Themis towing the dismasted Santa Ana after the battle before her recapture The British lost no ships in the battle and, in fact, added eight ships of the line to their fleet, Swiftsure (renamed Irresistible), Scipion, Formidable (renamed Brave), Duguay-Trouin (renamed Implacable), Mont Blanc, Bahama, San Ildefonso, and San Juan Nepomuceno (renamed San Juan). Duguay-Trouin/Implacable during WW2 in 1943 Phew, I think that’s all correct, but no doubt someone will spot any errors.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did Britain accept an "unconditional" German surrender without concluding peace with other countries first? Could they have refused and waited for all parties to agree on terms together?
Answer: Well, why not? If someone offers unconditional surrender you grab it with both hands whilst it’s there. As the surrender is unconditional you can impose whatever terms you want after the event - that’s what unconditional means - and so there is no need to agree terms with other allies at that point. As it happens, that’s not actually the sequence of events. General Alfred Jodl, Chief of Staff of the German Army, signed an unconditional surrender on May 7th, 1945, at Supreme Headquarters, Allied Expeditionary Force (SHAEF) in Reims. The Soviets were not satisfied with this and insisted that another surrender, this time signed by Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel, Chief of the OKW, on May 8th, 1945 in Berlin, represented the official, legal surrender of the Third Reich. What happened on May 4th was that Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery accepted the unconditional surrender of all German forces in the Netherlands, Denmark, and Northern Germany. This marked the end of the war as far as the British Sector was concerned, but was not a general surrender of all German forces. The surrender that Montgomery signed was entirely in line with the guidelines produced by the Combined Chiefs of Staff in August 1944. Admiral Hans-Georg von Friedeburg signs the surrender at Luneberg on May 4th 1945

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for German U-boats being unable to detect Allied convoys at night during World War II?
Answer: Because it is dark at night. For most of the war U-boats relied on visually locating convoys. The ocean is a big place and even when the U-boat had prior knowledge of where the convoy was likely to be, they still had to pinpoint it before the could attack it. As a U-boat sits very low in the water when surfaced, its visual horizon is correspondingly small at around 9km - and even less at periscope depth. Efforts were made to extend the visual sighting range by using collapsible masts or rotary wing kites but these, of course, could not be used at night. The Fa 330 autogyro could reach a height of 120m and had a visual horizon of around 46km. However it made the U-boat horribly vulnerable to air attack and was only used in very limited circumstances. The only ship known to have been sunk after being spotted by a Fa 330 was the Efthalia Mari, sunk of off Madagascar in the Indian Ocean by the U-177. Observarion mast and Focke Achgelis Fa 330 Bachstelze autogyro kite During the day the convoys gave off smoke which is visible, depending on weather conditions for up to 20km and this was probably the most common way of homing in on targets. This is not to say that U-boats didn’t attack convoys at night as they frequently did. But this was in situations where the convoy had already been detected and was being trailed by the U-boat(s) in question. U-boats were also fitted with hydrophones, Gruppenhorchgerat, which could, in theory at least, give a rough bearing on a ship at 20km and a convoy at up to 100km by day or by night, but these were highly dependent on sea conditions and could only be used when the U-boat was nearly stopped. As early as 1941 the U-boats were experimenting with radar but the U-boat version of the naval Seetakt radar was unsuccessful. In 1943 a better system, the FMG 41G (gU), was installed but this was easily damaged in the harsh environment that the U-boats operated in and many commanders feared that the radar might give their own positions away and so did not use the system. These radar systems could be used at night, but they only had a surface detection range of about 10km.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why are people downplaying America's role during WW2, saying it could have been won without them? They say America was useless and did not make a difference.
Answer: WW2 could certainly have been won without America, the question is who by? However, I don’t think that there is anybody who could possibly genuinely think that America didn’t make a difference in WW2 and so I regard this a troll question. The United States obviously played two vital roles in WW2. The first was, of course, direct military action both in Europe and in the Pacific with over twelve million men deployed overseas during the war. The second, arguably even more important, was the logistical support of the other Allied nations in terms of both materiel and other supplies. There is no doubt that the Lend-Lease programme was vital to the war effort of both the United Kingdom (receiving $31.4b) and the Soviet Union (receiving $11.3b). Arsenal of democracy A war without US involvement is difficult to parse. In Europe, the likely outcome would be a negotiated peace between Germany and Britain followed by a titanic battle between Germany and the Soviet Union. This is difficult to call, but with Britain and the US neutral, I think that Germany might well have won and Europe might well have, to paraphrase Churchill, sunk into the abyss of a new Dark Age made more sinister, and perhaps more protracted, by the lights of perverted science. However, like the current regime in Russia, the Nazi regime was inherently unstable and it is not clear that it could have stabilised the situation in the long term. In the Pacific, it is almost impossible to see how Japan could have embarked on its expansionist policies without triggering a reaction from the United States. If it could have managed this feat then it might well have swept away the distracted Europeans in the Dutch East Indies, French Indochina, and Malaya and Burma, but Japan’s logistical weaknesses would probably have brought it to a halt on the borders on India. Alternative histories are always fanciful because there are simply too many variables and interconnections. Within the appropriate Lyapunov time, months or years, the outcomes would become completely chaotic and unpredictable. Whatever else you might say, the war would not have followed the same course without the US playing a significant role.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was alcohol prohibited in Great Britain during World War II?
Answer: Nope. You might be thinking of Prohibition in the United States between 1920 and 1933. What we did have was the Defence of the Realm Act, introduced in 1914 and amended six times. DORA contained some draconian provisions and a host of minor ones, including banning, inter-alia, loitering, the possession of cocaine or opium, melting down gold or silver, flying kites, starting bonfires, buying binoculars, making white flour, whistling in London, feeding bread to horses or chickens, discussing naval and military matters in public, and buying alcohol on public transport. Specifically, as regards alcohol, in 1915, the then Minister for Munitions, Lloyd George, declared: We are fighting Germans, Austrians and drink, and so far as I can see the greatest of these deadly foes is drink. There were fears that over indulgence with alcohol by factory and munition workers would cost Britain productivity and starve the army of ammunition. In the areas containing the new munitions factories, cases of drunkenness, anti-social behaviour, and resulting convictions had quadrupled and there was also a heightened risk of hampering the war effort through increased sick absences and the threat of serious accidents as workers had to manually handle nitro-glycerine and guncotton. A a result, among the far-reaching powers granted to the government by DORA, was new legislation regarding the selling and consuming of alcohol. An experiment in Carlisle nationalised the local breweries and pubs (some of which remained state-owned until 1971) and closed nearly 40% of the pubs as well as revoking all off-sales licenses. All advertising referring to alcohol was made illegal and a ban was placed on the display of liquor bottles in windows. The sale of ‘chasers’ – spirits accompanying beer – was banned and it was forbidden to serve alcohol to people under the age of 18 or to sell spirits on Saturdays. It also became illegal to buy drinks for other people, thus ending the tradition of buying alcohol in rounds. Treating others carried a maximum penalty of six months imprisonment. The percentage of alcohol in beer was lowered to reduce drunkenness. The average Original Gravity (OG) of beer in England and Wales dropped significantly, from 1059 to 1029, between 1914 and 1919. The government also raised taxes on alcohol. The cost of a pint of beer roughly doubled and by 1918 a bottle of whisky cost five times its pre-war price. Most importantly, licensing hours, the time when public houses were permitted to sell alcohol, forced pubs to close during the middle of the day to prevent all day drinking. The new hours saw establishments open initially between midday and 2:30pm, before staying closed until 6:30pm when they would then stay open until 9:30pm. These enforced hours stayed in law until the Licensing Act of 1988. There was an effect and convictions for drunkenness fell dramatically during the war. In London in 1914, 67,103 people were found guilty of being drunk. In 1917 this had fallen to 16,567. During WW2, attitudes towards alcohol were more relaxed, as you might expect with Winston as Prime Minister, although, as mentioned, licencing hours remained restricted. My rules of life include as an absolutely sacred rite the smoking of cigars, as well as the consumption of alcohol before, after and, if necessary, during all meals and in the intervals between them. Winston Churchill The role of alcohol as a moral booster was specifically recognised: If we want to maintain at least some semblance of normal life, beer must be produced, even if it is not as strong as connoisseurs would like. The task of the government is to support not only life but also the moral spirit of the country. Lord Woolton, Minster of Food However, beer helped pay for the war, because just in the period from September 1939 to July 1940, the tax on it tripled. Cheers! A woman pours a beer for her husband in a bomb shelter in north London, 1940 Ad hoc beer supply to the troops in Normandy, 1944

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain produce its own tanks during World War II or did they rely on American lend-lease?
Answer: About half-and-half. Britain produced some 27,500 tanks domestically during WW2 and Lend-Lease supplied around 25,000 which included 17,000 M4 Shermans, 3,000 M3 Mediums Lee/Grants and 5,000 M3 Stuarts. As the question refers to tanks, I have not included some 2,000 M7 HMC self-propelled guns, nor some 1,600 M10 tank destroyers. Nor have I included the British Universal Carrier with around 70,000 produced during the war or the roughly 26,000 armoured cars produced by the British. It is possibly not well known that the most produced armoured vehicle of WW2 was the Universal Carrier. It should be noted that not all of these tanks were used by British forces as some of the Lend-Lease tanks went to equip Polish, Canadian, and French Divisions, and about 4,000 units of British tank production were sent as British Lend-Lease to Russia. In relation to the size of its population, Britain produced a reasonable number of tanks in WW2 with only the USA being significantly more productive. Britain produced a great number of different tank models, some of them real stinkers, due to a mixture of pre-war policy, poor coordination, and urgent necessity to rearm with something, anything, after Dunkirk. We’ll pass lightly over such disasters as the A13 Mk.III Covenanter. However, Britain did produce some very decent tanks both early and late in the war. The Matilda II was outstanding for its time. The Cromwell was decent and the Comet excellent (arguably better than the M4 Sherman). The Centurion, which just missed the war, is widely considered to be one of the most successful post-war tank designs, remaining in production into the 1960s, and seeing combat into the 1980s. Other decent tanks were the later marks of the Churchill, which was the Allied tank with the lowest loss rate in WW2, and the Valentine, which the Russians were particularly fond of. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the United Kingdom have to pay the United States for its help in World War II?
Answer: Help: to give assistance or support to (someone) : to provide (someone) with something that is useful or necessary in achieving an end. Help in this context could be considered as (a) the provision of armed assistance, (b) the provision of both war materiel and non-war related supplies, and (c) the provision of financial assistance. Obviously the United States did not require the United Kingdom to pay for the massive military contribution that the United States made to the defeat of Germany. There is, of course, no physical or financial standard of value by which we can measure the military contribution to the war on land or sea or in the air which has been made by our allies or ourselves. One thing is clear: By the help which our friends and allies have given us, and by the help which we have given them in the common cause, we have not only made progress in the war, but we have saved the lives of many of our own boys as well as those of our allies. Franklin D. Roosevelt In terms of the provision of materiel and supplies, prior to the start of the war the United States was bound by the Neutrality Act of 1937 which forbade both the selling of implements of war and lending money to belligerent countries. The background to this Act is itself quite interesting and I suggest an excursion into the 1934 Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry otherwise known as the Nye Committee, might be of interest. The confusingly known Pittman Act of 1939 amended the Neutrality Act to allow arms to be sold to belligerents providing that they were paid for in cash (as opposed to on credit) and that they were not transported on US ships, hence the commonly used term Cash & Carry. This provision was intended to assist the Allies and hinder the Axis, as the bulk of ready cash was held by the Allies as was most of the available shipping. However it did mean that Britain had to liquidate assets to buy goods and was soon running short of cash. By the end of 1940 the United Kingdom had reached crisis point. On November the 23rd Lord Lothian, Britain’s ambassador to the United States, arrived in New York and held an impromptu press conference. “Well boys,” he announced to the press, “Britain is broke; it’s your money we want.” Britain had been fighting Germany on land, at sea, and in the air and the cost of these operations had drained Britain’s reserves of currency and gold. Without those funds, Britain could no longer purchase the vital American-made war supplies it needed. Indeed, in early December 1940, Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt. “The moment approaches when we shall no longer be able to pay cash for shipping and other supplies.” Roosevelt’s response was the much misunderstood Lend-Lease. If there was no practical alternative, there was certainly no moral one either. Britain and the Commonwealth were carrying the battle for all civilization. Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Champion of Freedom, Conrad Black In March 1941, the Lend-Lease Act was introduced as An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States. This allowed the President to sell, transfer title to, exchange, lease, lend, or otherwise dispose of any defense article, and eventually resulted in $31.4b of aid to the Britain. All of this was free of charge; this was genuine aid, albeit designed to grow the US economy and promote US objectives. 15,085 M4 Shermans were shipped to the UK under Lend-Lease The United Kingdom did provide some $7.2 billion to the United States in what is known as Reverse Lend-Lease so it wasn’t an entirely one-way street. Reverse Lend-Lease covered the provision of all sorts of goods and services to the United States: the construction of bases, shipping, the provision of weapons, and even such mundanities as rubber from Ceylon, Trinidad, British Guiana, and British Honduras, sisal and pyrethrum from British East Africa, asbestos and chrome from Southern Rhodesia, cocoa from British West Africa, tea and coconut oil from Ceylon, and benzol and tar acids from the United Kingdom. In addition to Lend-Lease and often confused with it, there was the Anglo-American loan of $3.75b made in 1946 which did need to be paid back, although the loan itself was made on fairly generous terms of 2% over 50 years. The United Kingdom finally repaid the last instalment on this loan (not to be confused with the WW1 loans) in 2006. Finally, there was the Marshall Plan, an initiative to rebuild war-torn Europe whilst also benefitting the US economy. Many people think that Marshall Aid went primarily to Germany, but this is not the case. Germany received about 11% of the aid, but the UK received 26% and France 18%. In fact, the UK was the largest recipient with $3.3b. Marshall Aid was a gift, albeit with a few strings attached. Did the United Kingdom have to pay the United States for its help in World War II? All in all, the United States went above and beyond the call of duty to assist the United Kingdom in WW2 and, by extension, the whole of Europe. They did it because it suited their own purposes, but part of that purpose was a recognition of the evil of Nazi hegemony over Europe and that aid included the lives of 185,000 US servicemen. We don’t always have to like US policy today, but we should never belittle the help that the US provided during and after WW2.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there any instances of American pilots returning home via submarine after being shot down over enemy territory? How common was this practice?
Answer: Well, I don’t know about being returned home, you’d need to live by a river for a start. However, downed pilots were certainly rescued by submarines, placed specifically for that purpose, and, eventually, returned to the their bases. In the Pacific in WW2 US aircraft often had to fly very long distances. Damaged by fighters or flak, running short of fuel, or suffering from simple mechanical failures, it was not unusual for aircraft to have to ditch in the ocean a long way from anywhere. To attempt to assist downed pilots, allied submarines were positioned along the flight routes in what were known as Lifeguard missions. Famously, the USS Finback managed to pick up downed pilot, Lt. (jg) George Herbert Walker Bush of Torpedo Squadron 51 from the USS San Jacinto off Chichi Jima in September 1944. Future President George H.W. Bush being fished out of the Pacific During WW2 U.S. submarines rescued 504 airmen from all services and I know that British and Dutch submarines operating in the Pacific also participated in this duty. Originally the missions were primarily intended to keep bomber formations on course by picking up radio signals from submarines positioned along their route. However, aircrew rescue soon became a subsidiary mission. The first rescue was conducted by the USS Skate on October the 7th 1943 when she picked up two airmen downed off Wake Island. The airmens’ home carrier the Lexington was so grateful that they radioed to the Skate: Anything on the Lexington is yours for the asking. If it’s too big to carry away, we will cut it up into small parts The concept was later extended to the USAAF and ﬁrst rescue of a B-29 crew by a lifeguard submarine was on December the 19th 1944 when the USS Spearfish rescued seven airmen off the Bonin Islands. An interesting insight into the challenges faced by downed aircrew can be found in the following training film which is quite amusing and well worth watching (go back to the start of Part 1). Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many British children were killed in the German Blitz over Britain during World War II?
Answer: In WW1, 295 children died in German attacks on the UK. As there were 1,260 civilian deaths in total, this represents 23.5% of the total (another 411 or 32.5% were women). In WW2, 7,736 British children died during the Blitz. This represents around 19% of the total. A further 7,622 children were seriously injured. At the Sandhurst Road school in Catford thirty-eight children died when a Fw 190 dropped a single 500kg bomb on the school in January 1943. Innocents always suffer in war. Sandhurst Road school Casualties at Sandhurst Road

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How would history have been different if Austria had joined the Axis powers instead of aligning with France and Britain during World War II?
Answer: Austria was a member of the Axis. After the Anschluss of March 1938 it was actually considered part of a Greater Germany. The idea of an Anschluss or joining between Germany and Austria was not a new one and had been discussed since the early 19th Century, although originally as the thirty-seven or so German states uniting under the leadership of the House of Habsburg (Austria) in a Großdeutsche Lösung or Greater German solution. In 1918, in the wake of WW1, the Austro-Hungarian Empire collapsed, leaving a rump of Germans in Austria who largely favoured union with Germany. Do not be led into thinking that most Austrians did not want to unify with Germany even though, in the end, the Anschluss was a fait-accompli after a triumphal and unresisted German “invasion”. Crowds of Austrians greet the German “invasion” Between 950,000 and 1.3 million Austrians, out of a population of some seven million, served in the Wehrmacht or the SS during WW2 and Austria was fully integrated into the German war machine.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why do Britain’s leading political parties tolerate immigrants who are intolerant of Britain’s way of life?
Answer: Popper’s Paradox of Tolerance and its drawbacks. Popper’s paradox states that if a society's practice of tolerance is inclusive of the intolerant, intolerance will ultimately dominate, eliminating the tolerant and the practice of tolerance with them. Further, in order to maintain a tolerant society, the society must retain the right to be intolerant of intolerance. However, being intolerant of intolerance is a tricky proposition because it implies some level of action against intolerance that can all too easily be framed as, or actually be, discriminatory in any number of ways. The preferred approach is therefore to address intolerance through rational argument. This is all well and good in theory but is difficult in practice because the intolerant are not, generally, all that open to rational argument. The subsidiary idea that intolerance will be watered down automatically over the generations as immigrant communities integrate has been proved pretty decisively wrong over the last few decades. It also, of course, means that we have to define what intolerance we should be intolerant of. What we regard as intolerance depends on where the Overton Window is currently. What would now be regarded as intolerance (e.g. homophobia) would not have been regarded as intolerance a hundred years ago. Definition carries its own problems. Quis custodiet ipsos custodes? Essentially, the politicians don’t know what to do without laying themselves open to being anathemized by the left and others involved in proselytizing identity politics or by the right for restriction of individual liberties. The problem is now made harder by the emergence of a significant voting bloc related to identity politics which can only lead to politicians pandering to these elements. Therefore, the political parties don’t really attempt to address the issues raised by intolerance because it falls into the too hard box. The danger of this is that the intolerant - on both sides - see the lack of an approach as either weakness or betrayal (for instance, two tier justice, etc.) and act accordingly. The idea of tolerance needs to be instilled rigorously and universally, and this includes being overtly critical of any religion or political persuasion that practices intolerance. Explicitly it means being clear that religions, of every stripe, come loaded with doctrines that tend to promote intolerance: the sowing of discord, the demonisation of others, the justification of violence, resistance to social change, attacks on science, the repression of women, homophobia, etc. People need to be taught to think things through for themselves and not blindly follow religious (or other) leaders. I’d recommend compulsory Terry Pratchett in schools. The reason I say that is because Pratchett discusses issues of difference and toleration using non-specific groups. Reading about the problems faced by dwarves, trolls, werewolves, etc. allows children to think about the issues without making them specific. Other core requirements are that the laws of the land be applied, and be seen to be applied, equally and without apparent favour to any particular group or groups, and we also need to address the trend towards restricting freedom of speech (no-platforming, triggering, etc.) that is infecting Western societies. This itself is a significant form of intolerance - very often a wolf disguised in sheep’s clothing. Most importantly, every citizen needs to understand that they have no right not to be offended. As the late Christopher Hitchens said: Those who are determined to be ‘offended’ will discover a provocation somewhere. We cannot possibly adjust enough to please the fanatics. If someone tells me that I've hurt their feelings, I say, “I'm still waiting to hear what your point is.” There you go, I’ve probably managed to irritate everyone equally. Job done.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was Lord Nelson's previous position before becoming captain of HMS Victory?
Answer: Nelson was never the captain of HMS Victory (100) and indeed never captained anything larger than a third-rate. The captain of the Victory at Trafalgar was Thomas Masterman Hardy who was Nelson’s flag captain (the captain of an Admiral’s flagship). When he first boarded the Victory in 1803, Nelson was a Vice-Admiral of the Blue. By the time of Trafalgar, he was a Vice-Admiral of the White. Nelson lies fatally wounded with Hardy, wearing epaulettes, supporting him Nelson’s first command, as a Lieutenant was the tender Little Lucy in 1777 (West Indies). Promoted to Master and Commander, after only twenty months as a Lieutenant, he was appointed to the Badger (16) in 1778 (Mosquito Coast). After being promoted to Post-Captain in he was appointed to the frigates Hinchinbrook (28) in 1779 and Janus (44) in 1780 (both in the West Indies). After returning to England for health reasons he then commanded the frigates Albermarle (28) in 1781 (North Sea), and the Boreas (28) in 1784 (West Indies again). After a period on shore, he was appointed to the third-rates Agamemnon (64) in 1793 (Mediterranean) and then the Captain (74) in 1796 (Mediterranean). In 1796 Nelson was appointed Commodore by John Jervis (later St. Vincent) and hoisted his broad pennant in the Minerve (40). Commodore is an appointment rather than a rank and signifies a senior Post-Captain given temporary command of a group of ships. Junior Commodores generally retained command of their own ships but, as their responsibilities grew, handed command of their flagship to another Captain known as a flag captain. From that point on, Nelson then commanded fleets rather than individual ships. In February 1797 Nelson was promoted to Rear-Admiral of the Blue starting his rise through the ranks of Admirals. Nelson was promoted to Vice-Admiral of the Blue in 1801 and to Vice-Admiral of the White in 1804. Footnote: The promotion of admirals took place in the order Rear-Admiral, Vice-Admiral, and Admiral and, within that, Blue, White, and Red. Red (the senior) commanded the centre squadron, Blue the van, and White the rear. On promotion from Post-Captain, the first rank was Rear-Admiral of the Blue, then Rear-Admiral of the White, etc. Once he had reached Rear-Admiral of the Red, he would then become a Vice-Admiral of the Blue and so until he finally became an Admiral of the White. There was no Admiral of the Red until after Nelson’s death in 1805 and the most senior Admiral was the Admiral of the Fleet. Promotion path from Post-Captain

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for England having more privateers during the Napoleonic Wars compared to France and Spain?
Answer: Most nations employed privateers from the mid-17th to the mid-19th Centuries as they were a quick and cheap way for governments to wage war. GEORGE the Third, by the Grace of God of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, King Defender of the Faith; To all persons to whom these presents shall come Greeting. Whereas divers injurious proceedings have lately been had in France, in derogation of the honor of our Crown, and of the just rights of our subjects, and whereas several unjust seizures have been there made of the Ships and Goods of our subjects, contrary to the laws of nations, and to the faith of treaties. And whereas the said Acts of unprovoked hostility have been followed by an open declaration of war against us and our ally, the Republic of the United Provinces. We therefore, being determined to take such measures as are necessary for vindicating the honor of our Crown, and for procuring reparation and satisfaction for our injured subjects, did by, and with the advice of our Privy Council, order that general reprisals be granted against the Ships, Goods, and Subjects of France, so that as well our Fleets and Ships as also all other Ships and Vessels that shall be commissionated by Letters of Marque or general reprisals or otherwise, shall and may lawfully apprehend, seize, and take all Ships, Vessels, and Goods belonging to France, or to any persons being subjects of France, or inhabitating within the Territories of France, and bring the same to judgment in our High Court of Admiralty of England, or in any of our Courts of Admiralty within our Dominions, for proceedings and adjudication and condemnation to be thereupon had according to the course of Admiralty, and the laws of Nations. Bristol privateer Caesar engaging a 32-gun French frigate, 1782 Captain Valentine Baker took over the command of Caesar in October 1781. He came from a family with estates near Poole, Dorset, with a long tradition of service in the Royal Navy, but had resigned his commission to become a privateer captain. On 27th June 1782 Caesar was west of Lundy Island in the Bristol Channel, escorting a valuable homeward-bound merchant convoy from Jamaica. She was attacked by a 32-gun French frigate. Baker fought tenaciously and forced the surrender of the battered Frenchman, but Caesar was herself so badly damaged that the enemy frigate rehoisted her colours and escaped, later being recaptured by a British vessel and taken to Portsmouth. Although comparisons can be unreliable, the Enterprise privateer out of Liverpool cost £7,065/15/- to purchase and fit out for three cruises in 1799. That’s roughly equivalent to £1 million in today’s money and was shared between ten firms or individuals in sixteen shares of about £63,000 each. It might just be me, but I find the details interesting: Unfortunately, we do not know the aggregate value of the prizes that the Enterprise took on her three cruises but we know that she had some success because, On the 22nd of October, 1779, she returned to Liverpool, bringing in with her a valuable prize called L'Aventurier, of 22 guns and 50 men, bound from Martinico to Bordeaux with a cargo of cotton, tobacco, sugar, coffee, cocoa, and cassia fistula. We do know that, in 1779, that Liverpool, a major port, hosted a fleet of over a hundred privateers, whose aggregate tonnage was 31,305 tons, and who carried 1,986 guns and 8,754 men. I have read that the British issued some 4,000 letters of marque during the Napoleonic Wars, roughly three hundred per year on average, but this figure is complicated due to the fact that not all ships that possessed letters of marque actually acted as privateers - some were simply opportunistic. By way of comparison, I understand that the United States issued 1,172 letters of marque during the three year war of 1812. It is worth remembering that a different letter of marque was usually required for each nationality preyed upon, so there would be more letters of marque issued that privateers. It is notable that, apart from a blip during the War of the First Coalition (1792–1797) which was not part of the Napoleonic Wars, Great Britain seems to have employed privateers during the Napoleonic Wars far less than it had done earlier in the 18th Century. Letters of marque issued to ships from the port of Bristol in the 18th Century This relative drop in numbers may simply represent the growing importance of Liverpool but it probably does reflect a diminution in activity due to the growing domination of the Royal Navy which was, in effect, competition for the privateers. A subsidiary effect is that the merchant service was very short of seamen due to the manning demands of the Royal Navy. I suspect that Britain probably had more, but not significantly more, privateers than France and that where it did have more privateers than other countries (everybody was at it) that simply reflects the relative sizes of the merchant fleets of each nation.
