Question: Why did Britain import food from India during World War II instead of from countries involved in the war, such as Germany and Poland?
Answer: This is an AI generated question (QPG) and makes no sense because, to state the blindingly obvious, it would be very odd indeed to import food from an enemy, or enemy occupied, country during wartime. However, I have seen other Quora questions commenting on Britain importing food from India during WW2, usually in criticisms of the circumstances surrounding the Bengal Famine of 1943. Excluding the normal exchanges of rice for grain with Ceylon, food destined for Indian Army troops serving overseas, etc., I would be very interested if anyone has any information about foodstuffs from India being exported to the United Kingdom. I have seen it asserted more than once, that the United Kingdom imported significant amounts of food from India in WW2, but I have never been able to find any evidence that this is actually the case. To be clear, I am not interested in articles in The Guardian or from dubious websites, but only data, preferably quantitative, from verifiable contemporary sources. Any information that any of you Quora historians out there have on the matter or any data on convoys from India to the United Kingdom would be most gratefully received.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did Britain not provide assistance to Poland during the Warsaw Uprising? Did they have the resources to do so?
Answer: The British were, in fact, more or less the only ones to provide assistance to Poland during the Warsaw Uprising. The Warsaw air-bridge was a British operation to resupply the Polish Home Army that was carried out in August and September of 1944. RAF Lancaster flying over Poland The Soviets made the air resupply very difficult by refusing to allow Allied aircraft land and refuel, or even fly over, Soviet territory. Nearly all the drops were British-led. On the 18th September there was a single US drop and, from late September, there were some Soviet supply drops. These were carried out when the uprising was clearly defeated and one is forced to conclude that the Soviets only carried them out to avoid post-war criticism. The British missions, flown by British, Polish, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and South African crews had to fly long-distance from either Southern Italy or from the United Kingdom. The round trip took twelve hours and covered a distance of three thousand kilometres. The aircraft flew over enemy territory at four thousand meters above sea level. They had to drop to one hundred meters over dropping zone to drop supplies they had on board. F/WO George Robert Adams, 178 Squadron RAF described flying over Warsaw: We were being fired at because we were low, we could see Germans firing at us, we could see the guns operating at us. Our guns were able to shoot at the search lights which saved us because otherwise, if we were hit by the search lights, we couldn’t see anything and we would have crashed. Over a total of 24 days and nights, 199 individual sorties resulted in the loss of 36 aircraft and the deaths of 183 aircrew. This level of loss was among the highest suffered by the RAF during the war – higher in percentage terms than the raid on Nuremberg in March 1944, sometimes described as the RAF’s darkest hour. The RAF and SAAF squadrons lost one aircraft for every ton of supplies delivered. When I worked in Warsaw, I remember seeing a memorial to an RAF crew that was shot down over Warsaw. Memorial to 178 Squadron RAF in Warsaw Memorial to a crew from 148 Squadron RAF in Dębina Zakrzowska

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did a fascist party exist in Britain during WWII? If so, what happened to it after the war ended?
Answer: Oswald Mosley’s British Union of Fascists was formed in 1932 from the short-lived New Party. It was commonly known as the Blackshirts due to the uniform they adopted. They had some early success and may have had around 40,000 members but they lost support quickly in the lead up to the war, particularly when they stepped up their anti-Semitic rhetoric. It has to borne in mind that, before the war, fascism was seen as an opposition to communism, and communism was regarded by many ordinary people as a significant threat. By 1939 they had changed their name to the British Union and had probably declined to around 8,000 members although there was a blip in numbers when they took an overt anti-war stance. The party was declared illegal after the Battle for France in July 1940 and Mosley and around 750 members were interned under Regulation 18B of the Defence (General) Regulations 1939. In Mosley’s case internment lasted until November 1943 when he was released under house arrest until the end of the war. Mosley and his Blackshirts After the war, there was little appetite for fascism but the British People’s Party (1939–1954) and the Union Movement (1948–1994) were explicitly related to the BUF with, curiously, the latter being led by an ex-Labour Member of Parliament, John Beckett. Currently there are a scattering of far-right groups in the United Kingdom but, contrary to what some people would have you believe, they exert little influence. There are no equivalents to the major right-wing populist parties that exist in most EU nations such as Alternative für Deutschland, National Rally, Fratelli d'Italia, etc. Apart from those deadly-dull left-wingers who seem to believe that anyone that doesn’t agree with them is automatically far-right or fascist, the United Kingdom seems, mercifully, pretty immune to the far-right. Far right and far left are minority positions and the best way to treat both is to give them enough rope to hang themselves by allowing them to express their opinions and then the ballot box will put paid to them. I suspect that one of the reasons for this is that they tend to appear ridiculous to the British sense of humour. Indeed, the BUF were satirised by P.G. Wodehouse as the Black Shorts under their fictional leader Roderick Spode, an “amateur dictator” who leads a farcical group of fascists called the Saviours of Britain. "It is about time", I proceeded, "that some public-spirited person came along and told you where you got off. The trouble with you, Spode, is that just because you have succeeded in inducing a handful of half-wits to disfigure the London scene by going about in black shorts, you think you're someone. You hear them shouting 'Heil, Spode!' and you imagine it is the Voice of the People. That is where you make your bloomer. What the Voice of the People is saying is: 'Look at that frightful ass Spode swanking about in footer bags! Did you ever in your puff see such a perfect perisher?'" The Code of the Woosters (1938)

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was it wrong for the United Kingdom to invade Iceland during World War II?
Answer: Wrong? An interesting question - define wrong. The head of state of Iceland was King Christian X of Denmark who was under German control following the invasion of Denmark in April 1940. Both Denmark and Iceland had declared themselves neutral on the outbreak of the war as it had done during WW1. However, in WW2, Germany had decided to ignore that neutrality in the case of Denmark and would certainly have been happy to ignore it in the case of Iceland. In fact, we know that the Germans had a plan, Operation Ikarus, to do exactly that, utilising around 5,000 men from the 2nd Mountain Division stationed in Norway. Iceland’s position, in what is now known as the GIUK (Greenland, Iceland, UK) gap is one of major strategic importance - and still remains so in NATO considerations. The potential for German U-boats or aircraft operating from Iceland would have been a major threat to the UK’s Atlantic convoy lifeline and one that could not possibly be ignored. The UK offered assistance to Iceland to help it maintain its independence, which would have meant the establishment of a base on Iceland, but this offer was rejected and Iceland confirmed its neutrality. As a result, a month after the Germans occupied Denmark and assessing that Iceland would be unable to resist any German force, the UK occupied Iceland, Operation Fork, with a battalion of Royal Marines - having previously also occupied the Danish Faroe Islands, in Operation Valentine. British soldiers in Reykjavík By then, some locals had started gathering at the harbour. Among them was the British consul who asked a policeman whether he would mind asking people to stand back so that the soldiers could disembark from the destroyer. The policeman replied ‘certainly’ and explained to the small crowd that they were in the way of the invading army. The Royal Marines landed in the harbour and then proceeded to take control the key buildings in Reykjavík. Next was the city’s radio and telecommunication centre. There the marines knocked on the door, as a polite invading army does, but the night watchman was late in coming to the door (having fallen asleep by some accounts). Consequently the door was broken down causing what turned out to be the most substantial damage of the initial invasion. It was a bloodless occupation and there were no casualties on either side. The Icelanders complained that their neutrality had been flagrantly violated (which it had) and demanded compensation but there was no attempt at resistance. The British promised compensation, non-interference in Icelandic affairs, and the withdrawal of all troops as soon as the situation permitted. The British diplomats explained that they were terribly sorry about the inconvenience and gave a promise that the invading force would leave as soon as the war was over. They would not intervene in domestic affairs but would be willing to work with the government and make preferential arrangements for trade. The British occupation force was first bolstered by Canadians and then by US troops in July 1941 when, it should be noted, the US was still neutral. Relations with the occupying forces remained friendly for the most part. The main problem was the result of tens of thousands of young men living in a small country and coming in to contact with the island’s female population. The results of which were referred to as ‘The Situation’. This situation particularly worsened after the Americans arrived. Iceland’s economy, however, boomed – having never fully recovered from the Great Depression. Even though a considerable number of Icelanders lost their lives during the war (particularly in the North Atlantic convoys) many people referred to the Second World War as ‘the blessed war’ (with a bit of tongue in cheek). David Gunnlaugsson British sentry on guard Was it wrong? In the sense that it was an infringement of Iceland’s neutrality it was indeed wrong in international law. However, the Germans had shown no regard for Denmark’s neutrality and Britain could not afford to try and fight the war with one had tied behind its back. In this respect the occupation was justified by Realpolitik which is the conduct of policy based primarily on considerations of given circumstances and factors, rather than strictly following ideological, moral, or ethical premises. As the occupation was carried out with no damage to life or property and with full compensation, I think that it can be considered one of the lesser evils of WW2.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was the Battle of Trafalgar considered a pyrrhic victory for the British in their fight against France?
Answer: In one sense yes, but in another no. A Pyrrhic victory is specifically a victory that comes at a great cost, so great a cost in fact as to make the victory not worth it. It harks back to Pyrrhus, a king of Epirus who defeated the Romans in 279 BCE but lost many of his troops and commanders. Another term for a disastrously expensive victory is a Cadmean victory. The Battle of Trafalgar, which took place on the 21st of October 1805, appears to be the very opposite of a pyrrhic victory. It was actually a decisive victory for the British both tactically and strategically. An outnumbered British fleet (twenty-seven ships of line versus thirty-three) wiped the floor with the Franco-Spanish fleet. In the battle itself the British lost no ships and had 458 men killed whilst the Franco-Spanish fleet lost twenty-two ships and had 4,395 men killed and a further 7,000 or more captured. Two-thirds of the Franco-Spanish fleet was lost, its commander captured, and only eleven of their thirty-three ships escaped from the battle itself. The Battle of Trafalgar Strategically, the remains of the Franco-Spanish fleet were bottled up in various ports and the French fleet was never again a serious threat to the Royal Navy (the French turned on the Spanish in 1808). My arm was strong enough, it is true, to stop with a single shock all the horses of the continent. But I could not bridle the English fleet and there lay all the mischief. Had not people the sense enough to see this? Napoleon at St. Helena in 1816 So, in what sense could the Battle of Trafalgar be considered a Pyrrhic victory? There was, of course, one significant and traumatic loss for the Royal Navy and that was the death of Nelson. The Death of Nelson The King, George III, on receiving the news of Nelson’s death, is alleged to have wept and said: We have lost more than we have gained. The Times, breaking the news to the public on November the 6th 1805, opined: We do not know whether we should mourn or rejoice. The country has gained the most splendid and decisive Victory that has ever graced the naval annals of England; but it has been dearly purchased. The great and gallant Nelson is no more. Both these quotes make reference to what might be called a Pyrrhic victory by suggesting that the death of Nelson was too great a price to pay. However, there is obviously a certain amount of hyperbole in these statements as Nelson was already a national hero and fitting sentiments needed to be expressed. In a cold sober analysis, Britain had plenty of other capable Admirals and the Royal Navy continued to dominate the seas after Nelson’s death. It should be noted that, on his death, Nelson was a Vice-Admiral of the White which is the fifth most senior of the nine ranks of Admirals (see below). It is often not realised that there were thirteen admirals of Nelson’s rank in 1805 and sixty-one who were senior to him, including Parker, Cornwallis, St. Vincent, Keith, and Keppel (although not all of these sixty-one were still active). In the final analysis, Trafalgar was such a tactical and strategic victory that I don’t think that it can justifiably be called a Pyrrhic victory even when taking into account the death of Nelson. In a way, his final victory was so comprehensive that his country no longer had such need of him. Footnote: The promotion of admirals took place in the order Rear-Admiral, Vice-Admiral, and Admiral and, within that, Blue, White, and Red. On promotion from Post-Captain, the first rank was Rear-Admiral of the Blue, then Rear-Admiral of the White, etc. Once he had reached Rear-Admiral of the Red, he would then become a Vice-Admiral of the Blue and so until he finally became an Admiral of the White. There was no Admiral of the Red until after Nelson’s death in 1805 and the most senior Admiral was the Admiral of the Fleet.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How would Europe's military strength be affected if it was not part of NATO or had no other international alliances, similar to the situation during World War II?
Answer: Europe, being a continent rather than a political entity, doesn’t have any military strength. The European Union doesn’t have any real military forces either. There is an EU Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP) but this doesn’t amount to much. This has resulted in Eurocorps which is basically a corps headquarters which reports not to the EU but to the framework nations (Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Poland, and Spain) that set it up. Then there are the, rather grandly named, EU Battlegroups which are under the direct control of the Council of the European Union. Although there are theoretically eighteen of these, they rotate every six months and, in reality, only two battalion (+) sized units are operationally deployable at any given time. More recently, in 2022 the EU has announced the EU Rapid Deployment Capacity (EU RDC) of 5,000 men, to be drawn from the EU Battlegroups: As mentioned before the EU RDC is not a mere force. The natural tendency is to think in tangible elements. In the military context most people can picture a force, but the term capacity is less common. The EU RDC is a capacity, meaning that it not only consists of force-generated elements on standby, the EU Battlegroups plus their required Strategic Enablers, but also pre-identified modules. The elements in standby are required to ensure the aspired rapidness, whereas the modules provide flexibility and economy of force. The modules allow tailoring the EU RDC to the mission in a very flexible manner. Since the EU Member States’ military forces and capabilities are pre-identified for the modules, the targeted force sensing and force-generation in case of a crisis will be much quicker. Ho Hum - not a mere force, eh? I think that when the rubber hits the road, mere force can come in quite handy. I suppose that they can always try beating the enemy to death with their stakeholders. What this means is that Europe’s military strength resides within the individual European countries that make up NATO (one should bear in mind that Russia and Belarus are in Europe). To complicate matters, Austria, Cyprus, Ireland and Malta are in the EU but not in NATO, and the United Kingdom, Norway, and Iceland are in NATO but not in the EU. Anyway, despite all the chat, NATO is the only game in town. If the European countries of NATO were to withdraw from NATO, leaving just the USA and Canada in NATO, then the military strength of those countries obviously would not change at all. What would change is that those countries would then lack unified leadership, be unable to coordinate effectively, lose specialist US military abilities, lose US logistics support and industrial capacity, and be reduced to only a quarter of the current defence budget employed by NATO countries (not that all of the US defence budget is targeted at NATO).

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Napoleon read War and Peace after being defeated at Waterloo? How did he react to it?
Answer: War and Peace wasn’t published until 1869 (serialised from 1865) and Napoleon died in 1821 - so nope. Napoleon was, however, an avid reader of the classics (Pasquale Paoli reproached him for being entirely out of Plutarch), politics, history, military campaigns, military science, especially artillery (his branch) and siege warfare. We know he also read about foreign cultures and topography, economics, astronomy, geology, and meteorology. He favoured Montaigne and Montesquieu, Rousseau, Buffon and Mirabeau. Clearly, much of his reading was related to trying to understand his enemies and to plan his campaigns. On the ship taking him to Egypt, he familiarized himself with the culture, religion, history, topography and customs of the country using an on-board library containing nearly 300 books. Once he became Emperor, Napoleon gathered thousands of books in his various libraries in Trianon, Rambouillet, Fontainebleau and especially in Malmaison. He also put together a mobile campaign library, overseen by his personal librarian and researcher (conseiller littéraire), Antoine Barbier. The Emperor wishes you to form a traveling library of one thousand volumes in small 12mo and printed in handsome type. It is his Majesty’s intention to have these works printed for his special use, and in order to economize space there is to be no margin to them. They should contain from five hundred to six hundred pages, and be bound in covers as flexible as possible and with spring backs. There should be forty works on religion, forty dramatic works, forty volumes of epic and sixty of other poetry, one hundred novels and sixty volumes of history, the remainder being historical memoirs of every period. The campaign library also contained relevant works on A bookcase (literally) from Napoleon’s travelling library Napoleon used to carry about the books he required in several boxes holding about sixty volumes each, each box first made of mahogany and later of more solid leather-covered oak. The inside was lined with green leather or velvet, and the books were bound in morocco [leather] Barbier was also asked to write numerous reports regarding the history, geography and religious issues of various regions and countries which Napoleon used in his political and military planning. If a book had the misfortune to displease him, neither one nor two he threw it into the fire! And beware of those close to him who read a work of this kind because Bonaparte reserved the same fate for these books: the stake! Nothing annoyed him so much as wasting his time reading what he considered bad and Claude François de Ménéval, private secretary of the Emperor, conjured Barbier during the campaign of 1809 to send Bonaparte better volumes because disappointing books just “jump out of the mailbox into the fireplace”. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is USA today a greater superpower than the British empire at its prime?
Answer: The British Empire. The Empire was at its greatest extent just after WW1, but it was probably in its prime in the latter half of the 19th Century. In terms of relative population there is no contest. At one time the Empire contained about 25% of the World’s population, whilst the USA only has about 4.2%. The Empire also covered getting on for 25% of the World’s land area (13.7 million square miles) whilst the USA covers about 6.5% (3.8 million square miles). Quite a lot of that land area was in Australia and Canada and didn’t have much going for it except for its potential for raw materials, but the United States also has over 100 million acres of wilderness. In its prime the Empire also controlled most of the World’s shipping, most of its industry, and a very large proportion of its banking. None of this is true of the current United States. The Royal Navy also exercised uncontested dominance of the World’s seas - something that is probably currently true of the United States. It is difficult to make comparisons across technological eras Of course, the Empire didn’t have weapons of mass destruction or any other modern gizmos, so the pace of superpower life was rather slower and the risk of immediate immolation wasn’t something that needed to be worried about. In the matter of soft and cultural power, the Hollywood factor, it is arguable that the USA has more influence today than Britain did in the past, but that is simply because such a thing didn’t exist to any extent. No television, no radio, no telephones, no movies - every nation was still wedded to its own culture and traditions to a much greater extent than is true today. In terms of cultural influence, the Empire was probably on a par with France, Germany, and Russia. A final factor to consider is that the Empire actually maintained a tiny army and so, although it could bring maritime commerce to a halt at will, it had no real ability to project serious amounts of power inland and its army was a fraction of the size of the Continental Powers. Traditionally, the USA has also maintained a very small military but, since, WW2, it has taken on more responsibilities and maintains larger armed forces than the Empire ever did in peacetime.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In WWII movies, the gunners on bombers never seem to down a lot of enemy planes. What was the actual kill ratio like?
Answer: There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics. A mine of information is contained in the Army Air Forces Statistical Digest, World War II. From this source we find that US heavy bombers in the ETO cumulatively flew 2,158,017 hours in combat (Table 176) and claimed to have downed 6,098 enemy fighters (Table 167). Assuming, for convenience, that we’re talking about the B-17G, then that’s nine gun positions (13 guns) per aircraft, giving 19,422,153 gun position hours in combat. With 6,098 claims, that would be 3,185 gun position hours flown per claim, 0.03% of a fighter per gun position hour employed, or 354 bomber hours flown per claim. In addition we know that US heavy bombers expended 77,540,000 rounds of ammunition in the ETO (Table 150) which is 12,715 rounds expended per claim. However, bomber claims were exaggerated. US fighters in the ETO only claimed 7,422 kills and I don’t believe that the heavy bombers were anywhere near that number. Whilst a fighter pilot has a reasonably good idea whether he has downed an enemy plane or not, a US bomber flying in a combat box was part of a formation specifically designed to bring multiple guns, on multiple planes, to bear on any enemy rash enough to come in range. A single gunner can rarely have had any idea whether it was actually his shooting that brought down the enemy. This led to overclaiming on the part of the bomber crews. I’m not implying any wrongdoing, overclaiming was a natural consequence of the way the USAF flew. B-17s flying in a combat box To take a well known example. During the first Schweinfurt-Regensburg raid Spitfires claimed seven kills, P-47s claimed 14 kills and B-17s claimed 288 kills. Post-war analysis suggests that the Germans lost 27 fighters. If we assume that the fighters overclaimed by a factor of two (for 3 and 7 kills respectively) that leaves the bombers with 17 actual kills against 288 claimed - a 17:1 overclaim. With 376 B-17s participating in the raid, that’s 3,384 gun positions downing 17 fighters. That’s 0.5% chance of a kill per gun position, or a 4.5% chance per bomber. As that particular raid notoriously suffered a 15% loss rate, you were three and a half times more likely to be shot down than you were to bag a fighter. The German loss rate on that raid was 4.3%. Depending on how you look at it, the second Schweinfurt raid did better with an apparent overclaim rate of only 6:1 or 186 claims against 31 verified losses (plus an extra 6 assigned to fighters). In this raid the US bombers suffered 26% losses and the Germans between 9% and 12%. I’d say that overclaiming by the bombers probably ran at around 5:1 or higher compared with 2:1 for fighters. I can’t tell whether the figures contained in the Army Air Forces Statistical Digest have been adjusted to take into account overclaiming but, regardless, the figures indicate that it would take fifty or so missions for the average US bomber to bag a fighter which was significantly more missions than the expected life of the average US bomber.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Letters of marque were issued to hundreds of U.S. privateers during the war of 1812, and they captured 2,500 British merchant ships and severely damaged British trade. When and why did this effective means of privatizing war disappear?
Answer: It was exactly that, a way for cash-strapped governments to defray the costs of waging war at sea on to private shipowners. Issuing Letters of marque allowed governments to fight wars using private ships and sailors instead of funding their own navies in order to save both time and money. Instead of having to build, fund and maintain a navy in times of peace, a government could wait until the start of a war to issue letters of marque to ship owners, who then financed their own ships in expectation of prize money. The business was purely mercenary and could be very profitable. During the American Revolution, privateers from Guernsey captured French and American vessels and cargoes valued at £900,000 (equivalent to £145,000,000 in today’s money). The downside of the arrangement was, of course, that the government couldn’t order the privateers to coordinate or indeed do anything that the government happened to need to further the war. East Indiaman Kent being attacked by the French Confiance in 1800 The most cash-strapped government of the period was the United States during the Revolution and the War of 1812, but privateers were also used by Britain and France in the Napoleonic Wars, the Quasi War, and the War of 1812 (as well as by other nations). The United States may have done well during the War of 1812 although probably not quite as well as the question states. In December 1814, Lloyd's insurance underwriters advised the House of Commons that since the start of the war Americans had captured 1,175 British merchant vessels, of which 373 had been recaptured. However, even before the war the American merchant fleet had suffered losses. According to one estimate, by 1810 Britain had seized nearly 1,000 American merchant vessels and France 500, while a further 300 had fallen to the Danes, Neapolitans, Spaniards, Dutch, and the Barbary States. Between 1812 and 1815, Britain captured 500 additional American merchant vessels. Once Britain began its blockade and convoy policies, the American privateers became markedly less effective. By the time the War of 1812 ended, trade had ceased to be either free or active. Attacks on shipping pushed prices up and depressed commerce. Prohibitive insurance rates and uncontrolled prices caused severe personal and commercial hardships. The early damage inflicted on British trade by American privateers and the small but proficient US Navy, were soon countered by the British blockade that effectively ended the free movement of American maritime traffic. Simultaneously, Britain's strict enforcement of the convoy system deprived the few American vessels able to get to sea of likely prizes. The Fortunes of War: Commercial Warfare and Maritime Risk in the War of 1812, Faye M. Kert The point being that Letters of Marque were a double-edged sword and a nuisance to all concerned - particularly as some privateers were little more than pirates, changing allegiance at will and occasionally serving on both sides in the same war. The Paris Declaration respecting Maritime Law of the 16th of April 1856, initiated by Britain and France, banned the issue of Letters of marque and was eventually signed by fifty-five nations - not including the United States, and Article I of the United States Constitution still lists issuing Letters of marque and reprisal as one of the powers of Congress.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the reason behind some countries naming their ships after animals?
Answer: Usually because the name either suggests speed or fierceness. I think that I’m right in saying that the most frequently used name in the Royal Navy, historically, is Swallow (speedy) with thirty-nine Swallows between 1497 and 1984. Otherwise, when you have a large navy, you can run out of names - especially if you want names that run in series to help identify a class of ship. Various classes of Royal Navy ships have been named after animals, birds, insects, fish, flowers, tribes, admirals, towns, rivers, counties, islands, bays, biblical characters, dukes, jewels, classical heroes, weapons, castles, battles, types of soldier, hunts, and villages whose names end in ham. Don’t believe me? Check out the ninety-three Ham-class minesweepers launched between 1954 and 1959. In terms of animals, whilst we’ve had Lion, Tiger, and Panther (fierce), Greyhound, Antelope, and Gazelle (fast), and Cobra, Viper, and Anaconda (deadly), we’ve also had Ant, Bat, Beagle, Camel, and Gnat and many, many more running the gamut from Adder to Zebra. HMS Panther HMS Gnat For every stirring Relentless, Repulse, and Resolution, Vengeance, Venomous, and Vindictive we’ve also had a Pansy, Fairy, Dainty and Spanker, not to mention a Teaser, Tickler, Torrid, Thruster and Thrasher. HMS Fairy If you want to get really odd, we’ve had Black Joke (look it up), Happy Entrance, Adam & Eve, Dwarf, Cockchafer, and Doris. HMS Black Joke HMS Doris After that lot, naming ships after animals seems a relative safe and sane way to go…

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did the German armies surrender to the Allies in November 1918 at the end of World War I? Why could they not continue fighting and is it true that the Germans actually were winning against the British & French? Why do some people believe this?
Answer: Who knows why some people believe anything? As the saying goes: You can fool all of the people some of the time and some of the people all of the time. As a point of fact, the German armies didn’t surrender to the Allies in November 1918. Instead, an armistice, a temporary cessation of hostilities, was signed which brought all fighting to a stop. The Germans didn’t actually surrender until the Paris Peace Conference in 1919. The armistice is one of the reasons for the appearance of the Stab-in-the-back myth in Germany after the war. This maintained that the German Army didn’t lose the war on the battlefield but, instead, was betrayed by politicians and other elements at home - notably, and inevitably, including the Jews. The politicians that signed the armistice were denounced as November Criminals or November­verbrecher. However, the reality is different and Germany was most certainly not winning the war against the British and the French (and the Americans). Following the Russian withdrawal from the war after the signing of the Brest-Litovsk Treaty, the Germans transferred fifty divisions to the Western Front and made a last desperate attack, the Kaiserschlacht or Spring Offensive of March 1918. After some initial significant gains in Operation Michael, the Germans bogged down and the offensive ground to a complete halt in late July. German Spring Offensive - used novel tactics and equipment At the end of their offensive, the German armies were left severely depleted, losing nearly a million men, exhausted, and in exposed positions which greatly increased the length of the line to be defended. The failure of the offensive caused a loss of morale, both at the front and at home. By 1918, the situation in Germany itself was becoming intolerable with the British naval blockade causing widespread shortages and starvation which led to the deaths of around 500,000 civilians. This state of affairs eventually led to the Kiel Naval Mutiny and the November Revolution which brought down the Imperial Government. German civilians butchering a dead horse Kiel Naval Mutiny - Long live freedom November Revolution At the front, the Allies launched the Hundred Days Offensive at the beginning of August which drove the Germans back to the Hindenburg Line. Around 30,000 German soldiers surrendered during the Battle of Amiens. Ludendorff described the first day of this battle as the black day of the German Army. Huge numbers of German prisoners were also taken at the Battle of St. Quentin Canal. The battles of Meuse–Argonne, St. Quentin Canal, Fifth Ypres, and Cambrai broke the Hindenburg line and forced the Germans into headlong retreat. The Hundred Days Offensive General Campbell VC addressing men of the 137th Brigade (46th Division) on the Riqueval Bridge over the St Quentin Canal German prisoners taken during the 100 days On 29 September 1918, the Supreme Army Command informed the Kaiser that the military situation was hopeless in the face of the enemy's overwhelming advantage in manpower and equipment and that he should urgently seek an armistice. The German Imperial Army had been bled dry.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was it standard doctrine for the Royal Navy in WW2 to drop depth charges over known shipwrecks to deter enemy submarines from hiding over them?
Answer: Not as far as I know. I think that this idea comes from stories about the wreck of the Lusitania being used as a target for depth charges and is tied up with the various conspiracy theories relating to the Lusitania. Lusitania sinking If the wreck of any ship was indeed depth-charged, it is entirely possible that the wreck was picked up on sonar, reported as a potential U-boat, and attacked by accident. Another possibility is that wrecks could have been deliberately used for target practice being known datum points for a sonar target. It’s worth noting that U-Boats had no sensors that would allow them to locate wrecks accurately and hide in their sonar shadow.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did some German planes like the HE-111 drop their bombs upside down as they came out of the bombbays?
Answer: The early bomb racks of several nations (see also the Savoia-Marchetti SM.79 Sparviero) were sometimes designed in this way to maximise capacity in the face of design limitations. The vertical rack was an option, and not all He-111s carried their bombs in this orientation - especially as bombs became larger. In the German service, this rack was called an ESAC 250, an abbreviation for Elektrische-Senkrecht-Aufhangung fur Cylinderbomben 250/IX or Electric vertical suspension for cylinder bombs up to 250 kg. The HE-111 was equipped with 8 ESAC 250s in its Internal Bomb Bay, giving it a carrying capacity of 2,000 kg. Each could carry one 250 kg bomb or four 50 kg bombs. The German bombers tended to have narrow fuselages and so this was the most convenient way of carrying internal stores. It is also worth noting that German bombs did not have nose fuses and so the fused bombs could be lifted by their noses. You can see in the following photograph how quickly the bombs reorientated themselves to the familiar nose down orientation after they were released.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: People say the British Empire came to an "end" with the Hong Kong Handover. What if it had stayed entirely British or was never British, what moment would be considered the "end" of the British Empire?
Answer: That’s a complicated subject. The hard question is what is an empire? The definitions found in the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary that are relevant are: In the first sense, the British Empire clearly came to an end on the 22nd of June 1948 when George VI ceased to use the title Emperor of India. In fact, the title of Emperor or Empress of India dates only from the 1st of May 1876 in the reign of Victoria and so was only in use for around seventy-two years. As a matter of interest, George VI continued as monarch of India until 1950 and of Pakistan until 1952. In the second sense, the British Empire can be defined as an entity that includes, or included, all the territories controlled by Great Britain, explicitly an aggregate of previously existing states. As an aside, in this sense, most of the countries in the World are empires including, inter-alia, France, Germany, the United States, Russia, and China - all of which incorporate previously existing states, and England itself is an Empire consisting of the seven kingdoms of the heptarchy: East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Mercia, Northumbria, Sussex, and Wessex. The British Empire itself comprised all the dominions, colonies, protectorates, mandates and other territories ruled or administered by the United Kingdom and its predecessor states (including Great Britain). The Confederation of Canada became effectively independent in 1867 starting the process of rolling back the Empire and, since that point, some sixty-four countries have gained independence. The last dominion to gain full independence was Australia with the Australia Act of 1986, whilst Brunei was the last non-dominion to become fully independent in 1984. However, as of 2024, there are still fourteen Commonwealth realms where Charles III remains the head of state despite the fact that most are fully independent, These are Antigua and Barbuda, Australia, The Bahamas, Belize, Canada, Grenada, Jamaica, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Solomon Islands, Tuvalu. The last country to renounce the British monarch as head of state was, I believe, Barbados, in 2021. These countries are some of the fifty-six nations that now form part of the Commonwealth of Nations (previously the British Commonwealth). This still leaves fourteen Overseas Territories which are part of the sovereign territory of the United Kingdom. These are: Anguilla, Bermuda, the British Antarctic Territory, the British Indian Ocean Territory, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, the Falkland Islands, Gibraltar, Montserrat, the Pitcairn Islands, Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, and the Turks and Caicos Islands. There is also the enclave of Akrotiri and Dhekelia on Cyprus. Then there are, I suppose, the Crown Dependencies of Jersey, Guernsey (the Channel Isles) and the Isle of Man. The Balliwick of Guernsey includes the islands of Alderney, Brecqhou, Herm, Jethou, Lihou, and Sark. TLDR, it’s complicated. There’s the Empire, the Dominions, the Commonwealth, the Realms, the Overseas Territories, and the Crown Dependencies. This doesn’t even begin to consider oddities such as the Trucial States and the Protectorates (the last British protectorate was the Solomon Islands which gained full independence in 1978) or Papua New Guinea, which became independent from Australia in 1975. So, in the second sense (above), the Empire is still going - albeit to a limited extent.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for Britain's use of gliders in its airborne operations despite their vulnerability to enemy fire and aircraft attacks?
Answer: For the same reasons that everyone else did. Every major nation used both parachute and glider-borne troops in airborne operations during WW2, so there is nothing unusual about the British use of gliders. Gliders were indeed highly vulnerable to flak, but I am not aware of any British gliders that were lost to enemy fighters. Ideally glider landings should not be carried out in the face of unsuppressed flak, a lesson hard learned during Operation Varsity. The advantages of gliders were that they were cheap and could land untrained infantry behind enemy lines. There were also, at least theoretically, advantages in avoiding dispersion and improving forming up times. In addition, gliders could carry (relatively) heavy equipment, including jeeps, anti-tank guns and light armoured vehicles. British Hamilcar unloading a Tetrarch light tank US Waco Soviet Antonov A-7 German DFS 230 Japanese Ku-8

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for Britain's low tank production during World War II? Were there any efforts made to increase production?
Answer: Well, let’s see shall we. Low compared with what? Of course, it depends on what country we are discussing. It also depends what we are discussing. For the purposes of this answer I am going to consider medium and heavy tanks because that removes the complexities involved in discussing tankettes and armoured cars. The population of the United States was roughly three times that of the UK in 1939 and it was in the war for 66% of the time that Britain was. Therefore, we could reasonably expect the base ratio of armoured vehicles produced by the United States to be about twice that produced by Britain. According to Wikipedia, the British produced around 27,500 tanks during the war whilst the United States produced 71,000. A ratio of 2.58 rather than the expected 1.92 times. The population of the USSR was three and a half times that of the UK in 1939 and it was in the war for four and a half years. Therefore, we could reasonably expect the base ratio of armoured vehicles produced by the USSR to be about two and a half times that produced by Britain. According to Wikipedia, the USSR produced 78,000 tanks during the war. A ratio of 2.83 rather than the expected 2.67 times. The population of the Germany was nearly twice (1.81) that that of the UK in 1939 and it was in the war for six years. Therefore, we could reasonably expect the base ratio of armoured vehicles produced by Germany to be about twice that produced by Britain. According to Wikipedia, Germany produced 41,000 tanks during the war. A ratio of 1.49 rather than the expected 1.81 times. Therefore, a rough analysis would suggest that the Soviets did slightly better than Britain and the Germans rather worse. Only the United States did significantly better than Britain and, of course, the United States had the advantage that its industry was never subjected to bombing or being relocated as was the case with all the other combatants. This is not to say that the story of British tank production during WW2 is a pretty one. There are whole books written on this subject. I would particularly recommend Rude Mechanicals by A.J. Smithers if you are interested in this topic. By the end of the war Britain was producing decent tanks but, caught unprepared, the early years of the war, coming after years of complacency and cost cutting, were a mess. Lessons were learned the hard way, something that might well be of relevance today. Vickers Light Tank Mk VIB formed the bulk of British armour in France and the Desert in 1940 Comet I (A34), in service from 1944

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Would it be true to say that the English weren't fighting in WW1 & WW2 for democracy but to preserve their empire?
Answer: No, not really. Neither Belgium, in WW1, nor Poland, in WW2, were parts of the British Empire. Both were, however, the recipients of guarantees from Great Britain, the 1839 Treaty of London in the case of Belgium and the Anglo-Polish Agreement of 1939 in the case of Poland. Britain’s Empire was never under any really serious threat from Germany, but neither was Britain exactly fighting for democracy - which is a pretty nebulous concept in any case. In reality Britain entered both wars in order to try and maintain, or redress, the balance of power in Europe so that no one nation could dominate the Continent. This has been an important strategic objective for Britain for centuries, and in pursuing that objective Britain was acting in her perceived best interest - which is what nations do. However, had the politicians and diplomats known how WW1 would develop, they might have stayed their hands as they had with the Franco-Prussian War only a few decades earlier. A German soldier, Beaumont Hamel, 1916 If Britain had remained neutral, it might have avoided a lot of unpleasantness for everyone involved. However, unfortunately, foresight and hindsight are different beasts. As the German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck said: The mistakes that have been committed in foreign policy are not, as a rule, apparent to the public until a generation afterwards.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In the bomber War in WWII, what percentage of British and American bombers were shot down by flack and how many by enemy aircraft?
Answer: This is really and impossible question to answer as there are too many variables to account for: period of the war, day or night, number of fighters available, presence of escort fighters, location of the target, air defences around the target, etc., etc. It is also interesting to note that there is a difference between the number of bombers shot down and the number of casualties caused. In the latter case, flak is a clear winner, killing and wounding thousands of crewmen even if the bomber itself was not destroyed. After the war, the British Bombing Survey Unit (BBSU) described flak as “plentiful” but not “very lethal.” At the same time the official RAF history of the air war estimated that German flak accounted for 37 percent of Bomber Command’s losses between July 1942 and April 1945. However, BBSU wasn’t in an ideal position to categorise the cause of losses as RAF bombers were mainly flying at night and in streams (individually) rather than in formations and so there weren’t many witnesses to the fate of individual aircraft. Donald Nijboer in Flak in World War II, estimates that more American 8th Air Force planes were shot down by flak than enemy fighters. In November 1944 the Eighth Air Force Operational Analysis Section produced An Evaluation Taken to Protect Bombers from Loss and Damage. The report stated: During the past year enemy flak defenses have been concentrated and our bombers faced many more guns. The percentage of bombers lost to or damaged by enemy fighters has declined sharply, while the percentage lost to flak has declined only moderately. The percentage damaged by flak has remained almost constant. As a result, there has been a steady increase in the relative importance of flak until in June, July and August 1944, flak accounted for about two-thirds of the 700 bombers lost and 98 per cent of the 13,000 bombers damaged. Flak certainly shot down more bombers towards the end of the war, partly because of improvements in radar gun laying, etc., but also simply because there were less German fighters available to defend the Reich. B-17s flying through a flak barrage If you had to make an guess, I think that you wouldn’t be far wrong if you came to the conclusion that the overall ratio was probably not all that far from 50:50 although the ratio obviously varied wildly from raid to raid. We know that Hitler was a keen advocate of flak and that flak and fighters competed for resources, something that the Luftwaffe was making clear as early as 1941. In fact, the Luftwaffe claimed that the 47,000 tons of aluminium used to construct flak shell fuses between 1941 and 1945 could have been used to produce an additional 37,000 fighter aircraft - astonishing numbers. B-17 dropping out of formation after a fighter attack Also, we have to bear in mind that the purpose of flak was not actually to shoot down bombers, it was to make life as difficult as possible for bombers so that they missed their targets, by forcing them to fly high and by disrupting their formations and bomb runs. It is also worth commenting that carrying heavy defensive armament on bombers, taking into account the weight of weapons, mounts, ammunition, and gunners, was worthless in the case of roughly 50% of all losses. There is a calculation to be made regarding the potential impact of swapping defensive armament for a heavier bomb load on overall losses.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: England has no reagionalism (same grey old all over) as is not divided into states, unlike Brazil. England is a Unitary State, they need travel abroad to see cultural variation, whereas in Brazil we just go to another state. Isn't it sad for English?
Answer: Brazil is thirty-five times larger than England and half of the federative units (states) of Brazil are actually individually larger than the UK so the question makes no sense. Also, England not only has a very clear North-South divide, roughly marking the original extent of the Danelaw, but has thirty-nine historic counties which each exhibit clear differences in dialect and culture. I don’t know about foreigners, but these differences are very clear to the English and nobody would mistake someone from Sussex and a Yorkshireman, or someone from Cornwall with someone from Norfolk for example. These historic counties were established by the Normans after 1066, but in many cases were based on the earlier Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and, indeed, the original pre-Roman tribal boundaries. Note, for instance, how the present county of Kent harks directly back to the Iron Age tribal lands of the Cantiaci. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why wouldn’t RAF Fighter Command have warned their pilots not to attack the German Dornier sea-air rescue flying boats because they frequently carried British as well as German downed flyers rescued from the English Channel and North Sea?
Answer: The Seenotdienst (maritime distress service) was formed in 1935 and became part of the Luftwaffe in July 1940. Equivalent to the British Coastal Command’s Air Sea Rescue organisation, the Seenotdienst used Dornier and Heinkel flying boats and fast motor boats to rescue aviators downed at sea. Whilst there is no doubt that some of the aviators rescued were British, I wouldn’t necessarily use the word frequently. When the RAF shot down an escorted He-59 near the British coast it was found that the pilot had been marking the positions and courses of British coastal convoys. The British, rightly or wrongly, took this to mean that the German aircraft had been engaging in clandestine reconnaissance activity and the RAF was ordered (Air Ministry Bulletin 1254) to shoot down Seenotdienst aircraft. He 59 search-and-rescue aircraft The legal position is unclear, the aircraft were rescuing pilots who could then be returned to duty, and were also potentially being used for reconnaissance under cover of rescue operations. The Germans protested but the situation was unclear as the Geneva Convention had not considered this particular eventuality. The Germans eventually began to arm their rescue aircraft and the point became moot. As one of those unenviable decisions that have to made in wartime, the British assessed that the risk of shooting down an aircraft carrying downed British aviators was less important than the risk of letting German aircraft fly freely over airspace vital to British convoy operations. Do 24 V1 search-and-rescue aircraft German rescue buoy, Rettungsboje, used by (lucky) airmen awaiting rescue

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did HMS Hood compare to her contemporaries? Was she truly a big ship, or more of a glorified battlecruiser?
Answer: HMS Hood was technically a battlecruiser - an Admiral-class battlecruiser to be precise. Four of them were planned but the other three Anson, Howe, and Rodney were never built (although the names were later reused: Anson and Howe for King George V-class battleships and Rodney as the second of the Nelson-class battleships). Hood was therefore a one-off. She was originally intended to be an improved Queen Elizabeth-class fast battleship, but was modified during construction to be a battlecruiser intended to counter the new German Mackensen-class battlecruisers (none of which were ever completed). After multiple design changes, Hood was eventually laid down in September 1916. Essentially, she was, after all, an improved Queen Elizabeth-class fast battleship but faster and with much improved torpedo protection. As a result she was considerably larger and heavier than her predecessors. HMS Hood in 1924 To address the question directly, it is a common mistake to assume that battlecruisers have to be smaller than battleships. Depending on how you choose to look at her, she could be classified as either a battlecruiser (this was how the Royal Navy classified her) or as a fast battleship. In terms of her contemporaries, if you take that to mean ships commissioned in the 1920s, Hood was truly a big ship and remained the largest warship in the world until 1940. If you take it to mean ships existing in 1941 then, at 46,680 tons, she was very slightly lighter than Bismarck (49,500 tons) at full load, but rather longer. In May 1941, no other ship was bigger than the Mighty Hood, although the Yamato came along in December of that year. Of course, Hood was laid down in 1916 and commissioned in 1920 so she was, inevitably, not as recent a design as the Bismarck, commissioned twenty years later. However, it should be borne in mind that, as an evolution of the Queen Elizabeth-class that she was based on the same design as HMS Warspite and was by no means inadequately protected for 1940 as is sometimes suggested.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In All Creatures Great and Small, do you think vets like James Herriot were protected jobs in World War II's draft?
Answer: Vets were indeed in a reserved occupation during WW2 and therefore were not subject to conscription until 1943 when there was a surge in the use of mules in the Far East and in Italy and some vets were called up. Although the British Army was highly mechanised, there were some areas where vehicles simply could not be used and by 1942 the Army had 6,500 horses, 10,000 mules and 1,700 camels in service. Mules were so vital in Burma that some were even dropped by parachute. British mules being swum across a river in Burma Altogether, I believe that 519 officers and 3,939 other ranks served in the Royal Army Veterinary Corps (RAVC) during WW2. Apart from general veterinary duties, they were also required to devoice mules (vocal cordectomy) to stop them braying and giving away their location to the enemy. Apart from mules, the army vets also looked after horses, elephants, camels, water buffaloes, bullocks (draft animals), dogs and, no doubt, any number of pets. A sergeant of the Royal Army Veterinary Corps bandages the wounded ear of 'Jasper', a mine-detecting dog at Bayeux in Normandy, 5 July 1944 However, vets could volunteer for non-veterinary service and in fact both James Alfred Wight (James Herriot) and Donald Sinclair (Siegfried Farnon) volunteered for the RAF at various points in the war (although both were discharged quite quickly for medical reasons), whilst Brian Sinclair (Tristan Farnon) became a Captain in the Royal Army Veterinary Corps in the Far East. The Animals in War memorial in London

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Who was the youngest defendant in the Nuremberg Trials and what were their charges?
Answer: I suspect that you are asking the wrong question, but here goes. In total there were twenty-four defendants at the Nuremberg Trials, otherwise known as the International Military Tribunal or IMT. The youngest defendant was Baldur von Schirach who was born in 1907 and so aged around thirty-eight years of age. Von Schirach was head of the Hitler Youth and Gauleiter of Vienna. The oldest defendant was Gustav Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach who, at the age of seventy-five, was indicted more or less by mistake instead of his son Alfried but was deemed unfit to stand trial after a stroke brought on by the British bombing of his works. The defendants were generally indicted on one or more or four counts: (1) Participation in a common plan or conspiracy for the accomplishment of a crime against peace, (2) Planning, initiating and waging wars of aggression and other crimes against peace, (3) Participating in war crimes, and (4) Crimes against humanity. Von Schirach was indicted on counts (1), for building up the Hitler Youth, and (4) for deporting Jews from Vienna (bound for the concentration camps). He was found innocent of the first charge but guilty of the fourth and was sentenced to twenty years imprisonment. He was released from prison on the 1st of October 1966, after serving his full sentence in Spandau Prison and died in 1974 at the age of 67. Baldur von Schirach Of other war crimes trials, Irma Grese, a female concentration camp guard was twenty-two when tried for ill-treating prisoners and murder, and Rudolf Merkel was, I think, seventeen when he was tried for his involvement in the murder of a shot down U.S. airman.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why do Brits obsess over the Dambuster Raid even though it was a Brit failure with high losses for little gain? The Germans laughed.
Answer: What makes you think that the British obsess about the Dambusters Raid (Operation Chastise) which was carried out by 617 Squadron in May 1943? Come to that what makes you think that the raid was a failure? There was a book Enemy Coast Ahead written by the commander of the raid, Guy Gibson, in 1944 and a film based on that book and Paul Brickhill’s The Dam Busters, published in 1951, made in 1955. That was sixty-nine years ago you know. Great film though. More recently, Max Hastings published a book on the raid, Operation Chastise in 2019. As to losses, Operation Chastise cost the British eight aircraft and fifty-three aircrew. Are you aware that the German armed forces lost an average of around 2,150 men per day during WW2. Doesn’t look heavy to me in context. However, the raid itself experienced 40% losses which was indeed high for a Bomber Command Raid. Lancaster bombers carrying the bouncing bomb As to the success of the raid, it flooded mines, factories and houses for 50 miles downstream and over 1,600 people were drowned. Unfortunately about 750 of these were foreign conscripted workers or prisoners of war. Eleven factories and two power stations were destroyed and one hundred and fourteen factories and seven power stations damaged. The flood washed away roads, railways and bridges, and more than 7,000 workers had to be redeployed from other tasks in order to repair the dams. The impact on German power generation and coal and steel production was significant in the context of eight aircraft lost. Unfortunately, as with the Schweinfurt raids, there was insufficient follow up and the damage was relatively soon repaired. Damage to the Eder Dam after the raid German internal monitoring, the equivalent of the British Mass Observation programme revealed that the German population regarded the raids as a legitimate attack on military targets and thought they were "an extraordinary success on the part of the English". In fact, if you watch the film, I think that it struck a chord with the public was for two different reasons. Firstly, the heroism demonstrated by the British, Canadian, and Australian bomber crews (plus two Kiwis and an American flying in the RCAF) in their incredible low level attack, aided by spotlights to help them keep exact altitude and other ad-hoc bomb-aiming devices. Lancaster bombers using spotlights to keep at the critical altitude during the run Secondly, the depiction of Barnes Wallis, his extraordinary invention of the bouncing bomb and, even more so, his one-man struggle against bureaucracy to get his ideas accepted. The lines from the film that stick in my mind are when he is asking for an aircraft to test his ideas. You say you need a Wellington Bomber for test drops. They're worth their weight in gold. Do you really think the authorities will lend you one? What possible argument could I put forward to get you a Wellington? Well, if you told them I designed it, do you think that might help? Not a failure by any conceivable standard and the Germans certainly weren’t laughing. Good show chaps.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the age limit for joining the British Royal Navy during the golden age of sailing? What was the reason for this age limit?
Answer: Normally called the Golden Age of Sail which is normally taken to be the latter half of the Nineteenth Century. However, I am going to assume that the question is directed at the Georgian Navy in the latter Eighteenth and early Nineteenth Century. Age limit in which direction? The youngest that a ship’s boy would normally be employed in the Royal Navy was probably twelve to fourteen. The same is probably true for Midshipmen but these were sometimes carried on the ship’s books, but not on the ship itself, at an earlier age in a minor fraud intended to allow them to accrue sea time. However, there were certainly some younger boys, such as Midshipman Hamilton Davies who found himself in command of a fire-brig at the age of ten, and the young American at Trafalgar, Robert Holbrooke, aged eleven, Boy 3rd Class, of the Orion. Astonishingly, there were four or five other boys - British and Irish-born - younger than him in the fleet. Ship’s boys were often sent to the Navy from foundling societies, orphanages, or charity schools such as the Marine Society as a means of ensuring them a career. Both ships boys and midshipmen were often enrolled as officer’s servants. After complaints from the Navy that some boys had been too weak for service on a warship, the Marine Society set a minimum age of fourteen and a stature of at least 4ft 4in, with a possible exception for very stout [strong], tall thirteen-year olds. Marine Society boys being handed to Britannia by Charity To give an example, albeit not in the Royal Navy, one of my own, fairly distant, relatives, Thomas Dencer, was discharged from Bermondsey Workhouse school, on liking, into the care of a merchant captain, Captain Petty of the Brig Helen of Whitstable, at the age of 14 in 1858. Two of his brothers, William and George, were discharged in 1860 and 1861 to the bands of the 94th Regiment and 60th Rifles, aged 11 and 14 respectively, and their sister, Margaret was sent into service aged 15 and promptly sent back when she became pregnant. Only poor James, aged 6 when his parents died was retained in the workhouse school. The Dencer children As to the oldest that you could join the Royal Navy, it is probably worth remembering that many men would quite possibly not have known their exact age. Walter Burke, who was on board the Victory at Trafalgar, was apparently born in 1736, which would make in his late sixties time of the battle - however, there appears to be some confusion about his age. Certainly, we know that the rules regarding men liable to impressment, perhaps 20% of the Royal Navy, that they were to be "eligible men of seafaring habits between the ages of 18 and 55 years", but I don’t suppose that the press gangs were very picky if the man was reasonably hale and hearty. The oldest man at Trafalgar (pace Walter Burke) was Michael Leonard aged 62 born in Ireland and an Ordinary Seaman on the Temeraire, but there were two hundred and twenty men aged 50 or over and at least three men aged 60 or over present at the battle. Given the rigours of a life at sea, this is quite remarkable. Calls for volunteers specify no age limit. The only condition, tongue-in-cheek is that you be able to carry an hundred weight [112 lb or 51 kg] of pewter [prize money], without stopping, at least three miles.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why was the Battle of Kohima significant for Britain, despite Burma no longer being part of the British Empire?
Answer: The Battle of Kohima was fought in India, not Burma. Burma remained part of the British Empire until 1948 and was actually part of British India until 1937. That apart, the related Battles of Kohima and Imphal were significant for Britain because they protected the gateway into India proper. Specifically, the Battle of Kohima, which took place in April to June, 1944 was significant because it stopped the Japanese from cutting the road that connected Imphal to Dimapur and supplied the Empire forces fighting the larger Battle of Imphal. In the course of the two battles, the Japanese Army was stopped dead after bitter fighting in the largest Japanese defeat on land of the war up until that point. The battles marked the turning point of the Burma Campaign and became the springboard for the Fourteenth Army’s (the Forgotten Army) subsequent re-conquest of Burma under the command of Bill Slim. The Japanese suffered some 61,000 casualties in the two battles and more to disease and starvation when their logistics proved entirely inadequate, whilst the British Empire forces suffered some 16,500 casualties. I have a personal connection with the Battle of Kohima. Some of the bitterest fighting the, so called, Battle of the Tennis Court took place in April and May 1944 when a small Empire force held out against repeated attacks by the Japanese 31st Division. Part of the defensive position incorporated the Deputy Commissioner’s bungalow and tennis court. At one point the British, Indian and Gurkha defenders were dug in on the west side of the tennis court and the Japanese on the east side, exchanging fire at point-blank range for over a week. My Uncle Frank commanded a troop of Grant tanks and told me that he was asked by the infantry commander to demolish the remains of the District Commissioner’s bungalow because the Japanese were using it as cover. Years later, he met the District Commissioner in question, Charles Pawsey, at some function in the UK and was able to tell him that he had been responsible for destroying his house by repeatedly running over it in his tank. The tennis court as seen from the bungalow The Battle of the Tennis Court by Terence Cuneo Lord Mountbatten, Supreme Allied Commander South East Asia Command, later described the Battle of Kohima as: probably one of the greatest battles in history... in effect the Battle of Burma... naked unparalleled heroism... the British/Indian Thermopylae. [Thermopylae is famous for the heroic stand made by a small Greek force against a much larger Persian army in 480 BC. The difference being that the Spartans lost.]

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did the UK lose the throne to the US after World War 2?
Answer: Exhaustion as a result of the losses of manpower, talent and money in two world wars, combined with the disadvantages of the first mover effect. By 1900 both Germany and the United States were moving significantly ahead of Great Britain in terms of population (56.4m and 75.9m respectively compared with 44.5m) and were starting to outstrip Great Britain in areas of production such as steel and chemicals. This is what you’d expect with, in the case of the United States, a developing country with a large population. Indeed, we have the same process in reverse with the United States and China in last couple of decades with China now producing thirteen times as much steel as the United States. Great Britain was both the birthplace and leading force in the Industrial Revolution and throughout the 19th Century had reaped the advantages of being first mover. However, there are disbenefits to being first mover and these made themselves apparent in the 20th Century. First movers suffer penalties as capital equipment becomes obsolescent earlier and as other countries take advantage of the research and development paid for by the first mover. This is a natural process and only to be expected, but the effect of the two world wars magnified the process to an extreme degree, with little capital available for improvements and existing machinery, including the railways, being run into the ground by the huge demands of wartime. Quite apart from this, Great Britain, to a great extent financed WW1 (as the United States, to a great extent, financed WW2). In the end, Great Britain was financing its own and most of the Empire's war expenditures, all of Italy's, and two thirds of the war costs of France and Russia, plus various smaller nations as well. In total, the Empire funded over a third of the Allied costs, some $47b. Britain borrowed some $3.7b from the US but, at the same time, lent $6.7b, including $2.5b to Russia, $1.9b to Italy, and $1.6b to France. The funds lent to Russia were, of course, never paid back due to the 1917 Revolution. By 1918 Britain was spending 38% of its GDP on funding the war. The material cost was also high with Britain losing 7,600,000 million tons of shipping, over 3,000 ships in WW1 alone. In contrast the United States suffered very minor losses of material during WW1. In terms of manpower, the United Kingdom (not the Empire) lost 888,000 men dead and a further 1,700,000 wounded. In terms of the working age male population (15–64) in 1914, that’s over 7% of the workforce killed and another 14.8% wounded. The equivalent figure for the United States is 1%. Alongside the raw losses of manpower, many of them skilled workers, we must consider the loss of talent, as an entire cohort of young men, who should have formed the next generation of scientists, entrepreneurs, innovators, and managers, were decimated. Officers suffered disproportionately with 5.76 officers per thousand dying per month as opposed to 3.12 per thousand other ranks. This loss of talent must be regarded as a major drag on Great Britain’s sluggish economic recovery in the post-war period, compounded by the capital stock worn out by the war. Nothing like this occurred in the United States in either war. The net impact of this huge outpouring of resources was that Britain was exhausted by 1918, and it was still not in the best of conditions, nearly twenty-one years later when WW2 commenced. The costs and losses of WW2 simply compounded the previous problems. Military losses in WW2 were very similar in Great Britain and the United States (384k vs. 417k) but by this stage the population count had diverged further (47.7m and 138.5m respectively - which statistic alone indicates the serious impact of WW1) meaning that Great Britain’s losses in WW2 were, relatively speaking, much more severe than those of the United States. The factors are obvious. A more interesting question is what would have happened if WW1 had not occurred or if Great Britain had stayed out of the war. Tyne Cot holds some of the British Empire dead from the Battle of Passchendaele in 1917, 11,954 burials and the names of 34,959 men who have no known grave In Flanders fields the poppies blow Between the crosses, row on row, That mark our place; and in the sky The larks, still bravely singing, fly Scarce heard amid the guns below. Perhaps a note on perspective may be useful, as many people today don’t fully realise the immense destruction of WW1. Tyne Cot, above, holds some of the dead from the battle commonly known as Passchendaele or Third Ypres. This particular battle lasted for three months and ten days and the British Empire casualties in this one battle exceeded the entire US casualties of WW1, were 50% larger than the total number of US casualties in the nine years of the Vietnam War, and around five times larger than the total US casualties of the Gulf War, Afghanistan, and Iraq combined. One battle. On the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916, the British Army suffered 57,470 casualties, of which 19,240 men were killed. Some of the Pals battalions suffered losses, 584 of the 720 Accrington Pals and 750 out of 900 Leeds Pals died, that devasted entire cities. Current conflicts (apart from, possibly, in the Ukraine) pale into insignificance in comparison with WW1.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What would happen if they just kamikaze zeppelins into enemy forces in WW1? It would be pretty hard to hold a trench if a giant burning ball of fire was coming at you.
Answer: Zeppelins were at the mercy of vagaries in the wind are were incredibly difficult to steer at the best of times, often ending up hundreds of miles away from from their intended destinations despite the best efforts of the crews. A Zeppelin on fire would be effectively impossible to steer and, anyway, would have a miniscule effect on dug in troops, and, even then, over a very small area. They would, in any case expend most of their energy upwards as the flaming gas is lighter than air, and so this would be a monumentally stupid and cost-ineffective way of trying to engage in warfare. If you really want to make a trench difficult to hold, try setting off 95,600 lb of ammonal under it. That will do the trick. Troops on the rim of the Messines mine crater after the battle

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In 1940, Great Britain brought only 10 divisions to mainland Europe to fight the Germans. Is this a case of serious betrayal, for which everyone around the world paid a heavy price?
Answer: In 1939, Great Britain had one provisional armoured division and regular five infantry divisions available. In addition, it had twelve understrength and underequipped Territorial Army divisions and, in March 1939, six months before war broke out, the government announced the formation of another twelve Territorial Army divisions by splitting the existing twelve. In the event, all six of the regular divisions, including the 1st Armoured Division, nine Territorial divisions, and the 1st Canadian Division served in the Battle for France - this includes the 52nd (Lowland) Infantry Division (TA) which was part of the 2nd BEF. A total of sixteen divisions, not ten. Following the regular divisions, the first three Territorial Army divisions, the 48th (South Midland) Division, 50th (Northumbrian) Division and 51st (Highland) Division, took their place in the front line in February 1940. By April 1940 they had been joined by the 12th (Eastern) Division, 23rd (2nd Northumbrian) Division, 42nd (East Lancashire) Division, 44th (Home Counties) Division and 46th (North Midland) Division. However, the 12th, 23rd, and 46th were the new untrained 2nd line TA divisions and were deployed, minus much of their transport and equipment, as so-called 'digging divisions' to be used for infrastructure work. Therefore, overall, Great Britain deployed six (100%) of its available regular divisions, six (50%) of its 1st Line Territorial Divisions and three (25%) of its twelve 2nd Line territorial divisions (these latter largely untrained and unequipped). In contrast, in the Battle for France, the French deployed eighty-two divisions (including two Polish divisions), the Belgians twenty-two divisions, the Dutch ten divisions, and the Germans one hundred and ten divisions. Some people just don’t seem to understand that, not needing one, Great Britain simply didn’t have an army on the same scale of the continental armies. Great Britain essentially sent everything it had to aid France. In reality, Great Britain committed to supply nineteen divisions by the end of 1940 and had actually supplied sixteen when France fell at the end of June 1940. As befits its geography, Great Britain’s main strength was concentrated in the Royal Navy and, latterly, the RAF rather than in the number of ground troops it deployed. BEF in France, October 1939

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the British Company Bristol make any good aircraft during WW2?
Answer: Yes. They made the Bristol F.2B and Bristol Bulldog that remained in service into the 1930s. Then the produced the Blenheim light bomber, heavy fighter and night fighter, and the Beaufort torpedo bomber. The Blenheim was a good aircraft when it was first introduced but rapidly became obsolete in WW2 as technology evolved. However, the Beaufort evolved into the Beaufighter which served from 1940 to 1960. The Beaufighter was used by the RAF, FAA, RCAF, RAAF, RNZAF, SAAF, USAAF, and the PAF and successfully fulfilled a number of roles including heavy fighter, bomber, ground attack, torpedo bomber, and night fighter. Bristol Beaufighter I was privileged to know an ex-Beaufighter pilot, Robert Smith, who flew his Beau from England to India. He loved the plane and preferred it to the Mosquitos that he flew later on. Rugged, dependable, and heavily armed with 4x20mm cannon and 7x.303 machine guns as well as rockets or bombs, the Japanese were said to call it the Whispering Death.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the British term for "sandwich"? Are sandwiches eaten differently in Britain than in America, and if so, how do they differ (e.g., fillings)?
Answer: The British term for sandwich is, unsurprisingly, sandwich. Sandwich is a town in Kent, once England’s fourth largest port (one of the Cinque Ports) located on the Wantsum Channel but now a couple of miles inland due to the silting up of the channel. It was probably founded by the Saxons as Stonar and is located very close to the original Roman beachhead at Richborough. Sand is pretty self-explanatory, whilst wich probably comes from the Latin vicus or place. Sandwich in Kent John Montagu (1718–1792) the 4th Earl of Sandwich was, amongst other things, Postmaster General and First Lord of the Admiralty and he may also have been involved with the notorious Hellfire Club in the 1730s. Sandwich was the butt of the famous retort by Samuel Foote. When Sandwich declared "Foote, I have often wondered what catastrophe would bring you to your end; but I think, that you must either die of the pox or the halter” [Syphilis or hanging]. Foote replied "My Lord, that will depend upon one of two contingencies – whether I embrace your lordship's mistress, or your lordship's principles." However, Sandwich’s most enduring legacy is, of course, the sandwich.
