The popular story goes that Sandwich called for meat between slices of bread so that he was not forced to leave the gambling table to take a meal. Other gamblers saw this and began to order "the same as Sandwich", and, in this manner, the humble sandwich was born. As to fillings, you can put pretty much whatever you like between two slices of bread. I know that Tescos have produced both a lasagna sandwich and a strawberries and clotted cream sandwich (for Wimbledon), but I haven’t yet been able to verify the fabled Scotch Egg sandwich. Afternoon tea at the Ritz A little to the south of Sandwich is the tiny village of Ham which, rather serendipitously, gives rise to some amusing signposts.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If the European Defence Force acquired Army-like powers to call up EU member state Citizens who are NOT in the military to fight (bit like what the outgoing Tories tried to do in UK), would you stand up to them and firmly tell them to 'get lost'?
Answer: Well the outgoing Tories didn’t try to do that, but we’ll leave that aside. The point is that members of a society have both rights and responsibilities. It appears that quite a few people are well aware of their rights but keen to forget their responsibilities. If society, through the agency of the democratically elected government, decides that conscription is required then that becomes a responsibility and that’s that. Those who want to tell society to get lost would be termed conscientious objectors and have historically been dealt with in a number of ways. Essentially, if you don’t want to take on the responsibilities of being a member of society, you might well lose the benefits of being one. Conscription, by the way, is not uncommon in European societies, although it is now less evident than it was a couple of decades ago.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can British people explain? For A-level history, we learnt about British history from 1780-1928. Why did my teacher try to portray 1780 as “recent” British history whereas Americans see 1780 as ancient?
Answer: Context. I studied modern history at university and my course started in 410 AD (or CE if you are inclined that way). 410 is when the Romans departed these isles and so, in this case it is used to delineate the break between ancient (classical) and modern history. Ancient history is generally taken to cover the period between around 3400 BC (or BCE) and, in this case, 410 AD. 3400 BC marks the earliest currently known writing - Egyptian hieroglyphs and Sumerian cuneiform. Anything before that date is literally pre-historic. Nothing dating from colonial North America can technically be considered ancient although some pre-colonial archaeological remains are ancient. We can distinguish between ancient and old, and between old and recent. I would suggest that recent covers the period within living memory. What one of my history teachers (R.I.P. John King) once rather sniffily called current affairs. Therefore, I’d say that both statements are incorrect. 1780 is certainly not ancient, but it is not recent either. It is just about within the normal scope of modern. Last week, as of writing, I walked the Two Moors Way, 120 or so miles across Dartmoor and Exmoor starting on the Devon coast at Wembury and ending on the Somerset coast at Lynmouth. On the way across Dartmoor we walked through Grimspound, twenty-four late Bronze Age hut circles surrounded by a massive granite wall and dating to around 1300 BC - ancient. Dartmoor in July At one point we stayed at the New Inn in Coleford (highly recommended by the way). If you zoom in on the sign, you can see it says The New Inn since 1350 - old but not ancient. The parrot, Captain, has been there for forty years. In the 15th Century church of St. Peter, Washford Pyne - old, I noticed the Commonwealth War Graves Commission headstone of Company Sergeant Major F. A. Snowden, Machine Gun Corps, who died (of wounds I assume) in 1920 - recent (just about). As an aside, the reason it says (INF) on his headstone is presumably to differentiate him from the heavy branch of the Machine Gun Corps - the first tanks.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What percentage of German fighter pilots became ace pilots during World War II? How does this compare to other countries' fighter pilot units?
Answer: I don’t think that it is possible to answer this question accurately because there is no definitive data that I know of for the number of fighter pilots deployed in each air force. However… Using data from Wikipedia, we can derive very approximately that 73% of all the roughly 75,000 German claims were made by 963 pilots. In fact, just 35 pilots were credited with 6,848 kills, 9% of the entire total. Germany’s highest scoring ace was Erich Hartmann, nicknamed the Black Devil, with 352 claims, 345 Soviet and 7 American. Amazingly Hartmann survived the war. Erich Hartmann A further 1,500 odd pilots were also classed as aces and must therefore have shot down a minimum of five enemy aircraft each for another 7,500 aircraft, or 11%, leaving a rump of some 11,000 aircraft or less (<16%) to be shot down by non-ace pilots. Germany apparently produced (again from Wikipedia) some 53,200 fighter aircraft between 1939 and 1945. We know that a German fighter staffel (squadron) had between 12 and 16 aircraft and 20 to 25 pilots, or around 1.6 pilots per aircraft. If we extrapolate rather wildly, that would give us a figure of 85,000 fighter pilots. This figure is probably too high as you can write off an aircraft without writing off a pilot, but rarely vice-versa, so let’s arbitrarily settle on 80,000 fighter pilots. That would suggest that around 3% of German fighter pilots were classified as aces. Some sources suggest that the Luftwaffe only had 20,000 to 25,000 fighter pilots, but as they lost some 17,000 killed and 8,000 wounded, this seems unlikely. My figures are probably too high, but I do use the same metrics consistently. The German figures are a bit distorted because around two thirds of the claims were made on the Eastern Front where the pickings were, initially at least, pretty easy. This helps to explain the very high number of claims made by a few aces, as most of these will be found to have served in the East, at least at some point. See Hartmann above. The RAF produced some 742 aces during the war, whilst the USAAF produced 718 (some presumably in the Pacific). The highest scoring pilots from the Western allies against the German Luftwaffe were Johnnie Johnson (RAF) with 38 claims and Gabby Gabreski (USAAF) with 28 claims. A Russian ace, Ivan Kozhedub, is credited with 66 claims. The USN and the USMC produced 391 and 122 aces respectively, but I doubt if any of these served in the European Theatre. The RAF received around 50,000 fighters during WW2, including 13,400 produced in the US, so following the same rough metrics we can deduce around 80,000 pilots and therefore an ace percentage of around 0.9%. The USAAF received around 47,000 fighters during WW2 which also gives an ace percentage of around 1%. Now other sources suggest, without explanation, that around 5% of pilots became aces, but I think that is probably a bit high. My data may be wrong, but I think that the broad conclusion is probably correct. The Luftwaffe had around three times as many aces as the Western Allies and this is accounted for by their policy of not rotating pilots and the special conditions that existed initially on the Eastern Front. This post is mostly speculation, which has been more fun that working (oops), but I would be interested if anyone has any better hard data.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why didn't Hitler use his extensive stocks of poison gas when losing the war?
Answer: One of the hallmarks of WWI was the large-scale use of chemical weapons by both sides. However, chemical warfare caused less than 1% of the total deaths in this war and whilst the psychological impacts were significant, the real impact was less impressive. Some 91,000 men died of gas (mostly on the Eastern Front), around 85% of them from phosgene or diphosgene. Against a well prepared and equipped enemy, gas was basically not very effective. Gas was also a dangerous weapon to your own side because it depended on favourable conditions and could be blown back on your own troops by a flaw in the wind. It was also banned by the 1899 Hague Convention and the Geneva Protocol of 1925, and it was also seen to be an unsoldierly weapon. All sides has large stockpiles of gas during WW2, but it was not used on the Western Front and only to a limited extent on the Eastern Front. The essential calculation that the Germans made was that the likely Allied retaliation to any German use of gas would cause far more damage than the German attack could inflict. It is interesting to note that the Germans has significant stocks of chemical weapons in Normandy but chose not to use them. During the Nuremberg trials, Hermann Göring was asked about this. His response is illuminating: Q. We know you had Gas Blau [Tabun?] which would have stopped the Normandy invasion. Why didn’t you use it? A. The horses. Q. What have horses to do with it? A. Everything. A horse lies down in the shafts or between the thills [shafts] as soon as his breathing is restricted. We never have had a gas mask a horse would tolerate. Q. What has that to do with Normandy? A. We did not have enough gasoline to adequately supply the German Air Force and the Panzer Divisions, so we used horse transport in all operations. You must have known that the first thing we did in Poland, France, everywhere, was to seize the horses. All our material was horse-drawn. Had we used gas you would have retaliated and you would have instantly immobilized us. Therefore, it would appear that the main reason that Hitler didn’t use his chemical weapons was that he feared the retaliation that such use would bring and the crippling effect it would have on the German armed forces by immobilising its horse-drawn transport. The German Army used around a million horses and mules at any given point, whilst the Western Allies used next to none. German WW2 horse gas mask

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Brit historian Max Hastings has exposed the incompetence of the Brit WW2 military in many books and articles. Is he not given the attention he deserves because Brits care only about flagshagging, not about facts?
Answer: I would say that Max Hastings is certainly one of the most widely read popular historians in the UK and he definitely produces a prodigious output. I don’t think that you can say that he doesn’t get the attention he deserves. I have read most of Sir Max’s books and generally enjoyed then - although I have to say that I found Operation Pedestal a bit indigestible. It should be remembered that Sir Max is primarily a journalist rather than a historian and that he uses teams of researchers to help with his books - as, indeed, did Churchill, so there’s nothing very wrong with that. As a result, I consider Sir Max’s books as good general introductions to subjects that I don’t know very much about. However, they start to come across as a little superficial when you have some knowledge about the subject. The book that is probably being referred to is Overlord - D-Day and the Battle for Germany. It is worth noting that this is an old book now, being first published in 1984, and so does not represent the latest scholarship on the matter. If I remember correctly, Sir Max does rhapsodise somewhat about German equipment. Using first-hand reminiscences in historical works certainly makes them more immediate and compelling, but it does mean that your work is shaped by a very few voices. Allied soldiers were certainly cautious in the face of dug-in 88s and Spandaus (machine guns) - and who wouldn’t be - but that doesn’t reflect an inferiority of tactics or equipment. Where the Germans probably had an advantage was in their more flexible task oriented tactics, Auftragstaktik, which moved decision making further down their command structure. All military forces, of all nations, make mistakes all the time, large and small. These mistakes should not be ignored and swept under the carpet because, if that happens, no learning can take place. However, it is necessary to maintain context and realise that mistakes are also constantly being made by the enemy. At the end of the day, the Allies met and defeated the Germans at all levels: tactical, operational, and strategic on land, by sea, and in the air. I’ve just spent the last few minutes ferreting around for my copy of 18 Platoon by Sydney Jary. This is the story of a rifle platoon of the 4th Battalion Somerset Light Infantry and its fighting advance - not without losses - from Normandy to Bremen, as written by its platoon commander. Recommended reading. In it, Jary notes: It has become the custom for some of our younger military writers to extol the professional ability of the Wehrmacht whilst decrying that of our own fighting arms, particularly our armour and infantry. This has perplexed me because it runs contrary to my experience. My 18 Platoon were better soldiers than any we fought. So was "D" Company and the whole 4th Battalion, The Somerset Light Infantry. Admittedly it was a good battalion but I find it hard to believe that it was unique. This tendency among writers is understandable. They are too young to have taken part in the operations about which they write and therefore they have had to rely mainly on official records and personal interviews with those who were present. Sadly, interviews with all but a few ex-infantrymen must necessarily be of limited assistance because very few of them survived long enough to have much to contribute. Although they lost, the German soldiers and their families are proud of their exploits, many of which were considerable. It is, of course, very much in their own interest to encourage the theory and myth that, although superior as fighting men, they were beaten only by numerically superior forces and firepower. In my experience this was not so. In many attacks the prisoners we took outnumbered our attacking force and German units who would continue to resist at close quarters were few indeed. Unlike us, they rarely fought at night, when they were excessively nervous and unsure of themselves. Where we patrolled extensively, they avoided it. I can remember only one successful German patrol and not one successful night action. If our positions had been reversed, I doubt if they would have performed better than we did. Without doubt, some Wehrmacht formations were extremely professionally competent but many were not. Some of the enemy infantry fought with fanaticism but most did not. Churchill inspects the men of the 4th Somerset Light Infantry in May 1944

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did the number of infantry divisions in the British Army compare to those in the German and French armies?
Answer: When? I assume that the question is referring to the start of either the First or Second World Wars in order that a comparison of relative strength can be made. As usual sources vary on exact details, so feel free to chip in. I should note that the British and Indian Armies were separate entities during both wars but I will count them in the total. The question excludes cavalry and armoured divisions, but I have included fortress and motorised infantry divisions. In addition, there was no conscription in Britain and so Territorial divisions are not the same as French and German reserve divisions as they were volunteer organisations for home service only - although most men did volunteer for overseas service on the outbreak of war. In 1914, the British had 6 regular divisions and 14 territorial divisions. There were also 9 divisions belonging to the Indian Army but containing some British battalions and one light division of two brigades in Burma which was also part of the Indian Army. Hurry up and wait, British infantry on the march in France, 1914 The Indian Army divisions were obviously stationed in India/Burma. It is a fascinating side-note that Indian Expeditionary Force A, of two infantry and two cavalry divisions, arrived in France in September 1914, only six weeks after the declaration of war. Quite a feat of organisation in a pre-computer age. Indian Army infantry arrive in France, 1914 In 1914, the French had 47 regular divisions, 23 reserve divisions, and 6 colonial divisions and the Germans had 44 regular divisions (including 2 Guard divisions), 27 reserve divisions, and 11 Landwehr divisions. There were also 6 divisions of the Bavarian Army. In terms of regular divisions available for immediate deployment to the Continent before mobilisation the ratio is 6:47:50. In 1939, the British had 5 regular divisions and 24 territorial divisions together with 4 Indian Army divisions. Note, however, that the number of territorial divisions had been doubled in March 1939 and many of these units were seriously understrength on the outbreak of war. In 1939, the French had 51 regular divisions, 11 colonial divisions, 18 fortress divisions, 5 motorised divisions and 12 reserve divisions and the Germans had 103 infantry divisions and 10 motorised divisions. In terms of regular divisions available for immediate deployment to the Continent before mobilisation the ratio is 5:85:113. The general point is that Britain had no conscription before either war and relied entirely on volunteer forces and, of course, on the Royal Navy. Britain has never been a Continental land power and has never had a large peacetime army.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many German citizens were part of the Waffen-SS, excluding foreign volunteers?
Answer: The Waffen-SS was composed of German nationals, ethnic Germans (Volksdeutsche), and foreign volunteers from various countries. The part of the SS that became the Waffen-SS was originally the three Standarten: Deutschland, Germania, and Der Führer of the Verfügungstruppen (SS-VT) and they would have been composed of German citizens. Of the forty-one named Waffen-SS divisions, fifteen were composed mainly of Germans, three were composed mainly of ethnic Germans, six can perhaps be considered mixed, and seventeen were composed mainly of foreigners. I should mention that division in this case is a rather loose term as they ranged between 4,000 and 22,000 men. Many of the ethnic Germans came from Hungary and formed divisions such as Horst Wessel and Maria Theresia. These are not to be confused with the Hungarian Waffen-SS divisions such as Hunyadi which were manned by Hungarians. drawn from the Royal Hungarian Army. The primarily foreign divisions included three Hungarian, two Latvian, two Dutch, and one each of Albanians, Belarussians, Estonians, Flemish, French, Italians, Romanians, Russians, Ukrainians, and Walloons (Belgians). I’d guess that in 1944 approximately 45% of the Waffen-SS were German nationals, and a further 6% were ethic Germans. Assuming about 550,000 men in the Waffen-SS in 1944 then around 250,000 were probably German nationals and a further 35,000 ethnic Germans. Admittedly, it’s an educated guess, but it’s the best I can do. Waffen-SS soldiers in Normandy

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why do military symbols look the way they do? For example, why does an oblong represent armor or intersecting lines represent infantry?
Answer: I assume that we are speaking of the NATO Joint Military Symbology (APP-6). These symbols are in fact of relatively recent origin and are not universal. The Germans in WW2, used a different system and the Russians use a different system (as far as I am aware). German WW2 symbology In Kriegspiel which was developed starting in 1812, the units were actually differentiated by shape with infantry being oblongs and cavalry being squares. Kriegspiel symbology However, the common western (NATO) symbology consists of a frame, a constituent icon, and optional symbol modifiers. The latter are optional text fields or graphic indicators that provide additional information and may include a fill. When the symbols were first being derived, they only needed to consider infantry, cavalry and artillery and these were shown as a saltire for infantry (representing infantry cross belts), a diagonal for cavalry (representing the cavalry sabre belt) and a dot for artillery (representing a cannon ball). Once the basics were settled, it was easy to start combining the symbols: When tanks came along during WW1, the Germans adopted the lozenge shape of the first British tanks (see above) but the West eventually standardised on a track icon. And then more symbols could be combined or added: The final result is a standard set of several dozen symbols that represent all the common types of military unit and can be read at a glance by those with a bit of practice.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is Germany the sole cause of WW2?
Answer: Ah, the causes of WW2. What are causes? What, indeed, was WW2? I think that what it is safe say is that Germany was solely responsible for the outbreak of hostilities in Europe in WW2. Therefore Germany was certainly the proximate cause of WW2. That is assuming that you don’t believe, as some do, that WW2 started with the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937 (or in 1931 with the Mukden Incident according to preference). However, history unwinds backwards. Hitler didn’t wake up one morning and just decide to go to war with Poland, there are always reasons. The process was shaped by many factors, the outcome of the Russian Revolution, the terms of the Treaty of Versailles, the economic crisis of the 1930s, the rise of fascism in Germany, the cult of Hitler, the policy of appeasement by Western powers, the failure of the League of Nations, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the structure of the German economy. The list goes on and on, unwinding into the mists of the past. When considering jus ad bellum (the morality of going to war) and jus in bello (moral conduct within war) Germany failed on both counts. In initiating the conflict it demonstrated neither just cause nor last resort. Having said that, as we all know from personal experience, what is just and what is fair tends rather to be in the eye of the beholder. However, the failure of Britain and France to prevent the war is not nearly of the same moral weight as Germany’s decision to actually start the war. German troops demolish a Polish border crossing

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What would be the most effective combination of a battleship and an aircraft carrier in a naval battle?
Answer: There is no really effective combination of a battleship and an aircraft carrier in a naval battle; it is a case of chalk and cheese. The last major class of battleships deployed were the US Iowa-class with four completed. During the same period, the major class of aircraft carriers deployed was the US Essex-class with twenty-four completed. Iowa-class battleship Battleships were designed to fight in proximity to the enemy, with sensors and weapons limiting effective engagement ranges to around fifteen miles, whilst a carrier could seek out and engage the enemy at ten times that range - around two-hundred miles. Essex-class carrier In theory, a carrier can find a battleship and either engage or evade it before the battleship even knows that the carrier is there. A carrier had got itself into a very sticky situation if it found itself within fifteen miles of a battleship and would use its superior speed to evade if at all possible. Of all the WW2 battleships, only the Iowa-class themselves could keep pace with an Essex-class carrier. The only two incidents where a carrier was sunk by a battleship were the Glorious, which was sunk by the Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, and the escort carrier Gambier Bay which was sunk either by the Yamato or by the heavy-cruiser Chikuma. In both cases, the carriers were caught unawares. All the other carriers lost in WW2 were sunk as a result of air or submarine attack (the Chiyoda was crippled by aerial attack before being engaged by cruisers). Despite the two examples above there is no real case for suggesting that a battleship should be deployed to escort an aircraft carrier just in case an enemy battleship turned up unexpectedly - that was a job for cruisers and destroyers. Indeed, the Iowa-class battleships were not primarily designed to escort the Essex-class carriers, they were designed as fast battleships that would be capable of forcing the enemy battleships into action. It is an example of how fast naval aviation came to dominate during WW2 that whilst, at the start of the war, the carriers were seen as subordinate to the battleships the situation had completely reversed by 1944 with the evolution of the Fast Carrier Strike Force. By this stage of the war, the battleships were definitively subordinate and, arguably, not really required.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What happens if the US dissolves NATO? Can the European countries still fight as one coalition force or will that end immediately?
Answer: As other people have pointed out, the US can’t dissolve NATO. It could, however, potentially leave NATO and this would have serious repercussions. When considering defence expenditure US defence expenditure amounts to two-thirds of all defence spending in the NATO Alliance. The rest of the NATO countries combined spend only half what the US does on defence. Of course, not all US defence spending is relevant to NATO as roughly 50% of the US Navy operates in the Pacific. The US deployment in Europe is also a fraction of its former size, but we must consider the deterrent effect and reinforcement and logistical potential that comes from US participation in the Alliance. If the US left NATO then there would be the need to significantly bolster defence spending in Europe - unless for some unfathomable reason you believe that the world has become a kinder and gentler place recently. It is difficult to assess the amount of extra spending that would be required, but it is worth noting that, in terms of defence spending per capita, the UK spends 49% of the US figure, Germany 41%, and France 36%. These three countries account for 50% of the non-US defence spending in the Alliance, but still amount to only a quarter of US defence spending. However, without US participation, the remaining NATO countries could still fight as one coalition force, albeit one lacking in certain specialised capabilities. If the US were to leave NATO, the European countries (I don’t know what Canada would do if the US departed) would have to start taking defence seriously - which could mean significant cuts to social programmes. People tend to forget that defence spending in the UK used to be much higher until the mid-1980s, so talking about meeting a 2% commitment is a pretty low bar:

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What were the differences between escort carriers and regular carriers? Did escort carriers have hangars like regular carriers?
Answer: The early escort carriers were based on merchant hulls. The first escort carrier, HMS Audacity, which entered service in June 1941, was built on the hull of the captured German merchantman Hannover and had no hanger deck. All of her aircraft were stored on the flight deck. HMS Audacity Likewise the British MAC (Merchant Aircraft Carrier) ships based on the “triple-twelve” tanker hulls didn’t have a hangar deck either. Rapana Later classes of escort carriers, the Long Island, Charger, Bogue/Attacker, and Sangamon classes were built on merchant or oiler (tanker) hulls and it wasn’t until the Casablanca-class that the ships were actually built as aircraft carriers. Escort carriers were, essentially, cheap carriers designed for limited purposes - convoy escort and aircraft transport. They were smaller, carried fewer aircraft, were more lightly armoured and were, crucially, slower than full-sized carriers. On the other hand, they were cheap and quick to build in large numbers.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If HMS Habakkuk, the WWII aircraft carrier made of Pycrete (ice and wood pulp) had been successfully built and deployed, how would she have fared in combat, and would she have made a difference in the War of the Atlantic?
Answer: In the early years of the war, HMS Habakkuk would have been invaluable in the Battle of the Atlantic but, by the time she actually became feasible, events had overtaken her and she would have been a massive waste of resources. Project Habakkuk was an absolutely fascinating, if rather eccentric, experiment promoted by COHQ (Combined Operations Headquarters) under Mountbatten and designed to close the Mid-Atlantic gap. In outline, the idea was to build a very large aircraft carrier made of specially strengthened ice called Pykrete after its inventor Geoffrey Pyke. HMS Habakkuk concept The Mid-Atlantic Gap was the area of convoy routes between Canada and the UK that was beyond the range of Coastal Command aircraft based in Iceland, Newfoundland and Northern Ireland. The freedom of action allowed to U-Boats in the gap led to heavy losses amongst convoys and an urgent need to provide extended air-cover for convoys. One idea was to flatten the top off an iceberg and use that as temporary carrier, but Pye came up with the idea of a ship made of cast ice reinforced with 14% wood pulp - which considerably strengthened it - called Pykrete. In order to remain effective it was found that a Pykrete vessel needed to be insulated and kept at -16 C. Although a 1,000 ton scale model was built in Canada with some success, it was this requirement for continued refrigeration that eventually killed the idea. The specification of the vessel also started to suffer from scope creep and the final design would have weighed 2.2 million tons and had a flight deck 2,000 feet long. In addition, there was no possibility that Habakkuk could have been constructed before 1945. Project Habakkuk design During this period, there was a highly unedifying example of inter-command rivalry within the RAF, with Bomber Command refusing to give up long range aircraft to Coastal Command despite the fact that these were desperately needed to protect vital convoys. VLR (Very Long Range) aircraft equipped with radar did not necessarily need to sink U-Boats, although they did, but they also performed a vital role in forcing U-Boats that were shadowing convoys on the surface to submerge - which reduced their speed and caused them to lose the convoy. As an aside, I recommend Liberators over the Atlantic by Jack Colman for a vivid description of operating Liberators out of Iceland. Several events were occurring in the same time frame as Habakkuk was being designed that eventually scuppered the idea. A few, although never very many, VLR Liberators were coming into service and their range was being extended with additional fuel tanks, radar improvements made it much more dangerous for U-Boats to remain on the surface, escort carriers were becoming available as were dedicated U-Boat Hunter-killer groups as more ships became available, and, finally, VLR aircraft started to operate out of the Azores. Coastal Command VLR Liberator By the end of 1943 Habakkuk was dead in the water, found to be impractical because of the enormous production resources required and technical difficulties involved. However, the idea of floating bases remained attractive with spin-offs such as Project Tentacle, although nothing practical ever came of these ideas.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were Enigma machines never cracked? If so, how did the Allies locate U-boats during World War II?
Answer: Enigma was cracked and Enigma decrypts (Ultra) played a significant part in the Battle of the Atlantic, although perhaps not quite as much as is sometimes portrayed. As a starter, it is important to realise that Enigma was broken, lost, and broken again in a cycle as the Germans improved their procedures and the British countered them. It is also important to understand that even when Enigma was being broken, not every message was broken and some messages that were broken were not broken quickly enough to be of immediate use. The table below shows that in the ten months from December 1942, 18% of the U-boat traffic was never broken and another 36% took more than five days to break - probably making it of little use in locating the U-boats. Statistics relating to breaking the Atlantic U-boat key Where Enigma decrypts did play a major part in the Battle of the Atlantic was when Hut 8 at Bletchley Park started to read Dolphin (U-boat) traffic without delay in June and July 1941 using keys captured from German weather ships. Decrypts were translated and sent the Admiralty's Operational Intelligence Centre in London giving the U-boats approximate locations and allowing the OIC to re-route convoys away from the danger zones. However, Enigma decrypts were only part of the picture. U-boats were also located by Huff Duff (HF/DF) or High-frequency direction finding when they transmitted using their radios. At first these were shore based systems but eventually the technology was developed to mount them on ships. Bearings taken from multiple HF/DF stations could be used to triangulate the position of U-boats at long range with considerable accuracy. HF/DF aerial visible on HMCS Swansea a River-class frigate Another means of locating U-boats was when very long range (VLR) maritime patrol aircraft, Liberators and Sunderlands, were deployed to close the mid-Atlantic gap. These aircraft, particularly once equipped with centimetric radar, could detect and engage surfaced U-boats, but they also had the effect of keeping the U-boats down, which severely limited their speed and thus their effectiveness in closing with convoys. Aircraft flying from escort carriers had the same effect. Sunderland flying patrol over a convoy Sunderland W4030 of 10 Sqn RAAF sinking U-243 Finally, at a relatively short range, radar and ASDIC (Sonar) were deployed to locate and attack both surfaced (radar) and submerged (ASDIC) U-boats when they attempted to get into attacking positions on a convoy. Destroyer dropping depth charges

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What motivated Napoleon to support America in its war against Great Britain? Was his hatred towards GB the only reason for his support?
Answer: France and Spain both bitterly resented their losses to Britain in the Seven Years' War (1756-1763). In the Treaty of Paris, France lost nearly all of her North American possessions and Spain lost the territory of Florida. Humiliated, both countries sought revenge and a means of weakening Great Britain’s strategic position. Between 1776 and 1778 the French secretly provided supplies, arms and ammunition to the Americans through Roderigue Hortalez and Company. After the Treaty of Alliance in 1778, and up until 1782, they openly provided vital money, troops and naval support. Indeed, there were twice as many French troops engaged at the culminating Siege of Yorktown as there were American. The Siege of Yorktown. Note that the central figure is the French General Rochambeau with General Lafayette to Washington’s right, emphasising the vital importance of the French contribution to the Revolution The Treaty of 1778, however, was concluded between the Thirteen United States of America and His Most Christian Majesty, Louis XVI, not with Napoleon. Napoleon didn’t come to power until 1799, twenty-one years later. In 1778 he was nine. The cost to France was crippling, with over five million livres of aid sent by 1777. France’s Minister of Finance, Baron Anne Robert Jacques Turgot, prophesised that the funding, adding as it did to the already heavy burden of France’s military and naval costs, would lead to bankruptcy. In the final reckoning neither France nor Spain benefited from their support of the Revolution and France, at least partly as a result of that support, soon descended into the anarchy that cost Louis XVI his head and, in the course of time, brought Napoleon to power. When it came to the War of 1812, the Americans had rather queered the pitch by failing to repay monies owed to France, passing the Neutrality Act in 1794 and, in the same year, signing Jay’s Treaty (A Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, Between His Britannic Majesty and the United States of America). The undeclared Quasi-War between the United States and the First French Republic between 1798 and 1800 didn’t help relations either. These actions strongly suggested to the French that the Americans had abandoned their old allies, despite the assistance they had provided during the American Revolution. Although relations were normalised by the Treaty of Mortefontaine in 1800 the alliance was dead. In this light, the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 should not be seen as a friendly gesture towards the United States, but rather as a strategic move intended to stop the British from seizing what had been the vast Spanish Louisiana Territory. After the failure of Macon’s Bill No.2 of 1810 to improve the situation, relations between America and France were so poor that Madison was actually considering declaring war on France to stop French privateers from seizing American ships. In the event, Britain was considered the more pressing threat and this led to the War of 1812. In 1812, Napoleon was embroiled in his disastrous Russian Campaign and had no interest in supporting America in its war against Great Britain, nor had he the means to do so had he wished. Therefore, there is no evidence that Napoleon ever supported America either in the Revolutionary War or in the War of 1812.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How are decimals written in Roman numerals?
Answer: They didn’t use decimals for fractions. The Romans, rather confusingly, used base 10 for whole numbers and base 12 for fractions (as well as, occasionally, the Babylonian base 60). We still use base 60 today with 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 6 x 60 or 360 degrees in a circle, etc. Until the 15th of February 1971, Britain used base 12 in its coinage with 12 pennies in a shilling and 240 pennies in a pound. This is called a duodecimal system and is useful because base 12 has lots of factors. If I have a shilling, I can divide it equally between 2, 3, 4, or 6 people giving them each 2x6d, 3x4d, 4x3d or 6x2d respectively (d meaning penny). This is very handy for the most likely everyday transactions - try dividing ten between three people. So the Romans didn’t use decimals (tenths) as fractions, they used uncials (twelfths). These were sometimes simply spelled out, but there was another convention. There was a Roman coin was called an As and as half of As is S, the Romans used S to mean half (6 uncials). Fractions less than six were written as dots, either written in a line or as you might see one to five on a dice or, sometimes, as dashes. Therefore you end up with Unica 1/12 (.), Sextans 2/12 or 1/6 (..), Quadrans 2/12 or 1/4 (…), Triens 4/12 or 1/3 (….), Quincunx 5/12 (…..), Semis 6/12 or 1/2 (S), Septunx 7/12 (S.), Bes 8/12 or 2/3 (S..), Dodrans 9/12 or 3/4 (S…), Dextans 10/12 or 5/6 (S….), Denux 11/12 (S…..) and As 12/12 or 1 (I). So four and two thirds would be written as IV S.. or five minus one plus eight uncials. Uncia is the origin of the English words inch and ounce, Sextans and Quadrans for the English words sextant and quadrant. Quincunx is the proper name for shape made by the five dots on a dice and Semi, of course, still means half. However, if you want to see something really freaky you should see the way the Romans multiplied. If we want to multiply 20 by 31 it is easy to do the answer in our head: 31 x 10 = 310 x 2 = 620. The Romans used tables and abacuses (abaci) but they could also do it long hand as follows: Step 1: Divide the number on the left side by 2 successively until you reach 1 (ignoring remainders) Step 2: Multiply the number on the right side by 2 successively until you reach the 1 row Step 3: Take the right hand side numbers where the left hand side number is odd and add them up Step 4: Simplify the result: IIIII + V = X, XXXXXXX = LXX, LLXX = CXX, CCCCCCXX = DCXX Bingo! Roman multiplication made easy

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Which country had the most powerful navy during World War II: the US, UK, Germany, or Japan?
Answer: Specifying during WW2 makes this a difficult question to answer because the position changed during the course of the war as nations entered and left the war and due to building programmes and losses in combat. Indeed the only major nation to see the war through from beginning to end was Britain. I suppose you could count Japan and China but, perhaps parochially, I tend to think of that as a separate conflict. It also depends on how you define powerful and what you count. Is power measured in number of ships, types of ships, or the total tonnage of ships? When we count ships, are we counting just combat ships or are we including landing ships/craft and other supporting vessels? Are we counting light craft (PT/MTB boats), submarines, minesweepers? The rate of building was eye-watering to modern eyes. In March 1939, before the war had even broken out, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Admiralty, Geoffrey Shakespeare announced to Parliament that: Our dockyards and shipyards in the course of the year will be engaged in constructing some 200 vessels, or a total of 870,000 tons. An achievement like this has never been approached before in peace-time. We shall be building, in the course of the year, nine battleships, six aircraft carriers, 25 cruisers, 43 destroyers, 19 submarines, and a large number of small vessels. House of Commons Debate 16th of March 1939 vol 345 cc645-770 When the war actually got going some of the figures are barely believable. The Germans started the war with around 60 U-Boats and then built 1,100 more (and lost 785), launching them at the rate of roughly one every two days. In response, the Allies (mostly the US) started building merchant ships at such a rate that they were eventually averaging three per day. The US Navy (taking into account losses) expanded from 183 surface warships in 1939 to 917 by the end of 1944. U-249 surrenders to the Royal Navy What is not in doubt is that the British Royal Navy was the largest navy between 1939 and either late-1943 or early-1944 when it was overtaken by the massive US shipbuilding programme. Therefore it is clear who the two biggest navies belonged to. One analysis I have read suggests that, at the point that they entered the war, the size of the various national fleets was British 328, French 174, and German 103. When Italy joined the war, she had 261 vessels, and when the Soviets joined they had 272 (although most of these were relatively small craft). At the outbreak of the war in the Pacific, the Japanese had 238 and the USA 345 (but, by this point, the British had 363). According to the same analysis, at the end of the war, the USA had 803 significant vessels, Britain 518, the Soviets 227, the Germans 202, the Italians 77, and the Japanese 91. Then there were the Canadians who ended the war with 270 ocean-going warships, making them either the third or fourth largest navy depending on your definition. Therefore, assuming that we take the war to have started in 1939, the Royal Navy was the most powerful navy for the first 73% of the war and the US Navy for the latter 27%. The Japanese Navy was the third most powerful in terms of surface warships (including carriers) but the Germans specialised in submarines before being resoundingly defeated by mid-1943. However, in terms of the potential to do real damage to the Allied war effort, I believe that the Germans were a significantly greater threat than the Japanese. By the end of the war, the order of play was the USA, followed by Britain, followed by Canada and the Soviet Union.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were all airplanes used in World War I designed with two seats, one for each pilot?
Answer: If an aeroplane has two pilots it would be only polite to provide two seats, otherwise one of the pilots would have to stand up for the entire flight, which would be tiresome. In any case, I am not sure that any WW1 aircraft carried a co-pilot. Some of the late-war multi-engine heavy bombers such as the Vickers Vimy, Handley Page Type O/400, or Gotha G.V. may have carried a co-pilot (second pilot) and there is a reference to a Handley Page Type O/400 crashing and killing both the pilot and co-pilot whilst transporting T.E. Lawrence in 1919. Handley Page Type O/400 Many smaller aircraft had two crew members but these were always a pilot and an observer/gunner seated in tandem rather than two pilots. These tended to be called two-seaters and so, regardless of size, I’m pretty sure that all aircraft provided a seat of some kind for every crew member that they carried. Bristol f.2 two-seater

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is the 1917 mutiny at etaples during WW1 not widely taught in UK schools whereas the French military mutiny during WWI is taught?
Answer: Because the aren’t comparable in any meaningful way. The Étaples mutiny occurred out of the line at the Base Depot at Étaples and resulted from the unnecessarily harsh regime in the camp. It lasted for four days and was more of a riot than a mutiny. One man, William Wood, was shot by a military policeman during the rioting and one, Jesse Short, was tried for Mutinous Conduct and executed by firing squad. Three men received prison sentences of ten years and another forty-three received field punishment or short prison sentences. British soldiers training at Étaples The French Army mutinies of 1917 were a different kettle of fish altogether. They involved forty-nine divisions to one extent or another, nearly half of the French divisions on the Western Front, and lasted for six weeks with the men involved refusing all orders to attack and 27,000 men deserting. As a result, 629 mutineers were sentenced to death. Most of these sentences were commuted, but forty-nine men were executed by firing-squad.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Napoleon receive any formal training or mentorship from other generals before becoming one himself? Or did he rely solely on his own experience on the battlefield?
Answer: Napoleon’s formal military education started at the age of nine and consisted of five years at the military preparatory school at Brienne-le-Château (May 1779 to Oct 1784) followed by a year at the École Militaire in Paris (1784-1785). Napoleon was also a great reader and studied the historical campaigns of Alexander, Caesar and Frederick the Great amongst others. He was also greatly influenced by the works of Jean-Pierre du Teil, an artillery officer and theorist executed during the Revolution. On graduating from the École Militaire (where he was examined by Pierre Laplace) he became a Second Lieutenant of Artillery in the Régiment de La Fére and spent the next few years learning his trade as a junior officer or spending long periods of leave in Corsica. However, as far as receiving specific mentoring from generals, which is not something a junior officer normally receives, Napoleon served as a Captain under Generals La Poype, Carteaux and Dugommier at the Siege of Toulon in 1793. Following his outstanding performance at the siege, he was promoted directly from Captain to Brigadier General, slipping the rank of Colonel which is where one might normally expect to receive some mentoring. Napoleon as a student at Brienne

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the purpose of the British air raids on Dresden and how many were there?
Answer: Another Dresden question. There was one RAF raid, in two waves, on the 13th of February 1945 and two USSAF raids on the 14th and 15th of February. There had previously been two other, smaller, USAAF raids on the 7th of October 1944 and the 16th of January 1945 and there were three more follow-up USAAF raids, two on the 2nd of March and one on the 17th of April 1945. The total for all of these raids is that 772 RAF aircraft dropped 2,659 tons of bombs on Dresden whilst 1,676 USAAF aircraft dropped 4,441 tons. Therefore, clearly, the relevant question is not what the purpose of the British raid was, but, rather, what the purpose of the Allied raids were. In the main raids that took place between the 13th and the 15th of February 1945, the Allies had intended to drop some 2,157 tons of High Explosive (HE) and 1,570 tons of incendiaries on the city. However, the actual figures are slightly different. Firstly, 115 B-17s in the first USAAF raid (27% of the force) got lost and dropped approximately 168 tons of HE and 112 tons of incendiaries on Prague, Brüx and Pilsen in error. Secondly, the USAAF’s second raid had a primary target of Leipzig, but the town was obscured by clouds and so the raid diverted to Dresden, it’s alternative target. As a result, in the event, the Allies dropped some 2,431 tons of HE and 1,476 tons of incendiaries on Dresden; 3,907 tons in total in the raids of the 13th, 14th and 15th of February. It’s worth noting, as an aside, that the 431 USAAF aircraft that were intended to bomb Dresden on the 14th were just a part (around 21%) of the 2,100 bombers from the 8th Air Force active over Germany that day. Now, as to the purpose of the raids. There is controversy over two points. The first is that Dresden was a city of great cultural importance but of no military significance, and the second is regarding the number of deaths that resulted from the bombings. To deal with the second point first. Both the city authorities at the time (Rossberg, 1945) and a more recent analysis (The Historikerkommission, 2008) suggest that between 18,500 and 25,000 people died in Dresden. This is, of course, a tragic number, but WW2 abounds with tragic numbers, and the number of dead in the Dresden raids is less than the number of British civilians that were killed in the London Blitz. Which is London and which is Dresden? Sadly, there are still some people out there (usually with an axe of some kind to grind) who are taken in by Goebbels’ original, massively inflated, Nazi propaganda claim of 200,000 deaths. A claim that was later publicised by the USSR for its own purposes. It’s not correct. As to Dresden’s cultural importance, that’s largely irrelevant. London had great cultural importance too, but that didn’t stop the Luftwaffe bombing it on fifty-seven consecutive nights during the Blitz. Therefore, the remaining issue is whether the city was a legitimate military target. People have been arguing the toss about this since the war and so I’ll only provide some facts. Dresden was Germany’s seventh largest city (next to Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Cologne, Leipzig and Essen) and when compared with those cities, it actually experienced the smallest tonnage of bombs dropped per thousand population. Dresden was not, as is sometimes claimed, undefended although its defences were not as strong as the more heavily bombed cities. Relative bombing density per thousand population It was described by the Germans themselves as one of the foremost industrial locations of the Reich and the German authorities reported that over 200 factories were destroyed or damaged during the raids, 127 of which were supplying war materials to the Wehrmacht. The city was a major communications hub, the junction of three key routes: Berlin-Prague-Vienna, Munich-Breslau, and Hamburg-Leipzig-Prague. The Russians had asked the Western Allies if they could aid the Russian offensive by hampering the transport of German reinforcements to the East. The cities specifically mentioned were Berlin and Leipzig, but it doesn’t take much imagination to see how Dresden fits naturally into the pattern, being on both a major North-South route and the West-East route supplying the German counter-attacks around Breslau. Military position in February 1945 To my mind there are too many who use hindsight to declare that the war was effectively over in February 1945 and that the Germans were incapable of resistance. This is nonsense. It certainly didn’t appear that way to the Allies at the time and, in fact, hundreds of thousands were yet to die in the fighting in 1945.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: On WW2 B-17 equipped with H2X or Mickey radar for bombing in restricted visibility, how did the crew differ from a “standard” B-17 crew, and if extra crew members needed, what did the extra crew do?
Answer: H2X, also sometimes known as the Mickey or BTO (Bombing through overcast) set, was a derivative of the British H2S ground scanning radar. The advantage of H2S/H2X is that it allowed precision attacks to be carried out when outside the range of the standard, ground based, navigational aids such as Gee and Oboe and when the target was obscured by smoke or the weather - which it often was in the European Theatre. As such H2S/H2X was both a bombing and a navigational radar. There was a difference in usage between the RAF and the USAAF. The RAF eventually equipped most of their bombers with H2S whilst the USAAF tended to equip only pathfinder aircraft with the H2X. This reflects the difference in doctrine where the RAF bombers flew independently in a stream and therefore navigated individually whilst the USAAF bombers flew as part of a formation (box) and could, therefore, follow a navigation leader. H2S installation in a Lancaster, installed between the radio and navigation positions USAAF H2X installation in the navigator’s position of a B-17 In the RAF, because of the radar’s dual purpose, the navigator would assist the bomb aimer during the bomb run. Outside of the bomb run itself, when the bomb aimer was not manning the front turret he might also assist the navigator with general navigation tasks, including operating the H2S set to confirm landmarks for the navigator to check his position by. Therefore, in RAF usage, in the majority of aircraft no extra crew members were required to operate H2S. However, in some specialised roles, such as the Pathfinders, an extra Navigator/Radar Operator was carried. Nb. In the RAF the Pathfinders were specialised target marking squadrons belonging to No. 8 Group, the Pathfinder Force. In USAAF the term pathfinder applied to individual aircraft used to lead bomber formations. These individual aircraft were drawn from or trained by the 482nd Bombardment Group which specialised in this role. In the USAAF, a pathfinder aircraft normally carried a supplementary crew member, known as a Radar Navigator or Mickey Operator but, as the ball turret was eliminated to house the radar (except in some early conversions), the crew would presumably have remained at ten. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did Germany establish its Navy (Kriegsmarine) after World War I, considering they had no existing navy to rebuild from scratch like Britain did after World War II?
Answer: They did have an existing navy. The Reichsmarine, as it was called, was restricted by the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles (Article 181) to eight battleships (two in reserve), eight cruisers (two in reserve), sixteen destroyers (four in reserve) and twelve torpedo boats. No submarines were allowed (Article 191). Five of the battleships were Braunschweig-class pre-dreadnoughts, launched between 1902 and 1904, whilst the other three were Deutschland-class pre-dreadnoughts, launched between 1904 and 1906. Two of the cruisers were Bremen-class, built between 1905 and 1906, and the other six were Gazelle-class, built between 1900 and 1903. The destroyers were built between 1911 and 1913, and the torpedo boats between 1897 and 1902. Braunschweig The Versailles Treaty (Article 190) provided that Germany could replace ships when they reached twenty years of age, which happened between 1924 and 1928, but that the replacements could not displace more than 10,000 tons. Replacement cruisers were to be limited to 6,000 tons, destroyers to 800 tons and torpedo boats to 200 tons. As a general note, it is worth remembering that German torpedo boats were sometimes bigger than their destroyers. Between 1929 and 1932 the Germans laid down the Deutschland-class heavy cruisers Deutschland (later Lützow), Admiral Scheer, and Admiral Graf Spee which displaced 10,600 tons each. These three Panzerschiff or pocket-battleships replaced the old battleships Preussen, Lothringen, and Braunschweig. Deutschland The Germans started to build replacement cruisers, beginning with the Emden, which replaced the Niobe (1902), in 1925. The Emden was followed by the Königsberg (1927), Karlsruhe (1929), Köln (1930), Leipzig (1931), and Nürnberg (1935). Whilst the Emden was built within the Versailles limit, the later ships broke the 6,000 ton limit, becoming progressively heavier and ranging from 7,700 tons to 9,000 tons. German cruiser Niobe German cruiser Nürnberg In addition, the Germans were also starting to build the Type 1934-class destroyers, beginning with the Leberecht Maass in 1934 which displaced 2,250 tons, again breaking the Versailles limit of 800 tons. Most flagrantly of all, the Germans had commenced building U-boats in direct contravention of the treaty, with the first Type IIA U-boat, U-1, laid down in early 1935. When Hitler became Chancellor in 1933 he started to ignore the provisions of Versailles more openly and a British Foreign Office memo dated 1934 stated: Part V of the Treaty of Versailles... is, for practical purposes, dead, and it would become a putrefying corpse which, if left unburied, would soon poison the political atmosphere of Europe. Moreover, if there is to be a funeral, it is clearly better to arrange it while Hitler is still in a mood to pay the undertakers for their services. Recognising the de facto position, and in no mood to confront the Germans, the British tried to regularise and control the German building programme by concluding the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 which increased the allowed German tonnage to 35% of that of the Royal Navy. As a result the Germans immediately began building the 32,000 ton battleships Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, the Hipper-class cruisers and also began an extensive U-boat building programme. In the same year the Reichsmarine was renamed the Kriegsmarine. The rest, as they say, is history. The last of the Reichsmarine battleships to see active service was the Schleswig-Holstein. She fired what were probably the first shots of WW2 when she opened up on Polish positions in Danzig at 04:47 on the 1st of September, 1939. Schleswig-Holstein in the 1930s

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was General Montgomery considered for command of the Normandy landings instead of Eisenhower?
Answer: To be strictly accurate, General Montgomery did command the Normandy landings. During the landings, and until Eisenhower took over command of ground operations on 1st September 1944, Montgomery’s 21st Army Group had under command all ground elements, these being the 2nd British Army (Dempsey) and 1st US Army (Bradley). For the landings themselves, the ground element was commanded by Montgomery, the naval element by Ramsay (RN) and the air element by Leigh-Mallory (RAF). Montgomery reported to Eisenhower, who reported to the Combined Chiefs of Staff who, in turn, reported to Churchill and Roosevelt. As SCAEF (Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force) Eisenhower was in overall command of all Allied ground, air, and naval forces. The key players. Eisenhower with his deputy Tedder to his right and Montgomery to his left. On his right side are Ramsay and Bradley and on his left Leigh-Mallory and his Chief of Staff Bedell Smith. Missing is Bradley’s counterpart in 2nd Army, Dempsey Miles Dempsey At one point the leading candidates for SCAEF included both Marshall and Brooke, but they were deemed to be too important in the jobs that they were already doing, Marshall as Chief of Staff of the United States Army and Brooke as Chief of the Imperial General Staff. Both of them were the members of the Combined Chiefs of Staff who Eisenhower reported to. Other generals, including Montgomery, were probably considered for the role, but Montgomery didn’t have the diplomatic skills (to put it mildly) for the role. Eisenhower, on the other hand, had survived being assistant military adviser to the Philippine Government under MacArthur which provided him with valuable experience in the essential skill of handling challenging personalities.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was there ever a battleship that carried torpedoes?
Answer: Yes, there certainly were. Depending on what you choose to class as a battleship, the first one to carry torpedoes was probably HMS Devastation which was fitted with two 14″ torpedo launchers in 1879. HMS Devastation HMS Dreadnought, the progenitor of her eponymous class, commissioned in 1906, carried five 18″ submerged torpedo tubes, two on each broadside and one in the stern. Twenty-three torpedoes were carried for them. In addition six 14“ torpedoes were carried for her steam picket boats. HMS Dreadnought From that point, most battleships carried torpedoes. As far as I am aware, the last battleships to be fitted with torpedoes were the Andrea Doria (Italy) in 1916, the Baden (Germany) in 1917, the Mutsu (Japan) in 1921, the West Virginia (USA) in 1923, and the Rodney (Britain) in 1927. Tirpitz (Germany) was retrofitted with torpedoes in 1942. USS Florida (1911) in dry dock. Below the men working on the third stage is a 21″ torpedo port with its bar extended. The bar acted as a guide to prevent the torpedo being knocked off course by the force of water flowing down the ship’s side. An extended underwater torpedo tube on the German battleship Ostfriesland (1911) The Rodney carried two 24.5″ torpedo tubes, also the inspiration for the Japanese Type 93 Long Lance torpedo, and was the last battleship to fire a torpedo in anger when she launched six at the Bismarck on the 27th of May 1941. It is not known for certain whether there were any hits. HMS Rodney Obviously the torpedo was developed as a leveller, a way in which small, cheap ships - the first torpedo boat was HMS Lightning in 1876 - could take on and sink large, expensive ships. Although it seems counter-intuitive, battleships began to be armed with torpedoes almost at once. In the late 1800s engagement ranges were low and battleships were still being provided with rams The torpedo was seen as complimenting the ram in point blank engagements. The development of fuel injected torpedoes (heaters) in 1900 extended the range of the torpedo to several thousand yards and made it a much more potent weapon. This was an era where battleships were still expected to form a line of battle and steam on a parallel course with the enemy. Therefore the threat of the torpedo lay in the statistical chances of a hit in a well-spread launch. The British naval architect Sir Reginald Bacon calculated that for a typical line of dreadnoughts (say twenty four, the length at Jutland), that would amount to 4,800 yards of ships’ sides and 6,900 yards of empty space, which would yield a two-out-of-five chance of a hit. However, at Jutland only a few torpedoes were launched from capital ships as engagement ranges were already getting too large for torpedoes to be effective. The British battleships launched five and the battlecruisers eight, while the German battleships fired one, and their battlecruisers seven. There were no hits. However, carrying torpedoes also brought disadvantages and the battlecruiser Lutzow had her underwater torpedo flat opened to the sea by a 12″ shell which caused severe flooding and eventually sank her. In this photo of HMS Hood, you can see the armoured above water torpedo doors to the rear of the boat being lowered. Hood was having her tubes removed and the first two are blanking plates with the remaining tubes further aft. Apart from the danger of flooding, there was also the considerable danger posed by having multiple torpedoes, each with a warhead of 500 lbs of TNT, vulnerable to enemy fire. As a result of the opening of battleship engagement ranges and the subsequent reduction in the likelihood of obtaining a hit and the dangers of flooding and explosion, torpedoes were being removed from capital ships during refits from the 1930s onwards.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many German aircrafts were lost to RAF Spitfires and Hurricanes in the Battle of Britain?
Answer: It is always very interesting to me that even in such a relatively recent, not to mention exhaustively documented, war as WW2, you can often find considerable disagreement over matters of detail. This is partly a matter of definition. Are we discussing aircraft lost or aircraft lost or damaged? Are we discussing aircraft lost in combat or including aircraft lost in non-combat circumstances? Are we discussing only combat aircraft or all aircraft? What precise date range are we choosing to base our analysis on? Do the figures include the aircraft lost by the Corpo Aereo Italiano during their involvement with the battle? In addition, the question asks specifically about Spitfires and Hurricanes but German aircraft were also shot down by Blenheims and Defiants, and at least one He111 was intercepted by Gladiators of 247 Squadron without result. In addition, some German fighters were shot down by Wellington bombers during the battle - one documented case occurring on the night of 25/26th August 1940, when a Wellington from 99 Squadron shot down a German night fighter during a raid on Hanover. Hans Ring’s book, Die Luftschlacht über England 1940, published in 1980. suggests that the Germans lost 1,977 aircraft destroyed. Although I don’t have that book, the breakdown that I’ve seen on the web that is attributed to it is internally inconsistent. The He59 was a German float plane used for search and rescue. I have no idea what the He159 is supposed to be. The total adds up to 1,988 rather than the 1,977 stated, but this may be an error in the analysis. On the other hand, Hansard, the journal of the UK Parliament had the following to say on May the 14th, 1947: Mr. Keeling asked the Secretary of State for Air whether he will publish in the OFFICIAL REPORT a statement of the total number of enemy aircraft shot down during the Battle of Britain, according to contemporary R.A.F. estimates and German official records, respectively; and whether he will give the figures for the biggest days of the battle. The Secretary of State for Air (Philip Noel-Baker) Yes, Sir, I will circulate in the OFFICIAL REPORT the statement for which the hon. Member has asked showing the number of enemy aircraft which the R.A.F. claimed at the time to have been destroyed during the Battle of Britain, and the actual losses recorded by the German High Command. Between 10th July, when the action began, and 31st October, when the Germans broke it off, the R.A.F. estimated that 2,692 enemy aircraft had been destroyed. The German records show that, in fact, 2,376 of their aircraft had been put out of action; of these, 1,733 were destroyed and 643 were damaged. The figures I am circulating show that during the opening and concluding phases of the battle, while the numbers engaged were relatively small, and the fighting less continuous and intense, the losses actually inflicted on the enemy were higher than the numbers claimed by the R.A.F. When very large forces were in action, and when the battle raged without respite for many days, the estimates were well above the losses which the Luftwaffe sustained. Nb. I have reformatted the figures from Hansard slightly to make them more readable. Yes, I know that the totals don’t quite add up - they obviously didn’t have Excel in 1947. The 1980’s analysis is likely to be more accurate within its chosen parameters, so I would venture that somewhere in the region of 1,887 and 1,988 German aircraft were lost during the Battle of Britain depending on exactly what you count. Some 95% of them would have been shot down by Spitfires and Hurricanes.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: So what is this 'Black Rod' in UK Parliament as reportedly a 'bizarre scene'? What is at stake?
Answer: The Usher of the Black Rod, commonly known as Black Rod, is an official of the House of Lords whose symbol of office is an ebony (black) staff topped by a golden lion. Black Rod is simultaneously the Usher of the Black Rod, Serjeant-at-Arms in the House of Lords, and Secretary to the Lord Great Chamberlain. Sarah Clarke, Black Rod since 2018 The office originated as Usher of the Order of the Garter. Letters of Patent were issued in 1361 by King Edward III to create the Usher as a Court position involved in meeting with Parliament. By the sixteenth century, the role had evolved to become a position entirely associated with Parliament and, in essence, Black Rod became the monarch's representative in the House of Lords. Although Black Rod has other duties, the most well known is their official role in the State Opening of Parliament. This ceremony may seem silly or bizarre, but it makes a very important point in our system of government. In 1628, after disputes with the King, Charles I, Parliament passed the Petition of Right. This provided that no person should be forced to provide a gift, loan or tax without an Act of Parliament, that no individual should be imprisoned or detained without cause, and no soldiers should be billeted in private houses without the consent of the owner. Charles, forced into a corner by his need to raise money, accepted the petition with bad grace. He then promptly dissolved Parliament in 1629, starting eleven years of rule without a parliament. In 1640 Charles again needed money to fight the Bishops’ Wars against the Covenanters in Scotland and so he summoned Parliament, dismissed it again when it refused to provide funds and then, in desperation, summoned it again after the Battle of Newburn. Parliament promptly presented to the King the Grand Remonstrance, a list of two hundred and four grievances against Charles’ foreign, financial, legal and religious policies - although carefully not couched as an accusation against the King himself but against his ministers and a supposed Catholic conspiracy. This was too much and, in January 1641, Charles sought to arrest five Members of Parliament he believed to be the ringleaders: John Hampden, Arthur Haselrig, Denzil Holles, John Pym, and William Strode. Arriving at the Commons with around eighty armed troops, Charles entered the chamber without soldiers and called for the members by name. Pre-warned, the five members had fled by river to the City of London and when Charles asked the Speaker of the House of Commons, William Lenthall, where they were, he famously, and rather bravely, replied: May it please your majesty, I have neither eyes to see nor tongue to speak in this place but as this House is pleased to direct me whose servant I am here; and I humbly beg your majesty's pardon that I cannot give any other answer than this to what your majesty is pleased to demand of me. It may not seem much, but this was the first time that a Speaker had declared his allegiance to parliament rather than the monarch and it was a critical step in defining the changing relationship between the two and the independence of Parliament. It was also one of several events that led to the English Civil War and Charles’ eventual trial by Parliament and execution. At the State Opening of Parliament, after the King has been seated on the throne in the House of Lords, Black Rod is despatched to the Commons to summon MPs to hear the King’s Speech (which is, in fact, written by the Prime Minister and outlines the government’s policy). When Black Rod arrives at the Commons Chamber, the door is slammed in his or her face and Black Rod then has to bang on it three times to ask for admission. Black Rod summons the Commons In 1641, the custom, as noted in the House of Commons Journal, was ignored: Mr Maxwell, coming to the House, with a Message, without his Black Rod; and coming in, before he was called in: Exception was taken to both. The tradition has been continued as a way to symbolise the Commons' independence from both the Monarch and from the Lords. After knocking, Black Rod is admitted to the Commons chamber and requests the Members' attendance. The Members of Parliament then pair up and, led by the Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition, follow – in a deliberately boisterous way to signal their independence – Black Rod to the bar of the House of Lords to hear the King's Speech. Dennis Skinner (aka the Beast of Bolsover) now retired but an MP for that constituency for forty-nine years was known for his heckling of Black Rod when he arrived at the Commons Chamber, most famously: Ey up, here comes Puss in Boots and Get your skates on, first race is half-past two. That latter in reference to the fact that the speech had been rescheduled and the Queen had missed a morning’s racing at Ascot. If you want to watch the ceremony, Black Rod’s participation starts at 3:30. If you can’t see the video you can search for Queen's Speech : Black Rod heads to Commons to summon MPs.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you name the battleships that were involved in D-Day? How many of them survived the battle?
Answer: Seven battleships and two monitors were involved in the D-Day landings (Operation Neptune) and all of them survived the operation. The naval part of Operation Neptune was divided into two task forces, East and West and each of these was divided into assault groups, one for each of the five beaches, and bombardment groups. The Western Task Force bombardment group, covering the US beaches, included Arkansas (BB-33) and Texas (BB-35) supporting Omaha and Nevada (BB-36) supporting Utah whilst the Eastern Task Force bombardment group, covering the British and Canadian beaches, included Warspite and Ramilles and the 15″ monitors Roberts and Erebus with Rodney, and Nelson in local reserve. It also appears that Malaya was also held in reserve for the landings although not present on D-Day. The battleships were tasked to neutralise the German heavy batteries that could have engaged the assault forces. As many of these were in heavy fortifications, planners concluded that large-calibre naval fire was essential to suppress these positions. The most threatening German batteries, near Le Havre, were suppressed to the extent that the planned commando raid to capture them, landing on Band, D-Day’s forgotten sixth beach, was called off as unnecessary. The secondary role of the battleships was to break up German counter-attacks. German war diaries stress the devastating effect of battleship gunnery. The 16-inch guns of Nelson and Rodney engaged targets at a range of up to 19 miles, well to the south of Caen. Rommel himself reported on the impact of battleship fire: ‘The effect is so immense that no operation of any kind is possible in the area commanded by this rapid-fire artillery, either by infantry or tanks.’ HMS Warspite Warspite, for instance, fired three hundred 15″ shells in forty-eight hours and completely wore out her guns. On the journey to Rosyth to have them replaced she hit a mine on the 13th of June but only suffered relatively minor damage. Not until 23 July, D+46, did the front in Normandy finally move beyond the range of the battleships. The monitor HMS Roberts Although none of the battleships suffered any significant damage, Nelson was badly damaged after detonating two acoustic two mines on the 18th of June. and was sent to the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard for repairs not returning to the UK until January 1945. Apparently the Texas voluntarily flooded her torpedo blisters on one side in order to cause the ship to list so that her guns could reach a greater than designed elevation and thus hit targets further inland.
