Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you describe the experience of fighting in the hedgerows of Normandy? What materials were they made of and how large were they? Were there any instances of soldiers getting lost inside them?
Answer: Extremely dangerous for all concerned. The problem with bocage is that it is not simply a hedgerow, it is a hedgerow on top of a four to eight foot bank. The bocage is a network of small fields surrounded by these huge hedgerows and sunken lanes and an ideal place for infantry to dig in and create defensive positions. Typical bocage Lane through the bocage - not ideal tank country As well as being a severe problem for infantry, any tanks climbing the banks and bursting through the hedgerows were exposing their lightly armoured undersides and were easy meat for Panzerfausts. You can see the general effect illustrated here with Churchills of the Scots Guards. The eventual solution to fighting in the bocage was mixed infantry, engineer and tank teams supporting each other and working very methodically to break the German defences field by field. This process could include the use of various ad-hoc solutions such as the famous Culin hedgerow cutter and Rhino tanks to break through the banks without exposing the tank’s underside.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the naming convention for battles like Trafalgar, Waterloo, and Zenta? Why are they not simply named after their year or location?
Answer: They are named after their location, and possibly their year, although there is sometimes some disagreement. Waterloo is named after the village of Waterloo where Wellington had his headquarters and from where he wrote his dispatch. The French called the same battle the Battle of Mont St-Jean, which is perhaps slightly more logical as that village was immediately to the rear of the Anglo-Allied line and Waterloo was some little distance away. The Prussians knew the battle as the La Belle Alliance, which is where Napoleon had his headquarters. Waterloo Having two different names is not uncommon. In the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 the Germans call the main battle Sadowa, whilst the Austrians call it the Königgrätz. In the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, the engagement that the Germans call Gravelotte is known to the French as St. Privat. Likewise, in the ACW, what Northerners call First Bull Run is known by Southerners as First Manassas, etc. Trafalgar is named after Cape Trafalgar, one of the nearby prominent landmarks on the Spanish coast and immediately to the east of where the battle took place - although it could perhaps equally well be called the Battle of Cape Roche. Naval battles are normally named after some nearby bit of land but, when they are too far away from any land, may be given other names such as the Glorious First of June which was fought in 1794 some four hundred miles west of Ushant. The French called that one Combat de Prairial as it occurred during Prarial, the ninth month of the French Republican Calendar. Trafalgar Likewise Zenta, or Senta, was fought between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans close to the town on Zenta on the River Tisza in Hungary. Zenta Where there is scope for confusion a battle will also normally be associated with a date (different conflcts) or a number (same conflict) to make it clear what battle is being discussed. Thus we have the naval battles of the Dogger Bank in 1696, 1781, 1904 (Dogger Bank Incident), 1915, and 1916 and the First, Second, Third (Passchendaele), Fourth (Lys), and Fifth Battles of Ypres during WW1. As far as I know, the record is held by the twelve battles of the the Isonzo between the Italians and the Austro-Hungarians, also during WW1 - the Twelfth Battle of the Isonzo alternatively being known as Caporetto. The Isonzo is a river and, being a linear feature, the actual battlefields were not all in the same place. Whilst battles tend to be named geographically, people have really let their imaginations run riot when naming wars: the War of the Bucket, the Pastry War, the War of the Stray Dog, the War of the Golden Stool, all of which is an excuse for me to mention my personal favourite, the War of Jenkins’ Ear (1739–1748) fought between the British and the Spanish Empires. [The Spanish Captain] took hold of his [Robert Jenkins’] left Ear, and with his Cutlass slit it down; and then another of the Spaniards took hold of it and tore it off, but gave him the Piece of his Ear again, bidding him carry it to his Majesty King George. The War of Jenkins’ Ear

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the difference between a "Dame," "Earl," and "Baron" in British peerages?
Answer: After the Royal Family, the ranks of British nobility, in order of precedence, are Duke, Marquess, Earl, Viscount, and Baron. All life peers are barons, but not all barons are life peers - some being hereditary. All Earls, on the other hand are hereditary - the last non-royal Earl created being Harold Macmillan (an ex-Prime Minister) who was created Earl of Stockton in 1984. Ignoring royal and courtesy titles, there are 814 hereditary peers, 191 of them being Earls together with four Countesses in their own right (the female equivalent of an earl being a countess) and 426 of them being barons together with nine baronesses. There are also 667 life peers (all barons or baronesses) as of May 2023. Of the hereditary peers, 92 still sit in the House of Lords, along with the life peers. House of Lords for the State Opening of Parliament and on a normal business day Apart from the ninety-two hereditary peers (elected to represent their fellows) and the twenty-six odd bishops, the rest of the current 785 members of of the House of Lords are life peers, appointed by the Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister after vetting by the independent House of Lords Appointments Commission. They may be appointed to the Lords either for political services or for services to society in general. Before Canute (c. 994-1035) an ealdorman administered a shire for the king. Under Canute the Danish equivalent of earl was introduced, and under the Norman kings the title became hereditary, although the earls eventually lost some of their responsibilities as the king’s representatives in the shire to the sheriff. From the reign of Richard II (1377-99) earldoms were either life creations or hereditary with ‘remainder to heirs male’ (the inheritance of the title was restricted to direct male heirs of the original title-holder) although some Scottish earldoms may be inherited by a woman or pass through the female line. Both Earls and Barons are formally addressed as My Lord or My Lady - you have to be a Duke to be addressed as Your Grace. So apart from the fact that an earl’s coronet has eight strawberry leaves and eight pearls as opposed to a baron’s six pearls, there is not that much difference between them. A Dame on the other hand is the title given to a woman with the rank of Knight Commander or holder of the Grand Cross in the Orders of Chivalry. In this sense it is the female equivalent of a Knight. Dames and Knights are not peers and the rank is not normally hereditary unless the person is created a Baronet (which is not the same as a Baron) or Baronetess where a Baronetess is also styled Dame. To avoid confusion, the wives of Knights who used to be styled Dame are now styled Lady. Confusing ain’t it…

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Napoleon actually invade England or just threaten to do so? If he had invaded, would he have been successful in conquering Britain?
Answer: In February 1797, during the War of the First Coalition, a French raid consisting of around 1,400 men was mounted against Bristol but, due to bad weather, ended up in Fishguard in Wales where it unceremoniously surrendered to a some militia, sailors, and a group of Welsh women. Jemima Nicholas led a band of women on to Strumble Head to confront the invaders, capturing 12 of them and locking them up in a local church This is held to be the last invasion of the mainland of Great Britain and Napoleon was not involved in any way, being busy winning battles as a General in Italy at this time. From October 1797 to April 1798 Napoleon was notionally commander of the Armée d'Angleterre but no invasion was attempted a the army was repurposed in January 1800. A new army known as the Armée d'Angleterre or the Armée des côtes de l'Océan was formed in 1803 and concentrated near Boulogne, but this army too was repurposed in August 1805 after the French failed to win control over the English Channel after the Battle of Cape Finisterre in July 1805. Fanciful plans for invading England Therefore, despite his best endeavours, Napoleon never managed to launch an invasion of England because his naval commanders never managed to gain the upper hand over the Royal Navy. As Lord St. Vincent is reputed to have said: I do not say the French cannot come, my Lords, I only say they cannot come by sea. As far as answering what would have happened if he had invaded then the question must be invaded with what? Landing a few men would have been easy enough, landing hundreds of horses and heavy artillery is a different matter and it would have taken a significant amount of time - weeks probably - to get an army ashore and sorted out. The French army during the Waterloo campaign had around 130,000 men and 47,000 horses, one horse for every three men. The army that Napoleon gathered at Boulogne had 200,000 men and would probably have required more than 70,000 horses, plus guns, limbers, wagons, and all the other impedimenta of war. The French would have been required to perform an amphibious landing, an operation that they were utterly unfamiliar with - in the face of a probably determined opposition. In addition, Britain had mustered some 600,000 men in 1803 to oppose 200,000 Frenchmen who were without many strategic options. The average quality of the French soldiers and their leadership was probably better, but the French would have (like Hitler’s Sealion but to a lesser extent) been beset by logistics problems - even if trying to live off the land. In a scenario where the French have a temporary window to invade - Royal Navy blockade hampered by storms for instance - then a minor landing might have been possible but not a full scale invasion. This effort would have been doomed to failure. If the Royal Navy were somehow unable to intervene, then the French have a fighting chance if they can establish a working bridgehead before the British can concentrate their forces, but I would say that the odds are still 50:50 or less.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the U.S. Army have any special operations units similar to German or British commandos before World War II, such as the Office of Strategic Services (OSS)?
Answer: I don’t think that any of the three nations really had special operations units before WW2. The British retained one battalion of the Lovat Scouts between the wars, but the British Commandos (originally the Independent Companies) weren’t formed until 1940 and SAS not until July 1941. These were part of an explosion of British special forces units during the war: SAS, SBS, LRDG, COPP, the Libyan Arab Force Commando (LAFC), No.1 Demolition Company (Popski’s Private Army), the Small Scale Raiding Force (SSRF), SOE, etc., etc. The German Brandenburgers were formed in December 1939 and SS-Jäger-Bataillon 502 (Skorzeny) in 1943 although there was a small Marinestosstruppkompanie formed in 1938. The USMC Marine Raiders were formed in February 1941 and the U.S. Army Rangers in July 1942. Rangers near Pointe-du-Hoc, June 6th 1944 Marine Raiders, Bougainville, January 1944 SOE/OSS Jedburgh team before parachuting into occupied Europe, 1944 It is worth noting that the Commandos were not really fulfilling the same role as the SOE/OSS as the commandos were direct action amphibious forces while SOE/OSS were focussed on covert espionage and sabotage. The OSS (Office of Strategic Services) was formed in June 1942 and was based on the British SOE (Special Operation Executive), itself formed in July 1940.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were civilians involved in any way during the Battle of Britain?
Answer: The Battle of Britain is generally held to have taken place between the 10th of July and the 31st of October 1940 which means that it overlapped slightly with the Blitz which started in September 1940. During the Battle of Britain, Luftwaffe bombers targeted aerodromes and radar stations, ports, industrial complexes, especially those involved in aircraft production, transport Infrastructure and urban areas. Approximately 23,000 British civilians were killed, the first of the 70,000 civilians deaths in the UK during WW2, and around 32,000 were injured during the battle. The first civilian deaths that I am aware of (excluding merchant seamen) were on the 1st of August when six died and fifty-four were injured after the Luftwaffe attacked Norwich, bombing and machine gunning the train station. By the 7th of August the Luftwaffe had bombed Norfolk, Hampshire, Kent, Glamorgan, Denbighshire, Fife, Northumberland, Yorkshire, Lancashire, Gloucestershire, Buckinghamshire, Dorset, Somerset, Devon, Cornwall, and Lanarkshire - quite an eclectic selection of targets. August 24th 1940 was Ramsgate's worst day of the war. Described at the time as "the world's worst assault from the air", Ramsgate received more than 500 bombs from a squadron of German aircraft approaching Manston, and 1,200 houses were destroyed or damaged. Allegedly the leading aircraft as shot down over the harbour and in vengeance the Germans decided to release their bombs over Ramsgate. Remarkably only 29 civilians and 2 soldiers were killed, Aftermath of the raid on Ramsgate

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is Gold “Au” and Silver “Ag” while other elements are named after their names?
Answer: Elements named after the turn of the 19th Century have symbols (abbreviations) that reflect their names (e.g. Cf for Californium) but some elements, named prior to 1810 have symbols that do not match their (English) names, the most recent being Potassium (K) named in 1807. There are eleven symbols that don’t match the element’s modern name. Those are subtle reminders of the history of alchemy and chemistry and the process of the discovery of elements over the millennia. Eight of these elements were recognized by the ancient Greeks and Romans, and the abbreviations for those are based on a Latin or Greek term for the element. Therefore, gold is Au (aurum in Latin), silver is Ag (argentum in Latin), copper is Cu (cuprum in Latin), iron is Fe (ferrum in Latin), tin is Sn (stannum in Latin), lead is Pb (plumbum in Latin), antomony is Sb (stibium in Latin), and mercury is Hg (hydrargyrum in Greek). Roman gold and silver coins Tin (Sn) is interesting because the Romans called it plumbum candidum, or white lead and stannum meant an alloy of silver and lead - coming to mean tin in the fourth century. In French, tin is étain, in Spanish estaño, in Italian stagno, in Irish stán and in English the old name is remembered in the Stannary towns such as Truro and Tavistock where tin smelted in the area was assessed and coined. Potassium (K) was identified during the Middle Ages, but was named by Humphrey Davy who first isolated the pure element, K stands for kalium, a medieval Latin term for potash (from the root word alkali, which in turn comes from Arabic al-qalyah or plant ashes), tungsten is W because it was first identified in 1780 within the mineral known as wolframite by French scientist Antoine Lavoisier, and sodium is Na because it was first isolated by Humphry Davy (again) in 1807 and he was referring to natron, an Arabic word for the salt used by the Egyptians to mummify people. In fact, Davy is isolated, by using electrolysis, many elements for the first time: potassium (K) and sodium (Na) in 1807, and calcium (Ca), strontium (Sr), barium (Ba), and magnesium (Mg) in 1808 but, in these latter cases he followed the more modern naming convention.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What does "the high ground" mean in military context, as seen in Star Wars?
Answer: The question references the duel between Obi-Wan Kenobi and Anakin Skywalker in Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith. Holding the high ground can be referred to in either a moral or a military context, but they both have the same meaning and root. Sun Tzu’s The Art of War, which discusses military strategy in Ancient China and was written in the 5th century BC, discusses how the high ground is an advantage in battle. Being higher than your enemy means your enemy must fight against both you and gravity. On accessible terrain, He who occupies high Yang ground And ensures his line of supplies Will fight to advantage. On precipitous terrain, If we occupy it first, We should hold the Yang heights and wait for the enemy. If the enemy occupies it first, do not go after him, But entice him out by retreating. Holding the high ground is tactically advantageous in a military context because the holder has superior observation and can therefore observe the enemy’s positions and movements and react accordingly whilst concealing their own movements, thus putting the enemy at a disadvantage. In addition, in the days before vehicles, attacking uphill on foot or horseback was considerably more strenuous than attacking downhill or on the flat. Attacking troops arrive at the top exhausted and then have to face a fresh enemy. Also, in the days before gunpowder, gravity gives the uphill troops a longer range than those attacking them and more impetus if they choose to charge downhill. Holding the high ground is likely to confer a important additional morale advantage because of these factors. Always seek to hold the high ground! Gurkhas hold the hight ground in WW2

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: I realize some of the Allied forces that invaded North Africa in WWII came from Europe, but wasn’t the bulk of the force launched from the US East Coast? How did the Allies handle logistics?
Answer: The invasion of French North Africa, Operation Torch, consisted of three task forces. Whilst, the Western Task Force (35,000 men) came directly from the United States, the Central Task Force (39,000 men) and Eastern Task Force (33,000 men) both departed from the United Kingdom. Therefore, a little under a third of the men involved in Torch, those of the Western Task Force targeting Casablanca in Morocco, came directly from the United States. Ships of the Western Task Force heading for Morocco The Western Task Force sailed mainly from Norfolk, Virginia, on the 24th of October 1942, in a convoy (Task Force 34/UGF 1) of 102 troop transports, cargo ships, tankers, and escorts, including the US carrier Ranger, three battleships (Texas, New York, and Massachusetts), four escort carriers, seven cruisers and thirty-eight destroyers, in addition to troop and cargo transports and auxiliaries, under Rear Admiral Henry Kent Hewitt on the cruiser Augusta. USS Barnett (APA-5) an Attack Transport, note the landing craft carried on her sides The logistics for the invasion itself were self-contained with cargo ships and tankers included in the invasion force. Following the initial invasion the troops were supplied by the UGF (United States to Gibraltar Fast) and UGS (United States to Gibraltar Slow) starting with UGF 2 on the 6th of November 1942 and ending on the 28th of May 1945. There were twenty-six UGF convoys totalling 382 ships and one hundred slow convoys totalling 5,800 ships. Some twenty-five of these ships were lost to U-boats, aircraft or mines. One of the early UG convoys in November 1942

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In WW2 if an American Army Airforce wing was made up of groups and a Royal Airforce group was made up of wings was there an historical reason for the difference?
Answer: I don’t believe that there is any significant meaning to the differences in terminology. Air forces, Commands, Divisions, Brigades, Groups, and Wings were just intermediate levels of organising, commanding, controlling, and administering groups of squadrons. In 1912 the RFC was divided into an Military (Army) wing, previously the Air Battalion of the Royal Engineers, and a Naval wing. I think that the term wing was taken from the existing terminology for a sub-division of a military force, rather than being a reference to the aerial nature of the organisation. Expansion during WW1 meant that wings became groupings of squadrons that were in turn grouped into geographically based Brigades. When the RAF was created in 1918, Brigades became Groups. During WW1, American squadrons were grouped into pursuit or bombardment groups. Wings were then introduced just before WW2 in order to control the larger numbers of squadrons envisaged. The inversion of Group and Wing in the two air forces is simply historical happenstance and of no relevance.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Germany really destroy 30% of the world's merchant ships during the First World War?
Answer: No, but pretty close. A commonly quoted figure is that 12 out of 46 million tons of shipping was sunk during the war or about 26%. However, that eye-opening figure is for all the tonnage sunk - including German tonnage and may be a slight over-exaggeration. Comparing the Lloyd's Register of Shipping for 1919-1920 with that for 1914–1915 gives some interesting insights relating to vessels of one hundred gross tons or over. The changes, the result of the war, show a greatly lessened rate of growth for the world's mercantile tonnage as a whole, a marked deterioration in the vessels operating on the high seas, and a significant redistribution of the world's shipping. The war seriously reduced the tonnage of some countries and reduced the rate of growth of most others. The wastage, however, gave a powerful impetus to the development of the mercantile marine of the United States, which rose within a few years from a position of relative insignificance in the building and operation of vessels engaged in international commerce to one of commanding importance. In 1914, total steam tonnage was 45.4 million tons, with 20.5 million tons belonging to the British Empire and 2.0 million tons to the USA. By 1919 total steam tonnage of 47.9 million tons. Of this total, 18.2 million tons belonged to the British Empire and 9.8 million tons to the USA (this latter excluding the Great Lakes). There were also still around 3 million tons of sailing vessels in 1919 but these are excluded from this comparison. The net changes were a reduction of 11.2% in British Empire flagged ships, and a reduction of 13.5% in specifically British flagged ships. Austro-Hungary lost 32.2% and Germany 36.8% of their merchant tonnage, whilst Japan increased her merchant tonnage by 36.1% and the USA by a massive 382.1%. Therefore, whilst in 1914 Britain owned 41.6% of the world’s merchant tonnage, by 1919 this figure had reduced to 39.1%. In the same period the US share had increased from 4.5% to 20.4%. The total losses from belligerent action and marine risk, according to the Admiralty, amounted to 9,031,828 gross tons from the beginning of the war to October 1918. Over two thirds of this tonnage loss was the result of submarine activities. New construction in the United Kingdom during the same period was 4,342,295 tons, purchases from abroad were 530,000 tons, and enemy vessels captured amounted to 716,520 tons. SM U-35 attacking an allied merchant ship SM U-35 SM U-35, a German Type U 31 submarine, operated in the Mediterranean during WW1 and was the most successful U-boat participating in the war, sinking 220 merchant ships for a total of 505,121 tons of shipping.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were matchlock muskets used in the English War of the Roses?
Answer: Probably not in the proper sense of the term. Since 2010, we have known that there were handgonnes present at some of the battles of the War of the Roses because remains of them have been found at the site of the Battle of Towton which was fought on the 29th of March, 1461. This find indicates that guns were not just used at sieges in this period but were also used in open field battles. The Battle of Towton is important because it is reputed to be among the bloodiest in English history with an estimated 28,000 men killed or roughly one per cent of the entire English population at the time. The battle didn’t end happily for the gunner, because the gun exploded in his hands when it was fired. In fact, fragments of two gun barrels have been found - made of two different alloys of bronze - and chemical analysis has shown the component elements of gunpowder. A fragment of the oldest hand-held gun barrel found in Europe. These early handguns may have been operated by a two man team and were fired by the application of a slow match. The matchlock was a development where a trigger mechanism releases a spring-loaded serpentine holding the match. When the trigger is pulled, the serpentine swings down, igniting the priming powder in the flash pan and firing the weapon. This innovation marked a significant advancement in firearms technology by making the weapon far easier for one man to use. Early German matchlock The guns found at Towton probably weren’t arquebuses - matchlocks - because these weapons are not recorded in Europe (Germany) until the 1470s and the Wars of the Roses took place between 1455 and 1487. Therefore I think that it is not very likely that matchlocks were used during the Wars of the Roses, but it is, tantalisingly, just possible. Perhaps some future find of the remains of a serpentine will resolve the question once and for all.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Which European country had the largest colonial empire and was more powerful in terms of military and economic resources, Britain or France?
Answer: That would depend on when you were making the comparison. If we assume the second imperial age, around the turn of the 20th Century, then the British Empire had around 412 million people or about 23% of the world population, and covered around 14 million square miles or about 24% of the world's land area. France’s empire at this point was the third largest in the world and had about 55 million people, and covered around 4.3 million square miles. The second largest would have been Russia with about 175 million people and covering around 9 million square miles - but Russia’s empire was obviously not a maritime one like those of Britain and France. Therefore in terms of both population and area, Britain’s empire was considerably larger than that of France. Scope of the British and French colonial empires c. 1920 In terms of economics, the British Empire’s share of world trade was around 25–30% in 1900, its merchant fleet accounted for around 60% of total global tonnage, and it controlled around 40% of the world’s banking industry. Although already declining by the turn of the century, Britain was still the world’s leading economy, chased by Germany and the United States, with France probably taking fourth place. However, in terms of military resources the picture is a little different. The Naval Defence Act of 1889 adopted the two-power standard and, broadly speaking, required the Royal Navy to maintain a number of battleships equal to the next two largest navies - in this case France and Russia. Therefore, in naval terms, Britain had by far the world’s largest navy - a position it held until late 1943. However, in terms of land forces, the British Empire probably had in the region of 500,000 men, whilst the French Army possibly had up to 700,000. Moreover, in Europe itself, the British probably had around 100,000 men, whilst the French had possibly 500–600,000. All of these figures are subject to considerable variation depending on exactly when you try and make the comparison and exactly what you count. However, I think that they give a decent approximation of the relative sizes of the two empires at the turn of the 20th Century.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you explain the role of a sailing master?
Answer: This is a topic that seems to arouse an unusual degree of interest in Quorans. A sailing master, or simply Master, was the senior Warrant Officer on a Royal Navy ship. The easiest way of looking at it is that whilst the Captain, assisted by his Lieutenants, was responsible for determining where the ship was going and for fighting the ship, the Master was responsible for the day to day operation of the ship and getting it where is was going. The Master was expert in navigation and was responsible, aided by his mates, for charting the ship’s course and calculating its position and speed. Where his experience was relevant, the Master was also responsible for piloting the ship in coastal waters - although local pilots were also used in places that the Master was not familiar with. Like the Lieutenants, the Master would stand watches where he commanded the ship in lieu of the Captain. As part of his navigational duties, the Master was also responsible for maintaining and, where necessary, updating the ship’s charts. He also had a role in training his mates and probably also the midshipmen. In addition to navigation, the master was responsible for sailing the ship, handling the sails so that the ship was sailing as efficiently as possible within the parameters of safety and, as far as possible, at the speed agreed with the captain. Both the Bosun and the Carpenter reported to the Master. Finally, the master kept his own log and was responsible for taking and recording navigational sightings, noting weather conditions, recording the sail set, and the position, course, and speed of the ship as well as observations on navigational hazards, tides, etc. that could be used to update charts. The Master’s log supplemented the Captain’s log and the two were often compared during court-martials. When James, Lord Gambier (a blue light captain nicknamed Dismal Jimmy by his men) requested a court-martial to clear his name after the Battle of the Basque Roads, Thomas Stokes, the Master of his flagship HMS Caledonia, and the Masters of the Imperieuse and Caesar were all called to testify as to the accuracy of their logbooks before and during the action. Obviously, the precise distribution of duties on any given ship was down to the Captain. Whilst the Captain and Lieutenants were all competent sailors and navigators, the Master was the professional sailor.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did the UK manage to import tea during World War II?
Answer: An interesting and important question. Obviously tea was crucial to morale in the wartime UK. In 1938, the United Kingdom had accounted for about half the world imports of black tea and, at around 200,000 tons, the tea trade probably accounted for about 1% of UK foodstuff imports. Tea imports dropped by about 45% in the course of the war and, as a result, tea was rationed from July 1940, with each adult receiving two ounces of tea a week which would allow about three cups of tea a day. Tea didn’t come off the ration until the 5th of October 1952. To avoid a morale crisis, in 1942 the Government decided to buy every available pound of tea from all over the world. Some sources indicate that the largest government purchases in 1942 were, in order of weight, bullets, tea, artillery shells, bombs and explosives. The tea was imported by the same routes as all the other foodstuffs the UK needed to survive. It came across in convoys, either the Indian Ocean/South Atlantic convoys or the Atlantic convoys - all running the gauntlet of the U-Boats. Weekly adult ration in the United Kingdom during WW2

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What would have happened if the D Day invasion had been better planned and more accurately executed? What if the soldiers would have been trained better for what they were trained for what they were likely to encounter?
Answer: This is one of a run of recent questions that seem to be attempting to imply that D-Day was a botched operation - it wasn’t. The D-Day landings were, in fact, extremely well planned and executed - indeed they were an absolutely amazing feat in a pre-computer age. Thousands of people were involved in the planning of the operation over many months. By August 1943, the COSSAC planning staff alone included 320 officers and 600 other ranks and that was just the tip of the iceberg because, as with all military operations, there was a series of cascading plans created at various levels from the strategic to the tactical by many different staffs. Operation Neptune, the amphibious assault itself, was the largest seaborne invasion in history, comprising 6,939 vessels manned by 195,700 naval personnel. The fleet included 1,213 warships, 4,126 landing craft of various types, 736 ancillary craft, and 864 merchant vessels. 11,000 aircraft carried airborne troops, and provided close air support and bombing capability. 156,000 troops were landed on the beaches or dropped from the air on D-Day. The troops were pretty rigorously trained within the constraints of time and of not getting very large numbers of men killed during training. Even then several thousand were killed during training (see Exercise Tiger for example). On the whole, the operation went like clockwork on the operational scale. The weather and the enemy created some issues at the tactical level, but that’s only to be expected. Overall, casualties were fairly light - considering the scale of the operation - and within the predicted figures. You simply cannot remove the elements of chance and risk from war. No plan of operations extends with any certainty beyond the first encounter with the main enemy forces. Only the layman believes that in the course of a campaign he sees the consistent implementation of an original thought that has been considered in advance in every detail and retained to the end. Helmuth von Moltke the Elder However hard you try, the multiplication of small problems will nearly always disrupt your best laid plans. As long as we have no personal knowledge of war, we cannot conceive where those difficulties lie of which so much is said… Everything is very simple in war, but the simplest thing is difficult. These difficulties accumulate and produce a friction, which no man can imagine exactly who has not seen war… So in war, through the influence of an infinity of petty circumstances, which cannot properly be described on paper, things disappoint us, and we fall short of the mark. Carl Von Clausewitz, On War, Book 1, Chapter 7 - Friction in War D-Day was, without question, a massive success and an astonishing feat of planning and execution.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How different would D-Day be if the Royal Warwickshire regiment was better prepared for the "tremendous battle" they encountered?
Answer: I can safely say that it wouldn’t have made any difference at all to D-Day, as the action being referred to, the attack on Lebisey Wood, actually took place on D+1. The 2nd Battalion Royal Warwickshires made up, together with 1st Battalion Royal Norfolks, and 2nd Battalion King’s Shropshire Light Infantry, the 185th Infantry Brigade, which was one of the three brigades of the British 3rd Infantry Division which was tasked with assaulting Sword Beach on D-Day. On D-Day, the Battalion landed at Lion-sur-Mer at around 10:00 and was ordered to advance along the axis Colleville-sur-Orne - Orne - Benouville - Blainville. Benouville was taken by A Company and D Company was ordered to take over the defence of the bridges over the Orne (Pegasus Bridge) from 6th Airborne Division. The rest of the Battalion fought on to the outskirts of Blainville. On D+1 (June 7th) the Warwicks cleared the southern suburbs of Benouville/Blainville without serious resistance. The next stage called for the Warwicks(-) to advance from the river to Lebisey Wood. One Company (D) was left supporting Pegasus Bridge, and the Support Company, with the battalion’s anti-tank guns, was held at Bieville due to the marshy terrain. Men of the 2nd Royal Warwicks advance The wood was strongly held by elements of the 125th Panzer Grenadier Regiment and 22nd Panzer Regiment, part of the 21st Panzer Division. German Panzer IV dug in near Lebisey Wood Due to radio problems, the attack went in without artillery support and the situation deteriorated rapidly. The Colonel and many of the battalion officers were killed and German counter-attacks led to the battalion becoming virtually surrounded before being withdrawn in the evening with the loss of 154 officers and other ranks. The problems encountered in this attack were typical of those seen in small unit actions, poor communications (radio failures), a degree of confusion, lack of artillery support, infantry without anti-tank guns facing tanks, and the loss of key leaders. Whether the battalion could have been better prepared is doubtful. These are things that happen in war. Experience could have mitigated some of the issues, but experience is only gained in action.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain have the option to not participate in World War II? Was their involvement a voluntary decision or were they forced into it?
Answer: Unless you are physically attacked then it is always optional whether you participate in a war or not. In the case of WW2, Britain declared war voluntarily in fulfilment of its promises to render aid to Poland if it was attacked by Germany. On the 31st of March 1939, the Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, announced to the House of Commons that: As the House is aware, certain consultations are now proceeding with other Governments. In order to make perfectly clear the position of His Majesty's Government in the meantime before those consultations are concluded, I now have to inform the House that during that period, in the event of any action which clearly threatened Polish independence, and which the Polish Government accordingly considered it vital to resist with their national forces, His Majesty's Government would feel themselves bound at once to lend the Polish Government all support in their power. They have given the Polish Government an assurance to this effect. I may add that the French Government have authorised me to make it plain that they stand in the same position in this matter as do His Majesty's Government. On the 25th of August 1939, in a desperate last minute attempt to deter Germany, Britain and Poland signed an Agreement of Mutual Assistance in the event that Poland was attacked by Germany. This caused Hitler to delay the outbreak of war by a week. At this point, Britain was diplomatically obliged to enter the war in support of Poland but it could, of course, have ignored this obligation if it had wanted to and remained aloof. Therefore, Britain’s involvement in WW2 was a voluntary decision.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How would history have been affected if Churchill had been captured by Rommel during Operation Crusader?
Answer: It would have been quite a feat. Operation Crusader was a successful British operation to raise the siege of Tobruk that took place in North Africa (Egypt and Libya) during late November and December 1941. German tank brewing up during Crusader Churchill was in the United Kingdom in November and left for the United States, aboard the battleship HMS Duke of York, on the 12th of December. It would have taken unsuspected depths of cunning and resourcefulness for Rommel to have captured Churchill during Operation Crusader. Churchill on the deck of the Duke of York

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can D-Day be considered a Pyrrhic victory for the Allies?
Answer: No it can’t. A Pyrrhic victory is a victory that inflicts such a toll on the victors that it is tantamount to a defeat. The term comes from King Pyrrhus of Epirus, whose army defeated the Romans at the Battle of Asculum in 279 BC but suffered catastrophic casualties in the process: The armies separated; and, it is said, Pyrrhus replied to one that gave him joy of his victory that one other such victory would utterly undo him. For he had lost a great part of the forces he brought with him, and almost all his particular friends and principal commanders. Therefore, in order to consider D-Day a Pyrrhic victory, we would have to say that the Allied forces suffered such significant casualties that they were unable, or nearly unable, to continue with the battle. This is not the case. Firstly, the Allies were clearly perfectly able to continue the fight without any trouble at all. By the end of June, 850,000 men, 150,000 vehicles and 570,000 tons of supply had been landed in Normandy. Aerial view of the British Mulberry harbour off Arromanches landing troops and equipment US troops pour onto Omaha beach on D+1 Secondly, the casualties that were suffered on D-Day were less than the estimates made before the battle. In fact, total casualties on D-Day (killed, missing, prisoners of war, and wounded) were around 9,000-10,000 men or 7%, with perhaps 4,400 men killed in action, or just over 3%. Figures for expected casualties are often quoted of between 25% and 40%, but I have not been able to verify these and I suspect that they refer to the initial assault waves rather than the day as a whole. Other sources suggest that the planners expected casualties of around 10,000 men - which accords closely with reality. Many people equate D-Day as a whole with the events on Omaha beach where the initial assault waves suffered very heavy casualties as a result of a well known series of mishaps. However, even on Omaha beach, casualties for the day as a whole only amounted to the region of 7%. D-Day was in no respect whatsoever a Pyrrhic victory, it was a triumph of planning, organisation, and courage.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was a "sailing master" in the Age of Sail for the British Royal Navy a civilian expert or an RN officer?
Answer: The Sailing Master, or just Master, in a ship of the Royal Navy was one of the ship’s Warrant Officers. Unlike a commissioned officer, who held his rank by a commission conferred by the crown, warrant officers received their appointments through a warrant issued by the Admiralty or a similar authority. Therefore, the Master was neither a commissioned officer nor a civilian. However, the Master was considered one of the senior wardroom officers, dining in the wardroom and ranking after the Lieutenants but before the midshipmen and the standing warrant officers - the Gunner, Boatswain, and Carpenter. A Master could, sometimes, be promoted to Lieutenant and thus become a commissioned officer. One of the most famous example is William Bligh who was Captain Cook’s Sailing Master and was promoted to Lieutenant for his role in the Battle of Dogger Bank in 1781, eventually ending his career as a Vice-Admiral of the Blue. William Bligh as a Sailing Master Smaller vessels, captained by a Commander often didn’t rate a Master and so the officer was termed Master and Commander in order to reflect his dual role of both commanding and navigating the ship. Masters were examined by Trinity House (otherwise known as The Master, Wardens and Assistants of the Guild Fraternity or Brotherhood of the most glorious and undivided Trinity and of St Clement in the Parish of Deptford Strond in the County of Kent), an organisation founded in 1514 whose purpose was to: to improve the art and science of mariners; to examine into the qualifications, and regulate the conduct of those who take upon them the charge of conducting ships; to preserve good order, and (when desired) to compose differences in marine affairs, and, in general, to consult the conservation, good estate, wholesome government, maintenance and increase of navigation and sea-faring men; and to relieve decayed seamen and their relatives. and who were also responsible for: making, erecting, setting up, placing or laying out, all buoys, beacons, marks and signs, for the sea or seashore, to hold the same with all profits and emoluments thereunto belonging, as of the manor of East Greenwich, in free and common soccage. A Master may have started his career as a seaman or as a midshipman before becoming a Master’s Mate, a senior petty officer specialising in ship management and navigation, and then a Master, on receiving a warrant from the Navy Board of the Admiralty.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there any female officers in the British Royal Navy during World War II?
Answer: Technically, I think not. The Women’s Royal Naval Service, the WRNS or Wrens, was separate from the Royal Navy, although under control of the Admiralty, until finally integrated in the 1990s. The WRNS had female officers with the ranks (1941–45) of Third Officer, Second Officer, First Officer, Chief Officer, Superintendent, and Director, with Chief Officer being equivalent to Lieutenant Colonel (OF-4) but they were not formally enlisted in the Royal Navy itself as far as I can tell. Chief Officer Margaret Cooper, Deputy Director of the Women’s Royal Indian Naval Service (WRINS), with Second Officer Kalyani Sen, WRINS at Rosyth.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What countries regard the D-Day landings in Normandy as the most significant event of World War II?
Answer: That is an interesting question. Nobody? Neither the Germans or the Russians, who were locked into their appalling Götterdämmerung in the East. Not the Americans who tend to focus on Pearl Harbour and certainly not the Japanese or the Chinese who were on the wrong side of the world. Nor the Italians, Australians, Kiwis, or Indians who had no involvement in D-Day. The British were probably more focussed on the Battle of Britain and on El Alamein, and the Canadians, possibly, on Dieppe or the Battle of the Atlantic. Of the major nations involved in WW2 that only leaves the French and I have no idea what they regard as the most significant events of WW2. As far as victories go, probably the liberation of Paris. I think that for all of the Allies, the D-Day landings probably rank as one of the most significant events of WW2, but probably not the most significant event, partly because it was a joint endeavour rather than a distinctively national one. The D-Day landings in Normandy, a stupendous display of force I’ve just been reading Ian Macleod’s account of the D-Day landings, written in 1964 for the twentieth anniversary, and some of his words are striking. MacLeod was a Staff Officer, a Major, attached to the British 50th Infantry Division, itself augmented to nearly 40,000 men for the landings on Gold Beach. Of the approach to the beaches, he wrote: The coast of Normandy began to take shape through the haze. And then as full light began to come one saw the ships and the planes. It was a sight so paralysing that tears came to my eyes. It was as if every ship that had ever been launched was there, and even as if the sea had yielded up her wrecks. It was as if every plane that had ever been built was there, and, so it seemed in fantasy, as if the dead crews were there too. There had never been since time began such a rendezvous for fighting men: there never will be again. And I remember reciting, not in scorn, but out of sheer delight at being part of that great company in such a place, ‘And gentlemen in England now a-bed …’ That last is a reference to the end of the St. Crispin’s Day speech given by Henry V on the eve of the Battle of Agincourt from Shakespeare’s Henry V. And gentlemen in England now a-bed Shall think themselves accurs'd they were not here, And hold their manhoods cheap whiles any speaks That fought with us upon Saint Crispin's day. Of his own landing at H+40, he wrote: The beach was alive with the shambles and the order of war. There were dead men and wounded men and men brewing tea. There were men reorganising for a battle advance, and men doing absolutely nothing. There were even some German prisoners waiting patiently for heaven knows what. There was a whole graveyard of wrecked ships and craft and tanks of every size. It was like an absurdly magnificent film by Cecil B. DeMille. It was like war.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for Germany to stop building new battleships? When did this decision take place?
Answer: The four battleships built by Germany before WW2, as is fairly well known, were the Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, both laid down in 1935, and the larger Bismarck and Tirpitz, both laid down in 1936. These ships could only be constructed after the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935, as this removed the restrictions that had been imposed by the Treaty of Versailles, which had limited German replacement ships to a maximum of 10,000 tons. Tirpitz, the last German battleship The Kriegsmarine’s Plan Z, authorised by Hitler in January 1939, called for a fleet that comprised ten battleships, three battlecruisers, and four aircraft aircraft carriers, together with fifteen Panzerschiffe, basically the Deutschland-class heavy cruisers, and a large number of smaller vessels. In total, Plan Z envisaged a fleet of some two hundred and thirty warships. Taking into account the four ships already building, this meant that the Germans were committing to building an additional six H-class battleships. The design for the new H-class battleships was started in 1935 and then revised in 1936 and 1937. This resulted in the H-39 specification, an enlarged Bismarck-class ship with a displacement of 55,500 tons and a main armament of eight 40.6cm (16″) guns. By way of comparison, the Bismarck had a displacement of 41,700 tons and a main armament of eight 38cm (15″) guns. Possible photo of an H-class keel being laid Subsequent design revisions (H-41 to H-44) gradually increased the displacement of the designs to 129,000 tons with a main armament of eight 50.8cm (20″) guns, but these were nothing more than fantasy. The Kriegsmarine imaginatively named the ships H, J, K, L, M and N and orders for H and J were let in April 1939, the keels being laid down in July and September of that year. Work on the ships was suspended on the outbreak of the war as it was not expected that the ships could be completed by the end of the war. As the war progressed the Germans started to suffer from severe material shortages, especially of high-grade steel and so, in November 1941, the work that had been carried out was scrapped so that the steel could be used for other purposes, and the dockyards and their personnel freed to work on new U-boats. As well as the purely material reasons Hitler, never very interested in naval affairs, had lost patience with the Raeder and the Kriegsmarine by the end of 1942, after a series of losses and botched operations. The truth is that the Kriegsmarine’s surface fleet simply wasn’t powerful enough to perform any role that might have justified its cost. [The Führer said that] our own navy was but a copy of the British and a very poor one at that. The ships were not in operational readiness; they were lying idle in the fjords… utterly useless like so much old iron… it was now his irrevocable decision to do away with these useless ships. He would put the good personnel, the good weapons, and the armour-plating to better use. Vice-Admiral Theodore Krancke, naval liaison officer to Hitler

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did former colonies, such as Canada, react to Britain giving up control over them after World War II?
Answer: It’s so much more complicated than that. Britain didn’t give up control over Canada after WW2, it was a more nuanced process than that and extended over a long period of time. In reality Canada had a large measure of independence after 1867. During each of these steps, the provinces of Canada had various forms of legislature, operating with various degrees of success and various levels of authority. Effectively, Canada became largely self-governing with the British North America Act in 1867. The Act set up the House of Commons and Senate of Canada and delineated the powers of the Federal and Provincial governments. Canada remains part of the Commonwealth and recognises Charles III as King of Canada. As to the other colonies and dominions, there is no simple, universal, answer. Some sixty-five countries (according to Wikipedia) have gained independence from the United Kingdom over the last 250 years. Some have done very well and transitioned into full democracies whilst others have done less well. I’ll leave you to consider which is which, but I think it’s reasonably safe to say that Canada has done pretty well. Countries that have gained independence from the United Kingdom

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is the 2/ part of 2/14th Battalion (Aus.) A Second World War recognition of the First World War Battalion of the same area, place, etc.? So if called up again, would it possibly be 3/ 14th Battalion?
Answer: This is an interesting one. Normally, when we see a prefix such as 2/14th, we’d understand it to be the 2nd service battalion of the 14th Regiment, but this is not quite the case here. During WW1, the British Army underwent expansion and the number of battalions in a regiment increased, sometimes dramatically. For instance, the Northumberland Fusiliers (a regular regiment) eventually counted 52 war service battalions, and was surpassed only by the London Regiment (a territorial regiment created in 1908) which had 88 battalions. So, for instance, there was the 3/4th Northumberland Fusiliers, which was the 3rd service battalion raised from the 4th battalion of the Northumberland Fusiliers. Slightly more obviously, the US practice is to number battalions within regiments so the 16th Infantry (the equivalent of a Commonwealth brigade) had the 1/16th, 2/16th, and 3/16th battalions with the companies being lettered sequentially A-L (no J). During WW1, the Australian Army raised sixty infantry battalions, numbered sequentially. At four battalions per brigade, the 14th Battalion was therefore the 2nd battalion in the 4th Brigade of the AIF (Australian Imperial Force). The 14th served at Gallipoli and on the Western Front and was disbanded at the end of WW1 before being raised again in 1921 as a militia battalion. Under the Defence Act of 1903 men in militia battalions could not be forced to serve outside Australia or its territories unless they volunteered to do so. Men of the 14th Battalion at Ypres When the second AIF was raised at the beginning of WW2 it was an expeditionary force designed specifically for overseas service. The new battalions raised for this force were given a new numbering system designed to distinguish them from the militia force. Thus the 2/14th was specifically the 14th battalion on the 2nd AIF. Although tradition and logic would normally suggest that there should be a 1/14th, there was no such unit because of the structure of the numbering system did not follow the commonly used format. Both the 14th and the 2/14th were raised from the Melbourne area (Victoria) and so were closely related, with the 2/14th adopting the 14th’s yellow over blue colour patch. During WW2, the 14th battalion was eventually merged with the 32nd battalion to become the 14th/32nd battalion which served in New Guinea and New Britain, mostly on garrison duties, before being disbanded in 1945. The 2/14th served in Egypt, Palestine, and Syria before being redeployed to serve in New Guinea and Borneo. Men of the 2/14th at Kokoda Therefore, unusually in the normal run of things, it is correct to say that the 2/ does identify the battalion as part of the 2nd AIF whilst still maintaining the link to the original 14th battalion raised in the same area. I suppose that it is indeed possible that in a future conflict, Australia could raise a third AIF (or equivalent) and distinguish its battalions with the prefix 3/. There could yet be a 3/14th Australian infantry battalion.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain have a strategic reason for not building more battleships after HMS Dreadnought, despite having a significant advantage over other navies?
Answer: Well, of course Britain did build many more (some forty-two more) battleships after HMS Dreadnought. What the Royal Navy didn’t do was built any more ships in that particular class. Dreadnought was a revolutionary test-bed, her very name becoming synonymous with battleship, but she was a test-bed nonetheless. HMS Dreadnought, commissioned 1909 18,120 tons, 10 x 12” guns, 21 knots, 4”-11” belt BL 12-inch Mk X, 850 pound shell, 25,000 yards Building HMS Dreadnought with her all big gun armament and steam-turbine propulsion was a double-edged sword because she made all previous battleships obsolete. However, if Britain hadn’t built Dreadnought, a competing nation would soon have introduced the technology. The succeeding class was the three Bellerophon-class ships, Bellerophon, Superb, and Temeraire, followed by the St. Vincent, Collossus, Orion, King George V, Iron Duke, Queen Elizabeth, and Revenge-classes (and a handful of one offs) all of them commissioned between 1909 and 1917 - which is a staggering rate of evolution. HMS Revenge, commissioned 1916 29,590 tons, 8 x 15” guns, 22 knots, 13” belt BL 15-inch Mk I, 1,938 pound shell, 33,550 yards

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Could the British navy have rebuilt its fleet after losing most of its capital ships at the Battle of Jutland?
Answer: In WW1 the capital ships of a navy comprised its battleships and battlecruisers. At the Battle of Jutland the Royal Navy lost fourteen ships out of the one hundred and fifty-one deployed or 9%. Of these losses, three (Indefatigable, Invincible, and Queen Mary) were battlecruisers and therefore capital ships. There were thirty-seven battleships and battlecruisers deployed and so the loss rate of capital ships was 8%. The other losses were three armoured cruisers and eight destroyers. HMS Invincible The Germans lost eleven out of ninety-nine ships deployed (11%), but only two of these (Lützow and Pommern) were capital ships out of the twenty-seven that the Germans deployed and so the loss rate of capital ships was 7.5%. The other losses were four light cruisers and five heavy torpedo boats (destroyers). SMS Lützow Between June 1916 (the date of the Battle of Jutland) and the end of the war, the Royal Navy brought into service the battleship Ramillies and the battlecruisers Renown, Repulse, Courageous, Glorious, and Furious. HMS Ramillies HMS Renown Therefore, it is wrong to say that the Royal Navy lost most of its capital ships at Jutland. At the end of the battle, the Royal Navy had thirty-four capital ships present and the Hochseeflotte twenty-five, so the Royal Navy still retained a decisive advantage. The three capital ships lost at Jutland were replaced by six new capital ships and so the Royal Navy more than rebuilt its fleet; it enlarged it.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there any American soldiers involved in the Battle of Britain? If not, why?
Answer: No American soldiers were involved in the Battle of Britain because the Battle of Britain took place between July and October 1940 when the United States was not yet at war with Germany (Germany declared war on the United States on the 11th of December 1941). Several American citizens were, however, involved in the Battle of Britain, although they were present illegally as they were breaking the provisions of the US Neutrality Acts. The RAF recognises seven United States citizens as having taken part in the battle and another three who presented themselves as Canadians, making a total of ten (some sources say eleven). They were De Peyster Brown, Carl Raymond Davis, Art Donahue, Billy Fiske, John Kenneth Haviland, Vernon Keough, Phillip Leckrone, Andrew Mamedoff, Eugene Tobin, and Alexander Zatonski. Billy Fiske’s US passport - note the endorsement Phillip Leckrone of 616 Squadron in his Spitfire Mamedoff, Keough, and Tobin travelled to Europe intending to join either the Finnish or French Air Forces, but found themselves joining the RAF after the fall of France. De Peyster Brown, Donahue and Fiske claimed to be Canadian. Davis is listed at South African American-British and was educated in England and Canada, whilst Havilland was Anglo-American and educated in England. Zatonski was born in the United States but his family moved to Canada before the war. Andy Mamedoff of 609 Squadron shows off damage to his Spitfire Only De Peyster Brown and John Kenneth Haviland survived the war. Billy Fiske and Carl Raymond Davis were killed during the Battle of Britain and the others later in the war. “Shorty” Keough, flanked by Tobin and Mamedoff, model the proposed Eagle Squadron insignia The first of the three Eagle Squadrons (71, 121, and 133), formed of US personnel, was only created at the end of the Battle of Britain, in September 1940, and did not become operational until February 1941, therefore missing the Battle itself. American pilots of No 71 Eagle Squadron scramble to their Hurricanes in March 1941 By the time that the United States entered the war in December 1941, two hundred and forty-four US citizens had served with the Eagle Squadrons and some 6,700 had applied to join either the RAF or the RCAF. In September 1942, the Eagle Squadrons were turned over to the Eighth Air Force as the 4th Fighter Group.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is life on an air force base really that much cushier than on a marine or army base?
Answer: There’s a very old joke that sums it up pretty well and reasonably accurately. A group of officers from the different branches of the armed services are attending a joint training course and are asked what they would do if they found a scorpion in their tent. The Royal Navy officer said that he would call a rating to remove it; the Army officer said that he would hit it with his boot; the Royal Marine officer said that he would catch it, break off the stinger and eat the rest; whilst the RAF officer said that he’d call room service and ask why there was a tent in his suite…

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for the introduction of conscription in Britain and when did it occur?
Answer: Leaving aside older mechanisms such as the Fyrd the Press Gang and the Militia Ballot, there was a strong reluctance towards conscription in Britain due to a long-standing public antipathy towards standing armies and continental-style militarism. Having said that, there were calls for conscription from as early as 1902 when the National Service League advocated four years of compulsory military training for men aged between 18 and 30. In fact, there have been two periods of conscription in recent British history, coinciding with the two World Wars and their aftermaths. The first was from 1916 to 1920 and the second from 1939 until 1960. The last National Serviceman, Richard Vaughan, Royal Army Pay Corps, was demobbed in May 1963. During WW2 and up to 1948, conscription was not just limited to the military but also extended to the mines, the so-called Bevin Boys. As to the reasons for conscription, it exists to provide men and women to fill shortages in areas deemed essential by the government.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During the Napoleonic wars, if an officer or officer’s mate died while on a long voyage, would their position be filled immediately, or would the ship dock before anyone was promoted? Did they keep spare uniforms on the ship for such an occasion?
Answer: I can answer for the Royal Navy, although I don’t know what an officer’s mate is. If an officer died the next most senior officer would step into the role. A Captain would be replaced by the First Lieutenant who would become the Captain, whilst remaining in the rank of Lieutenant until a suitable replacement could be appointed which, depending on where the ship was, could take some time. If a vacancy occurred amongst the Lieutenants they would move up in seniority order from 4th to 3rd to 2nd to 1st. If it became necessary, the captain could always promote a midshipman or a master’s mate to be a temporary Lieutenant. However, such an appointment would not be permanent until the man had officially passed for Lieutenant. Likewise, if a Warrant Officer (Gunner, Boatswain, Carpenter, Surgeon, Master) died, he would be replaced by one of his mates (mate was a rank) who had the relevant experience. Uniform was unlikely to be a problem as officers in the Royal Navy quite often didn’t wear uniform on a day to day basis - instead wearing whatever working clothes they had handy. It was the custom to auction a dead man’s clothes and possessions at the mast for the benefit of his family, and so if a uniform was required it would be available - and all sailors were handy with a needle and thread.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is Britain's defense plan on the eve of a Napoleonic Invasion before Trafalgar should the Royal Navy failed? Does it involve plans similar to a Fabian or Scorched Earth tactics and could it sustain them long enough for a proper counteroffensive?
Answer: At the start of the War of the Third Coalition in 1803, Napoleon assembled a second Armée d'Angleterre of around 150,000 men in a camp at Boulogne and commenced building an invasion flotilla. Inspection of the troops at Boulogne This concentration was noted by the British who took the threat seriously and went to very considerable lengths between 1803 and 1805 to build up their forces and construct fortifications. Invasion! The government raised fifty new infantry battalions for a new Reserve Army and called for volunteers. As with the LDV (Home Guard) in 1940, the response was tremendous with over 480,000 men volunteering. British view of the likely outcome The government also built fortifications in likely invasion areas, including the Martello Towers that still dot the British coastline, the Royal Military Canal, and major fortifications at Dover. Martello Tower The Royal Military Canal is built like that so that cannons can fire in enfilade down its length A British defeat Trafalgar would not have destroyed the Royal Navy, although it would have seriously weakened it, and so an invasion was very far from a sure thing. Only about a quarter of the Royal Navy’s ships of the line were present at Trafalgar and only four of her roughly one hundred and twenty frigates. Some of these were scattered at stations around the World but there would still have been a formidable number left for home defence. Even if he had managed to invade, Napoleon would have faced the same issues that confronted Hitler a hundred and thirty five years later - how to maintain an army on a hostile shore with contested command of the seas.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is is true that Admiral Raeder said"Let's we enter the war in 1943".I learned this while listening to 2 Turkish professors.If Hitler had listened to this suggestion, could he have changed the fate of the war?
Answer: Erich Raeder was made Oberbefehlshaber der Kriegsmarine, the commander-in-chief of the German Navy, the Kriegsmarine, in 1935. When war was declared between Germany and Britain and France on the 3rd of September 1939, Raeder was shocked. He wrote in the Seekriegsleitung war diary on 3 September 1939: Today the war against England and France, which the Führer had previously assured us we would not have to confront until 1944 and which he believed he could avoid up until the very last minute, began... As far as the Kriegsmarine is concerned, it is obvious that it is not remotely ready for the titanic struggle against England. To be sure, the brief period of time that has elapsed since the Agreement of 1935 [the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935] has witnessed the creation of a well-trained and well-conceived force of U-boats, of which approximately twenty-six are currently ready for Atlantic operations, but these boats are still far too few to exert a decisive influence upon the war. The surface forces, moreover, are so weak and so few in numbers vis-à-vis the British fleet that the only course open to them-presupposing their active employment-is to show that they know how to die gallantly and thereby to create the basis for an eventual rebirth in the future. This is all in reference to Plan Z, the grandiose German plan to challenge the Royal Navy. Plan Z was conceived in late 1938 and is not to be confused with the Replacement ship construction program of 1932, the second phase of which was intended to be complete by 1943. At the point that Plan Z was initiated in January 1939, Hitler had promised Raeder that war would not come until 1948, although the initial part of Plan Z was to be completed by 1942. Numbers vary in different drafts but, in outline, the plan required the Germans to build, by 1948, thirteen battleships (the H-class battleships) or battlecruisers, four aircraft carriers, fifteen Panzerschiffe (i.e. Deutschland-class heavy cruisers) and over two-hundred smaller warships. The Tirpitz , one of the few ships completed under Plan Z, although laid down before it The cost of the program would have amounted to 33 billion reichsmarks spent over the span of nine years - a truly colossal sum by any standards - and also required the Kriegsmarine to grow to over 200,000 men. None of this came to pass and of the planned thirty-two heavy units, only seven were built and this didn’t include any of the aircraft carriers - although the Graf Zeppelin reached an advanced stage of construction. The carrier Graf Zeppelin under construction It is doubtful whether the German economy, which Hitler ran hot, could have sustained the building programme without collapsing, and Germany almost certainly couldn’t have sourced the six million tons of fuel oil per annum that the fleet would have required to operate. Plan Z concentrated on building a balanced surface fleet rather than on the U-boat arm, and this was almost certainly entirely the wrong emphasis. Had Plan Z been possible to build (which it probably wasn’t) and had Hitler managed to postpone the war until 1944–48 (which he probably couldn’t) and had the German fleet managed to defeat the British blockade (perhaps), then it might well have made a difference to the war but, frankly, it was never going to happen in the face of competing priorities and was probably unattainable from the start - a fantasy, a pipe dream.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many ships were in the British and U.S. navies during the Napoleonic Wars? Was there a significant difference in the number of ships between the two sides?
Answer: The Napoleonic Wars lasted from 1803 to 1815. When the Continental Navy was disbanded it had eleven ships remaining of the approximately sixty-five that had served at some point. The last ship in the Continental Navy, the frigate Alliance was sold out of service for $26,000 on the 1st of August 1785. After 1785, the United States effectively had no navy until 1797 when the heavy frigates United States, Constellation, and Constitution came into service following the Naval Act of 1794. In the War of 1812, the US Navy had no ships of the line and of their sixteen ships only nine were frigates, including the heavy frigates Chesapeake, Congress, Constellation, Constitution, United States, and President, the rest being brigs, sloops, and schooners. The Independence, a 74-gun ship, was launched at Charlestown, Massachusetts, in June 1814, while, four months later, the Washington, another 74-gun ship, was completed at Portsmouth. USS Franklin 74, commissioned in 1817 In 1816, after the Napoleonic Wars had ended, Congress provided for a million dollars a year for six years to build nine 74-gun ships of the line, twelve 44-gun frigates and three steam-propelled batteries for harbour defence. However, these ambitions were later scaled back and only four and two, respectively, had been launched by 1826. In 1815, the Royal Navy had around 150 ships of the line and 180 frigates and, taking into account other smaller vessels, the total size of the fleet probably exceeded 500 vessels. However, fairly obviously, the North American station was not a priority for the Royal Navy during the Napoleonic Wars and was starved of resources as the Navy sought to contain Napoleon and maintain the Channel blockade. Therefore, the early successes of the American heavy frigates against their lighter British counterparts in the War of 1812 caused consternation in Britain and the station was rapidly reinforced. By 1813 the Royal Navy was successfully blockading New York City, Charleston, Port Royal, Savannah, and New Orleans, causing American exports to drop from $45 million in 1811 to $7 million in 1814 and largely confining the US Navy in its ports. Therefore, I think that it is fair to say that there was a pretty significant difference in size between the two navies during the Napoleonic Wars - even though the bulk of the Royal Navy was not deployed on the North American Station.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did British regiments mix colonial troops with English troops during WWI and Two, or did they keep them separate, other than English officers?
Answer: Depends on what you mean by regiment. In the British Army the infantry battalion is the basic combat unit and the regiment is purely administrative. What the US called regiments were called brigades in British service - a combat formation, generally of three infantry battalions plus supporting units. In the British service, that is to say the British and Indian armies which were separate entities, battalions were generally always composed of the same nationality, tribe, caste, or religion. This doesn’t mean that there wasn’t the odd Englishman in a Scottish battalion, etc. but that was the general rule. Recruiting the men for a battalion from the same general area reduced possible sources of religious or cultural friction within the battalion whilst also increasing cohesiveness and efficiency as different tribes spoke different languages or dialects. In fact, in the Indian Army, it wasn’t until 1894 that the three, geographically based, Presidency armies (Bengal, Madras, and Bombay) were unified into a single army. This geographical distinction carried on all the way up to the Divisional level. So, for instance, the 1st (Peshawar) Division contained Punjabis, Sikhs, and Dogras, the 4rd (Quetta) Division Pathans, Mahrattas, and Hazara, and the 5th (Mhow) Division Rajputs, and Jats, etc. A Gurkha, a Sikh, and a Rajput, receiving the Victoria Cross at Buckingham Palace in 1945. The East and West African divisions were also manned by regionally recruited battalions: the King’s African Rifles, the Gold Coast Regiment, the Nigeria Regiment, etc. Above the battalion level, brigades and divisions mixed troops of different nationalities relatively freely and Indian Army brigades frequently had one Indian, one Gurkha, and one British battalion. For example the 7th Indian Infantry Brigade at Second Alamein consisted of the 1st Battalion Royal Sussex (British), the 4th/16th Punjabis (Indian), and the 1st/2nd King Edward’s Own Gurkha Rifles (Nepalese). When we come to the other Dominions, the 2nd New Zealand Division contained the 28th (Maori) Battalion, but Maoris also served in standard New Zealand battalions and can’t be classed as colonial troops. Likewise, some 3,000 First Nations people served in the Canadian armed forces in WW2 but, again, can’t be classed as colonial troops. Finally, several thousand Australian aborigines and Torres Straits islanders served in Australian units, including Reg Saunders, who was one of the first Indigenous commissioned officers in the Australian Army, again not colonial troops - albeit from the colonies. Reg Saunders (as a Sergeant)

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During WW2, the USAAF shot down multiple times the amount of German fighters that the RAF shot down. Isn't this embarrassing? Wasn't Europe supposed to be a Brit theater?
Answer: It really is a shame that Quora contains so many examples of this kind of question. I’m sure that the vast majority of the Allied airmen who risked their lives in the war over Europe would not be impressed by the childish point scoring attempted by some of their more chairborne descendants. The answer is no, it’s not remotely embarrassing. The question simply demonstrates the same poor grasp of the subject that we see in similar questions about the Battle of Britain. The RAF had two primary roles in WW2. The first was to protect the United Kingdom from German bombers. The second was to pursue economic warfare through the strategic bombing of Germany. Neither of these objectives required the RAF to concentrate on shooting down Luftwaffe fighters. These were simply a nuisance that either impeded the shooting down of Luftwaffe bombers or impeded RAF bombers that were attempting to reach their targets. Luftwaffe fighters needed to be dealt with when they were encountered, but they were never a primary target. Now as to the claims that the US shot down multiples, this may or may not be true even though it is irrelevant. What is known is that US claims were highly exaggerated. During the first Schweinfurt raid for instance Spitfire pilots claimed thirteen German fighters and P-47 pilots claimed nineteen, but the gunners on the B-17s claimed 288. Post war analysis showed that the Germans lost 26 fighters. If we assume that the Spitfires actually shot down five Luftwaffe fighters, and P-47s six - it’s easier for a fighter pilot to know whether he has shot down an enemy - then we are left with a plausible scenario of the B-17s claiming 288:15 or nineteen Luftwaffe fighters claimed for every one that they actually shot down. During the second Schweinfurt raid the ratio of claims to reality was around 5:1. We can call it an average of a 9:1 overclaim across the two raids. That’s an easy way to obtain multiples for a start. I don’t blame the B-17 gunners in the least for overclaiming. If a Luftwaffe fighter dived through a US bomber box then multiple gunners were going to take a pot at it. If the fighter is seen to burst into flames then multiple gunners were going to make a claim. There is no way to know which gunner actually made the kill. Furthermore, as these combats were taking place over enemy territory, there was no way to validate the actual number of kills. In comparison, during the Battle of Britain, which obviously took place largely over Britain where enemy losses could be verified, the RAF ratio of claims to reality was about 1.6:1, still exaggerated but much closer to reality. Then there is the question of opportunity. Between 1939 and late 1943, bombers, on all sides, took heavy losses to fighters when they attempted to operate in daylight. This was because there were no long range fighter escorts to protect them - with the exception of the not very effective Me110. First the Germans and then the British switched to night bombing as a result of these unsustainable losses. The night war was very different to the day war and, as a result, there wasn’t much opportunity to shoot down Luftwaffe fighters at night. It wasn’t the job for the bombers and there were no escort fighters except for Mosquito night intruders which are rather a different kettle of fish. The US learned this same lesson the hard way in the two raids mentioned above. Bombers, however heavily armed, could not survive in daylight without heavy escort. The US ceased deep penetration raids (not all raids) for several months until the brand new long range escort, the P-51, became available in December 1943. Once the P-51s were available, the USAAF resumed its daytime deep penetration raids and the Germans had no choice but to respond by bringing up their own fighters, which were then decimated - not by the bombers, but by the escorts.
