P-51 little friends with drop tanks Finally, there is the question of quality. By this stage of the war, the Luftwaffe was in a very poor state indeed and a kill in 1944/45 can hardly be regarded as the same as a kill in 1939/43. The Luftwaffe had lost most of its skilled experten pilots by this stage of the war and replacement pilots were relatively poorly trained due to shortages of both time and fuel. German aircraft and in particular engines were hampered by shortages of critical materials and lowered quality control which led to reductions in durability and performance, especially as the Germans also had to manage with low (87–88) octane and synthetic fuels compared to the 100 octane fuel used by the Allies. I’m tempted to use the American term turkey shoot, but I think that would be disrespectful to all the pilots involved. So there we have it. The RAF and the USAAF were operating different doctrines. The USAAF day doctrine brought them into conflict with the bulk of the depleted Luftwaffe day fighter force over Germany, whilst the RAF night doctrine only brought them into conflict with a relatively small number of Luftwaffe night fighters. Therefore, although remaining mindful of the exaggerated claims ratio, it wouldn’t surprise me at all if the USAAF shot down more Luftwaffe fighters than the RAF by the end of the war - they simply came across more of them.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain or France attempt to invade Italy during World War II? If not, what were the reasons for not doing so?
Answer: Britain, together with her Canadian and US allies, invaded Italy on five occasions in WW2. These were Operation Husky (Sicily) in July 1943, Operation Baytown (Calabria) in September 1943, Operation Slapstick (Puglia) in September 1943, Operation Avalanche (Salerno) in September 1943, and Operation Shingle (Anzio) in January 1944. Men of the 51st Highland Division wading ashore as part of Operation Husky France remained on the defensive during the Italian invasion of France in June 1940 and then took no further part in the war as an independent nation following the French Armistice at the end of June 1940. Free French troops fought in Italy but they did not, as far as I am aware, participate in the invasions themselves. The 4th Tabor of Moroccan Goums (French Colonial troops) fought in the Sicilian Campaign after landing at Licata on the 14th of July 1943, and the French Expeditionary Corps (Corps Expéditionaire Français en Italie) fought in mainland Italy from November 1943 to August 1944. These troops fought under the command of the US Fifth Army. French Colonial Goumier Following Operation Dragoon, the Allied invasion of Southern France in August 1944, French troops of the newly formed Armée des Alpes, nominally under command of the US 6th Army Group, were fighting on the Franco-Italian border. These units were barred, by the provisions of the Armistice of Cassibile (the Italian surrender) from entering Italy but they drove the remaining Italian and German defenders out of occupied French territory along the border by April 1945 in what is called the Second Battle of the Alps. General de Gaulle had been considering seizing Italian territory along the border: the Aosta valley, western Piedmont, and the coastal city of Ventimiglia and, following the Axis collapse and the end of the war in Europe in May 1945, French troops advanced across the border into the chaos that was Italy, although I don’t think that this can really be considered an invasion except in the very loosest sense of the term. Under heavy pressure from the other Allies, the French withdrew from Italian territory after a month, except for the villages of Tende and Brigue, which were later annexed as part of the treaty that formally ended hostilities between France and Italy in 1947.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What date did the WWI conscription end in the UK?
Answer: It was surprisingly difficult to locate an answer to this one as some sources say 1919 and some 1920. The correct answer is that conscription in the UK, under the terms of the Military Service Act of 1916 and its Amendments, ended on the 31st of March, 1920. Conscription was never applied to Ireland. Conscription was introduced in January 1916 targeting single men aged 18 to 41. The scope was expanded to include married men in May 1916, and in late 1918 the upper age limit was extended to 51 - with a provision to extend it to 56. Some 4.9 million men were enlisted in the British army between 1914 and 1918. Of these 2.4 million enlisted prior to the introduction of conscription and 2.5 million after the introduction of conscription. However, it has been suggested that only 1.3 million men were actually conscripted. The man responsible for announcing the end of conscription was one W.S. Churchill, then Secretary of State for War and Air. His speech to the House of Commons is worth reading: On the 31st of next month conscription will be abolished, and within a month from that date the last conscript is entitled to be released from; the Army. The vast process of demobilisation will then be completed. In the interval, and only just in time, we have succeeded in raising and organising, unit by unit, an entirely new Volunteer Army, which by the time conscription lapses will, we estimate, number about 220,000 men, exclusive of those serving in India… In other words, we have recruited in a single year what is, broadly speaking, the pre-war Regular Army, and we have organised the additional troops which are needed to discharge our temporary and new liabilities. I venture to think that that is a remarkable achievement… I will invite the Committee to consider what sort of language would have been used supposing we had not succeeded, and supposing I had had to stand here to-day, as I might easily have done, and point out that, owing to the fact that we had not been able to recruit a volunteer army, I must ask for a prolongation of compulsory military service, keeping at any rate the younger conscripts who took no part in the War for another year to come. We have abolished conscription. At the General Election we pledged ourselves to fight for the abolition of conscription at the Peace Conference, but we were very careful to add that our own action must depend on what others did. Our representatives fought at the Peace Conference for the abolition of conscription, but they fought with singularly little success. In fact, there was no response at all to the representations which they made. The only other great nation whom we have succeeded in persuading to abolish conscription is Germany, and that is only under dire compulsion and as part of her punishment for having lost the War. The following States, among others—I do not pretend for a moment that my list is exhaustive—retain compulsory service as the basis of their military system, and apparently have no intention of departing from it: France, Italy, Japan, Spain, Portugal, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Holland, Denmark. Rumania, Greece, Poland, Jugo-Slavia, Czecho-Slovakia, the United States, the originator of the League of Nations, Russia—here we tread on controversial ground—the home of advanced political thought, where there is not only military conscription but industrial conscription also. Undiscouraged and undeterred by our failure to convert others, we have proceeded to set an example ourselves. Alone among the nations we have decided to abolish compulsory military service, and I venture to think that this action, coming as it does apart from the action of all other nations, deserves additional recognition from those who have so vehemently demanded it. We alone, who have far greater extent of territory to control, who are responsible for a far larger mass of human beings in every part of the world, have returned to that voluntary system which we pursued before the War. At the Armistice we had on the whole the strongest army in the world. Our normal army and our present army will be weaker than the army of Belgium. And then we are called militarists. Alone among the nations we have abandoned compulsory service. Yet I suppose we shall be treated to a continuance of the line of criticism which brands us as a Jingo Government and accuses the Secretary of State for War as being a bellicose and ambitious administrator. House of Commons, Monday the 23rd February 1920

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were the 13th colonies British colonies or English colonies? I've heard both terms used interchangeably.
Answer: Virginia (founded in 1607), New York (1626), Massachusetts (1630), Maryland (1633), Rhode Island (1636), Connecticut (1636), New Hampshire (1638), Delaware (1638), North Carolina (1653), South Carolina (1663), New Jersey (1664), and Pennsylvania (1682) were all English colonies until the Acts of Union in 1707, during the reign of Queen Anne, created the Kingdom of Great Britain by combining England and Scotland. After 1707 they were all British colonies. Georgia (founded in 1732) was established after the Acts of Union and was, therefore, never an English colony. As an aside, there were a lot more than thirteen British colonies in the Americas depending on how and when you count them. Leaving aside the more modern (western) Canadian provinces, these included Quebec, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, New Brunswick (Acadia), Rupert’s Land, the British Arctic Territories, the Indian Reserve, East Florida, West Florida, Bermuda, Jamaica (including parts of Honduras and Nicaragua), Barbados, The Bahamas, Trinidad and Tobago, the Windward Islands and the Leeward Islands.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During the Second World War, were four engine RAF Lancaster bombers able to carry parachutists, and if so, how many?
Answer: The Lancaster was far too valuable to Bomber Command to carry parachutists (apart, of course, from its own crew if needs be) and was never used either for this purpose or as a glider tug. The primary troop carrier of the Allied air forces was the Douglas C-47, named the Dakota in British service, and the C-53 Skytrooper, which could carry 18–22 paratroopers and allowed them to exit rapidly through its side door. The British did make limited use of their other four-engined bombers, the Halifax and the Stirling, for dropping paratroopers and towing gliders. However, these were less than ideal as they could only carry a very limited number of men who had to drop through a hole in the floor. Exiting from the rear of a Whitley two-engined bomber proved to be unsatisfactory As did dropping through a hole in the floor in a Halifax or Stirling However, Lancasters did do more than drop bombs and they made 3,156 sorties and dropped 6,684 tons of food supplies to the starving Dutch in May 1945. I did wonder if Lancasters were used to drop Ruperts, the dummy explosive paratroopers, about five hundred of which were dropped to confuse the Germans on D-Day, but it appears that they were not used and this role was filled by the Whitleys and Halifaxes of the Special Duties squadrons. Rupert - dummy paratrooper

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How much did the Royal Navy and US Navy support the 1944 (Monte) Cassino battles, shelling the Germans?
Answer: To the best of my knowledge, there was no naval gunfire support by either the Royal or US Navies during the Battle for Monte Cassino - which took place between January and May 1944. At first glance the prospect seems ridiculous, as the battle for the monastery was fought deep in the interior of Italy, on a hilltop in the Latin Valley, 120 kilometres south-east of Rome. However, Italy being the shape it is, a quick look at the map shows that the monastery is actually only 30 kilometres from the coast. This is within range of the 16″ naval rifles of the Iowa-class battleships. As it happens, there were no Iowa-class ships present in the Mediterranean, but the British battleship HMS Ramillies and the French battleship Lorraine, which were deployed in support of Operation Dragoon in August 1944, had BL 15-inch and 340mm/45 guns respectively, which could just about reach the vicinity of the monastery. That is if, of course, the ships didn’t mind firing from just off a hostile shore - which wouldn’t have been very healthy for them. None of the warships deployed in support of Operation Shingle (the Anzio landings) which occurred at the same time as the Battle of Monte Cassino, had the range to shell the monastery. HMS Ramillies In the event, the monastery was subjected to a furious air bombardment on the 15th of February, when 230 B-17s, B-25s and B-26 bombers dropped over 1,150 tonnes of explosives. Sadly, the only significant effect of this was to turn the ruins of the monastery into an excellent defensive position for the Germans. The ruins of Monte Cassino after the bombardment

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is the EU right to start legal action against the UK for banning sandeel fishing in the North Sea in an attempt to increase the number of endangered species?
Answer: It’s not really legal action, depending on how you want to define the term. The EU is submitting a claim that there has been a breach of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement to independent arbitration. The arbitration tribunal will be composed of three members selected from a list of potential arbitrators previously agreed by the UK and EU. One will come from a list proposed by the UK, one from a list proposed by the EU, and one from a list of potential chairs who must not be citizens of either the UK or the EU. The UK’s case is that it has banned all sand eel fishing by bottom trawlers and that there is therefore no discrimination because fishermen of all countries are being treated equally. The EU’s case is that most sand eel fishing, some 99% of it, is carried out by Danish vessels and so they are disproportionately affected - amounting to discrimination. The EU’s case is likely to be somewhat diminished by the fact that, on the 21st of February 2024, the Commission called on Member States to phase out bottom trawling from all marine protected areas by 2030. As a result the Commission is in the awkward position of having to support a member state that wishes to maintain a practice that it itself is trying to ban.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Which country has a history of more invasions: Germany or Great Britain/England? Can this be explained statistically?
Answer: Germany. This could be demonstrated statistically, but it can be explained geographically. Germany sits at the centre of Europe and, as a result, has always been both an invasion route and battleground - although Germany may be pipped at the post by Belgium, which is known as the Cockpit of Europe because of the number of battles fought there. Germany has been the target of multiple invasions and historical migrations since (and presumably before) recorded history began. The most famous are still bywords for violence and general mayhem: Goths, Vandals, Huns… In fact, I believe that Germany has the oldest known major battle site in Europe, the Tollense valley battlefield in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern which, human remains indicate, was the site of a pitched Bronze Age battle between up to 4,000 warriors in the 13th Century BC. Then you have every man and his dog from Charlemagne to Napoleon fighting across Germany, with a special mention to the Thirty Years’ War which ravaged Germany multiple times as the French and the Habsburgs fought for dominance. During this period, Germany was laid waste, losing an estimated third of its population. The British Isles, on the other hand, are both less strategically situated and much more difficult to invade being, as is obvious, islands. You can’t just march into Britain as you can Germany, you need a navy, or at least naval transports, to mount an invasion. Even Julius Caesar had to gather ninety-eight transport ships for his first invasion, and eight hundred for his second invasion - a significant investment in time and resources over just mustering his legions. However, nothing on the scale of the Thirty Years’ War has taken place in Britain since the Harrying of the North in 1069–70. You’ve got to get to the British Isles before you can invade them

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: As a Christian, did you know that the name Daniel is Islamic?
Answer: That would be odd indeed. The Book of Daniel was authored in the 2nd Century BC, probably around 165 BC, during the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid Empire. The events in the Book of Daniel are supposed to have taken place in the 6th Century BC and Daniel is a Jew exiled in Babylon in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. The book was originally written in Hebrew and Aramaic and appears in the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh, specifically in the Ketuvim or Hagiographical section, between Esther and Ezra or between Lamentations and Esther. However, the Book of Ezekial, which may have been written as early as 570 BC, more contemporaneously with the supposed events, also mentions a DN’L (Hebrew words are written without vowels) which might, or might not, be a reference to the same Daniel. The Islamic period, on the other hand, dates from the 610, at least some 800 years later than the probable writing of the Book of Daniel. However, Daniel is recognised in the Shia branch of Islam as an imported prophet, although he is not mentioned in the Koran. Therefore, Daniel appears in the Jewish, Christian, and Islamic religious traditions, as well as making an appearance in The Thousand and One Nights as a twelve year old boy on Night 394, The pious Jewish woman and the two evil old men.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Winston Churchill ever regret not joining the military during World War II, like many other young British men did?
Answer: Churchill was 64 when WW2 broke out. The National Service (Armed Forces) Act of 1939 set the limits to conscription for men as those aged between 18 and 41, and the normal limit to military service as 51. Soldiering is a young man’s game and Churchill was not a young man. Indeed he would only have been eligible for the LDV (the Home Guard) until November 1940, as the upper age limit for that was 65. Churchill held military commissions of various sorts between 1895 and 1924 when he resigned his commission in the Queen’s Own Oxfordshire Hussars (QOOH), a Yeomanry regiment in the Territorial Army, at the age of 50. Churchill as a captain in the QOOH c. 1905

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was Britain warned by Russia about a potential German invasion before World War II? If so, what information was given and who delivered the warning?
Answer: No, Russia didn’t warn Britain about a potential German invasion (Sealion) before WW2. In fact, Russia both wouldn’t and couldn’t have warned Britain about any impending invasion for two very good reasons: Firstly, the Russians had signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact non-aggression pact with Germany on the 23rd of August 1939 and were, as a result, significantly more closely aligned with German interests than they were with Britain - for example, planning to split the spoils of Poland between them. Secondly, the Germans had no plans to invade Britain before the start of WWII and so there was nothing to warn Britain about. It wasn’t until the 15th of November 1939 that Grand Admiral Raeder instructed his chief-of-staff Vice Admiral Schniewind to begin even a preliminary study of the matter. Hitler himself issued no instructions until the 6th of July 1940 when he issued Führer Directive #16 authorising Sealion. As England, despite her hopeless military situation, still shows no signs of willingness to come to terms, I have decided to prepare, and if necessary to carry out, a landing operation against her. This operation aimed to eliminate the English Motherland as a base from which the war against Germany can be continued, and, if necessary, to occupy the country completely. Prior to this point, Hitler’s thinking (Führer Directive #9 – Instructions For Warfare Against The Economy of the Enemy) was to bring Britain to the negotiating table through an economic blockade carried out by the Kriegsmarine and the Luftwaffe. On the other hand, Britain certainly warned Stalin about Hitler’s plans to invade Russia in Operation Barbarossa. As early as March 1941 decrypted Luftwaffe Enigma messages revealed that three armoured divisions and other important elements had been ordered to move from the Balkans to the Kraków area of Poland, a sure sign that Germany was building up its forces in the East. Operation Barbarossa - the Germans invade Russia The British Ambassador to the Soviet Union, Stafford Cripps informed the Russians of some of the details of the planned German attack, and less than three weeks before the attack Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden also warned the Soviet Ambassador in London, Ivan Maisky, that the Germans were about to launch an attack. Finally, Churchill himself sent Stalin a personal message: I have sure information from a trusted agent that when the Germans thought they had got Yugoslavia in the net - that is to say, after March 20 - they began to move three out of the five Panzer divisions from Roumania to Southern Poland. The moment they heard of the Serbian revolution this movement was countermanded. Your Excellency will readily appreciate the significance of these facts. Stalin ignored these warnings as he had ignored multiple others.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason behind German soldiers calling the British "Tommy"?
Answer: The Germans called British soldiers Tommy because the British soldiers called themselves Tommy. The term Tommy Atkins was used as early as 1743 and was embedded in the British Army when the name was used as an example in official forms from 1815. In the same way it entered King’s Regulations in 1837 as quoted by Richard Holmes (a very nice man by the way) in his eponymous book Tommy: The British Soldier on the Western Front. Part of a sample form from the Soldiers’ Book of 1815 Rudyard Kipling famously entrenched the name in the public mind with his 1890 poem Tommy: I went into a public-'ouse to get a pint o' beer, The publican 'e up an' sez, "We serve no red-coats here." The girls be'ind the bar they laughed an' giggled fit to die, I outs into the street again an' to myself sez I: O it's Tommy this, an' Tommy that, an' "Tommy, go away"; But it's "Thank you, Mister Atkins", when the band begins to play, The band begins to play, my boys, the band begins to play, O it's "Thank you, Mister Atkins", when the band begins to play. Obviously some British soldiers were actually called Tommy Atkins and they probably came in for a bit of stick: A real Thomas Atkins, discharged in 1825

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did Great Britain manage to survive as an independent country during World War II, despite being surrounded by enemies and having limited allies?
Answer: There are three main elements that ensured Great Britain’s survival in 1940. Firstly, Great Britain is, famously, an island and has always benefitted from the defensive advantage of having at least twenty miles of sea between itself and the Continent. As Shakespeare put it in Richard II: This fortress built by Nature for herself Against infection and the hand of war, This happy breed of men, this little world, This precious stone set in the silver sea, Which serves it in the office of a wall Or as a moat defensive to a house, Against the envy of less happier lands… The Germans had neither the logistics capability (shipping) required to support an invasion of the British Isles, nor did they have the specialist landing craft that would have been required to conduct the assault landings themselves. Such German plans and preparations as were created for Seelöwe (Sealion) were laughably amateur in their lack of scope, and no planning whatsoever for an invasion of Great Britain had taken place before the outbreak of the war. German officers, Göring towards the right, looking at the White Cliffs of England Secondly, as a maritime nation, Great Britain had the world’s largest navy in 1940. The Germans, on the other hand, even with the potential assistance of the Italians, didn’t have anything like the naval strength required to protect the invasion armada or subsequent supply convoys from the cruisers and destroyers of the Royal Navy. Nor did the Germans have the minesweeping capabilities required to clear a safe path for their shipping. As an aside, it is extremely unlikely that either side would have deployed capital ships in the Channel except in extremis. German Panzer III als Tauchpanzer submersible tank - this was never going to end well Thirdly, the Germans failed to defeat the RAF in the Battle of Britain. In fact, despite popular myth, they were never ever close to doing so. Short-ranged German fighters would have had a hard time defending either shipping or the beachheads against the RAF fighting on home turf. To succeed in even initiating an invasion, the Germans required command of the air, command of the sea, detailed planning and preparation, and specialised logistic and other technical support. They had none of these things. If the Germans had not invaded Russia, if they had not declared war on the United States, if they had devoted months or years to planning, preparing, and building for the invasion, if they had made different decisions regarding the U-boat arm, if they had equipped the Luftwaffe with heavy bombers, then, with the resources of a conquered continent at their backs, they might have been able to wear down the British to the extent that an invasion became possible, but it would have been a tremendous risk.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the British and Americans land at different beaches on D-Day? What was the reason for not landing together?
Answer: The British landed on two beaches (Sword and Gold), the Canadians on one (Juno), and the Americans on two (Omaha and Utah). The British provided some support to Juno, including 48 (RM) Commando and elements of the 79th Armoured Division (Hobart’s Funnies), but the main combat elements of each beach were all drawn from a single nationality. This makes sense because troops of different nations had different weapons, different ammunition, different communications equipment, different doctrine and tactics, and, of course, different chains of command. Although the latter could be varied if necessary, it is always going to be much more efficient use troops who belong to the same division (except on Omaha where two divisions landed), who have trained together and whose commanders have worked together, than it is to mix nationalities up. In the latter case, there are no readily apparent advantages to be gained. Commandos landing on Sword, in case you’re wondering what strange weapon the foreground figure is carrying, it’s Bill Millin and his bagpipes… US troops landing on Utah

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is cheddar American or British?
Answer: The Cheddar Gorge in Somerset, England has been inhabited since at least the Mesolithic period (Middle Stone Age) and human remains found in Gough’s Cave date back to 8500–8000 BC. The genetic markers derived from Cheddar Man (as he is called) suggest that he was from what is known as Western Hunter-Gatherer population. This population forms about 10%, on average, of the ancestry of Britons without a recent family history of immigration. Mesolithic skeleton shares DNA with English history teacher Adrian Targett When humans started making cheese in the Cheddar Gorge is unknown but it goes back to at least the 12th Century when the cheese was stored in the caves to keep it cool. There are records of Alured of Lincoln purchasing 10,240 lbs of cheddar (forty weighs at an estimated 256 lbs each) in 1171 for £11. Alured submitted his expenses to the Exchequer and they were recorded in the Pipe Roll for the 17th year of Henry II’s reign (1171). Being relatively imperishable, the cheese was probably destined to feed Henry’s army during his Irish campaign of 1170–1175. As Alured had estates in Somerset, it is assumed that the cheese was from Cheddar (Somersetshire Archaeological and Natural History Society Proceedings during the Year 1880, vol. XXVI). The Cheddar Gorge Cheddar being matured in caves in the Gorge Rather later, British colonists who moved to America took their cheesemaking techniques with them, and by 1790, cheddar was being produced in the United States. Being so widespread (cheddar is produced in Australia, Argentina, Belgium, Canada, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand, South Africa, Sweden, Finland, and Uruguay as well as the United Kingdom and the United States) cheddar has no protected designation of origin but, traditionally, the cheese has to be made within 30 miles of Wells Cathedral to be a true cheddar. 1964 New York World's Fair cheddar - 17.5 tons of cheese

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Do the people of the United Kingdom generally embrace a British-centric perspective on World War II?
Answer: Yes, of course. I don’t think that it would be possible to name a nationality that doesn’t place its own efforts at the centre of its own history. This is an entirely rational point of view, regardless of whether you are talking about the Second World War or any other international event. In fact, it is difficult to imagine how you could do otherwise unless, of course, the affair being discussed didn’t involve your home nation at all, or perhaps if you are a professional historian looking from a specific angle. Having an country-centric point of view doesn’t mean dismissing the contributions of other nations, and nor does it mean being blind to the faults and errors of your own country and its leaders. Other people, looking at the course of events from their own country’s viewpoint, may well have a different perspective on the details even though the overall narrative must, perforce, remain the same. We would also be well advised to heed L.P. Hartley's words: The past is a foreign country: they do things differently there. The past was populated by men and women with passions like our own, but with entirely different customs and codes of behaviour.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Where do the English Armed Forces keep their right-tenants and right-tenant generals?
Answer: As the OP probably knows perfectly well, there’s no connection between the words left and lieutenant, and therefore no connection with the word right. The OP is attempting a humorous comment, a pun, on the British pronunciation of leftenant. Lieutenant is a compound word from the Latin locum meaning in place of, and teneris meaning holding. Taken together the phrase applies to someone holding in place of someone else. Over time the word locum evolved into the French word lieu, which is pronounced in French as it is spelled. I don’t know about American usage but, in the UK, we still use the term locum for someone holding a temporary appointment, particularly doctors. A lieutenant is therefore someone who is standing in for, or these days assisting, a captain, a colonel, or a general. Lieutenant, Lieutenant Colonel, and Lieutenant General In the United States, the word is pronounced semi-phonetically, thanks to Noah Webster, as lootenant, although the actual French pronunciation is closer to lootenon. In England and Scotland we can see formulations such as luftenand dating from as early as the 14th Century. This may be because the original Old French for lieu was, apparently, luef or because u and v were considered interchangeable in early English, or because the labial glide at the end of the first element of a compound word was heard by English-speakers as a v or f. Interestingly, this same formulation can be seen in Russian, where лейтенант is pronounced leytenant.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did Germany build so many tanks before World War II in such a short amount of time?
Answer: I’m not sure that the statement holds up. The Germans started the war with 3,872 tanks. German tank production, technically banned by the Versailles Treaty, started in 1934 (although design and prototyping started as early as 1926 with assistance from Sweden and Russia), so they had five years in which to produce their starting stock of 3,872 tanks. Of these, 78 of were Czech Panzer 38(t) that were not produced in Germany, so that leaves 3,794, which is a production rate of 759 tanks per annum. However, 1,893 of these (50%) were Panzer I tankettes which were never supposed to be used in combat (although, in the event, they were pressed into service) and a further 1,223 (33%) were the marginally more useful Panzer II. Panzer I, based on the British Carden Loyd tankette The remarkable fact is that the Germans started the war with only 510 medium tanks (255 Panzer III and 255 Panzer IV) produced between 1937 and the outbreak of the war. Of these, 202 were produced in 1939, which can hardly be seen as a rapid rate of production for a highly industrialised nation. In fact, only 310 mediums (Pz III or IV) were available at the start of the Polish Campaign, during which the Germans lost about 30% of their armour. It is a myth that the Germans started the war with overwhelming armoured forces. During the war, the Germans produced around 117,000 armoured vehicles during WW2, the British around 95,000 (including fully-tracked carriers), the US around 108,000, the Soviets around 120,000. The Italian and Japanese contributions were nugatory with around 4,500 and 7,000 respectively. Given that the Germans were at war longer than everyone else except the British, that makes their production of armoured vehicles nothing out of the ordinary run. Stug IIIs being produced One of the curiosities of the war is actually that the Germans put so little effort into tank production, especially in the early war. The annual figures are 1940 : 1,888, 1941 : 3,623, 1942: 5,530, 1943: 11,601, 1944 : 18,956, and 1945 4,406 (13,000 annualised). The rapid expansion in tank production from 1943, in the face of intensive Allied strategic bombing, shows that German industry had significant amounts of spare capacity and tends to suggest that the German planners were rather caught napping by the developing scale of the war. In fact, the production of civilian cars was not suspended until 1943 and this points to the Germans anticipating a short war. It wasn’t until after Albert Speer’s appointment as Reich Minister of Armaments and War Production in early 1942 that tank production was was properly planned and organised.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for the Germans using a variety of tanks compared to the US who used only a few types?
Answer: Well, let’s see. The German deployed seven basic varieties of tank (we’re talking about tanks not tank destroyers here) helpfully numbered I to VI. There were the Panzer I, II, III, IV, V (Panther) and VI (Tiger and King Tiger). In case you are wondering, I’m ignoring the Panzer 35(t) and 38(t) as these were captured Czech vehicles. The Germans were at War from September 1939 to May 1945, so let’s call that 69 months and so the Germans rated around one tank for every ten months at war. German Tiger II (King Tiger) The US, on the other hand, deployed the M3/M5 Stuart, the M3 Lee, the M4 Sherman, the M24 Chaffee, the M22 Locust, and the M26 Pershing. The US was at war from the December 1941 to May 1945, so let’s call that 41 months. That’s six tanks over 41 months, so the US rated around one tank for every seven months at war. US M4 Sherman I’ve ignored various prototypes, etc., and only included the tanks that saw some combat. Therefore, empirically, and adjusting for duration, the US actually developed more types of tanks than the Germans. Admittedly, the Germans also pressed captured Czech and French tanks into service or adapted them into other vehicles. If we were to include the main tank destroyers, ignoring half-tracks the US used three types, the M10 GMC, the M18 Hellcat, and the M36 Jackson, whilst the Germans used the field expedient Marder I, II, and III, the Hetzer, the Jagdpanzer IV, the Jagdpanther, the Jagdtiger, the Elefant, the Nashorn, and the redoubtable Stug III. That’s three US tank destroyers to ten German ones, which would bring the ratio down to one German tank/tank destroyer deployed every four months at war versus one US tank/tank destroyer deployed every 4.5 months at war - not much to choose between them really. The most commonly deployed tanks on either side were the M4 Sherman for the US and the, often overlooked, Panzer IV for the Germans. Both of these tanks went through too many marks to bother enumerating in detail: twelve for the M4 Sherman and ten for the Panzer IV.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In studying the History of WW2 in Europe, we always hear of the air army airforces need to destroy Germanys ball bearing factories. After the war, was an assessment done to see how effective ballbearing production was to Germanys war efforts?
Answer: This question is referring to the two Schweinfurt raids, the first (Schweinfurt-Regensburg) on the 17th of August 1943 and the second (Schweinfurt only) on the 14th of October 1943. The raids are famous for the very heavy losses taken by the Eighth Air Force. The impact of the two raids was so severe that the Eighth Air Force was forced to stop deep-penetration raid for several months until sufficient long-range fighter escort could be provided. B-17s over Schweinfurt Bombing Schweinfurt When discussing the damage caused by the two raids, it is important to differentiate between the damage caused to the site and the damage caused to the German war effort, as these are two very different things. After the first raid, German ball bearing production dropped from 140 tons in July to 69 in August and 50 in September, but the effect on the German war effort was minimal because adequate stocks were available to cover the short-term. After the second raid, production of ball-bearings in Schweinfurt was halted for six weeks whilst production facilities were dispersed but, again, the impact on the overall German war effort was minimal. Damage caused to the Kugelfischer factory after repeated raids Post-war investigation by the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey showed that while production fell by early 1944 to about half of the pre-attack totals, it rose again to about 85 percent by mid-1944. The key failure was in not rapidly following up either raid - party as a result of the heavy losses suffered by the bombers - which allowed the Germans time to disperse manufacturing, and use existing stocks and alternate sources, including imports from Sweden, to cover the deficit whilst they rebuilt production. Despite further raids by both Eighth Air Force and Bomber Command at the end of the war production was still estimated at 98 percent of pre-bombing totals in late 1944. One of the most quoted lines from the US Strategic Bombing Survey said that “there is no evidence that the attacks on the ball bearing industry had any measurable effect on essential war production.” Less noticed was the judgment of the Survey that the outcome might have been different had Eighth Air Force been able to follow up on the two 1943 attacks.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can a shot trap on a tank effectively defend against an Abrams or a Leopard II? What is the purpose of a shot trap on a tank?
Answer: A shot trap is a defect in the design of a tank, not a defensive measure. A shot trap is a place where when a non-penetrating round strikes the tank and instead of ricocheting away harmlessly, the geometry of the trap ricochets the round into vulnerable location where it may cause more damage that the original strike. Typical shot traps are found in under-curved turret designs that deflect hits down into the thinner top armour of the hull. Here you can see where a shot trap, the original under-curvet mantlet, has been reinforced on a Panther Ausf G with an additional piece of armour, known as a chin mantlet, that removes the shot trap. Having said that, the issue of shot traps is much less of an issue in modern warfare as anti-tank long-rod penetrators have a much higher velocity that they did in WW2 and are more likely to shatter than to ricochet if they do not penetrate.

Question: Does NATO understand well that the notorious Article 5 also works in the opposite direction? All NATO countries as a whole and each individually will be responsible for the entry of one of the NATO countries into the territory of Ukraine.
Answer: You clearly need to read Article 5. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is Alan Lester right to call the idea that the military costs of Britain’s Empire outweighed the benefits “risible” and is he right to point to temples’ presentation to the Royal Statistical Society as evidence of the economic benefits of empire?
Answer: In truth, it is impossible to make a single judgement like that on something that lasted for several hundred years in a period when conditions were constantly changing. It also, of course, depends on what you mean by military costs. Do military costs include the Navy? Also, why are we discussing the military costs rather than the administrative costs of the Empire? Ever since Adam Smith economists and other have argued about the costs of the British Empire. The ‘imperial accountancy’ approach has generally held that the empire was a waste of money: The majority of the English people cheerfully and even proudly shouldered a tax bill for an empire from which they derived very little in the form of tangible pecuniary gains. Labour politician Dennis Healey wrote: As early as 1880, the British empire was producing an economic return lower than investment in Britain itself, while to preserve it the British taxpayer was paying two and a half times more for defence than the citizens of other developed countries. Trade was the raison d'etre of the Empire Sir Richard Temple’s presentation The General Statistics of the British Empire dates from 1884. What Temple has to say is that: The annual revenue and receipts collected in the British empire for the general government or administration amounts to 203 millions sterling annually. Of this mighty sum, 89 millions pertain to the United Kingdom, 74 millions to India, and 40 millions to the colonies and the dependencies. Central Government spending in the UK in 1885 was £85.4 million of which defence accounted for £28.5 million or 33%, a not inconsiderable amount. As Central Government receipts, as above, were £89 millions, this suggests that the UK was self-financing, with no net income from the Empire. Also, in the 1880s at least, 44% of the running costs of the Empire were raised in the United Kingdom which means that the Empire was certainly not self-financing. Still the sum is not apparently high for the total population, amounting to £1 5s. 4d. per head per annum. But the average incidence varies greatly, being £4 7s. 5d. per head in the United Kingdom, £2 14s. 1d. per head in the colonies and dependencies, and only 7s. 11d. in India. Taxation per head was clearly higher in the UK than in the white colonies. The lower taxation in India is, presumably, a reflection of much lower average wages on the sub-continent. Now the men trained to arms in the British empire may be stated at 850,000, including the regular British forces at home and abroad, the militia, and volunteers in the United Kingdom and in the colonies, the British native forces in India and other countries. Thus the military forces of the British empire are much smaller relatively to the territory and the people than those of any other great State, excepting only the United States of America. There remains, too, the cardinal fact that the British military forces are raised entirely by voluntary enlistment, a circumstance almost unique in the military arrangements of the present age. The defensive armaments of the empire by sea and land cost 41 millions sterling annually, or 20 per cent. of the total of [Imperial] revenue and receipts, which proportion is less than that shown by any great State in the world, except the United States. If the expenditure be compared with the whole population of the empire, then it amounts to less than 4s. a head, which (always with the exception of the United States) is the cheapest rate to be found in any great State of the world. We can see from this data, that defence was costing the British Exchequer some 33% of its revenue and the overall Imperial Exchequer some 20%. Temple certainly seems to believe that this is good value for money when compared with the military spending of other European powers, but I don’t know that one-fifth can be described as risible. However, whilst the costs are quite easy to see, the benefits of empire are much more difficult to ascertain, because benefits are more than simply tax revenue. Temple makes no comment on the economic benefits of the Empire and, indeed, there is no consensus on this matter. It is difficult, if not impossible, to unravel the relative impacts of the industrial revolution, the Napoleonic Wars, and imperial policy when trying to assess the growth of the British economy. What we can say is that in this period the Empire accounted for over 24% of the world’s economy and 34% of the world’s commerce - which are pretty amazing statistics.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is jaywalking allowed in the UK?
Answer: Jaywalking is a peculiarly American concept in origin, where the term Jay originally meant rube or bumpkin. The earliest citation of jaywalking dates to 1913 according to Peter Norton’s book Fighting Traffic - The Dawn of the Motor Age in the American City, and implied someone wandering in the street aimlessly and without care. The term is now used to denote any crossing of a street illegally. Early automobiles were recognised as a danger to pedestrians. In the UK the Locomotive Act 1865 required all road locomotives to travel at a maximum of 4 mph in the country and 2 mph in the city, as well as requiring a man carrying a red flag to walk in front of road vehicles hauling multiple wagons. In 1896 the speed limit was raised to a heady 14 mph. The State of Vermont passed a similar ‘Red Flag’ Law in 1894: the owner or person in charge of a carriage, vehicle or engine propelled by steam, except road rollers must have a "person of mature age… at least one-eight of a mile in advance of the vehicle, to warn those with livestock of its impending arrival. If at night, it also required the aforementioned person to carry a red light. The onus for safety was clearly on the driver. Although American pedestrians used to the same rights to use the roads as motorists, the motorist lobby gradually won the legal battle for supremacy. This came about through a rather cynical campaign by the motor industry to shift the blame for accidents from motorists to pedestrians. The origin of this appears to have been a 1923 petition in Cincinnati to limit the speed of motor vehicles to 25mph. This so alarmed the local car lobby that they started to lobby against jaywalkers using boy scouts, clowns, and the press. By the 1930s the tide of public opinion had been turned and anti-jaywalking laws had become the norm in most American cities. Traffic at Piccadilly Circus, London around 1895, lots of pedestrians on the road In the UK on the other hand, pedestrians have a right to cross a road wherever they please, with the exception of motorways and their slip roads. Rule 204 of the Highway Code states: The road users most at risk from road traffic are pedestrians, in particular children, older adults and disabled people, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists. It is particularly important to be aware of children, older adults and disabled people, and learner and inexperienced drivers and riders. In any interaction between road users, those who can cause the greatest harm have the greatest responsibility to reduce the danger or threat they pose to others. Note that pedestrians are also road users and that the onus is on drivers to reduce the danger they pose to other road users. This does not mean that pedestrians always have the automatic right of way though. The statistics would tend to indicate either that British drivers are better trained or that British pedestrians are more careful, or, possibly, both. Despite the Jaywalking laws, as a pedestrian you are at least twice as likely to be killed on the roads (per million head of population) in the US than you are in the UK. British children are educated from an early age to cross the road safely. In my day, it was Tufty the Squirrel, but nowadays I believe that it is the Green Cross Code. Both of these codes originated from the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you name any battles where German forces were completely surrounded and surrendered en masse?
Answer: The large scale organised surrenders that spring immediately to mind were Stalingrad, Tunis, and the Ruhr. Obviously, in the last months of the war, hundreds of thousands more German soldiers surrendered, but they didn’t do so in an organised manner. Of the men who surrendered, some 34,000 died in French POW camps, 22,000 in American camps, 21,000 in British camps and between 363,000 (Deutsche militärische Verluste im Zweiten Weltkrieg) and 1,094,000 (Maschke Commission) in Soviet camps. The en masse surrenders, on the other hand, were sanctioned, at least tacitly, by army commanders, Paulus, Arnim, and Model, when the situation had clearly become untenable. In late January 1943, 91,000 German personnel of the 6th Army trapped in the Stalingrad pocket surrendered after the failure of Manstein’s relief operation, Winter Storm. Of these, only around 6,000 survived their capture. German prisoners after Stalingrad In May 1943, 267,000 German (perhaps 100,000 Germans) and Italian personnel of 5th Panzer and 1st Italian Army surrendered after being encircled by British and American forces at Tunis. German troops surrender in Tunisia In April 1945, 317,000 German personnel of Army Group B in the Ruhr Pocket surrendered after having been encircled by the US 12th and British 21st Army Groups. Model dissolved Army Group B on the 15th of April and there was a general surrender on the 17th. German POWs after the surrender in the Ruhr

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did JRR Tolkien base the character Golem on Jews as he is sneaky and the word Golem is a Jewish word?
Answer: Well, leaving aside the implication in the question that Jewish people are sneaky, Gollum (not Golem) was actually called Sméagol. Tolkien was, of course, a professional philologist (Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford) and Sméagol‘s name derives from the Old English smēag: creeping in; penetrating; subtle; crafty. However, Sméagol was also variously nicknamed Trahald (burrowing), Stinker, Slinker (by Samwise), and Gollum. And when he said 'gollum' he made a horrible swallowing noise in his throat. That is how he got his name, though he always called himself 'my precious‘. A Golem, on the other hand, is an animated being made of clay and activated by a shem written on a piece of paper and inserted in the mouth or in the forehead of the golem. The Golem is most famously associated with Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel of Prague. JRR Tolkien As an aside, although Gollum’s name has no Jewish connotations, in an interview with the BBC in 1971, Tolkien mentioned the dwarves: I didn’t intend it, but when you’ve got these people on your hands, you’ve got to make them different, haven’t you? The dwarves of course are quite obviously, wouldn’t you say that in many ways they remind you of the Jews? Their words are Semitic, obviously, constructed to be Semitic. Tolkien took his languages seriously, he was a philologist remember. According to Tolkien scholars, his dwarves are an inversion of Wagner’s negatively “Jewish” dwarves in the Ring Cycle. As a lover of Norse mythology, Tolkien despised the Nazis’ distortion of ancient tales to incite hatred. Anyway, I have in this war a burning private grudge… against that ruddy little ignoramus Adolf Hitler. [Hitler is] ruining, perverting, misapplying, and making forever accursed, that noble northern spirit, a supreme contribution to Europe, which I have ever loved, and tried to present in its true light. When asked confirm his Aryan ancestry before a German version of the Hobbit could be published in the 1930s, Tolkien responded: If I am to understand that you are enquiring whether I am of Jewish origin, I can only reply that I regret that I appear to have no ancestors of that gifted people. In modern Hebrew, golem is apparently used to mean ‘dumb’ which kinda brings us back to the question.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the Germans develop a high altitude fighter to counter the Mustangs over Britain during World War II?
Answer: There is quite a lot wrong with this question that needs addressing before we get the meat of the answer. Firstly, P-51s were bomber escort fighters not air-defence fighters. The air defence of Great Britain (ADGB) was primarily a job for RAF Fighter Command. The RAF did have around 1,500 P-51s, but they never replaced the Spitfire as the main frontline fighter. Secondly, the P-51′s ceiling was not significantly different to the contemporary Spitfire IX and so it would be wrong to imply that the P-51 was specifically a high-altitude fighter. Thirdly, as the Battle of Britain came to a close, the Luftwaffe began arming its single-engine fighters with bombs, using them in preference to twin-engine bombers against many daylight targets. These aircraft engaged in the so called tip and run nuisance attacks with light bombs and were conducted at low, not high, altitude. The emerging V1 attacks were also made at low altitude and the V2s could not be intercepted at all. Fourthly, by the time that the P-51 arrived in the UK in numbers in late 1943, the Luftwaffe was no longer posing a serious threat over Great Britain. Operation Steinbock, the so called Baby Blitz, ran from late 1943 to mid-1944 but had very little impact compared with the Blitz and cost the Germans some 70% of the 500 odd aircraft involved. Therefore, one would have to question why the Luftwaffe would need to develop a high altitude fighter to counter Mustangs over Britain when they were concentrating on low level attacks. Any Allied aircraft at high altitude could simply be ignored. Having said that, the Luftwaffe did develop a high altitude fighter, the Focke-Wulf Ta 152, a variant of the excellent Fw 190. The Ta 152 and the Bf 109H were developed to intercept the bomber offensive over Germany, not aerial activity over Britain. The Ta 152 had a service ceiling of 49,500′ which was better than a P-51, but it was a case of too little, too late, and probably only scored seven aerial victories. The Germans also developed the Junkers Ju 388 heavy interceptor, a variant of the Ju 88 for high altitude operations, with a ceiling of 43,000′ but few were built. There were also a number of prototypes including such rarities as the Me 155/BV 155 but they never entered service. Captured Focke-Wulf Ta 152 Junkers Ju 388

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason behind the Germans making most of their tanks open-topped?
Answer: The Germans didn’t make any of their tanks open-topped. What they did do was make some, but not all, of their tank destroyers open-topped. The role of a tank destroyer is, in theory at least, defensive. This means that they are intended to stand back from the front lines and engage enemy tanks at long range and, ideally, from hidden, hull down positions. Because of this, speed was emphasised over armoured protection and, as they were not expected to be engaged by infantry an open top was acceptable and gave better visibility as well as more room for the crew to work and more room for the gun to recoil. We can identify three basic types of German tank destroyers, open-topped, turretless but fully armoured, and mounted on half-tracks. Although not the subject of this answer, the fully armoured casemated tank destroyers included the highly successful Sturmgeschütz III, the Elefant/Ferdinand and the Jagdpanzers, the Jagdpanzer 38 Hetzer, Jagdpanther, Jagdtiger, etc., whilst many half tracks were also modified for the tank destroyer role such as the Sd.Kfz. 251/22 with the 75 mm L/46 Pak-40 gun. Sd.Kfz. 251/22 The early German tank destroyers or Panzerjäger were of the open-topped design and were expedient designs mounted on obsolete light tank or captured tank chassis. Thus the Panzerjäger I mounted a Czech 4.7cm gun on a Panzer I chassis, the Marder I mounted a 75 mm Pak-40 on a French Lorraine 37L chassis, the Marder II mounted a 75 mm Pak-40 or captured Soviet 7.62 cm gun on a Panzer II chassis, and the Marder III mounted the same guns as the Marder II but on a Czech Panzer 38(t) chassis. The last of the German open-topped tank destroyers was the Nashorn, sometimes called the Hornisse, which mounted a 8.8 cm Pak 43 on a chassis that used components from the Panzer III and Panzer IV as a chassis. Panzerjäger I Marder I Marder II Marder III Nashorn It should be noted that the open-topped tank destroyer was not limited to the Germans with the Allies deploying the 3″ armed M10, the 76mm M18 Hellcat, and the 90mm armed M36 as well as the 17-pdr Archer. M10 M18 M36 Archer

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What were the reasons for William's victory at the Battle of Hastings and his later loss of Normandy? Why did he not engage in another battle after Hastings?
Answer: Possibly because the Angevin Dynasty, under the unfortunate King John, didn’t lose Normandy until June 1204, which was 138 years after the Battle of Hastings and William I had died in 1087, twenty-one years after the Battle. The Battle of Hastings (Senlac Hill) was, as far as we can tell, a close run thing and was lost when the English leader Harold Godwinson (Harold II) was killed and the English lost heart. How Harold was killed is subject to debate, but the common legend is that he was shot in the eye by an arrow - as depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. Earlier in the tapestry, William is shown lifting his own helmet to show his faltering men he was still alive after a fall from his horse. At this moment, he would have been equally vulnerable. On such tiny chances does the course of world history depend. Harold Rex Interfectus Est: Harold the King is killed Earlier in the battle William lifts his helmet to show that he is still alive in order to encourage his faltering men.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the name of the Allied invasion of Normandy that took place on June 6, 1944?
Answer: In common parlance it is often called D-Day, although D-Day is a generic term that can be used for any military operation. In this usage D simply stands for Day and, in the same way, H stands for hour. This is a simple way of providing offset references, especially useful when the target date may change during the planning process. D-1 indicates one day before the operation, and D+5 indicates five days after. In the same way, H+1 indicates one hour after the operation and H-5 indicates five hours before it. Other people might refer to the Normandy Landings or Operation Overlord. However, what you don’t so often hear is the correct name for the landings themselves, which was Operation Neptune. Operation Neptune in full swing Operation Overlord was the umbrella plan for the invasion and the breakout from the beachheads and lasted until German forces retreated across the Seine on the 30th of August, whilst Operation Neptune was the plan for the invasion itself. Some people incorrectly define Operation Neptune as the purely naval part of Operation Overlord, but this is not quite correct. The objective of Operation Neptune was defined as: to carry out an operation from the United Kingdom to secure a lodgement on the Continent from which further offensive operations can be developed. This lodgement area must contain sufficient port facilities to maintain a force of 26 to 50 divisions and to enable this force to be augmented by follow-up formations at the rate of from three to five divisions a month Operation Neptune was terminated in the British Sector on the 30th of June (D+24), when responsibility for the reception and defence of shipping was transferred to the Flag Officer, British Assault Area and the Eastern Naval Task Force was formally disbanded. By this date, 570 Liberty Ships, 180 troop transports, 788 coasters and 905 LSTs, as well as 1,814 LCTs and LCI(L)s, had delivered their cargoes to the far shore, landing 861,838 men, 157,633 vehicles and 501,834 tons of stores.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How were the SA like compared to the SS?
Answer: The SA (Sturmabteilung) or Storm Troopers or Brownshirts (the inspiration for P.G. Wodehouse’s Black Shorts), created in 1921, were the original paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party. The SS (Schutzstaffel) or Protection Squad wasn’t created until 1925 and was, until 1929, part of the SA. An SA parade The SA was a much larger organisation than the SS and were more radical (Strasserist) than Hitler and the core leadership of the Nazi Party and believed in mass action rather than the preferred method of co-opting the political, army and industrial leadership. The leader of the SA, Ernst Röhm, openly stated that he saw the SA as the replacement of the Reichswehr (army) and the SA was growing out of control with over three million members. Röhm (SA) right and Himmler (SS) left An unholy coalition of jockeying factions in the Nazi Party, the SS, the Reichswehr, industrialists, and President Hindenburg, emerged, determined to destroy the SA and during the Night of the Long Knives on June the 30th 1934, Röhm and the senior SA leadership was arrested on the pretext of a coup plot and shot by the SS. Although the SA continued to exist, and was prominent during Kristallnacht, its power was broken and it became little more than a training organisation for the army - including the Hitlerjugend, the Hitler Youth. The members of the SA were typically of a lower class than those of the SS and the organisation was primarily more of a mass movement dedicating its time to combatting rival political organisations on the streets. They are often characterised as thugs. The SS on the other hand was a many-headed monster, incorporating the police, including the SD, the Kripo, and the Gestapo, the SS-Totenkopfverbände or concentration camp guards, Hitler’s personal guard units, and the Einsatzgruppen, the paramilitary death squads, as well as the the military Waffen-SS and peculiar groups such as the Ahnenerbe. Having said that, it was always a smaller organisation than the SA, probably never having more than 800,000 members. An SS parade The SS also developed a curious neo-pagan ideology centred around Wewelsburg castle in Westphalia which Himmler plainly intended to supplant Christian practices within the SS. The SA and the SS, two more unpleasant groups of humanity you could hardly wish for.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did British pilots navigate during World War II without GPS or satellite technology? Did they use maps with grid coordinates or another method?
Answer: In WW2, pilots used maps, compasses, chronometers, sextants (celestial navigation), dead reckoning and just plain old looking out of the window. Larger planes had astrodomes from which the navigator could make sextant shots although, certainly later in the war, celestial navigation was very much a last resort. The elements of aircraft navigation are the air speed and heading of the aircraft, the wind velocity and direction at the current altitude, and the speed and track of the aircraft against the ground. Of these the accurate determination of wind drift is the most difficult problem, especially on long flights where there was no visible ground reference. Astrodome on a C-47 Taking a sextant sighting through an astrodome Where available radio navigation aids such as Gee, Oboe, and later H2S were also used. The Allies also used the Loran (US) and Decca (UK) long-range (which is what Loran stands for) radio navigational systems. Pilots used specialised slide rules, usually strapped to their leg, the most famous of which was the E6B, which was still standard issue when I was learning to fly in the 1990s. These slide rules allow the pilot to make calculations of many sorts, including the calculation of the effects of wind drift. I still have mine and it is entertaining to demonstrate the concept of a slide rule, particularly a circular one, to anyone under about forty. Below is a section of a navigational chart maintained by the navigator of a Lancaster bomber during a raid on the French port of Le Havre. The ‘x’ marks are Gee plots and the vectors drawn between them and the triangle plots are so that the navigator can calculate the impact of wind drift on the plane’s course. Gee was a hyperbolic VHF navigation aid using a master and two slave stations. The stations were synchronised so that they transmitted with a known time difference which created a series of hyperbolic lines. By measuring the time differences, the navigator could position the aircraft on the hyperbolic grid. The RAF also deployed medium frequency (300-400 kHz) radio beacons that the radio operator could take bearings on, allowing the navigator to take bearings on two beacons and, adjusting for the time between bearings, plot his position at the intersection. Earlier, there was the low frequency radio range, the predecessor of the modern VOR, where pilots could fly along a beam where a uniform tone could be heard. If the signal of a single letter (A or N) became audibly distinct, the aircraft would be turned as needed so that the modulation of the two letters would overlap again. This was similar to the Knickebein and X-Gerat systems used by the Germans to navigate during the Blitz. Individual airfields also used Pundit Beacons which used red lamps to flash a two letter code in Morse that uniquely identified the airfield. From 1942, there were also Eureka beacons that were used by ground troops to help aircraft, using Rebecca, locate their position for air drops. Pundit light in action This only skims the surface of the topic but, in conclusion, I’d like to mention my friend and neighbour, now sadly no longer with us, Arthur ‘Robert’ Smith, who, in 1943, at the age of around twenty and having never previously left the country, picked up an unarmed Beaufighter from Filton in Bristol and flew it, mostly alone to save weight, in stages to India. His journey took him from Filton to RAF Perranporth in Cornwall, across the Bay of Biscay (where he was chased down to sea-level by Luftwaffe Ju 88s), in a dog-leg out into the Atlantic, to RAF Luqa in Malta, to RAF Idris in Libya, to one of the RAF airfields near Cairo, to RAF Habbeniyah in Iraq, before the final leg to RAF Mauripur near Karachi. I’d dearly like to be able to pop across the road and ask him what navigational equipment he had, but sadly I can’t. Whatever it was, it was a damned brave thing to do at that age. Robert and friends on his 90th birthday

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the reason for Captain Sobel's animosity towards Private Ryan during the Normandy invasion?
Answer: Captain Herbert Sobel was a real person who commanded Easy Company, 2nd Battalion, 506th PIR in the 101st Airborne Division between 1942 and late 1943, whereas Private Ryan is a fictional character in the film Saving Private Ryan, an account of the fate a group of men from a Ranger company during the D-Day landings and their aftermath. The fictional Private Ryan that the Rangers are trying to find was serving in Baker Company, 1st Battalion, 506th PIR of the 101st. Sobel, no longer with Easy Company, parachuted into Normandy on D-Day with the 506th’s service company. Therefore, the real and fictional characters were not a million miles apart on D-Day, but there is no suggestion in the film that they ever met. The only connection would be Stephen E. Ambrose, who wrote a book, Band of Brothers, about the exploits of Easy Company and who was also a consultant during the making of the film Saving Private Ryan. I do have concerns about the portrayal of Sobel, played by David Schwimmer, in the TV series. We shouldn’t forget that he was a real person, seen from a very limited perspective and portrayed as a slightly cartoonish baddy. The poor man had an unhappy life and eventually tried to commit suicide.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did artillery units not charge with cavalry units on horseback during the Napoleonic Era? Was this not a feasible strategy or was it considered unwise?
Answer: Artillery units don’t charge, what would be the point? They need to unlimber their guns in order to fire them. Where horse artillery is depicted as charging, it is normally moving away from the enemy at high speed in order to save the guns. Saving the guns at Maiwand, 1880 - a case of a rapid advance to the rear Napoleonic armies fielded three different types of artillery. The heaviest was very slow moving siege artillery. Then there was foot artillery, horse drawn (the gunners walked) and designed to keep up with and support the infantry. Finally, there was horse artillery, light guns that were designed to keep up with moving cavalry units in order to provide mobile support. In a horse artillery unit the gunners all rode. British Napoleonic horse artillery Horse artillery and lancers in 1898 waiting to advance British 13-pounder horse artillery in WW1 Horse artillery was designed to designed to move with the cavalry and disrupt enemy formations in order to make them vulnerable to a cavalry charge. In the rock-paper-scissors nature of Napoleonic warfare, infantry in square formation was, generally speaking, invulnerable to cavalry. However, an infantry square is a dense formation and it will suffer disproportionate casualties if artillery can be brought to bear on it, especially at cannister (grapeshot) ranges. So horse artillery moved with cavalry (and bear in mind that cavalry actually moved quite slowly, until the very last part of a charge) but did not charge with them. Ideally, they would unlimber in close proximity to the enemy to soften them up and disrupt them before the cavalry tried its hand at a charge to finish them off. In turn the horse artillery needed to be protected by the cavalry from attacks by enemy cavalry.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why didn't Hitler invade the UK through the chunnel instead of attempting an amphibious landing?
Answer: Leaving aside the slight temporal inconvenience that Hitler was contemplating invasion in 1940 and the Chunnel (aka Channel Tunnel/Eurotunnel) wasn’t opened until 1994, there are a number of factors that should be borne in mind. Project of attack against England by Napoleon - French troops walk through the Channel Tunnel while ships and balloons attack by sea and air (1803) Firstly the Chunnel, being a tunnel is, perforce, underground, up to 115 metres below sea-level in fact, and could therefore be flooded, which would have rather unfortunate consequences for the invaders. Secondly, in consequence of the Chunnel being under the sea, there are no ventilation shafts and this rules out invasion either on foot or in internal combustion powered vehicles, because of the exhaust fumes and, er, suffocation. Thirdly, the military does dearly love a chokepoint and the Chunnel is nothing if not a chokepoint from a military perspective. Trying to debouche an invading army through its two twenty-four foot wide tunnels doesn’t sound like a brilliant tactical idea. In the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC, 300 Spartans and 700 Thespians led by Spartan King Leonidas defended the pass against 10,000 or more Persians under Xerxes I and, famously, Horatius defended the Pons Sublicius, a bridge across the River Tiber in Rome, against an entire Etruscan army. In reality, there would be no problem either in defending the tunnel mouths or indeed in blocking them, either temporarily or permanently. However, the British did have real concerns regarding the prospect of a tunnel. The idea was championed by Napoleon III in the 1880s but the scheme was not pursued on the grounds of national security. The possibility of constructing a tunnel was raised repeatedly in 1906, 1914, 1919, 1924, and 1930 but, on each occasion, the Committee of Imperial Defence (CID), chaired by Sir Maurice Hankey, objected. After the initial wave of German victories, the British authorities, for perfectly comprehensible reasons, had developed an invasion complex, together with a healthy respect for German efficiency in waging war, and this led them to consider the prospect that the Germans might construct their own tunnel. In 1941, Major-General King, Chief Engineer of Home Forces, consulted Sir Leopold Savile, President of the Institution of Civil Engineers, on the possibilities. Despite technical advice that building a tunnel would take two to three years, Hankey was concerned that the Germans might deploy advanced technology such as reducing the spoil to slurry and pumping it out, in order to speed up construction. The Joint Intelligence Committee (JIC) then reviewed the question and determined that it would take at least six years. Despite being dismissed by civil engineering experts, Hankey developed a bee in his bonnet about the German tunnel and continued to press the issue through two committees that he chaired, the Engineering Advisory Committee (EAC) and the Scientific Advisory Committee (SAC). The matter was pursued throughout 1942 and experiments were conducted to see whether the sounds of tunnelling could be detected. Plans were put in place to monitor stretches of the coast and forwarded to the Chiefs of Staff, but at this point the suspension of disbelief broke, and the whole matter was shelved for good. The Germans never had any intention of tunnelling under the Channel, but the British certainly had concerns that, in the event of a long war, they might.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Eisenhower purposely avoid landing in Cherbourg during D-Day?
Answer: Well, if he intended to land in Cherbourg then D-Day was a bit of a cock-up. Yes, the Allies did purposely avoid landing in Cherbourg on D-Day. Wars are won by logistics and logistics loomed large in the minds of the Allied planners. To capture a port would be of the first importance. However, capturing a deep-water port and, equally importantly, capturing it in working condition, was not an easy ask. Part of the reason for the Dieppe Raid in 1942, apart from testing out various aspects of amphibious operations, was to assess the feasibility of capturing an occupied port. The lessons learned at Dieppe were not encouraging and it was deemed that an direct attack on a heavily-defended port was not feasible. Dieppe, at the time of the raid, had a garrison of 1,500 men whilst Cherbourg had a garrison, on D-Day, of around 25,000 and was designated a fortress (festung) port; it was going to be a tough nut to crack. The landings at Utah were designed to provide a springboard to cut across the Cotentin Peninsula and allow the investment of Cherbourg. The US 9th Infantry Division cut the Peninsula on the 18th of June, twelve days after D-Day, and the assault on Cherbourg began on the 22nd. After hard fighting, the port surrendered on the 29th. However, the port facilities had been so thoroughly demolished that it was only back in limited use in the middle of August. Given that a deep-water port was not going to be immediately available, the Allies had to come up with an alternative and the British floated the idea (actually Churchill had come up with the basis for the idea as early as 1915) of bringing a harbour with them - the famous Mulberries. There were two Mulberries, one off Gold and the other off Omaha, and they were designed to handle 12,000 tons of cargo a day in all weathers. They were huge undertakings, involving blockships, breakwaters, giant pontoons, and prefabricated roadways. The American harbour was abandoned after a storm on the 19th of June, but the British harbour operated until March 1945 during which time it landed two and a half million men, half a million vehicles, and four million tons of supplies.
