Question: Why in the 1920s-1940s European battleships had guns smaller than the 16-inch guns that were the norm with American and Japanese battleships (with the sole exception of Britain's Nelson class)?
Answer: Standard arms race leapfrog. The Japanese introduced 16” guns with the Nagato-class battleships, first commissioned in 1920, and then moved to 18″ guns with the Yamato-class in 1941. Nagato, 1920 The first US battleship to have 16” guns was the Colorado-class Maryland, commissioned in 1921. Before that both Japanese and US battleships had 14” guns, whilst the British Revenge-class, first commissioned in 1916 had 15” guns. USS Maryland (BB-46), 1921 The French used 12″ guns until the Bretagne-class in 1916 which had 13.5″ guns and then the Richelieu-class in 1936 which had 15″ guns. The Italians used 12″ guns until the Littorio-class in 1940 which which had 15″ guns. The Germans also used 12″ guns until the Bayern-class in 1916 which had 15″ guns. The Scharnhorst-class reverted to 11″ guns in 1928, but with plans to replace them with 15″ weapons, and the Bismarck-class had 15″ guns in 1940. The Kriegsmarine’s Plan Z called for six H-39-class battleships with 16″ guns, but these were never laid down. The story starts with HMS Dreadnought, commissioned in 1906, which, amongst other innovations, introduced a uniform main battery of BL 12-inch Mk X guns and set a standard for all other navies. By steps the Royal Navy increased the calibre of it’s guns to 13.5″ with the Orion-class in 1912, 15″ with the Queen Elizabeth-class in 1915, and 16″ with the Nelson-class in 1927. The N3-class, designed in the 1920s was planned to have 18” guns but, in fact, the following King George V-class battleships reverted to 14” guns in 1940 (see below). The British had also experimented with 18″ guns on HMS Furious, a Courageous-class battlecruiser. BL 18-inch Mk I naval gun, 1916 Why did this happen? It happened because of a series of naval treaties designed to stop the arms race. The first was the Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 which limited battleships to 35,000 tons and a maximum of 16” guns. This killed the British 48,000 ton, 18″ N3-class design and none were ever laid down. The following Nelson-class was a compromise designed to meet the terms of the treaty and they were often referred to as the Cherry Tree class because they had been cut down by Washington. The Washington Naval Treaty was signed by Britain, the United States, Japan, France, and Italy. The Germans were already limited by Article 181 of the Treaty of Versailles which effectively restricted them to 11″ guns. HMS Nelson, 1927 The Washington Treaty was followed by the London Naval Treaty of 1930, also signed by Britain, the United States, Japan, France, and Italy, and then the Second London Naval Treaty of 1936 which was only signed by Britain, the United States, and France as both Japan and Italy withdrew. Battleships were limited to 14″ guns - which explains the apparent retrograde step of the King George V-class. However, the treaty contained an escalator clause which allowed 16″ guns if either Japan and Italy had not signed up by 1937. As Japan did not sign, this allowed the United States to build the 16″ armed North Carolina, South Dakota, and Iowa-classes - the so-called treaty ships. It was too late to change the design of the King George V-class ships, but the planned Lion-class would have been armed with 16″ guns. Therefore, the answer to the question is that 16″ guns became the standard in the Pacific because of the Japanese. However, the European nations, with the exception of the Royal Navy and the 16″ Nelson-class, were not expecting to come into conflict with the Japanese and thus had their own arms race that, by the outbreak of WW2, had reached the point of arming battleships with 15″ guns in order to keep up with their local rivals.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the most powerful battleship in history? Were any battleships ever used as aircraft carriers?
Answer: I don’t know, how do you define most powerful? The ones with the biggest guns was the Japanese battleships Yamato and Musashi with nine 18″ guns. Their likely opponents, the US Iowa-class battleships only had nine 16″ guns and rather less armour (a 16″ shell weighs 2,700 lbs whilst an 18″ shell weighs 3,219 lbs, a 19% difference). However, the Iowa had better radar and fire control and would probably be able to land more hits. The point is moot anyway, as both the Yamato and the Musashi were sunk by carrier aircraft marking an emphatic end to the dreadnought era. Most battleships carried catapult aircraft for scouting purposes, but few were used as aircraft carriers. The British Courageous-class battlecruiser, HMS Furious was converted into a hybrid aircraft carrier whilst building in 1916 and ended up with the rather bizarre configuration of having a flying off deck forward and a single 18″ gun aft. She has the distinction of being the first moving ship on which an aircraft was landed but was otherwise not a success and was eventually converted into an aircraft carrier. HMS Furious The obsolete Japanese Ise-class battleships, Ise and Hyūga were converted into hybrid aircraft carriers by removing their two after turrets and replacing them with a hangar and two catapults. These ships could launch but not recover aircraft (except for floatplanes which could be lifted aboard by crane). They could carry up to twenty-two aircraft, mostly the Yokosuka D4Y Suisei (Judy) dive bombers. The experiment was not a success. Hyūga after conversion During WW2 there was a plan to convert the Illinois (BB-65) and Kentucky (BB-66) into carriers but this came to nothing and would, anyway, have been a conversion of a battleship into a carrier rather than a battleship being used as a carrier. There were, in the 1970s and 1980s, various plans to convert the Iowa-class battleships into hybrid battlecarriers, also called the Interdiction Assault Ship, that could potentially carry a dozen AV-8B Harrier jump jets as well as a battalion of marines and hundreds of cruise missiles. These plans risked creating a jack-of-all-trades, master of none ship and ultimately came to nothing. Iowa-class battlecarrier concept - note the cruise missile silos between the ski ramps

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: The EU Organization has threatened to cut off supply of weapons to/from UK in the event that the EU goes to war with anybody. Is this a deliberate tactic to arm-twist Keir and Lammy into accepting the superiority of the EU over the UK military?
Answer: The EU cannot go to war with anybody because that is not, at least yet, one of its core competencies. However, Thierry Breton, the EU’s industry commissioner has announced a European Defence Investment Programme that contains within it prioritisation measures that include the ability to block exports of weapons or components, including to the UK. There are pros and cons to this initiative from the EU’s perspective, and only time will tell whether it will be effective or simply a giant exercise in pork barrel politicking. It is clearly a high risk situation for the UK, or indeed anyone else, to rely on other nations to supply their weapons, particularly consumable items. This is true regardless of whether the supplier is in the EU or not, as, in an emergency, the supplying nations’ own needs will inevitably take priority over those of their customers. The posturing of the EU just reflects this reality and adds an extra layer of complexity. Of course, the EU will have its own problems as, in a real crisis, its constituent nations will follow their own interests rather than its rules. At any rate, there is no cause for panic about the EU’s intentions just yet. In reality 81% of the UK’s arms imports come from the United States and a further 16% from South Korea and Israel. We import about the same amount of arms from the EU as we do from Israel. It is potential US protectionism we need to worry about, not the EU. However, I am somewhat concerned about the UK’s reliance on Franco-Italian Aster missiles for the Royal Navy, as this is a very clear weakness. HMS Defender fires an Aster missile We rely on economies of scale and it would be very expensive to move all manufacturing in house even where this is possible. In the big picture, these are false economies, but the situation it is what it is. The best that we can hope for is that the government identifies critical weaknesses and seeks to mitigate them by gradually moving production into the UK - although, in reality, this is unlikely to amount to much. Long term self-sufficiency in weapons is probably no longer possible, so the only answer is to build significant reserve stockpiles of consumable items (pigs might fly).

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you provide a historical example of a larger battleship losing to a smaller, faster ship in ship-to-ship combat?
Answer: That depends on what you mean by losing. If we are assuming that we’re discussing a fully operational, undamaged, battleship being sunk by a smaller ship, then there is at least one example that springs to mind. On the night of 12–13 May 1915, the Canopus-class pre-dreadnought battleship HMS Goliath was moored in Morto Bay off Cape Helles with HMS Cornwallis and five destroyers. The Ottoman destroyer Muâvenet-i Millîye, captained by Ahmet Saffet Okay, managed to slip past the patrolling destroyers at about 01:00 hours, taking advantage of darkness and patches of fog, and launch three torpedoes. The first two hit almost simultaneously, the first near the bridge and the second by the funnel, causing a large explosion. Goliath was already capsizing and was lying on her side when a third torpedo struck near her after turret. The ship was lost with 570 of her 750 crew whilst the Muâvenet-i Millîye escaped in the confusion. HMS Goliath HMS Goliath displaced 14,300 long tons whilst the Muâvenet-i Millîye displaced 753 long tons, almost exactly one nineteenth of the size of Goliath. Muâvenet-i Millîye Obviously, the Muâvenet-i Millîye with its two 3″ and two 2.2″ guns could never take on the Goliath with its four 12″, twelve 6″, and ten 3″ (12-pounder) guns and 6″ of belt armour in a gunfight. However, the Gallipoli naval campaign and this engagement in particular were stark illustrations of how cheap weapons such as mines and torpedoes rendered battleships vulnerable. Two more pre-dreadnoughts, Triumph and Majestic, were to be sunk by the German submarine U-21 in the next fortnight, and the battleships Irresistable and Ocean together with the French battleship Bouvet had already been sunk by mines in March of 1915. In fact the Goliath’s loss and related events were to have serious consequences within the British Government, leading to the resignation of the First Sea Lord Admiral “Jackie” Fisher on the 15th of May and, shortly after, that of the First Lord of the Admiralty, Winston Churchill and triggering the decision to withdraw all heavy naval units from the area which changed the whole course of the campaign. Other examples include the sinking of the Austro-Hungarian SMS Wien by the Italian MAS 9 and, as mentioned by Michael below, the sinking of the Austro-Hungarian SMS Szent István by the Italian MAS 15. There is some cracking footage in Michael’s comment. Edit: To avoid repeating myself in the comments, submarines are boats not ships, and are therefore excluded from this question.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is coal necessary for an industrial revolution? If not, what alternative sources could have been used to power steam engines and factories during that time period?
Answer: No, it is not necessary, but it is very handy. It is worth noting at the outset that the industrial revolution was about far more than steam engines, it was about standardisation, specialisation and the division of labour (see Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations for example), the invention of tool making machinery (lathes for example), extensive scientific research, etc. The alternatives to coal are human power, animal power, wind power, water power, and burning wood (or peat, heather, or furze). Arkwright’s Water Frame for spinning cotton, and Cartwright’s Power Loom for weaving fabric were both powered by water. Power loom weaving, driven by shafts and belts Therefore, wind and water power can certainly be used in industrial processes, and wood was used extensively to produce steam in early-industrial America. However, wood has many other uses as well as simply burning it. You can’t build houses, or ships, or make railway ties out of coal for instance. Captain Cuthbert Collingwood, later to become an admiral and Nelson's second in command at Trafalgar, had his home at Morpeth, in Northumberland, and when he was there on half pay or on leave he loved to walk over the hills with his dog Bounce. He always started off with a handful of acorns in his pockets, and as he walked he would press an acorn into the soil whenever he saw a good place for an oak tree to grow. Some of the oaks he planted are probably still growing more than a century and a half later ready to be cut to build ships of the line at a time when nuclear submarines are patrolling the seas, because Collingwood's purpose was to make sure that the Navy would never want for oaks to build the fighting ships upon which the country's safety depended. Life in Nelson’s Navy, Dudley Pope The late Sixteenth and early Seventeenth centuries in Britain (Elizabeth I and James I) saw significant increases in the population and a soaring demand for wood for all purposes, as can be seen from the rising prices. The smelting of metals at high temperatures required huge amounts of wood to be turned into charcoal, and by 1615, we see James I issuing a ban on burning firewood for glass production by declaring that “the great waste of timber in making glass is a matter of serious concern.” Coal, readily available in Britain, was the obvious alternative. Anthracite (high grade) coal burns hotter than wood, and takes up less volume for transport and storage than wood, burns for longer, and provides more consistent heat. The hottest wood fire burns at around 1,600 degrees F, whilst anthracite burns at about 3,000 degrees F. It takes roughly two tons of bulky wood to provide the energy equivalent of one ton of more compact coal. Therefore, I think that the answer to the question is that coal is not necessary to power industrial processes but that there simply wasn’t enough wood available to meet industrial demands at the scale required. The industrial revolution could still have occurred, but it would have been much more limited in scope because of the limitations in the fuels available and its supply.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In a tank with no ammo left, do the crew members have to abandon the vehicle for it to be captured? Can they continue fighting from inside like in WW2 movies?
Answer: Continue to fight with what? If a tank had no ammo, it would be prudent to withdraw out of sight of the enemy until it can resupply. If the tank is unable to move for some reason, a shed track, etc., the crew would have to make a decision based on the tactical situation. In some cases it might be safer to stay in the tank until recovered, in other cases it would be safer to leave the tank and seek shelter with friendly forces. In WW2, it was standard to keep on shooting at a tank until it started to burn, as otherwise you can’t tell whether it has actually been knocked out of not. Therefore sitting in a tank doing nothing in sight of the enemy is a bad idea. Having said that, bailing out of a tank is not an easy option as it is generally not possible to do in a stealthy way and the enemy is likely to machine gun the occupants as they emerge. For obvious reasons, there aren’t many (any?) photos of crews actually bailing out, but this photo gives an idea of how exposed the crew would be when bailing out. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was the US considered allies to Napoleon’s France?
Answer: The new United States had a rocky relationship with both Britain and France. In 1778, the United States signed the Treaties of Alliance, the Treaty of Amity and Commerce and the Treaty of Alliance, with Louis XVI (not Napoleon). The Treaty of Alliance was a mutual defence pact and had no specific end date. Treaties signed with both France (left) and Great Britain (right) Following the signing of the Treaty of Paris in 1783 which marked the end of the Revolutionary War, the Treaty of Alliance became contentious in the United States. Alexander Hamilton and the Federalists wanted to cancel the treaty, but Washington and the Anti-Federalists (the Democratic-Republican Party) were determined that the treaty should stay in force. Technically the treaty was automatically invalidated on the death of Louis XVI in January 1793 and, regardless of diplomatic niceties, it was effectively killed by Washington’s Proclamation of Neutrality in the same year and the Neutrality Act of 1794. The French believed that the Treaty of Alliance bound the United States to defend French possessions in the West Indies during the War of the First Coalition between 1792 and 1797. The United States was, by this time, benefiting hugely from trade with Great Britain and demurred. In the same year, 1794, the United States signed the Jay Treaty, or Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, with Great Britain. Although not a military alliance, this treaty decisively moved the United States away from the French orbit. The Jay Treaty was in force until 1806, at which point it lapsed and was not renewed as Britain and the United States headed towards conflict in the War of 1812. Before that point, in 1793 the United States was having trouble repaying the large sums of money that it had borrowed from France to pay for the Revolutionary War and suspended payments. This and the signing of the Jay Treaty caused relations with France to deteriorate and by 1796 the French started to seize over three hundred American ships. Following a failed diplomatic mission to France, the XYZ Affair, the United States officially nullified the Treaty of Alliance in July, 1798, a year before Napoleon became First Consul. At this point, the United States was very close to declaring war with France and this led to the Quasi-War of 1798–1800, during which period American ships were allowed to sail in convoys under the protection of the Royal Navy (the Continental Navy having been stood down in 1785 and the United States Navy not having any ships until 1797) and American privateers operated from British ports in the Caribbean. The Quasi-War involved multiple small ship actions against privateers and frigates and included the capture of the frigate L'Insurgente and the corvettes Le Berceau and Flambeau. However, over two thousand American ships were seized, some 38% of the United States merchant fleet. British view of the Quasi-War - Five Frenchmen plunder the female America The Quasi-War ended with the Convention of 1800, or Treaty of Mortefontaine, which finally terminated, for about the fourth time, the original 1778 Treaty of Alliance. Although not viewed very favourably in the United States at the time, the Convention of 1800 did set the scene for the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 after Napoleon gained control of Louisiana from the Spanish in 1800 as part of the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso. This 828,000 square mile purchase more or less doubled the theoretical size of the United States. In practice, France did not control most of the territory that it sold and Napoleon probably had no legal right to sell it. The United States purchase was therefore legally dubious on several grounds and, in any case, they had to seize most of the lands from the indigenous inhabitants who had not ceded their lands to Spain, France, or the United States. Ultimately, this led to the Trail of Tears and the forced resettlement of tens of thousands of Native Americans. After the winding down of the Quasi-War between the United States and France, the scene was set for the outbreak of the War of 1812 between the United States and Great Britain, which lasted until 1814. This war, in turn, was partly caused by British restrictions on America’s trade with France, just as the Quasi-War was partly caused by French restrictions on America’s trade with Great Britain. Between 1804 and 1807, some 731 American ships were seized by either Britain or France. The United States was simply being tossed to and fro as a side-effect of the Great Powers’ struggles in Europe. Internal politics within the United States also confused matters. The Federalists were criticized by the Democratic-Republicans for being too close to Britain, while the Democratic-Republicans were criticized by the Federalists as being too close to France and the tyrant Napoleon. Thus during the thirty six years between 1778 and 1814, the United States signed treaties with both France and Great Britain and went to war with both France and Great Britain. However, as Napoleon did not become First Consul until 1799 (he became Emperor in 1804), and the 1778 Treaty of Alliance was nullified by the United States in 1798, it was not in force when he came to power and the United States was never allied with Napoleon.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: I've read somewhere, that the armour of the Panzer 38(t) wasn't RHA. If not RHA, what was it?
Answer: RHA is the abbreviation for rolled homogeneous armour, a hot-rolling process that changes the crystalline structure of the steel, homogenising it throughout. The Pz 38(t) armour was produced at the Poldi steel works in Kladno, Czechoslovakia and had either 25mm front armour or 50mm front armour made from a pair of 25mm plates, probably because the mill could only produce plates with a maximum thickness of 25mm. It appears that the inner plate was homogenised and the outer homogenised and the cemented (carburized) - treated with carbon-bearing gases to harden the surface. Panzerkampfwagen 38(t) Ausf A The alternative to homogeneous armour was cast armour. Obviously cast armour allows any shape to be produced whilst RHA plates are generally flat but rather more durable. I think (but am happy to be corrected) that the Panzer 38(t) did have RHA armour but with a cemented face. Panzer 38(t) riveted double plate front armour

Question: What light armed reconnaissance helocopter flying or in development offers better performance than the OH-58D Kiowa?
Answer: I don’t think that there will ever be any more reconnaissance helicopters now that the OH-58 has been retired. From now on their role will be filled by UAVs and drones. Sikorski Raider FARA concept Bell 360 Invictus concept This was actually the fourth OH-58 replacement program to be cancelled prior to reaching production: the Comanche LHX program (1982–2004), the Bell ARH-79 Arapaho Armed Reconnaissance Helicopter (2004–2006), and the Armed Aerial Scout (2012–2013) which evaluated various off-the-shelf designs. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How badly did the Battle of Britain deplete the resources of the German Luftwaffe?
Answer: The Battle of Britain (10th July - 31st October 1940) was a body blow for the Luftwaffe and one from which it never fully recovered. A Junkers Ju 88 brought down over England To be specific, the Luftwaffe lost 518 single-engine fighters (47% of strength), 235 twin-engine fighters (66%), 88 dive bombers (21%), 621 (45%) bombers, and 89 other aircraft. A total of 1,462 aircraft lost or 45% of their starting strength. General Werner Kreipe, later Chief of the Luftwaffe's General Staff, and the commander of III./KG 2 during the battle, described the Luftwaffe as "bled almost to death, and suffering losses that could never be made good throughout the course of the war". Messerschmitt Bf 109s The Luftwaffe had lost 26% of its combat aircraft in the Battle for France (May-June 1940) and together with the losses incurred during the Battle of Britain that means that between May and September 1940 the Luftwaffe had lost 63% of its starting strength or 2,472 combat aircraft in total. However, whilst aircraft can easily be replaced, other consequences have a more lingering impact. The Battle of Britain was the Luftwaffe’s first major defeat and its effects were far more than the merely material. We have looked at aircraft, but we should also consider aircrew losses, morale, intelligence, leadership, strategy, tactics, equipment, and policies. Messerschmitt Bf 110s The loss of an aircraft does not necessarily imply the loss of its crew. However, as much of the Battle took place either over Great Britain or over the sea, the Luftwaffe suffered very high attrition rates in aircrew. In the sample that I have for August 1940, 71% of the aircrew assigned to written off aircraft were lost permanently (e.g. killed, missing, or captured) and a further 12% were injured. As a result the number of operational crews dropped steadily despite replacements, dropping to 59% for bomber crews by September. The battle also clearly showed up that there were significant problems with Luftwaffe intelligence, leadership, and tactics which the aircrews could hardly fail to notice. Combined with the Luftwaffe policy of not rotating their aircrews, this led to a decrease in morale as which became known as Kanalkrankheit, or Channel sickness, where aircrew increasingly reported sick or aborted missions for minor technical reasons. JU 87 Stukas In addition, it soon became clear to the Germans that their air strategy had not equipped them for strategic bombardment and that they did not have aircraft with the range or bombload to support such demands. Some Luftwaffe equipment was also found lacking. It soon became clear that the Ju-87 Stuka, could not survive without air superiority and that the other German bombers lacked defensive armament. It is being said that the British are already on their last legs, but when you hear what the operation pilots - and particularly the bomber crews - have to report... the losses suffered by our bomber crews must be terrible. Heinkel He 111 bombers Dornier Do 17 bombers Junkers Ju 88 bombers The Battle of Britain was the moment the shine came off; the first time that the flaws inherent in the Luftwaffe became glaringly apparent and an abrupt halt to its string of victories. The psychological impacts were perhaps more important than the material losses. Although the number of aircraft produced continued to rise, the problems with pilot replacement were already apparent by the end of the battle. The Luftwaffe lost a high proportion of its best aircrews and never recovered to the same level of quality. A Luftwaffe pilot in the Battle of Britain would have received around 240 hours of training and would probably have had months of operational experience. His counterpart coming into service in 1943 or 1944 would have been lucky to have had 80 hours of training and pilots on squadrons only averaged eight to thirty days of operational experience. The Germans started the war with a cadre of well-trained, experienced pilots, but training was to become the Luftwaffe's Achilles’ heel. As the war progressed the growing disparity in training between the Germans and the Allies became critical. The Battle of Britain marked the start of that process. Replacement pilots in the Luftwaffe were so poorly trained they did not need Allied fighters to bring them down in large numbers Why Air Forces Fail In the midst of the Battle of Britain, Churchill made a speech where he said of the pilots: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few. The Few, the 2,937 British and allied aircrew who flew in the Battle, dealt the Luftwaffe a blow from which it would never fully recover. Two years later, after El Alamein, Churchill said: Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning. These words were written in a different context, but are perhaps equally appropriate to the Battle of Britain as it marked the end of the beginning for the Luftwaffe. It’s final end that would be protracted through five more long years of war and cost the Luftwaffe 76,875 aircraft (about 43,000 lost in combat) and the lives of 113,650 aircrew. The Few. Front row (left to right) are Bernard Jennings, Colin McFie, Howard Burton and Philip Leckman.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Are some people in Britain envious, jealous, bitter about and/or resentful of Germany’s success and status in Europe since the end of WW2?
Answer: I dare say that some are, people are people and hold all sorts of views. Germany caused untold death, grief, and destruction over the course of the 20th Century and older people may have had friends or relatives who died in the war and remember that. There are also things that cause offence. You can find apologists on this site attempting, for instance, to blame Great Britain for WW1 (laugh out loud), and other people peddling false statistics about Dresden and trying to claim some form of moral relativity on that basis. These people are not even necessarily German, but this sort of nonsense is likely to get short answers, which some people might interpret as anti-German. However, I don’t think that you could say that many people in Britain are bitter about Germany’s success. The Germans worked extremely hard to rebuild their economy from the ruins after WW2, the Wirtschaftswunder, and they fully deserve to reap the rewards for that. Trümmerfrauen or “rubble women” start to rebuild Germany by salvaging bricks Germany is a big country and it is always going, for good or ill, to play a significant role in pan-European politics. The trick is to keep the Germans and the French from each others’ throats and that is what the ECSC/EEC/EU is for. It seems to be working reasonably well so far. Given the general tone of this question, it is also worth noting that Germany is no longer quite the economic miracle that it once was, and that its status has also taken a pasting recently - particularly with regard to its approach towards Russia. No country gets it right all the time. Resentment is, anyway, a pointless activity. The best thing is to look at what the Germans did well, and what they did badly, and try to learn and apply the appropriate lessons. One of which is that you don’t get something for nothing - you have to work hard for it.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Germany consider invading England after France surrendered and before The Battle of Britain?
Answer: No. The suppression of the RAF, aka the Battle of Britain, was considered a vital pre-condition for the launch of Unternehmen Seelöwe (Operation Sealion) the invasion of the British Isles. German shipping under attack by the RAF Führer Directive 16, issued in July 1940, set out four pre-conditions for the launching of Sealion. These four conditions were: All four were huge tasks and it was utterly beyond the capability of the Germans to achieve any of them in either the short or medium term. In any case the French signed the Armistice on the 25th June 1940 and the Battle of Britain started on the 10th of July 1940. The two weeks between the two events wasn’t anywhere remotely near sufficient time to plan, assemble, and launch an invasion. In any case, Führer Directive 16 wasn’t even issued until a week after the Battle of Britain started. A Squadron of Hurricanes Not only was an early invasion logistically completely impossible, any attempt to launch it would have been utterly slaughtered unless the RAF had been suppressed first.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is there such a hatred towards Scotland and Scots from England when it comes to Scottish Independence? It seems there is an anger, dare I say xenophobia for daring to ask for a vote to leave the UK.
Answer: I think that if the rest of the UK were to be given a vote on Scottish independence, you’d very quickly see how completely and utterly wrong you are. There only appears to be xenophobia on one side of this debate.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What factors influenced the Allies' decision to land on Utah Beach instead of Omaha Beach during D-Day?
Answer: Well, clearly the Allies landed on Omaha and Utah beaches as well as Gold, Sword, and Juno beaches. Silly question, so on to a spot of D-Day trivia. In general, Normandy was chosen by planners because it lay within range of air cover from over 200 fighter fields in the United Kingdom and was less heavily defended than the more obvious Pas de Calais sector whilst still providing the shortest distance between Great Britain and the Continent. The Bay of the Seine had flat, sandy, load-bearing beaches, the necessary frontage, reasonable tides, at least some protection from the weather, and ready access to the hinterland. Sword and Utah, the beaches at each extremity of the landings, were added quite late in the planning process in December 1943. Adding these two beaches doubled the frontage of the invasion and necessitated a month-long delay so that the required landing craft and personnel could be assembled. Utah was added both because the whole scope of the invasion was increased and also because the Allies had their eyes on capturing the port of Cherbourg. US infantry landing on Utah Beach The American beaches were originally called X-Ray and Yoke from the phonetic alphabet. The names were changed by Bradley, the commander of the US First Army, in March 1944. Apocryphally, Bradley discovered that two soldiers doing some work for him were from Omaha, Nebraska, and Provo, Utah respectively. Why the beaches weren’t called Omaha and Provo, which would make more sense, I do not know. Apropos of nothing, I seem to remember having a very decent breakfast in JD’s restaurant in Provo in 1994. I remember it because it was either on, or very close to, the 50th anniversary of D-Day. The British beaches were originally named after species of fish, Goldfish, Jellyfish, Swordfish, and Bandfish. However, the Canadians objected to their beach being called Jelly and the name was changed to Juno instead. Band beach is the forgotten sixth beach and was the intended landing beach for 46 and 47 Royal Marine Commandoes for an assault on the German batteries at Houlgate (Battery de Tournebride) and Benerville (Mont Canisy). This operation was cancelled after the naval bombardment of the batteries as they were deemed to be no longer a threat to the landings at Sword.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How does the UK deal with Winston Churchill being both an adversary to Hitler and a heinous proponent of the Bengal famine?
Answer: This really doesn’t deserve an answer but, unfortunately, there are too many people who might give this sort of rubbish credence. If anyone was responsible for the Bengal Famine it was the Japanese who cut off all food imports from Burma. Churchill was neither a heinous proponent of the famine nor, indeed, a proponent of any kind. Churchill was, of course, not directly responsible for the governance of India or for the food situation in Bengal. There were many layers between him and the situation including the Government of Bengal, the Prime Minister of Bengal, A. K. Fazlul Huk, the Viceroy, the India Office, and the Secretary of State for India. Churchill did not concern himself with the day-to-day running of India and a perusal of the cabinet minutes shows that issues connected with India came up rarely. The Cabinet was made aware of the poor harvest in Bengal but was assured that there was enough food in India itself to supply Bengal. When the severity of the situation became known the cabinet put measures in place - as far as could be done in the middle of a World War - to mitigate the problem. Any decision made regarding the Bengal Famine will be recorded in the cabinet minutes or in Hansard. If you have any comments on how Churchill encouraged the famine, please provide the appropriate reference from these documents as they are available online - otherwise you are simply talking out of your fundament.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it true that U.S. Admiral Ernest King, when refused a British aircraft carrier for support for a Pacific Operation, never again requested British support or participation in the Naval aspect of the Pacific Theater?
Answer: The public perception of Admiral King is heavily based on the mythology that has grown around him rather than the ascertainable facts. King is often portrayed as anti-British when in truth he was probably just anti-everyone. Famously, one of his six daughters (unspecified) is supposed to have said that "he is the most even-tempered person in the United States Navy. He is always in a rage". King served with the Royal Navy in the later stages of WWI and apparently evaluated the experience positively. Moreover, as a personal sartorial touch more in line with Royal Navy than US Navy uniform regulations, King often carried a white pocket square in the breast pocket of his service dress blue uniform jacket. The British General Ismay described King as “…tough as nails and carried himself as stiffly as a poker. He was blunt and stand-offish, almost to the point of rudeness. At the start, he was intolerant and suspicious of all things British, especially the Royal Navy; but he was almost equally intolerant and suspicious of the American Army. War against Japan was the problem to which he had devoted the study of a lifetime, and he resented the idea of American resources being used for any other purpose than to destroy the Japanese”. Admiral King, complete with “British” pocket square My guess would be that he was just hard-driving and intolerant of slackness “I don’t care how good they are. Unless they get a kick in the ass every six weeks, they’ll slack off”. He did not suffer fools or disagreement and had a volcanic temperament that would rule him out from high command these days. In a similar vein, Admiral Rickover, the father of the US Navy’s nuclear submarine force, was also described as intolerant, "not too easy to get along with" and "not too popular". Not suffering disagreement is a double-edged sword. Things need to get done and decisions need to be made; a military service is not a talking shop. However, a wise commander should not rely entirely on his own certitudes. I would be very tempted to draw a comparison between King and the British Admiral Jackie Fisher, who was also not known for suffering fools gladly but, by sheer force of personality, drove the modernisation of the Royal Navy in the early years of the 20th Century. King certainly made his share of mistakes, but, as Chief of Naval Operations and Commander-in-Chief U.S. Fleet, he had very wide responsibilities and so it would have been remarkable if he hadn’t. In 1942 the US Navy had lost the carriers Lexington, Yorktown, and Hornet, and Saratoga was undergoing repair in Pearl Harbour. This left the US with only the damaged Enterprise operational in the Pacific. King had asked for a Royal Navy carrier in June after Midway. Being rather busy engaged against the Axis in the Atlantic, Mediterranean, and the Indian Ocean at the time, the British only freed up the Victorious (often referred to as the USS Robin) in December after the loss of the Hornet, which must have caused King some anxious moments in the intervening months. Therefore, his request wasn’t refused, but it was somewhat delayed. HMS Victorious in Pearl Harbour King’s later objections to the role of the British Pacific Fleet are not unreasonable in the light of the huge logistic preparations required for the campaign and the additional complexity required to support the British Fleet. I imagine that, had the situation been reversed, the same considerations would have applied. However, there was definitely also an element of chauvinism for his own service involved. At the Octagon Conference, King clearly wanted the US Navy to have all the glory for the final defeat of the Japanese in the Pacific. From a serving admiral this is an entirely understandable if rather short-sighted point of view. In this matter King was quickly overridden by both Marshall and Arnold. War sometimes requires hard-driving to get things done. However, it is an interesting exercise to compare Eisenhower’s conciliating style of leadership with the antagonistic style of King. Perhaps sometimes it is possible to become so focussed on immediate objectives that you lose sight of the bigger picture.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During WWII in the Pacific did the British army (note: not the Australians or New Zealanders) ever fight against the Japanese army in any place not part of the 1939 British Empire? If so, where and when?
Answer: The British Army, as opposed to the Royal Navy and the RAF, played no part in the Pacific Theatres as the Pacific was an American endeavour with assistance from Australia and New Zealand. Edit: Stephen Phillips points out below that the British Army, in the shape of 16 AA Brigade (6 and 77 Heavy AA Regiments and 21, 35, and 48 Light AA Regiments) supported by B Squadron of 3rd Hussars, did take part in the defence of Java in February and March 1942. Java was not part of the British Empire. In the Far East, the British and Indian Armies, as XIV Army, were occupied fighting the Japanese 15th, 28th, and 33rd Armies in the South-East Asian Theatre, generally known as the Burma Campaign. As a result, the XIV Army, nearly a million men by 1944, were fighting in Singapore, Malaya, Burma and India from 1941 to the end of the war. As far as I am aware, this fighting was all within the extent of the British Empire. The British Army was later involved in some local conflicts in the Dutch East Indies, Thailand/Siam, and Vietnam, which were not part of the British Empire, but this was immediately after the Japanese surrender. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Regarding the 1962 version of Mutiny on Bounty, in terms of actual British history, did Mills get off light with only two dozen lashes?
Answer: No, I think that would have constituted a very heavy punishment. I have written about William Bligh before as he is an interesting character (see below). One of the salient points regarding him is that he was most definitely not a flogging captain. His overall flogging rate was exceptionally low for the time, lower for example than that of Captain Cook. A naval flogging The Mutiny on the Bounty occurred in 1789 which is an interesting date because it is the year of the French Revolution and there is evidence that the severity of punishments in the Royal Navy increased in the wake of the Revolution as commanders imposed tighter discipline on their crews. However, the French Revolution commenced in May 1789 and the Bounty sailed for Tahiti in December 1787 and so cannot have been affected by these events. In the period 1740 through 1789, the average rate of punishment per member of a ship’s company per annum was 1.34 lashes, with an average punishment of per flogging of 13.6 lashes (Threat, Deterrence, and Penal Severity: An Analysis of Flogging in the Royal Navy, 1740–1820, Underwood et al). Up to 1806, a Captain could only order 12 lashes on his own authority without a Court Martial. This limit was exceeded in practice but, prior to 1789, 12 lashes seems to have been the customary limit. The main offences that merited a flogging were Neglect of Duty (23%), Drunkenness (22%), Insolence (16%) and Theft (14%), followed by Mutiny (7%), Assault (6%), Desertion (6%) Forbidden Commerce (2%) and Sodomy (a capital crime) and Filthiness at (1%) each. The Bounty had a crew of 46, including Bligh, but 15 of them could not be flogged, being officers (2, Bligh and Fletcher Christian a Master’s Mate appointed acting-Lieutenant during the voyage), warrant officers (5, including the surgeon), midshipmen (6), or civilian botanists (2). The remaining 31 were petty officers, seamen, or idlers and could be flogged. It is known that Mathew Quintal received 12 lashes for insolence and mutinous behaviour in March 1788, the first flogging in five months of voyaging. In January 1789, three men, Churchill, Muspratt, and Millward deserted and were flogged on recapture (the second time Muspratt had been flogged). This is interesting because, in the film, Mills sets fire to the ship whilst, in reality, this act was carried out by Mathew Quintal. John Mills was a Gunner's mate on the Bounty and I have not seen any evidence that he was ever flogged as he seems to have been well behaved before the mutiny itself. Therefore, as the events occur prior to the tightening of discipline in the wake of the French revolution, I would suggest that a flogging for insolence was certainly possible (see above) but that in the light of Quintal’s punishment and Bligh’s known leniency, it was more likely to have been 12 lashes than two dozen. In another ship, it could have been more, but the most likely number would still have been 12. A few years later the punishment would probably have been more severe but even a grotesque example like Robert Corbet of the Nereide (134 floggings in 211 days for a crew of around 250) only averaged 17 lashes per punishment.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Japanese build a good ship and fighter planes during WW II, but why did they only make tanquetee and light tank?
Answer: What’s a light tank? There is quite a range, but if we consider the German Pz 35(t), the Soviet BT5, the US M5 Stuart and the British Vickers Mk VI, all of which are classified as light tanks, we can perhaps characterise them on average as weighing 11 tons, having 28mm of armour, a 31mm main weapon, and 3.5 crew. As for medium tanks, the Pz IV, T34/76, Sherman, and Cromwell can be characterised on average as weighing 28 tons, having 70mm of armour, a 75mm main weapon, and 5 crew. The most common Japanese light tank was the Type 95 Ha-Go with 2,300 built. The Ha-Go weighed 7 tons, had 12mm of armour, a 37mm main weapon and 3 crew - quite close to the German Pz II in size but more heavily armed. Type 95 Ha-Go However, the Japanese did produce Medium tanks. Of these the Type 97 Chi-Ha was the most common, with 3,000 produced. The Chi-Ha weighed 16 tons, had 25mm of armour, a 57mm main weapon and 4 crew. Heavier than a light tank, but light for a medium. Type 97 Chi-Ha Produced in limited numbers (around 170 each) were the Type 1 Ch-He and Type 3 Chi-Nu mediums. These weighed in at 20 tons, had 50mm of armour, a 47mm and 75mm main gun respectively and 5 crew. Therefore the Chi-Nu in particular was quite comparable with other nations’ medium tanks if a tad on the light side. Type 3 Chi-Nu tanks and Type 3 Ho-Ni III tank destroyers The Japanese obviously used tanks but they lagged behind somewhat. This is due to a number of reasons: firstly, the Japanese Navy had prior claim over steel stocks, secondly, the main deployment of armour was in China and the Chinese didn’t have much in the way of tanks and, thirdly, the terrain that the Japanese fought in wasn’t the most suitable for armoured warfare. As a result, tank development didn’t feature highly in Japanese priorities.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain consider using a fighter plane like the P-51 Mustang during World War II instead of their outdated Spitfires?
Answer: The RAF did actually use about 1,500 P-51 Mustangs for limited purposes, but the P-51 never replaced the Spitfire as the RAF’s main front line fighter. Regrettably, this is either a trolling question or one from someone who is ill-informed on the topic. The Spitfire continued to evolve throughout the war and didn’t become outdated until the advent of the jet sounded the death knell all piston-engined aircraft. Time didn’t stand still, and the Spitfire Mk XIV of 1944 was a very different beast to the Spitfire Mk II that took part in the Battle of Britain in 1940. Spitfire XIV Rather than us armchair aficionados, I think that we have to give the last word to Eric “Winkle” Brown, the Royal Navy test pilot, who flew 487 different types of aircraft and remains the world record holder: I have flown both for many hours, and would choose the Spitfire [over the Mustang] if given a choice in a fight to the death. The Spitfire Mk XIV was designed from the ground up as an interceptor and had the advantage over the Mustang in a dogfight. The Mustang was an escort fighter and had the advantage in endurance. They had the same top speed but the Spitfire was a much faster climber and more agile. The FW190D-9 was broadly equal to both. Personally, I would like to have been allotted a P-47D Thunderbolt because of its outstanding record in getting its pilots home in one piece. Horses for courses. FW190D-9 Thunderbolt William “Poppy” Dunn (US Eagle Squadron ace who flew both Spitfires and P-51s) wrote: Now, if I had to make the choice of one fighter aircraft above all the others - one that I'd rather have tied to the seat of my pants in any tactical situation - it would be, without any doubt, the world's greatest propeller driven flying machine - the magnificent and immortal Spitfire. Spitfire and Mustang All fine fighters. You’d think yourself lucky to be assigned any of them.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there any British people who fought for William at the Battle of Hastings, or were all the fighters Normans who had moved there before then? If there were British fighters, what might have motivated them to fight for William?
Answer: It is certainly not impossible that exiles or others with a grudge against Harold fought with William at Hastings, but if so there is no record of them. It is believed that William’s forces included men from Normandy, Brittany, Maine, Anjou, Poitou, Isle de France, Picardy, Boulogne, and Flanders, but not, as far as we know, from England. The Battle of Hastings was fought quite a while ago, on the 14th of October 1066 to be precise, and, as you might expect, there is not much in the way of documentation. The only reliable contemporary, or near contemporary, sources are the Bayeux Tapestry (c. 1075) the Gesta Guillelmi II Ducis Normannorum (c. 1075) and the Historia Ecclesiastica (c. 1120). Although there were probably around 8,000 men on each side, these sources provide the names of only fifteen individuals who fought with William: Robert de Beaumont; Eustace, Count of Boulogne; William, Count of Évreux; Geoffrey II, Count of Perche; William FitzOsbern; Haimo, Vicomte of Thouars; Walter Giffard, Lord of Longueville; Hugh de Montfort, Lord of Montfort-sur-Risle; Raoul II of Tosny; Hugh de Grandmesnil; William de Warenne; William Malet; Odo de Conteville, Bishop of Bayeux; Turstin FitzRolf; and Engenulf de Laigle. This is not to say that none of these men had links with England. For instance it is said that William Malet’s mother was English and that his sister, Ælgifu, was married to Ælfgar, the Earl of Mercia. Their daughter Ealdgyth (Edith of Mercia), William Malet’s niece, married Harold in January 1066. Therefore, there was obviously the potential for close ties between the Normans and the English, even with the Royal Family in some cases. Above is a detail from the Bayeux Tapestry. At the left is Bishop Odo holding a club or mace (Hic Odo Eps Baculu Tenens) rather than a sword as bishops were not supposed to shed blood. The man on the right, holding the standard, is identified as Eustace, Count of Boulogne but may actually have been Turstin FitzRolf. William is second from the right. On the English side, we only know of a very few individuals who fought with Harold: his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, Godric the Sheriff, Thurkill of Berkshire, Breme, and someone known only as the son of Helloc.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What do you think of Rheinmetall's goal to produce up to 1.1 million artillery shells a year by 2027?
Answer: It’s a start, but possibly too little too late, as several estimates suggest that the Russians are already producing around 3 million shells per year and still ramping up. The absolute number is irrelevant, it’s the ratio that matters. It’s going to be difficult for the NATO nations to compete whilst maintaining a peacetime economy if the Russians have moved to a wartime economy. NATO could certainly out produce Russia if it wanted to, it has a much larger economy even in PPP terms, but at what cost? What tax rises and cuts to services would be required to match or out-perform Russia? I notice that the MOD recently (Jan 2024) issued the following statement: The Ministry of Defence (MOD) placed an order in June 2023 with BAE Systems to provide an eight-fold increase in production capability of 155mm shells. Call me cynical, but those look like weasel words to me - shorthand for we’re increasing from virtually nothing to not very much - otherwise why not just state the number? I hope I’m wrong. I understand that a 155mm shell can cost anything between $1,000 and $100,000 depending on production volumes and on how smart it is (Excalibur for instance). Even with volume production and dumb shells, we’re talking about billions of dollars per year to outperform Russia and that’s before we start looking at the, much more expensive, missiles that we will also need to be producing in volume. In 1917, Britain produced over 76 million artillery shells. If things continue this way, it’s going to get expensive fast folks.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why were women originally allowed to retire at 60 years of age in the UK, rather than 65?
Answer: Until the 1993 White Paper 'Equality in State Pension Age' set out the UK Government's intention to equalise men and women's State Pension age at 65 there was a clear inequality. Women live longer than men, so it makes absolutely no sense for them to retire earlier - if anything, they should retire later than men if both sexes are to receive an equal number of pensionable years. In fact, in 1990 the statistics were as follows, with women receiving pensions, on average, for over twice as long as men. I wondered how this obvious inequality came about and the background is quite indeed interesting. The Old Age Pensions Act 1908 established a pension of 5/- per week (approximately £25 today) for both men and women over 70 (or 7/6d for a couple) who had resided in the UK for at least 20 years and who were of good character. Excluded were those in receipt of poor relief, those being held in lunatic asylums, those who had served a prison sentence and been released less than ten years before, those convicted of drunkenness under the Inebriates Act 1898 (vide Jane Cakebread), and any person who was guilty of ‘habitual failure to work’ according to their ability. Discrimination based on sex began with the Old Age and Widows' Pensions Act 1940 and was promoted by the National Spinsters’ Pensions Association (NSPA) which was established in Bradford in 1935 by a confectioner, Florence White. By 1939, the NSPA had over 150,000 members (The Spinster, ii, May 1939) and was probably the largest women’s reform movement in the country. This was, needless to say, related to WW1 and the resulting 38% of eligible women who found themselves spinsters (British Social Trends since 1900, Halsey, 1988) in the 1930s. As an aside, the UK suffered 888,000 dead and a further 1,700,000 wounded which, in terms of the working age male population (15–64) in 1914 was 7.7% of the workforce killed and another 14.8% (badly) wounded. Under the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act 1925, widows could claim a pension of 10/- per week regardless of their age, and the average age for widows claiming a pension was 55. White and the NSPA believed this to be discrimination, describing unmarried women as ‘war widows’ and suggesting that they should be treated as such to ensure equality. The NSPA became a formidable pressure group collecting over a million signatures to a petition demanding the reform of spinsters’ pensions, sponsoring mass meetings and marches (shades of the suffragettes) and resolutions at the TUC. This led to the creation of a government appointed Committee on Pensions for Unmarried Women in 1938 and a parliamentary campaign supported by 200 MPs. The actual change happened indirectly when it was decided that married women aged 60 or over should receive their pensions when their husbands retired – to avoid household income dropping precipitately. As married women were generally younger than their husbands that meant that, on average, they would receive their pensions at 60. This was obviously inequitable, as married women who had never worked would potentially receive a pension at 60, whilst women who had worked had to wait until they were 65. This was politically unsustainable, and that’s how the pension age for all women came to be 60 rather than 65. Bravo Florence (bottom right).

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How active was the US Navy during WW2? What was the fatality rate of US Navy compared to US Marines, US Air force, and US Army?
Answer: How active was the US Navy during WW2? Pretty active. Mostly fighting in the Pacific against the Japanese, but also lending a hand in the Atlantic. Carriers at war Here are some statistics from the Naval History and Heritage Command showing the growth of the US Navy from mid-1941 to the end of WW2. This staggering expansion, and the logistics associated with it, must be one of the most phenomenal technical feats ever accomplished. US Navy during the Marshall Islands Campaign As far as casualty data is concerned, this was fun. There are more contradictory statistics out there than you can shake a stick at. Also, the AAF was part of the Army until 1947 and so there is extra work to try and disaggregate the statistics for that. I’ve also included the Coast Guard and the US Merchant Marine as they also served. My main source of data is from the Defense Casualty Analysis System which is maintained by the Defense Manpower Data Center, part of the Department of Defense. They should know what they are doing. I have supplemented this with data derived from other sources as necessary and this as accurate as I can make it. What can we deduce from these statistics? Firstly, you were much more likely to be wounded in the Army or, even more so, in the Marines - which makes sense. Secondly, you were more likely to be killed outright than wounded in the Navy or, even more so, the AAF. Thirdly, you were much more likely to be killed in an accident in the AAF - which, again, makes sense. The AAF lost 65,164 aircraft in WW2, of which only 22,948 (35%) were lost in combat. The other 65% were lost in non-operational accidents, including 21,583 (33%) lost in the Continental United States. More than 13,000 US pilots lost their lives whilst training. How does the fatality rate compare? Join the Navy, it had the lowest fatality rate of all the services by a considerable margin. Avoid the Merchant Marine, the Marines, and the AAF. The US Navy at the surrender of Japan

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Churchill and Monty go over the Rhine River together? If so, when did this occur?
Answer: There are photographs of them crossing the Rhine on the 25th of March 1945, so yes, they did go over the Rhine together. Churchill continued to tempt fate, even as the war drew to a close. In March 1945, the Germans were in retreat. By 10 March, the Allies were on the west bank of the Rhine, the traditional border of Germany that no foreign army had crossed in 140 years (since Napoleon on 1805). On 24 March, the Allies started crossing the Rhine under a barrage of two thousand guns. Churchill, never one to miss out on the action, watched the momentous crossing with General Bernard Montgomery – and even had a picnic lunch on the banks of the river. He and Montgomery then crossed the Rhine into enemy territory. They later went to the railway bridge at Wesel, in sunshine, when they came under enemy fire, with shells falling only a few hundred yards away, into the river, and sending up great jets of water. This adventurous expedition was later criticised by Eisenhower – who felt it was far too daring – saying that if he’d been there, he’d never have allowed Churchill to cross the river when it was still so dangerous. International Churchill Society In fact there are two photos in two different vehicles. The photo above is of a US LCVP landing craft with Montgomery (21AG), Alanbrooke (CIGS), and a bunch of US brass including Simpson (9A) and three other generals. In the photo below, Churchill, Montgomery, and Alanbrooke have embarked on a British LVT-2 Buffalo with some British brass - perhaps to make the return trip across the river (Monty is at the rear right).

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is the quote "You cannot invade mainland United States. There would be a rifle behind every blade of grass." attributed to General Isoroku Yamamoto based on a true story?
Answer: Admiral Yamamoto, not General. No, it is almost certainly bogus as there is no known citation for this supposed quote. The words have sometimes been attributed to the Gordon Prange, a historian on the staff of Douglas MacArthur, but it is found nowhere in his writings either. The quote should be regarded as bogus until someone can cite when and where it originated. Nor did Admiral Yamamoto ever say: I fear all we have done is to awaken a sleeping giant and fill him with a terrible resolve. That quote appears to be derived from the 1970 film Tora! Tora!, Tora! (great film). What he did say was: A military man can scarcely pride himself on having smitten a sleeping enemy. This is a reference regarding his disappointment over the bungled Japanese declaration of war which wasn’t delivered until a few hours after the attack on Pearl Harbour. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many aircraft did the Royal Air Force lose during World War II?
Answer: This is not an easy question to answer. Are we including RCAF, RAAF, and foreign squadrons that flew under RAF command? Are we discussing operational losses or all losses? Are we including written off aircraft? Training and, indeed, simply flying were dangerous activities in WW2 even without enemy intervention, and many aircraft were lost in training accidents and to other non-operational causes. My best guess would be that a little over 19,000 aircraft were lost, with Fighter Command losing 4,790, Coastal Command 2,060, and Bomber Command 12,330. That latter figures comes from the Bomber Command Museum of Canada and is higher than the typically quoted 8,325. I assume that the lower figure covers operational losses and the higher figure losses to all causes. I believe that this figure only covers the British Isles and North-West Europe and therefore excludes RAF aircraft deployed in other theatres and other Empire contingents - probably bring the total up to around 22,000 excluding training aircraft lost in North America. To illustrate the point, 14% of Canadian casualties occurred training at OTUs or HCUs (Operational Training units and Heavy Conversion Units) and this doesn’t count the significant losses of aircrew during basic training or other losses due to non-operational causes. Likewise, the US AAF lost 43,581 aircraft overseas and a staggering 21,583 in the Continental US. A good book to read to get a feel for training losses is Murray Peden’s A Thousand Shall Fall. Per Ardua ad Astra.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Which presidential son served in three wars and was awarded the Medal of Honor?
Answer: Aha! Most people would probably nominate Theodore Roosevelt Jr. (1887–1944) who was the son of Theodore (Teddy) Roosevelt, the 26th President. Theodore Roosevelt Jr. Served in WW1 and WW2. As far as I know, he only served in those two wars although, during WW2, he served in both the North African and European theatres. Aged 56, he was almost certainly the oldest man to land with the assault waves on D-Day. Theodore was awarded his Medal of Honor for rallying and directing troops on Utah Beach. Sadly, he died of a heart attack a little over a month later. For gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty on 6 June 1944, in France. After two verbal requests to accompany the leading assault elements in the Normandy invasion had been denied, Brig. Gen. Roosevelt's written request for this mission was approved and he landed with the first wave of the forces assaulting the enemy-held beaches. He repeatedly led groups from the beach, over the seawall, and established them inland. His valor, courage, and presence in the very front of the attack and his complete unconcern at being under heavy fire inspired the troops to heights of enthusiasm and self-sacrifice. Although the enemy had the beach under constant direct fire, Brig. Gen. Roosevelt moved from one locality to another, rallying men around him, directed, and personally led them against the enemy. Under his seasoned, precise, calm, and unfaltering leadership, assault troops reduced beach strongpoints and rapidly moved inland with minimum casualties. He thus contributed substantially to the successful establishment of the beachhead in France. However, James Webb Cook Hayes (1856–1934) was the son of Rutherford Birchard Hayes, the 19th President, and he was also awarded the Medal of Honor, and arguably served in five, albeit smaller, wars: the Spanish American War, the Philippine Rebellion, the Boxer Rebellion, the Russo-Japanese War (as an observer) and WW1. At any rate he was awarded the Spanish, Philippine, and China Campaign medals and the WW1 Victory Medal. James won his Medal of Honor in the Philippines in 1899 for his role in the Battle of Tangadan Pass. The President of the United States of America, in the name of Congress, takes pleasure in presenting the Medal of Honor to Lieutenant Colonel Webb Cook Hayes, United States Army, for most distinguished gallantry on 4 December 1899, while serving with 31st Infantry, U.S. Volunteers, in action at Vigan, Luzon, Philippine Islands. Lieutenant Colonel Hayes pushed through the enemy's lines alone, during the night, from the beach to the beleaguered force at Vigan, and returned the following morning to report the condition of affairs to the Navy and secure assistance.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there any other fighter planes in World War II that used Merlin engines, or was this technology exclusive to the British Spitfire and Mustangs?
Answer: With regards to fighter planes, various marks of the Merlin engine were used in the Spitfire and Mustang as mentioned, and also the Hawker Hurricane, Boulton-Paul Defiant, de Havilland Mosquito, de Havilland Hornet, Fairey Fulmar, Westland Welkin, some Bristol Beaufighters and, at one point if I remember correctly, an Me Bf 109. There were also a number of test beds, including the Hawker Hart, and prototypes such as the Hawker Hotspur and Vickers Type 432. The Westland Welkin, a forgotten fighter The Merlin was used in several bombers, including the Avro Lancaster, Avro Manchester Mk III, Handley Page Halifax, Fairey Battle, Fairey Barracuda, Armstrong-Whitworth Whitley, Avro Lincoln and some Vickers Wellingtons. There were also three Vickers Windsors built. The Merlin was also used in transport aircraft, namely the Avro Lancastrian, Avro Tudor, and Avro York, all Lancaster derivatives.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why does the Brit narrative of WW2 think of Lend-Lease as some dirty attempt to drain Brit money even though the reality is that it was generous aid? Why can't Brits be more thankful to the Americans for pouring billions into their country?
Answer: It’s because this is a much more complicated topic than most people, on both sides of the Atlantic, are aware and people, on both sides, make sweeping generic statements that may have elements of the truth to them, but are not the full truth. There are several different elements to this story that are easily confused including (a) cash-and-carry, (b) destroyers for bases, (c) the Tizard Mission, (d) lend lease itself, (e) reverse lend lease, (f) the Anglo-American loan, and (g) payments received under the Marshall Plan. Firstly, you have to consider the background. During WW1, by 1916, Britain was financing its own and most of the Empire's war expenditures, all of Italy's, and two thirds of the war costs of France and Russia, plus various smaller nations as well. In total, the Empire funded over a third of the Allied costs, some $47b. Britain borrowed some $3.7b from the US but, at the same time, lent $6.7b, including $2.5b to Russia, $1.9b to Italy, and $1.6b to France. The funds lent to Russia were, of course, never paid back due to the 1917 Revolution and Britain didn’t fully repay its various debts from WW1 until 2015. By 1918 Britain was spending 38% of its GDP on funding the war. The material cost was also high with Britain losing 7,600,000 million tons of shipping, over 3,000 ships, from its merchant fleet. In comparison, the US lost 339,000 tons. In terms of manpower, the United Kingdom (not the Empire) lost 888,000 men dead and a further 1,700,000 wounded. In terms of the working age male population (15–64) in 1914, that’s over 7.7% of the workforce killed and another 14.8% wounded - over 22% in total. The equivalent figure for the United States is 1%. The net impact of this huge outpouring of resources was that, to use a technical term, Britain was a bit buggered by 1918, and it was still not in the best of conditions, nearly twenty-one years later when WW2 commenced. Any analysis of the financing of WW2 needs to bear this in mind. At the start of the war and after the passing of the Neutrality Act of 1939, the US initiated a policy called cash-and-carry for belligerent nations. All goods had to fully paid for immediately in cash (no credit allowed) and transported in non-US ships. This was certainly not generous aid and drained the British of their liquid assets. Cash-and-Carry aircraft being pulled across the Canadian border to abide with the Neutrality Act In September 1940, the US swapped fifty WW1 era destroyers in return for basing rights in the Bahamas, St. Lucia, Jamaica, Trinidad, Antigua, British Guiana, Bermuda, and Newfoundland. This was not aid either, although it is sometimes depicted as such, but was the US seeking to secure its Eastern seaboard against possible German attacks. In the same month, the British dispatched the Tizard Mission carrying details of secret British research and development to share with the US. This research included the cavity magnetron, the VT fuse, the jet engine, the Frisch–Peierls memorandum and the MAUD report (key foundations of the Manhattan Project), and a host of other important developments. This research was freely shared with the US and does rather contrast with the shabby treatment later doled out by the US to its nuclear partners with the McMahon Act in 1946. The financial value of this research cannot be estimated. When the members of the Tizard Mission brought one cavity magnetron to America in 1940 they carried the most valuable cargo ever brought to our shores. Scientists Against Time, James Phinney Baxter Finally, it became clear that Britain, at this point pursuing the war more or less single-handedly, had exhausted its reserves. If there was no practical alternative, there was certainly no moral one either. Britain and the Commonwealth were carrying the battle for all civilization. Franklin Delano Roosevelt, Champion of Freedom, Conrad Black In March 1941, the Lend-Lease Act and introduced as An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States which resulted in $31.4b of aid to the Britain, offset by some $6.8b in Reverse Lend-Lease from Britain to the US. Lend-Lease also applied to the Soviet Union, China, and France, but Britain received about 60% of it. About 54% of Lend-Lease spending was on war material, including naval and merchant ships, 21% percent was on industrial materials and products, such as aviation gasoline, metals and machine tools, surgical and medical supplies, rolling stock, lumber, etc., 13% percent was food and other agricultural products, and 12% was spent on services such as the construction of factories in the United States to produce lend-lease goods, repair and rental of ships, the ferrying of aircraft, and building of air and naval bases. The Arsenal of Democracy, lend-lease tanks being produced Lend-Lease is often misunderstood in the wider context but this was genuine aid, albeit designed to grow the US economy and promote US objectives. However, no payment was required for Lend-Lease goods and they were critical to the British war effort. We should always be grateful that the US recognised at this point that it had a key role to play in defeating Germany even before Pearl Harbour. It should also be borne in mind that, at the same time, Britain provided Russia with about $0.5b of material as well as running the Artic Convoys and was also hosting and supporting Free French, Polish, and other Allied contingents that found themselves exiled in the UK. A different matter was the Anglo-American loan of $3.75b made in 1946 which did need to be paid back, although the loan itself was made on fairly generous terms of 2% over 50 years. The United Kingdom finally repaid the last instalment on this loan (not to be confused with the WW1 loans) in 2006. Finally we come to the Marshall Plan, an initiative to rebuild war-torn Europe whilst also benefitting the US economy. Many people think that Marshall Aid went primarily to Germany, but this is not the case. Germany received about 11% of the aid, but the UK received 26% and France 18%. In fact, the UK was the largest recipient with $3.3b. Marshall Aid was a gift but it did come with some conditions requiring Britain to balance its budget, control tariffs, and maintain adequate currency reserves. Lend-Lease TNT from the Tennessee Powder Company being stockpiled 100 feet below ground in the UK Therefore, it is the case that the US provided Britain with a net $24.6b of aid through Lend-Lease during the war, less a payment of $1b at for goods received after the termination of the agreement, and a further $3.3b in Marshall Aid after the war ended, for a total (if my maths is correct) of $26.9b. To put this in context, Lend-Lease to the United Kingdom amounted to around 12% of US war spending, or about 2.9% of total US GDP over the period 1940–45. It is worth noting that the US economy grew by 71% over the same period, adding some $72b a year by 1945 which puts these figures into context. Lend-Lease not only helped Britain, it helped the US as well, serving to jumpstart the US economy out of the doldrums of the Great Depression with dramatic effect. In 1940, government-financed capital spending accounted for 5% of the annual U.S. investment in industrial capital but, by 1943, the government accounted for 67%. Massive war spending doubled economic growth rates, essentially ending the Depression. Businesses ignored the mounting national debt and taxes, redoubling their efforts to increase output to take advantage of generous government contracts. TLDR: Lend-Lease was free, Marshall aid was free, other elements were not free. Lend-Lease was a boon to both Britain and to the US economy. Anyone who knows the facts should be grateful to the US for recognising its responsibilities and acting on them. …and even if, which I do not for a moment believe, this Island or a large part of it were subjugated and starving, then our Empire beyond the seas, armed and guarded by the British Fleet, would carry on the struggle, until, in God’s good time, the New World, with all its power and might, steps forth to the rescue and the liberation of the old. Winston Churchill, June 1940

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did Germany choose not to use its heavy ships (Bismarck, Tirpitz) during the Battle of Britain? What was the reason behind this decision?
Answer: Because they couldn’t fly? The Battle of Britain was an air battle. Also neither the Bismarck nor the Tirpitz were operational when the Battle of Britain was being fought. The Battle is generally held to have ended in October 1940, while Bismarck wasn’t worked up until December 1940 and Tirpitz only started her sea-trials in February 1941. Also, apart from the Channel Dash in February 1942, the Germans were careful to keep their heavy units well away from the coast of the British Isles. To lurk around anywhere near the South Coast (where the Battle of Britain was being fought) would have been utterly suicidal because of the minefields, coastal artillery, and land-based air cover alone, never mind the Royal Navy’s reaction. Likely fate of any German heavy unit entering the Channel Even in the planning for Operation Seelöwe (Sea Lion), the proposed invasion of the British Isles, it was never anticipated for a moment that any Kriegsmarine heavy units would operate in the English Channel. If they did anything, they would have been running interference in the North Sea - and that would, most likely, have been another suicide mission. Anyway, with regards to the Battle of Britain, what useful effect could these ships have had? Their guns had a range of only twenty odd miles, which was nowhere near enough for them to hit most of the Battle of Britain airfields belonging to 11 Group (defending the South Coast), and those few airfields that could have been hit, Tangmere for instance, would simply have been evacuated inland. Also, why blindly fire a 6,400 kg broadside inland when a Luftwaffe bomber Staffel could carry 20,000 kg much further, and actually see what it was dropping its bombs on? A military operation can potentially still be useful even if it is probably suicidal, but this one would have been suicidal and pointless - and anyway, the ships weren’t available. So much more useful, not to mention so much cheaper!

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you provide some examples of merchant vessels that have been used by navies in the past?
Answer: I’m going to restrict myself to the Royal Navy and to WW2, otherwise the remit of the question is far too large. I will also look at civilian owned boats and ships rather than merchant vessels as the latter would limit us to just looking at cargo carrying ships. During WW2, the Royal Navy requisitioned everything from Thames barges and fishing trawlers to ocean liners, for any number of different purposes. If we consider the Little Ships of Dunkirk, we can also include the 850 privately owned fishing boats, pleasure yachts, cabin cruisers, life boats, and ferries, the smallest probably being the little 15-foot Tamzine, that were requisitioned for use in the evacuation. Little Ships being assembled to take part in the Dunkirk evacuation in 1940 Transporting troops back from Dunkirk The inshore fishing boat Tamzine, now preserved at the Imperial War Museum Early in the war, there were also some sixty Thames barges requisitioned and moored offshore as lookout posts, with others used for transport, and, once again, at Dunkirk where thirteen were lost, including Claude and Doris. Thames sailing barges off Dunkirk in 1940 Thames lighters and barges were also used during D-Day. Originally the barges (LB - landing barges) were simply towed. Then some had a ramp added for loading and unloading vehicles (LBR or Landing Barge, Ramped). Adding an engine created a more flexible barge (LBV or Landing Barge Vehicle) which were mainly used to carry vehicles and supplies from ship-to-shore, especially equipment that was too bulky or heavy for DUKWs. They were also used to provide the specialist vessels needed to form Supply & Repair (S&R) flotillas, which included Landing Barges Oiler (LBO), Water (LBW), Kitchen (LBK), and Emergency Repair (LBE).
