Another, but more restricted use was as Landing Barges Flak (LBF) and Gun (LBG). There was also one Landing Barge Cable (LBC). Landing barge kitchen - perhaps not very glamorous but nonetheless essential Moving up the scale slightly, we have the 816 English and Welsh trawlers and 200 steam drifters requisitioned for use in harbour service, minesweeping, balloon barrage, net laying, submarine tender, auxiliary patrol, boom defence, anti-submarine, boarding and examination, and degaussing duties. HMT D’Arcy Cooper, lost in April 1941, courtesy Barry Banham HMT Northern Sky operating off Iceland, she made the last attack of WW2 on a U-boat. Moving on to the larger vessels, we, of course have the merchants ships that were used to support naval operations and for troop transport. These were converted to DEMS (Defensively Equipped Merchant Ships) and armed a low-angle gun as defence against surfaced submarines and a high-angle gun and/or machine guns for defence against air attack. By the end of 1943, all merchant ships were DEMS. Although they remained under civilian masters, they carried Royal Navy or Royal Artillery personnel to man the guns (some 38,000 men in total). A merchant seaman passing a shell to the Royal Navy gunners on a DEMS ship in 1942 As regards specialised naval uses for requisitioned ships. off the top of my head (and I’m sure that other people can come up with more) there were Q, AMC, CAM, MAC, OBV, auxiliary anti-aircraft, and Headquarters ships, as well as such exotica as the railway ferry HMS Daffodil. Nine Q-Ships were deployed by the Royal Navy in WW2. These were decoy vessels that were heavily armed with concealed weaponry and were designed to lure U-boats into surface attacks (preferred as they conserved torpedoes). A typical Q-ship armament might include seven single 4-inch guns, four Lewis machine guns, four 21-inch torpedo tubes and 100 depth charges. Q-ship armament concealed in a fake deck house The Royal Navy also deployed some fifty-one Armed Merchant Cruisers (AMC) including the well known HMS Jervis Bay and HMS Rawalpindi, the first sunk by the Admiral Scheer and the second by the Scharnhorst and the Gneisenau. AMCs were requisitioned merchantmen intended as a stop-gap to supplement actual cruisers by fulfilling patrol and escort duties. Armed with seven or eight 6-inch guns and a couple of 3-inch AA guns, they could take on a German raider by not a heavy warship. HMS Jervis Bay, Captain Fegen was awarded the Victoria Cross For valour in challenging hopeless odds and giving his life to save the many ships it was his duty to protect. On the 5th of November, 1940, in heavy seas, Captain Fegen, in His Majesty's Armed Merchant Cruiser Jervis Bay, was escorting thirty-eight Merchantmen. Sighting a powerful German warship he at once drew clear of the Convoy, made straight for the Enemy, and brought his ship between the Raider and her prey, so that they might scatter and escape. Crippled, in flames, unable to reply, for nearly an hour the Jervis Bay held the German's fire. So she went down: but of the Merchantmen all but four or five were saved. Thirty-five Catapult Armed Merchant (CAM) ships were converted. These were ordinary merchantmen that were armed with a catapult launched Hurricane (Hurricat) fighter. They were another stop-gap, intended to drive off German aerial reconnaissance. Pity the poor pilot, who had to ditch in the sea after his mission if he couldn’t make land. Hurricat on the CAM Ship SS Empire Darwin The nineteen Merchant Aircraft Carriers (MAC ships), on the other hand, were limited aircraft carriers converted by adding a flight deck to a bulk grain ship or oil tanker. They were peculiar in that they retained their civilian status and continued to carry a reduced cargo. Equipped with four Swordfish aircraft, they were effective at keeping U-boats off the surface, thus severely limiting their speed when attempting to intercept a convoy. Swordfish launching from the MAC MV Empire Macdermott, a bulk grain ship Some twenty merchant ships were requisitioned as Ocean Boarding Vessels (OBV) and used to enforce the blockade by intercepting, boarding, and inspecting foreign vessels to determine whether they were carrying contraband. HMS Cavina, an OBV converted from a banana boat Other Merchantmen were converted into auxiliary anti-aircraft cruisers. For instance HMS Palomares, originally MV Palomares another banana boat (banana boats were fast to avoid the fruit spoiling), was equipped with three twin 4" DP guns, two quad pom-poms, and two quad Vickers .50 calibre guns and was used to escort Arctic convoys, including the notorious PQ-17. HMS Palomares, auxiliary anti-aircraft cruiser, in 1941 HMS Royal Eagle, Auxiliary Anti-Aircraft Vessel (Coastal) Then we have the Headquarters ships, converted merchantmen that were used to support amphibious operations and equipped with the space and sophisticated communications capabilities required to coordinate the naval, land, and air aspects of a landing. HMS Bulolo, the first headquarters ship Finally, it is worth mentioning the some of the odder ships that were requisitioned such as the SS Train Ferry No. 3 purchased from the London and North Eastern Railway (LNER) and converted as a landing craft carrier, or HMY (His Majesty’s Yacht) Viva II sunk by bombing in 1941, or the cable ship SS Lady of the Isles, built in 1875 and sunk by a mine in 1940. I’d dearly like to include Pneumatic Elevator No. 11, but although listed as a merchant shipping loss, I don’t think that she was in Royal Navy service when she was lost in May 1941. HMS Daffodil, ex SS Train Ferry No. 3, sunk in March 1945 Sorry, this got a bit long, but I hope you’ve found it interesting. It’s worth remembering that Britain lost over two and a half thousand civilian owned ships during WW2, ranging from the 3-ton fishing vessel Mouette, sunk at the cost of two lives in December 1941, to the 16,243-ton RMS Lancastria, sunk during Operation Aerial with an estimated toll of 4,000–7,000 lives in June 1940, to the 42,348-ton RMS Empress-of-Britain, sunk in October 1940, happily (if that is the right word) at a cost of only 45 lives. Whether these ships were in Royal Navy service or not, it’s a sobering number.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did the US Navy assign nicknames to their airplanes during the Vietnam War, such as "Wild Weasel," "The Cockpit," and "Crazy Horse"?
Answer: I’m not sure about this one as I don’t know that I’ve ever seen nose art on a Vietnam era aircraft - feel free to correct me. During WW2, aircraft frequently had nose art which included a nickname for for the aircraft, e.g. Memphis Belle, Enola Gay, Bockscar, etc. Aircraft nicknames in WW2 However, I believe that, even in WW2, the US Navy was pretty averse to nose art and the practice seems to died out generally by Vietnam, except for helicopters. Helicopter nose art in Vietnam Given the range of names given in the question, I think that we need to distinguish between pilot nicknames, aircraft tail numbers and package call signs, individual aircraft nicknames (nose art), aircraft model names, mission types/aircraft, and, possibly, the names of military operations. Pilots have nicknames (personal callsigns) which are assigned by their colleagues on the basis of some personal quirk, characteristic, or embarrassing experience they have suffered. Individual aircraft can be identified by all or part of their side/tail numbers and flights, packages, and squadrons of aircraft would have a call sign. Appending the side number of the aircraft to the call sign e.g. Black Lion 105, for all air traffic communications. On a tactical frequency, this might be shortened to Black Lion 2 or even Black 2, as the second aircraft in the flight. In the US Navy, individual aircraft nicknames, as already mentioned above, didn’t exist to the best of my knowledge. On the other hand, aircraft models did have names: A-1 Skyraider, A-3 Skywarrior, A-4 Skyhawk, A-6 Intruder, F-8 Crusader, F-9 Cougar, and F-4 Phantom, as well as many others. Grumman A-6 Intruder - one of my favourite aircraft As for mission types/aircraft, Wild Weasel is the name given to aircraft and missions tasked with destroying or supressing enemy air defences as part of a strike package - SEAD missions. These aircraft were typically armed with anti-radiation missiles to destroy enemy radars. In the US Navy in Vietnam this would probably have been a A-4 Skyhawk armed with the AGM-45 Shrike. US Navy A-4 Skyhawk launching a shrike TLDR: Crazy Horse could well be a pilot’s nickname. It is also the name of the RC-12G Crazyhorse electronic snooper aircraft, but that was post Vietnam, as well as the name of a US Army operation that took place in late May 1966 in Bình Định province. Wild Weasel almost certainly refers to a SEAD mission or aircraft. The Cockpit doesn’t sound like anything that I have ever heard of apart, of course, for the place where a pilot sits in the aircraft. The original meaning was literally the pit where a cockfight happens, and in the 18th Century, cockpit became the Royal Navy's term for the area where the coxswain was stationed to steer the boat and this was then transferred to the pilots position in an aircraft.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Britain lose more aircraft carriers than Japan during World War II, even though they had a larger number of carriers?
Answer: No, the Royal Navy didn’t lose more carriers than the Japanese Navy in WW2, in fact it suffered less than a third of the Japanese losses. The Royal Navy lost five fleet carriers (Courageous, Glorious, Ark Royal, Hermes, and Eagle) and three escort carriers (Audacity, Avenger, and Dasher) during WW2. A total of seven carriers lost to enemy action (Dasher was sunk by an internal explosion). None of the nineteen MAC ships (Merchant Aircraft Carriers) were lost during the war. Ark Royal sinking The Japanese Navy lost eleven fleet carriers (Akagi, Amagi, Hiyo, Hiryu, Kaga, Shinano, Shokaku, Soryu, Taiho, Unryu, and Zuikaku), five light carriers (Chitose, Chiyoda, Ryujo, Shoho, and Zuiho), four escort carriers (Chuyo, Shinyo, Taiyo, and Unyo), two merchant converted carriers (Akitsu Maru, and Nigitsu Maru), and the two battleships converted into hybrid aircraft carriers (Ise, and Hyuga). A total of twenty four carriers lost to enemy action. Note that several of these carriers were scuttled by Japanese destroyers after being crippled or settled in their harbours after bombing and I have counted these as lost in combat. Amagi, sunk in Kure Harbor Therefore, the Japanese lost three and a half times as many carriers as the British, despite the British fighting for 2,211 days as opposed to the Japanese fighting for 1,385 days. By means of comparison, the US Navy lost five fleet carriers (Hornet, Lexington, Wasp, Yorktown, and Langley), the latter having been converted to a seaplane tender before being sunk, one light carrier (Princeton), and six escort carriers (Bismarck Sea, Block Island, Gambier Bay, Liscome Bay, Ommaney Bay, and St. Lo). A total of twelve carriers lost to enemy action. Again, ships scuttled by US destroyers are counted as lost in combat. USS Lexington sinking An analysis of the causes of carrier losses is interesting. Whilst 71% of the British losses resulted from submarine (U-boat) attacks, the Japanese losses were split fairly evenly between air bombing and submarine attacks, whilst the US losses were, again, split fairly evenly between air bombing, submarine, and Kamikaze attacks.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was Jimmy Carter ever in the military?
Answer: James Earl Carter Jr., a truly admirable man, is one of six Presidents to have served in the US Navy: Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, Ford, Carter, and Bush (Snr). Influenced by his uncle, Tom Gordy, a radioman in the Navy, he seems to have set his eyes on a naval career from an early age. He was admitted to Annapolis in 1943 on an accelerated war programme, having first commenced studying engineering and mathematics at Georgia Southwestern College and the Georgia Institute of Technology. Carter graduated 60th out of 821 in the class of 1947 and was appointed as an Ensign to the battleship USS Wyoming and a radar and CIC (combat information centre) officer and was then posted to the USS Mississippi as a training officer before transferring to the submarine service. Midshipman James Earl Carter Jr. After completing the six month submarine course at New London, Carter was assigned to USS Pomfret (SS 391) based at Pearl Harbour, Hawaii in December 1948 where he served as Communications Officer, Sonar Officer, Electronics Officer, Gunnery Officer and Supply Officer and was promoted to Lieutenant (junior grade). In February 1951, Carter was assigned as Engineering Officer to the USS K-1 (SSK 1). K-1 where he served as Executive Officer, Engineering Officer, and Electronics Repair Officer and qualified for command of a submarine. Jimmy Carter in the control room of USS K-1, 1952 In June 1952, Carter was promoted to Lieutenant and was selected by Admiral Hyman G. Rickover to work on the nascent nuclear submarine programme. Carter was assigned to the Division of Reactor Development in Schenectady, New York and Washington DC where he assisted in the design and development of nuclear propulsion plants for naval vessels. USS K-1 and USS Seawolf (SSN-575) Between March and October 1953, Carter was preparing to become the nuclear engineering officer for the USS Seawolf (SSN 575). However, after his father's death in 1953, Carter resigned from the Navy to run the family business and was honourably discharged in October 1953. He remained in the Navy reserve until December 1961 when he transferred to the retired reserve with the rank of Lieutenant.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Enigma give no hint that British/Allied naval codes had been broken by the Germans?
Answer: No, not Enigma, Lorenz. Before getting into the meat of the subject, there are a couple of points to bear in mind. Firstly, there were lots of naval codes and ciphers, not just one. Secondly, traffic needs to be broken not once but every time the key changes, and this means that the traffic must not only be broken but broken quickly enough that it is useful. Breaking traffic after days or weeks may be useful, but it is unlikely to yield information that can be used operationally, as the immediate opportunity for action will already have passed. U-442 near a torpedoed tanker, January 1943 This is usefully illustrated by the following analysis of the U-boat traffic broken between December 1942 and September 1943. 18% of the traffic was never broken, and a further 36% took more than five days to break. The main code that we are discussing here is Naval Cypher No. 3, which was broken by the Germans with great success. The Royal Navy cyphers were actually a two stage process. The message was first encoded using a codebook (where numbers stand for words or phrases) and the result was then enciphered using a key sequence from one of a number of tables depending on location and type of message. To take an example from the excellent Christos military and intelligence corner, the message Enemy frigate sighted South-West of Malta would be encoded by the operator, using the code book, as enemy=2591, frigate=7482, sighted=5556, SW=3309, Malta=4610, so the message becomes 2591 7482 5556 3309 4610. Because a four digit code group might stand for any word or, indeed, for a whole phrase, no useful data can be derived regarding word length or letter frequency. The operator would then choose a random page and starting point from subtractor table valid for the time period, location, and message type and use the resulting numerical sequence for enciphering the code groups. This might provide the key groups 5668 8301 3496 3540 7778. The operator then subtracts the code groups of the message from these key groups, without carrying. 5668 8301 3496 3540 7778 - key groups 2591 7482 5556 3309 4610 - code groups ------------------------------------- 3177 1929 8940 0241 3168 – cipher groups Naval Cypher No. 3 used to provide interoperability between the British, American and Canadian navies and consisted of a 4-figure book and subtractor tables with 15,000 groups. Originally the subtractor tables were changed every month but from September 1942 every 15 days and in 1943 every 10 days. Because of the sheer amount of traffic generated and the consequent reuse of keys (depths), the Germans were able to break into the traffic and by February/March 1942 they were able to read a large proportion, but not all, of the traffic sent using the General table. This situation lasted until June 1943 when Naval Cypher No. 5 replaced No. 3 and the Germans lost most of their access. In August 1942 Bletchley discovered that Naval Cipher No. 3 had been penetrated. This was revealed by the decrypt of a German Tunny (Lorenz) message that revealed that the B-Dienst was solving Naval Cyphers Nos. 3 and 4. However, the Admiralty did not change the cypher until the following June. The logistical effort involved in creating, printing, and distributing a new system should not be underestimated, but this seems an unconscionably long time. There is no clear answer as to what went wrong but it seems to be a mixture of miscommunication, poor organisation, and divided responsibilities. A summary of the report into the affair stated: Minor economies in this detail of code and cipher security not only cost us dearly in men and ships but very nearly lost us the war. It serves as a salutary reminded that it is not just good enough to break into the enemy’s codes but that the security of one’s own codes must be constantly evaluated and that they must be updated frequently - however bothersome that might be. There is no room for complacency in the code war. TLDR: Enigma itself gave no hint that Naval Cypher No. 3 had been broken by the Germans, but the decrypt of an even more secure Lorenz message did provide this vital information.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: When did Germany find out that Enigma was broken?
Answer: Although some people had suspicions, particularly Karl Dönitz the head of the Kriegsmarine, the full story of the breaking of Enigma (Ultra) was not finally revealed to the world until 1974 when The Ultra Secret was published by F.W. Winterbotham. However, other works hinting at the fact that Enigma had been broken, such as Battle for Secrets by Władysław Kozaczuk and The Codebreakers by David Kahn, had been published before that in 1967. During the war, the Germans dismissed evidence that Enigma had been broken. Indeed, Kapitän zur See Heinz Bonatz, the former head of the Kriegsmarine's B-Dienst (Beobachtungsdienst), part of German Naval Intelligence, asserted in his history of German naval intelligence, Die deutsche Marine Funkaufklärung 1914–1945, published in 1970, that Enigma had never been broken. Enigma decrypts (Ultra) were shared with a very small and select audience and the British went to great lengths to disguise their sources, both from their own people and from the Germans. Intelligence was generally only acted on when its source could plausibly be ascribed to some other source, such as a fake reconnaissance flights that “discovered” the target independently. As a result, the Germans had suspicions that Enigma might have been broken but never had a smoking gun that proved that it had been. The Germans were not aided in their efforts by the highly fragmented nature of their own intelligence operations and by the, ever present, inter-service lack of cooperation. Enigma in use The German’s were aware that information was leaking to the Allies, but they tended to ascribe the leaks to other sources: agents (for instance Rudolf Roessler and the Lucy spy ring), new technology, or random bad luck, etc. Of all the services, the German Navy (Kriegsmarine) appears to have been the most security conscious and they made several improvements to their encryption machinery (four rotor Enigma) and procedures which caused the code-breakers at Bletchley Park major headaches. Both Admiral Kurt Fricke and Konteradmiral Ludwig Stummel of B-Dienst, conducted investigations into the possibility that Enigma had been compromised, specifically into the sinking of the merchant raider Atlantis (Schiff 16) in November 1941 by the heavy cruiser Devonshire (which was indeed the result of an Enigma decrypt). However, these investigations concluded that Enigma had not been compromised. When the Germans investigated various incidents where Enigma could have been compromised, they concluded that Enigma was not at fault. For instance, when convoys avoided Wolfpacks, the Germans assumed that the cause lay with Huff-Duff (high-frequency direction finding) and radar rather than Enigma. In 2001, a book, Action This Day: Bletchley Park from the Breaking of the Enigma Code to the birth of the Modern Computer, by Michael Smith and Ralph Erskine, reported that an American-Swiss spy in the US Navy Department had informed the Germans that Enigma had been broken for several months. However, the German investigation concluded that although specific, short-lived, keys may have been captured, Enigma itself was not compromised. It wasn’t the case that the Germans thought that Enigma couldn’t be broken, they were well aware that, theoretically at least, it could be broken. What they failed to assess correctly was the extraordinary effort that the British were prepared to put into breaking the code and the technical innovations that they developed in order to do so (the Bombes, etc). It’s not that the Germans didn’t understand that there was a risk, it’s simply that they gave it a very low priority in their list of things to worry about.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it realistic for the main character of a historical fiction novel to be present at multiple major events of their time, such as Pearl Harbor and D-Day?
Answer: That would depend on how many major events were involved. It would be wholly plausible that a US Navy officer, for instance, be present at both Pearl Harbour and D-Day. I am put in mind of the excellent Flashman Papers series written by George MacDonald Fraser. Based on the character from Tom Brown’s Schooldays, Flashman is a coward and poltroon who always comes out smelling of roses. Through the twelve book series, Flashman finds himself involved in everything from the last stand at Gandamak (1842) to the Battle of Isandlwana (1879), via the Charge of the Light Brigade, the Indian Mutiny, the Battle of the Little Bighorn, the Taiping Rebellion, The Raid on Harper’s Ferry, and many other adventures. The timeline is plausible for the wars of Victoria’s reign. If you haven’t read these books and you enjoy history, you really should. They are meticulously researched and worth it for the extensive footnotes alone. Returning to the question, James Delingpole took this idea and reversed it. His character, Dick Coward, is a Coward by name but not by nature, who has the unfortunate knack of being in the right place at the wrong time. Coward is a hero whose feats always go unnoticed. Unfortunately, Delingpole only wrote two books in the series: Coward on the Beach and Coward at the Bridge (you should be able to guess the subjects), but the books allude to his presence at Stalingrad (somehow fighting for the Germans), Pearl Harbour, and other pivotal events of WW2. It is a great pity that James didn’t pursue the idea, as the two books he did publish are very funny and well worth reading. In short, I see no reason why a character could not be present at multiple events providing that the time lines don’t overlap and that there is a reasonable explanation of how they came to be there.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the size comparison between an American destroyer and the British ship HMS Belfast?
Answer: HMS Belfast is a Town-class light cruiser displacing 11,550 tons and armed with twelve 6” 50 calibre guns. A contemporary US destroyer might be the Gleaves-class displacing 1,630 tons and armed with five 5” 38-caliber guns. Although the guns sound fairly similar, there’s quite a difference between a 5” and a 6” shell. A 5” shell weighs around 55lbs whilst a 6” shell weighs 112lbs. Belfast is 613 feet long with a 63 foot beam whilst Gleaves was 348 feet long with a 36 foot beam. Modern destroyers are much bigger than their WW2 predecessors. An US Arleigh-Burke-class Flight II or a British Daring-class (Type 45) both weigh in at around 8,400 tons. HMS Belfast USS Gleaves

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why couldn’t Britain build its own U-boat force to sink Nazi commerce and starve the Germans?
Answer: There was no need for a British equivalent of the wolfpacks to sink German commerce because Germany had essentially no maritime commerce once the British blockade was imposed in 1939. When WW2 began the Royal Navy had 60 submarines based in the Far East, the Mediterranean, and in home waters. These were manned by 350 officers and 2,800 ratings and, including the crews of their depot ships, the strength of the submarine branch was 5,150 - less than 4% of the Royal Navy. In 1939, Germany had a very similar 56 U-boats. However, the strategic situation between the two countries was not symmetric. Germany had no choice but to rely on U-boats, whereas submarines were only a relatively minor part of the Royal Navy’s armoury. Where British submarines were very useful was in the Mediterranean where they interdicted the German and Italian supply lines to their armies in North Africa. Germany’s maritime trade during the war was limited to iron ore imports from Sweden through the Baltic (in the summer) or along the Norwegian coast (in the winter), a limited amount of coastal trade along the European Atlantic coastline, and a very small number of fast blockade-runners to and from Japan. In fact Germany’s main source of imports from neutral countries were Sweden (as already mentioned), the Soviet Union (until June 1941), Romania, Bulgaria, Spain, and Turkey. Apart from Sweden, trade with these countries was not conducted by sea, so there was nothing for the British to intercept. The British naval blockade was extremely effective. Because the Royal Navy commanded the sea lanes to Europe, they could stop and search neutral ships rather than simply sinking them. Any contraband items were confiscated and the ships allowed to continue. Early in the war, this did cause considerable friction with the United States who regarded the interception of mail bound for Germany as unwarranted. However, the British refused to back down and continued to intercept and search neutral ships, including those from the USA. HMS Cavina, Ocean Boarding Vessel, 1941 As the war progressed, the number of neutrals declined as countries were either occupied by the Axis (Yugoslavia, Greece, etc.), voluntarily joined the Axis (Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, etc.), or were invaded by the Axis (The USSR). However, Sweden, Spain, Portugal, Switzerland, and Turkey remained neutral throughout. German shortages caused by the British blockade were partially offset by the ruthless looting of occupied countries and the manifestly unfair terms imposed on their farmers. Despite these efforts, Europe found itself with agricultural deficits caused by the loss imported fodder and fertilizer from Britain, the British blockade, the requisitioning of millions of horses for the German Army, and manpower shortages. Even by the end of 1940, Europe’s food supply had been reduced by 15% by the effects of the blockade and a further 15% by the fall in agricultural production and Herbert Hoover wrote: The food situation in the present war is already more desperate than at the same stage in the World War… If this war is long continued, there is but one implacable end... the greatest famine in history. Food shortages were therefore one of the reasons behind the German invasion of the USSR and the seizure of the rich agricultural region of the Ukraine. The situation continued to deteriorate and there was agonized debate in Britain as to whether the blockade should be lifted to assuage suffering in the occupied countries. I will just refer to some of the countries concerned. I will take first Belgium because it is, after all, the closest to us, and we have had authoritative declarations from representatives of that country. Belgium, be it remembered, is dependent in normal times on about half its food supply being conveyed to it by sea… The population… is in a state of famine, which even now is leading to very serious consequences, so far as public health and the future of youth are concerned. It looks as if this situation may turn into a catastrophe towards the end of this winter… Norway is in want of food. Spain, as we see from the declaration of General Franco to-day, is in want of food; and perhaps the most serious case that has been brought to the information of the public at large is that of Greece. Greece, too, has been dependent for about half its food supply on ships and sea-borne trade. If the war lasts another year one-third of the population of Greece will die from lack of food… I am not asking the Government for any cut-and-dried solution of so vast a problem, but I hope they are not going to dismiss it by saying that it is Germany's responsibility and that we have nothing to do with it. We can abuse the Germans and Hitler, but that does not feed these children. Lord Ponsonby, Hansard, 27th January 1942 I think we have also to remember that Belgium, Greece, Norway, Holland and Poland have all suffered invasion, with the train of misery, famine, disease, and starvation following invasion, on behalf of the cause for which we are all fighting. Their sufferings, the famine and the disease which accompanies famine, as we found in the last war, have got steadily worse, and will get steadily worse unless some steps are taken to find a remedy… I entirely agree that the responsibility for the Belgians, the Greeks and those in the other occupied territories is Germany's responsibility—Germany's responsibility under International Law—but I am sure that your Lordships know well enough that such a consideration does not in practice weigh much with our enemy. It is a question of interest with our enemy, and it may not be to the interest of Germany to feed these unhappy people unless it is to prevent typhus, pestilence and a great contagion covering Germany as well as the rest of the world. We are influenced by higher considerations than those which influence our enemy. I need not touch on them. But we are also influenced, I claim, by a consideration of our interest. The despair of the Belgians, the Poles, the Greeks, the Norwegians and the Dutch, is not to our interest. The Lord Bishop of Chichester, Hansard, 27th January 1942 Of course, the blockade is an odious weapon—everybody thinks that. But it is one of our strongest weapons, and it is almost our only definitely offensive weapon at the present time. Even if it is imperfect in its effects… it has already, I think, had a very material and, possibly, a profound effect upon the resistance of the Germans. What the noble Lord, Lord Ponsonby, and the right reverend Prelate the Bishop of Chichester are, in effect asking us to do, and asking of course with the highest possible motives, is to blunt that weapon if not actually to throw it away. What would be, in effect, the result of that? It would mean, first of all, that we might risk actually losing the war. If not that, at any rate, we should risk seriously prolonging the war with all the miseries which are connected with war. That is a fact which all those in this country—the noble Lord and others—who suggest the relaxation of the blockade must face. Lord Cecil (Viscount Cranborne), Hansard, 27th January 1942 By 1945, German civilians were receiving approximately 1,200 calories a day, as opposed to British civilians rationed to 2,300 calories and US civilians on 3,200 calories. There was no need for British wolfpacks, Germany was starving anyway - and taking its allies and the occupied countries down with it.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was Churchill aware of Operation Sea Lion before publicly announcing it after the attack on Pearl Harbor?
Answer: Say what? Sea Lion (Unternehmen Seelöwe) was a German operation - the planned invasion of the British Isles. It wasn’t a British operation, so there was no reason for Churchill to “announce” it. Churchill did issue instructions to the public on how to behave in the event of invasion and, of course, their is his famous beaches speech, part of which reads: Even though large tracts of Europe and many old and famous States have fallen or may fall into the grip of the Gestapo and all the odious apparatus of Nazi rule, we shall not flag or fail. We shall go on to the end. We shall fight in France, we shall fight on the seas and oceans, we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be. We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender. Come on Adolf - if you think you’re hard enough At any rate, the Germans abandoned Sea Lion as unachievable in September 1940, well over a year before the attack on Pearl Harbour. British Intelligence was well aware of the German preparations from photo-reconnaissance and other intelligence means, not least the German’s own propaganda broadcasts (the much derided Lord Haw Haw) and Churchill was, as a matter of course, kept informed on a daily basis. In September 1940, Hitler told an approving Berlin crowd: “And when people in England today nosily inquire: ‘Well, why isn’t he coming?’ Calm yourselves: he is coming! Curiosity killed the cat.” In October 1940, Churchill responded, “We are waiting for the long-promised invasion. So are the fishes.” Keep calm and carry on

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Winston Churchill ever drink to the point of being drunk or just to a point of being tipsy?
Answer: Montgomery: I neither drink nor smoke and am 100% fit! WSC: I both drink and smoke and I am 200% fit! Memoirs of Field Marshal Montgomery There are a lot of unnuanced answers to this question, some of them clearly from people who either have an agenda or have taken wartime Nazi propaganda at face value. Nazi propaganda cartoon: Churchill tries to find luck in drink, but the bottle distorts the view, Der Stürmer, 26th of February 1942 - Churchill would never drink whisky from a champagne glass! The first point to make is that people drank a surprising amount in the past. If you read, for example, NAM Rodger’s The Wooden World, his analysis of the amounts of alcohol consumed by officers in the Georgian Royal Navy will make you stretch your eyes. For ratings, the daily ration of rum was 71 ml at 57% ABV, compared with the current notional safe limit of 150 ml at 12.5% ABV - less than half of a Georgian sailor’s daily allowance - and they operated heavy machinery all day. In civilian life, it was not unusual for men to drink ten pints of small beer per day (ABV ~3%) because it was deemed safer than water. Indeed Churchill developed the habit of adding whisky to water during his service in India and South Africa where the water was barely potable. The water was not fit to drink. To make it palatable, we had to add whiskey. By diligent effort I learned to like it. WSC Remark in Silver Spring, Md. USA, Feb. 1947 I certainly wouldn’t deny that Churchill liked alcohol, he drank a lot, but claims that he was often seen inebriated or that he was an alcoholic are simply not supported by the historical record. Whether or not he was alcohol dependent is arguable. In 1936 he won a bet with Lord Rothermere that he would not drink spirits for a month, which doesn’t sound like dependency to me. I had been brought up and trained to have the utmost contempt for people who get drunk, except on very exceptional occasions and a few anniversaries. My Early Life It appears that Churchill probably drank approximately six glasses of champagne or wine daily along with 5 to 6 ounces of whisky or brandy spread over a 12 to 15 hour period. By any standards that’s a lot of alcohol, but there is virtually no evidence that it affected his performance or meets the clinical definitions of alcoholism or alcohol dependence. [Churchill’s] consumption of alcohol continued at quite regular intervals through most of his waking hours without visible effect. Robert Sherwood, Whitehouse speechwriter It is interesting that Churchill expressed concerns over Roosevelt’s drinking habits, particularly his afternoon ritual of concocting martinis which Churchill hated. Churchill apparently became adept at using the nearest bathroom or flower pot to dispose of the drinks. Churchill dodges prohibition as he recovers from being knocked down by a car in New York For your elucidation, I have transcribed the alcohol consumption of the Churchill household in Kent (Chartwell) and London for two months in 1949. I must say that 62 bottles of spirits and 453 bottles of wine a month is a little more than I get manage to through myself, but it obviously wasn’t all for his personal consumption - he did a lot of entertaining, and lived with both family members and a staff. The many stories about his consumption of whisky are misleading. What his daughter called his “Papa Cocktail” was just enough Johnnie Walker to cover the bottom of a tumbler, which was then filled with water and sipped throughout the morning. Jock Colville, his private secretary, said it was more akin to mouthwash than a highball and that it had no perceptible effect. It is quite clear that Churchill used alcohol as a prop to his persona but, contrary to revisionists, he was rarely drunk. He believed his peers liked leaders who could hold their alcohol and so he did nothing to discourage rumours and, indeed, actively seems to have encouraged them. However, no colleague who can be taken seriously ever reported seeing Churchill frequently the worse for drink. WSC: Prof! How many pints of Champagne in cubic feet have I consumed in twenty-four years at the rate of a pint a day, and how many railway carriages would it fill? Professor Lindemann: (consulting his slide rule): Only a part of one Winston. WSC: So much to achieve, so little time remains. In their book Winston Churchill’s Illnesses 1886–1965, Allister Vale and John Scadding conduct a search for all known reports of Churchill being the worse for drink and only two such occasions are reported. One was during the Tehran conference in 1943, when Churchill and Eden chose to walk back to their legation in order to enjoy the clear and starry night. Apparently, both men benefitted from a helping arm to hold them steady. On the other occasion, on the 6th of July 1944, Churchill was very tired and stressed as a result of giving a speech in the House of Commons concerning the new threat of flying bombs (V-weapons). He tried to recuperate with drink, resulting in bad-tempered behaviour and a “deplorable evening” according to Field Marshall Lord Alanbrooke - the only comment of this kind in all of Alanbrooke’s diary entries. These two incidents are now repeated ad nauseam. Lord Moran also expressed concerns about Churchill’s consumption of alcohol, but we might be more concerned by the fact that Moran was feeding Churchill with Seconal, a powerful barbiturate that can easily kill in higher doses and is particularly lethal when mixed with alcohol, and Drinamyl, half barbiturate and half amphetamine! I could not live without champagne. In victory I deserve it. In defeat I need it. WSC Churchill lived to the age of 90. Cheers!

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the Allies continue to use gliders during World War II after their success at Arnhem in Operation market Garden?
Answer: Operations Neptune/Overlord (Normandy, June 1944) and Market Garden (Arnhem, September 1944) are, by far, the most famous Allied glider operations, but other operations where gliders were used took place, including Operation Husky (Sicily, July 1943), Operation Thursday (Burma, March 1944), Operation Dragoon (Southern France, August 1944), Operation Repulse (Bastogne, December 1944), and Operation Varsity (Rhine River Crossing, March 1945). Operations, Choker I (Saarbrücken, December 1944) and Choker II (Worms, March 1945) were also planned but never carried out. Operation Repulse was carried out by IX Troop Carrier Command to deliver urgently needed supplies in the area of Bastogne between the 23rd and 27th of December 1944 during the German Wacht am Rhein offensive (the Battle of the Bulge), and involved the landing of gliders through German fire to deliver the urgently needed ammunition, motor fuel and medical supplies that would make it possible for the US defenders of Bastogne to hold out against the German siege of their position. IX Troop Carrier Command comprised three troop carrier wings, fourteen troop carrier groups, and a pathfinder group, totalling approximately 1,380 operational aircraft and 2,000 gliders at its maximum strength in March 1945. Operation Varsity was the airborne part of Operation Plunder, the crossing of the Rhine by 21st Army Group and involved dropping the British 6th and US 17th Airborne Divisions. C47s and Waco gliders waiting to take off for Varsity This was an immense operation. As usual with these things, the various sources don’t all agree but these numbers give an impression of the sheer size of the operation. Stephen Wright, in The Last Drop, counts 226 USAAF C-47s and 72 C-46s dedicated to carrying paratroops, 610 USAAF C-47s towing 906 gliders plus 1,123 RAF aircraft, total 2,937, whilst Martin Bowman in his book Air War Varsity counts 541 paratroop transports, 1,050 tow aircraft and 1,350 gliders: total approximately the same at 2,941. The aircraft belonged to IX Troop Carrier Command and 46 Group Transport Command. When fully assembled over Brussels, the train of aircraft taking part was over 200 miles long and is often quoted as having taken more than two and a half hours to pass overhead. Paratroopers being dropped during Varsity The 6th Airborne Division lifted 7,220 personnel, transported by 42 Douglas C-54 Skymasters and 752 C-47 Dakotas, together with some 420 Horsa, Hamilcar and Hadrian (Waco) gliders, whilst the 17th Airborne Division lifted 9,387 personnel, transported in 836 C-47s, and 72 C46 Commandos together with 930 Waco gliders. Gliders landed during Varsity The aircraft were protected by 889 escort fighters, and more than 2,000 other ground support aircraft, Spitfires, Typhoons, P-51s and P-47s, were probably involved in the overall operation. Operation Varsity was the largest ever single airborne drop and was judged to be a success, landing nearly 20,000 troops. Fifty-six aircraft (3.3%) were lost, together with another 16 flying resupply missions and a further 357 damaged. Around fifty gliders (3.8%) were destroyed and many of the remainder, probably around 60%, were damaged by flak or on landing. The 21st Army Group ORS (Operational Research Section) report records that 41.6% of gliders released below 1,000 ft, 44.1% released between 1,000 and 1,500 ft, 50.5% released between 1,500 and 2,000 ft, and 69.4% released at over 2,000 ft were hit by flak. Ken Cooper, of the Glider Pilot Regiment, described coming under fire as he crossed the Rhine: Over to my right, a Hamilcar took a hit in the belly and the tank dropped out, complete with its crew. It was common practice for the tank crew to man the tank before landing so that they could drive straight out of the glider and be in action immediately. The Hamilcar was now unbalanced and would have crashed. I was flying the 12th glider in the stream, and the aircraft about the fourth along was hit by flak and one wing broke off and came perilously close to me whilst the rest of the glider plummeted to earth. All around, various aircraft were hit by flak or fighters, and some of the C47s were in flames. It looked like the safest place to be was on the ground… The signaller on my tug flashed the release signal and I cast off. It wasn’t possible to see Haminkeln in the early morning fog but the church spire was sticking up out of it, and using this landmark I manoeuvred to where I thought my allocated pin point was. As I turned over the unmade autobahn, now the E36, a feature we were not to cross, my glider was hit by flak in both flaps which were down and were in shreds. This made the landing difficult because it wasn’t possible to reduce speed. Troops with rifles and machine guns were firing at this sitting target slithering towards them. To add to the difficulty, the ground was covered in “Rommel’s Asparagus”, pieces of railway line dug into the ground to deter an airborne invasion. The Germans had obviously expected us somewhere in the area. The element of surprise we had when we first arrived quickly disappeared shortly after landing. It was impossible to avoid these obstructions, and the starboard undercarriage was knocked off and a piece of wing went, too. An officer from one of the glider battalions, the 12th Devons recorded: I was in the glider carrying my battalion’s engineer detachment. They had a jeep with a trailer full of explosives. We could see the flak bursting around us before casting off and then it followed us down as we made our relatively silent approach from 2,500 feet. While we were still quite high, about one thousand, a shell splinter penetrated the petrol tank in the jeep and set the whole centre section of the Horsa ablaze. We did not have parachutes, of course, so there was nothing for it but to hope that we might land before the machine broke up or went out of control. Seconds seemed like minutes, and minutes, hours. Then, at last, it seemed that we would survive. The pilot made his final turn, lowering his flaps and approached to land. That is the last thing I remember. Sometime later, I suppose about half an hour, I regained consciousness to find myself lying on a haystack. Slowly I gathered my thoughts and looked about. All around where I lay, scattered over the field and farm buildings, were the fragments of my Horsa, the wreckage of the jeep and the bodies of the passengers and crew. Of the trailer there was no trace. The fire must have reached it and at the crucial moment it exploded. Loading a jeep into a Horsa glider It appears that the casualties from the landings amounted to around 20% of the troops involved and that, of these, some 30% (i.e. 6%) were occurred in the air or immediately after landing. The casualty rate suffered by the glider troops appears to have been significantly higher than that of those dropped by parachute, probably because of their longer, slower approach runs. Heavy equipment also suffered badly, with the final losses including 46% of 6th Airborne's jeeps, 44% of their trailers, 44% of their carriers, 50% of their light tanks, 29% of their 75mm Howitzers, 50% of their 25 pounders, 56% of their 17 pounder anti-tank guns, 29% of their 6 pounder anti-tank guns, and 56% of their Dodge 3/4 ton weapon carriers. A daylight landing in the face of heavy, mostly unsuppressed, flak (probably over 500 guns) was clearly a dangerous proposition, and the flak suppression provided by 336 medium bombers, 24,000 rounds of artillery, and 316 anti-flak sorties by Typhoons appears to have been ineffective, especially as the Germans had constructed many dummy sites. One conclusion drawn was that, in the future, glider landings should be preceded by parachute drops that would aim to neutralise flak positions before the more vulnerable gliders arrived.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How many ships did the UK lose during World War II? Did they lose any major capital ships, such as battleships or aircraft carriers?
Answer: At the start of World War Two, the Royal Navy was the largest navy in the world and it remained so until late 1943 or early 1944. It fought for six years in every theatre, including the Atlantic, the Mediterranean, the Arctic Ocean, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. During WW2, the Royal Navy lost in the region of 2,785 craft including 313 significant warships. These losses do not include the Canadian, Australian, New Zealand, Indian, or South African naval forces According to Admiralty figures, some 2,548 merchant vessels (11.86 million grt) were lost to war related causes. This excludes vessels of under 200 grt which would include most of the 136 fishing vessels and any other smaller craft lost. The Royal Navy lost 51,578 men over the course of WW2 and the Merchant Navy and fishing fleet some 30,250 men. HMS Hood - the largest warship in the world at the outbreak of the war. Of course, it rather depends on what you mean by “ship”. The breakdown of Royal Navy losses is itemised below and ranges from the Mighty Hood to the Armed Merchant Cruiser Jervis Bay to the Drifter George Albert, and includes such exotic vessels as the Monitor Terror, Chariot LXXIX, Landing Barge Kitchen No. 8, and the Train Ferry Daffodil. Most of these classes should be self-evident. The Escort category includes Frigates and Corvettes. Coastal Forces includes MTBs, MGBs and MLs. Mine Warfare includes Mine Layers and Minesweepers (excluding three mine-laying cruisers that are counted with the cruisers). Large Landing Craft includes LSIs, LSTs, LCTs, etc. Supply & Support includes Tankers, Colliers, and a whole range of other types. Miscellaneous contains larger auxiliaries including Armed Merchant Cruisers, Anti-aircraft ships, Fighter Catapult ships, etc., and Minor includes all the smaller vessels from manned torpedoes to tugs, etc. HMS Terror HMS Jervis Bay Drifter George Albert Landing Barge Kitchen HMS Daffodil Chariot human torpedo As far as warships are concerned, you can see that the landlocked seas of the Mediterranean were where the heaviest losses were taken and that aircraft and submarines were the real killers. The era of surface ship engagements had already largely passed. Analysis of data from Royal Navy and Naval History.Net As far as merchant shipping losses are concerned, it is clear that submarines were by far the main cause of losses, and it is interesting to note that losses to large surface warships are barely noticeable.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In a hypothetical battle, who would win between the Bismarck and an aircraft carrier?
Answer: The answer is that it is entirely situational. If the Bismarck started within a few miles of the carrier then the Bismarck would win hands down. If the Bismarck was much further away, then the carrier would probably win and certainly wouldn’t lose. WW2 carriers normally carried cruiser or destroyer armament to fend off destroyers and had very light armour; they were in no way designed to take on a battleship. In June 1940, the carrier HMS Glorious unexpectedly encountered the Scharnhorst and the Gneisenau at a distance of around 28 miles. Scharnhorst opened fire at 26,000 yards, and Glorious was hit within six minutes. Scharnhorst firing on Glorious Glorious’ sixteen 4.7” guns and 3” belt armour were in no conceivable way a match for the Scharnhorst’s nine 11” and twelve 5.9” guns and 13.8” belt armour. The action lasted for a little over an hour and only that long because one of Glorious’ two escorting destroyers, Ardent, managed to lay a smokescreen which blinded the Germans for 20 minutes. Glorious listing and on fire On the other hand, the attack that resulted in fatal damage to the Bismarck was launched from the Ark Royal when she was some 70 miles away. The Bismarck had no idea where the carrier was and no means of engaging her. Her FuMO27 radar could only see about 18 miles in ideal conditions.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did the Kriegsmarine ever possess the tactical ability to control the English Channel, even for a little while, at any point in WW2?
Answer: No, the Kriegsmarine never possessed tactical control over the English Channel although they did contest control with the British. Each side was able to run shipping along its own coastline, albeit at some risk from coastal craft and aircraft, but the British always held the balance of power. This is not the same as saying that the Germans never had any tactical successes in the region. Two examples spring to mind: During the Channel Dash of the 11th to 13th of February 1942 (Operation Zerberus) the German battleships Scharnhorst and Gneisenau and the cruiser Prinz Eugen were successfully relocated from Brest on the Atlantic coast to German ports in the Baltic. Scharnhorst During the Slapton Sands incident (Exercise Tiger) the Germans managed to sink two LSTs and damage two more, killing around 750 US servicemen in what came to be known as the Battle of Lyme Bay. USS LST-289 docks at Dartmouth, England, after being torpedoed by German MTBs during Exercise Tiger But these were isolated tactical successes, the Germans never gained tactical control over the Channel at any point.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How did the British give Winston Churchill the premiership after the disaster he caused in the Dardanelles at the Battle of Galipoli as First Lord of the Admiralty? I am Polish, we Poles believe that Britain has betrayed us?
Answer: This is a classic non-sequitur as the two sentences have no link whatsoever. To take the first one first, Churchill was not responsible for the Dardanelles debacle but, as the senior politician involved, he took responsibility for it and resigned, which is a different matter. The idea behind the Dardanelles campaign was actually reasonably sound and the fact that it was, ultimately, a failure can be attributed more to the lacklustre performance of the commanders on the ground than to politicians in Westminster. The initial failure of the Royal Navy to force the straits lies with Carden and, to an extent, with his replacement, de Robeck. The poor performance of the following land campaign lies with Hamilton and Birdwood. I’m all for the principle of politicians taking responsibility for outcomes, but we need to distinguish between the viability of the strategic concept and errors in the tactical handling of the campaign. The report of the Commission of Enquiry did not conclude that Churchill was personally responsible for the failure of the campaign. British artillery firing during the Gallipoli Campaign To take the second, totally unrelated, point, I once spent eighteen months working in Warsaw and I never came across anyone who held that view, so I suspect that yours is a minority opinion. If you think that Britain betrayed Poland, then you are going to have to articulate exactly what you think that Britain could have done differently, apart, of course, from fighting Germany for six years. In 1939, Poland only held out for thirty-five days before surrendering. There is no viable naval route to Poland, it was out of range of the British aircraft of the time, and any land campaign would have needed to fight right across Germany. In the event, Poland, which was expected to be able to hold out for a lot longer, surrendered before any meaningful action could take place. German troops invade Poland In 1945, there was nothing at all that Britain could do in the face of the fait accompli of the Russian occupation of Poland. It’s not Britain’s fault that Russia failed to honour the promises it made at Yalta. As is fairly well known, Churchill did, in fact, instigate planning for Operation Unthinkable, but it was clear from the outset that this would have zero chance of success without whole hearted American support. If you hold the view that Britain, in some way, betrayed Poland, then the onus is on you to present a credible counter argument as to what could have been done to save Poland that wasn’t done.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was Germany's plan after the successful operation Wacht am Rhein?
Answer: Wacht am Rhein was the codename for the unsuccessful German operation that the Allies called the Battle of the Bulge. This was the last major German offensive on the Western Front during WW2, and took place between December 1944 and January 1945 (the last major German offensive of the entire war was Frühlingserwachen, or Spring Awakening, which took place in Hungary on the Eastern Front in March 1945). The ultimate objective of Wacht am Rhein was to take the port of Antwerp, splitting the Allied armies and leaving several of them cut off from their tenuous supply lines. The idea was that this defeat would so disturb the British and the Americans that they would sue for a separate peace - providing the Germans with some breathing space and allowing them to concentrate their efforts on the Eastern Front. A German Panther advances during the Ardennes offensive. The plan was born of desperation and most of the senior German commanders believed that Hitler’s plan was simply unachievable in the face of Allied air superiority. Model and von Rundstedt both came up with less ambitious plans Herbstnebel (Autumn Wind) and Martin which both envisaged an attack from the Ardennes that did not attempt to cross the Meuse River. However, Hitler rejected these plans as simply delaying the inevitable and insisted on one last big gamble that relied on poor weather mitigating or negating Allied air superiority and that would see Antwerp taken in four days. Neither the weather nor the Americans cooperated and, although the Germans achieved surprise and casualties on both sides were relatively even, they never got closer than 85 miles to Antwerp. At the end of the day, Wacht am Rhein was never really more than an exercise in wishful thinking. Even had the Germans succeeded in capturing Antwerp the impact on the Western Allies would have been significant but not fatal. The fundamental strategic balance was simply too heavily against the Germans by this point in the war.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why isn't the Greek Navy mentioned in the Italy and Normandy landings even though it took part? Was its participation that minimal to be mentioned in history and maritime history?
Answer: The small Royal Hellenic Navy was pretty much destroyed in the Greco–Italian War (1940–41) and the subsequent German invasion of Greece. The remains of the Greek fleet, a cruiser, 6 destroyers, and 5 submarines relocated to the British fleet anchorage at Alexandria in Egypt where it was supplemented by ships loaned from the Royal Navy. Several RHN ships did indeed later participate in Operations Husky and Avalanche, including the destroyer RHN Vasilissa Olga. RHN Destroyer Vasilissa Olga There were two Royal Hellenic Navy warships present on D-Day, both Flower-class corvettes on loan from the Royal Navy. They were RHN Kriezis (ex-HMS Coreopsis) and RHN Tombazis (ex-HMS Tamarisk), and they were assigned to Force G and tasked with escorting the transports of the 50th (Northumbrian) Division and 8th Armoured Brigade landing on Gold Beach. RHN Kriezis/Coreopsis The Greek ships were part of the force of some 265 warships (corvettes or larger) and some 255 minesweepers, danlayers, and MLs that took part in the landings. Exact numbers are very hard to pin down as it depends on exactly what you count and sources vary. Broadly speaking this force (which excludes light units) consisted of 7 battleships, 2 monitors, 25 cruisers, 105 destroyers, 26 destroyer escorts, 27 frigates, 2 gunboats, and 71 corvettes. Of these 61% belonged to the Royal Navy, 23% to the US Navy, 11% to the Royal Canadian Navy, and 5% to other allied navies - of which 12 were Free French, 3 were Polish, 3 were Norwegian, 2 were Dutch, and, as discussed, 2 were Greek. According to the US Naval History and Heritage Command, Operation Neptune utilised 1,089 naval vessels, 1,373 merchant ships, and 4,021 landing ships and landing craft, for a total of 6,483 vessels of all kinds - a staggering number. Therefore, the contribution of the RHN to the D-Day was indeed small but no less welcome.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did tanks used to have a "back door" for escape in case of catastrophic failure or damage? Why was this feature discontinued in later models?
Answer: The only tank that I am aware of that literally has a back door is the Israeli Merkava. This is only possible because, unlike most other tanks, the Merkava has its engine positioned at the front of the hull rather than to the rear. Obviously, having the engine to the rear of a tank means that there is no egress for the crew to the rear. Merkava back door However, other tanks have been equipped with escape hatches, in addition to their normal access hatches, in a variety of positions. Escape hatches have been placed in the tank floor (Sherman), turret side (Tiger, Panther) or hull side (Panzer IV, Churchill). I understand that the Leopard II still has a floor mounted escape hatch, but that there isn’t one on the Challenger II or Abrams tanks, probably because every opening is also a potential weakness. Churchill escape hatch on hull side Sherman hull floor mounted escape hatch Tiger I escape hatch on turret side Panther turret escape hatch Panzer IV escape hatch

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why does the navy have such stupid looking hats? They don't even have a brim to block the sun. Do they serve a purpose?
Answer: Nearly all the world’s navies wear a similar hat. There are definite fashions in military wear and these are usually based on cues taken from victorious armies. When thinking about hats, other examples include the German pickelhaube, which was adopted by various countries including Great Britain and the United States, the Prussian Grenadier mitre cap, widely copied, and the bearskin of the French Imperial Guard which was adopted by Great Britain, Italy and assorted other countries. Before the mid-Nineteenth Century sailors had no specific uniforms and generally wore round straw hats, usually tarred, or knitted caps, depending on personal preference or possibly the sartorial ideas of the ship’s captain. Over time the round hat came to be replaced by the sennet hat in the Royal Navy, a kind of wide-brimmed boater. Royal Navy round ‘tarpaulin’ hat and later sennet hats In European armies, the official shako or stovepipe headgear then in fashion was too heavy and clumsy to be worn all the time. Therefore, for barracks use, they were replaced by forage caps, often knitted or home-made from remnants of discarded uniforms. Originally unofficial, or regimentally sanctioned, they became official in all armies over time. The sailor cap originates from the military forage cap and is a pretty close relative of both the tam o’shanter and, to an extent, the military beret - all being low crowned, comfortable to wear, cheap to produce, easily stowed, and, in most cases, immune to being crushed. Tam o’shanter and beret The modern sailor cap appears to have originated when Russian sailors had their uniforms standardised and based on those of the Russian Army, which included a round forage cap. This kind of forage cap continued in military use into WW1. Brodrick cap and feldmutze The sailor cap became commonly adopted because it was convenient in low decked ships with minimal headroom, didn’t obstruct the sailor’s view and wouldn’t get entangled in rigging. From a common basis, various styles evolved that included tallies (ribbons, often with the ship’s name on them), ribbons, bows, and pom-poms. US, British, German, and French sailor caps

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If German tanks had been sent to Omaha Beach on D-Day, could they have stopped the Allied invasion?
Answer: No, because Omaha Beach was only one of five beaches stormed on D-Day. Failure on Omaha would have been a significant setback, but it wouldn’t have stopped the whole Allied invasion. Also no, because there were no significant armoured forces within reach that could have been sent to Omaha Beach on D-Day. The divisions that were holding the coast were mostly static infantry divisions and thought themselves lucky if they had a company of assault guns assigned. Whilst Army Group B, consisting of the 7th and 15th Armies, holding the Channel Coast from Amsterdam to Lorient was under the command of von Rundstedt, the Panzer divisions were initially formed in Panzer Group West, under the command of von Schweppenburg. These nine divisions (2nd, 21st, 116th, 1st SS, 12th SS, 17th SS, 2nd SS, 9th and 11th) were tasked with covering the entire coastline of France, Holland, and Belgium, including the Mediterranean coast of France. The Germans decided to hold their main armoured units in reserve and at some distance from the coast so that they could react to wherever the invasion occurred. Their plan called for a mobile defence in depth to hold the allied invaders in check until a mobile strategic reserve could be brought to bear for a decisive counterattack and a battle of annihilation. Bearing in mind that the most likely invasion site was still thought to be the Pas de Calais rather than Normandy, the disposition of the Panzer divisions on June 6th 1944 was as follows: 2nd SS and 9th were on the Mediterranean coast, 11th Panzer was on the Atlantic coast, and 1st SS and 2nd were covering northern France and the Low Countries. That leaves a central group consisting of 116th, Pz Lehr, 12th SS and 21st roughly centred to the west of Paris and about 90 miles from the Normandy beaches. Rommel wanted to position the Panzer divisions nearer the coast where they could react more quickly but his views were opposed by von Rundstedt, von Schweppenburg, and Guderian. In reality, the Germans were in an impossible position. Stationing the Panzers nearer the coast would have allowed them to react more quickly, but it would also have put them directly under the guns of the immensely powerful Allied naval task forces stationed off the beaches. They would have entered the fight with less attrition, but would then have been rendered combat ineffective very quickly by Allied air and sea-power. Rommel had wanted to position 12th SS Panzer in the vicinity of Isigny, which would have put it around 12 miles from Omaha Beach rather than more than 100 miles to the east near Evreux. If 12th SS had indeed been stationed at Isigny, it would very probably have had a significant impact on the landings at Omaha Beach as it could have intervened before the Allies had managed to land much armour of their own, and it might possibly have caused the landings on Omaha to fail. Panzerkampfwagen IV Ausf H of 12. SS-Panzer-Division In fact, the nearest Panzer division to the US beaches was 21st Panzer, which was initially positioned near Falaise about 45 miles from Omaha Beach. In the event 21st Panzer was the only German panzer division to play a part on D-Day when it attempted to drive between the British and Canadian beaches in the vicinity of Caen. Whilst one kampfgruppe did succeed in reaching the coast at Lion sur Mer, their position was clearly untenable and they were forced to withdraw north of Caen, losing significant numbers of armoured vehicles in the process.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were flak towers only used by the Germans in World War 2? Were they effective?
Answer: This question has been coming up in my feed regularly for months, so I’ve decided to take a hack at it in the hope that it will go away. No, flak towers were not only used by the Germans in WW2. The British also built flak towers of various kinds for specific purposes, but they were by no means as monumental as the German versions. British army type Maunsell sea fort in the Thames Estuary British navy type Maunsell sea fort in the Thames Estuary Bofors flak towers at Caterham (left) and West Malling Before considering whether the towers were cost effective it is worth considering why they were built in the first place. The British towers were built either for local airfield defence or to protect the seaward approaches to vulnerable targets - London (seven) and Liverpool (three). In the case of these main British forts, they were all built in the sea and thus basically had to be towers of one kind or another. The most famous German flak towers, Flaktürme, were built to protect the major cities of Berlin (three), Hamburg (two) and Vienna (six). There were also unrealised plans to build towers in Bremen and Munich. German flak towers were built in pairs with a gun tower (Gefechtsturm) and a command tower (Leitturm), and came in three different designs or generations, getting smaller but taller as the war progressed. The L-Towers carried the radar, searchlights, and command control facilities and were lightly armed against low level attack. The first generation G-Towers were 70.5 m square and 39 m high and were ideally armed with four twin 128 mm guns and thirty-two 20 mm guns. The L-Towers were armed with four quad 20 mm guns. The second generation G-Towers were 57 m square and 41.6 m high and ideally armed with four twin 128 mm guns and four quad 20 mm guns. The L-Towers were armed with ten quad 20 mm guns. The third generation G-Towers were 43 m square and 54 m high and ideally armed with four twin 128 mm guns and eight quad 20 mm guns. Pairs of twin 12.8 cm guns on a flak tower Type 3 tower in Vienna (left) and Type 1 (right) in Berlin - the Zoo Tower Heiligengeistfeld Type 1 G-Tower, Hamburg - the windows had armoured shutters The Germans, and Hitler in particular, tended to emphasise flak over fighters and the towers were built to engage bombers during their final approach when the were most vulnerable because they had to fly straight and level. This meant that the flak guns would be most effective near the centre of the target city. However, in this position they would have poor lines of sight due to the buildings surrounding them - hence the idea to put them on towers where they could have an unobstructed 360 degree view. Ideally, the towers were to be arranged in a triangle to provide all round protection for the city. With concrete up to 3.5 metres thick, the flak towers also served a secondary purpose as air raid shelters and one of the towers in Berlin is said to have provided shelter to 30,000 civilians during one raid. The Type 3 tower in Vienna shown above consists of more than 45,000 cubic metres of reinforced concrete. The Thames estuary forts shot down twenty-two aircraft and about thirty V1s flying bombs and can be considered to have been moderately effective considering that they were relatively cheap to build. In terms of effectiveness, Flakturm III the Humboldthain flak tower in Berlin had a total of 32 confirmed kills (~£1.6 million) and probably cost around 90 million Marks (~£7 million?) to build. How many civilian lives it saved, and how many bombers it caused to miss their targets is unquantifiable. Steven Zaloga says that the flak force consumed between a quarter and a third of German ammunition production and half of the military’s electronic production. The quartermaster general of the Luftwaffe estimated that and 88/L36 anti-aircraft gun required 16,000 rounds expended per bomber downed, the 88/L41, 8,500 rounds, the 105/L39, 6,000 rounds, and the 128/L40, 3,000 rounds. Interestingly, there is evidence that the Russians are building towers around Moscow to house the radars of their Pantsir air-defence systems - presumably to increase its unobstructed radar horizon. Modern Russian tower

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were bazookas used by British forces during World War II? If not, why not?
Answer: Not, to any significant extent, in World War II. In September 1942, a consignment of 600 M1 bazookas was shipped to Egypt for use by the British Army in the Western Desert campaign. The first iteration of the bazooka and its ammunition both had issues and the weapons were not really ideal for use in the wide-open spaces of the desert where their blast and rocket trail were sure giveaways. When considering anti-tank weapons in WW2 we run into the fact, which many people either don’t understand or choose to ignore, that technology advanced so quickly during the war that weapons from one period of the war can seem ridiculously antiquated only a year or so later. In this case, an evaluation of the M1 bazooka would be very different to an evaluation of the M9A1 only two years later. M1 bazooka The British used the PIAT (Projector, Infantry, Anti Tank) which replaced the earlier Boys anti-tank rifle and the anti-tank rifle grenade. In this respect, it was a great leap forward as it utilised a shaped charge which could penetrate 4″ of armour as opposed to the Boys which could only penetrate 1″ (the M1 bazooka could penetrate around 3″). Both the PIAT and the M1 bazooka had a maximum effective range of around 100 yards and both suffered from early problems with their ammunition. In terms of accuracy in the field there seems to have been no appreciable difference between the two weapons - which might come as a surprise to some people. The advantages of the PIAT were that it could be used by one man, that the lack of blast and smoke made it harder to spot, that it could be fired from inside buildings and that it could be used, and frequently was, as an indirect fire weapon with a maximum range of around 350 yards. I’m not sure whether the Bazooka was commonly used, or could be used, for indirect fire. The PIAT was well liked, at least by those who didn’t have to carry it, and in a survey regarding the effectiveness of different infantry weapons the PIAT was ranked the number one most “outstandingly effective” weapon, followed by the Bren gun in second place. The main advantage of the Bazooka was that it was considerably lighter at 18lbs compared with the PIAT’s 32lbs and it didn’t have the fearsome recoil of the PIAT. Essentially, there wasn’t much difference between the two weapons when they were introduced in 1942 and both were significant advances over the previous means that infantry had been given to deal with armoured vehicles. PIAT Although there was no difference between the two weapons in 1942–44, in the longer run the spigot mortar was an evolutionary dead-end and the British eventually adopted the M20 super-bazooka after the war.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: I am falling from 900,000 feet. I have no parachute nor a backup parachute. If I were able to make my landing in the ocean, could I survive?
Answer: The Kármán line, the boundary of outer space, is conventionally set at 100 kilometres (62 miles) whilst 900,000 feet is 275 kilometres (170 miles), so you’d be in outer space and in Low Earth orbit. Not having a parachute would be the least of your worries. Barring really, really, freak circumstances, from any reasonable height you’ll accelerate at 32 feet per second per second, reaching terminal velocity for the human body, which is around 120–140 miles per hour, in less than six seconds and after about 700 feet. At that point, wind resistance will keep your speed stable. This assumes that you are not wearing anything that creates a significant amount of drag like a wingsuit. There is only about a 2–2.5% chance of surviving falling off the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco and that is only 245 feet above the water. Jumpers hit the water after about four seconds and at around 75 miles per hour and generally die of massive cardiothoracic, traumatic brain or spinal injury, or by drowning. The highest recorded survival from a fall is Vesna Vulović who fell 33,000′ (6.3 miles) in 1972 but she fell in the wreckage of an aircraft. In WW2, Nicholas Alkemade of the RAF fell 18,000′ (3.4 miles), Alan Magee of the USAAF fell 22,000′ (4 miles), and Ivan Chisov of the Soviet Air Force fell 23,000′ (4.3 miles) and survived. Their falls were broken variously by trees, snow, slopes and a glass roof. In normal circumstances, the FAA (US Federal Aviation Administration) concludes that the upper survival limit for impact into water is 100 ft/sec (68.2 mph), the equivalent of a 186-foot fall. Try and land feet-first to minimise deceleration shock. Nicholas Alkemade, Alan Magee, and Ivan Chisov

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If battlecruisers were superior and could sink enemy cruisers, why didn't HMS Hood sink or at least damage KMS Prinz Eugen, while the German cruiser accurately landed all shots on the dated battlecruiser during the Battle of Denmark Strait?
Answer: Lack of time, pure and simple. From the Hood’s perspective the Battle of the Denmark Strait lasted less than eight minutes. In that time she straddled Prinz Eugen, mistaking her for Bismarck, and would probably have hit her in the next couple of minutes if she had not been blown up as a result of a lucky shot from Bismarck. As some people don’t seem to understand the nature of luck in sea battles, I should explain that whilst the shooting from both the Bismarck and the Prinz Eugen was excellent (although it should be borne in mind that it was Prince of Wales that landed the first hit) they were only shooting at the target ship, not at a specific part of her. The location of the hit that destroyed the Hood was pure luck and she might have withstood dozens of similar hits without critical damage. In the same way, the torpedo that disabled the Bismarck was good shooting by the Swordfish crew, but its impact was pure luck. If it had hit further forward, it would have damaged but probably not crippled her. As for why the Prinz Eugen landed shots on Hood and not vice-versa there are probably several reasons. Firstly, Hood was approaching from an angle that only allowed her to open fire with her forward turrets. Secondly, her approach provided her fire control, which was not as modern as that of the Germans, with a difficult high rate of change problem. Thirdly she was approaching upweather which may have blinded some of her rangefinders with spray. The German ships were in a better tactical position for the fight but Holland probably assumed that, having the speed advantage, they would attempt to turn away, gefechtskehrtwendung, and he therefore chose to force the Germans to battle as fast as possible, even if that was disadvantageous from a tactical perspective. A better example of the intention behind the battlecruiser concept was the Battle of the Falkland Islands in 1914 where the British battlecruisers Invincible and Inflexible annihilated the German armoured cruisers SMS Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, suffering only ten killed compared to the 1,871 Germans lost. The battlecruisers were faster and better armed than the German ships, which could neither run away nor fight with any real hope of victory. This was exactly Fisher’s conception of what the battlecruisers were for. It is worth noticing that Prinz Eugen, a Hipper-class heavy cruiser had virtually the same 8x8″ armament as the SMS Scharnhorst and, although faster, was less heavily armoured. The Hood would have soon finished her off if the Bismarck had not been present. HMS Inflexible rescuing German survivors from Gneisenau

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How close was HMS Hood to landing shells on the Bismarck before she was hit and sunk herself?
Answer: The problem with the Battle of the Denmark Strait is that there are many conflicting accounts and, of course, only three men from the Hood survived the battle, none of them in a position to know what was in the mind of Vice Admiral Holland. As a result much of the analysis of the battle must forever remain speculative. Bismarck from Prinz Eugen As the battle commenced, Prinz Eugen was leading Bismarck as the latter’s radar had been put out of action by the concussion of her guns firing on Norfolk the previous day.
