Therefore, given their similar silhouettes, the British ships both opened fire on the Prinz Eugen thinking that, as she was in the lead, she was the Bismarck. The mistake was recognised and the order given by Holland, on the Hood, to switch fire to the Bismarck - which was the far more dangerous opponent. However, for reasons unknown, it is not clear whether the Hood ever actually switched her fire to the Bismarck and certainly her last salvo was aimed at Prinz Eugen. The battle commenced at 05:52 and the Hood blew up either just before or just after 06:00. Therefore, there was a maximum of eight minutes for her to adjust her fire. The simple answer is that, although she straddled Prinz Eugen, albeit without hits, she doesn’t appear to have fired at Bismarck at all. It was Prince of Wales that landed the three hits on Bismarck.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did Germany use an Enigma machine despite the risk of their codes being broken by cryptologists? Can this be compared to leaving a door unlocked with keys easily accessible?
Answer: They had to use something, so the question begs the further question of what else could they have used that would have been better? The answer is that nothing better was available. Any cryptographic scheme except for a one-time pad can potentially be broken. Whilst the Germans must have been intellectually aware that Enigma could be broken, they deemed that the time and effort required would far outweigh any benefits the Allies might get in the form of timely - and being timely is of critical importance - intelligence. As it happens, the Germans made several key mistakes which led them to overestimate the security of Enigma. Firstly there was a design flaw in the machine in that a letter could never be encoded as itself, secondly German procedure was sometimes lax and allowed cribs to be developed where the contents of a message could sometimes be deduced, and thirdly they completely underestimated the amount of effort that the British, with some Polish and French assistance, would be put into breaking Enigma and the organisational, mathematical and engineering genius that would be deployed in cracking the machine. The British deployed more than ten thousand men and women in the effort to break Enigma, not only in the code breakers themselves, but in the wireless intercept Y-Stations, the analysts who kept vast cross-referenced filing systems of all the information gleaned, the operators of the machinery, the translators of the messages, and many, many, more. The keys to Enigma were most certainly not easily accessible by any possible standard. Multiple keys had to broken with huge effort every single day. Getting timely intelligence from Enigma, without the Germans realising what was happening, was a triumph of brains, organisation, and sheer willpower. Daily solutions of Fish messages at GC&CS reflect a background of British mathematical genius, superb engineering ability, and solid common sense. Each of these has been a necessary factor. Each could have been overemphasised or underemphasised to the detriment of the solutions; a remarkable fact is that the fusion of the elements has been apparently in perfect proportion. The result is an outstanding contribution to cryptanalytic science. US Cryptanalyst Albert W. Small As to why the Germans used Enigma, they used it because it was the most secure deployable system that they had until Lorenz came along. Their problem was that they became overconfident in its security and did not take all the measures that they could have done to make life difficult for the British. In fact, it is a little known fact that the British also used an adapted Enigma, the Typex, into the 1950s. German Enigma machine British Typex machine

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In a hypothetical battle, could modern ships defeat WWII-era ships?
Answer: Assuming that carriers aren’t involved, possibly to probably. If the WW2 ship was a major unit, heavy cruiser or above - one with decent armour - then the modern ship might or might not be able to make a serious impression on it, depending on what weapons it had to hand. Certainly any modern warship that found itself without anti-ship missiles would have problems against a capital unit from WW2. Bismarck-class vs Arleigh-Burke-class - modern navies don’t really do big ships if we exclude the carriers. On the other hand if the ships found themselves in close proximity, a WW2-era ship could knock seven bells out of any modern ship. No modern warship carries anything more than splinter armour and so even the guns carried by destroyers and the secondary batteries of larger ships are going to wreak havoc. In fact shells from larger guns might actually go straight through the target without detonating as they wouldn’t meet much resistance. The modern weapons are going to fire faster and be targeted more precisely, but the WW2-era weapons are going to be available in much larger numbers and be better protected. The problem, of course, would be getting into close proximity in the first place. With current sensors, the modern ship is going to be able to spot the WW2-era ship before the WW2-era ship is going to see it. Depending in when in WW2 we are talking about, the WW2-era ship might be able to pick something up out to about thirty miles, whilst the a modern search radar might be able to see up to one hundred miles.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If Germany in WW2 had spent all the money and expended all the labor they did on heavy cruisers and battleships instead of on subs and torpedo boat, would the sea fight have turned out differently?
Answer: This question is asking whether the Germans would have been better off spending money on heavy surface units than on submarines. The answer is NO, it would have been a disastrous strategy for the Germans. German surface raiders (excluding light units) sank around 1,100,000 tons of shipping whereas submarines sank over 14,500,000 tons in the Atlantic alone. It gets even worse. Of the 1,100,000 tons sunk by surface raiders only about 300,000 tons was actually sunk by warships, the most successful being the Admiral Scheer with 113,223 tons sunk. Admiral Scheer The other 800,000 tons was sunk by humble auxiliary cruisers. The top scoring ship being the auxiliary cruiser Pinguin (Raider F) which sank over 136,000 tons, more than the Admiral Scheer. Pinguin (Raider F), the most effective German surface ship Therefore, Kriegsmarine heavy units only sank around 2% of British shipping losses, which was a very poor showing and far, far less than submarines, aircraft, or even mines. U-boats were extremely efficient in terms of cost to build and run, steel required, crew required, and oil consumption whilst on operations. Estimates vary widely, but you could probably get around 50 Type VII U-boats, the most common class, for the cost of a Bismarck. The average U-boat sank around 15,000 tons in its career, whereas the average German heavy unit (Graf Spee, Scheer, Deutschland, Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, Hipper) sank around 54,000 tons. If the Germans had built no U-Boats, they could, in theory, have built (very) approximately twenty more Bismarcks. That would have been trading 14,500,000 tons sunk by the U-Boats for around 1,100,000 additional tons sunk by heavy units based on actual outcomes. Of course, its not really that simple a comparison, but, whichever way you look at it, its not a good exchange rate. Regardless of any of this, the basic fact is that the Germans simply didn’t have enough time or shipyards to build large numbers of heavy units, or enough oil to deploy them.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the British mission in Operation Unthinkable?
Answer: There were two operational plans named UNTHINKABLE. The question probably refers to the first which was a planning scenario developed in early 1945, whilst the war was still in progress, to study the possibility of liberating East Germany and Poland from the Soviets. The plan assumed that British, American, Polish and German forces would fight a short sharp action to drive Russian forces back to the lines of the Oder and Neisse rivers with the objective of forcing Stalin to abide to the terms of the Yalta agreement and thereby achieve a “square deal” for Poland (and other Eastern European nations), particularly by allowing free elections. The British mission or objective under this scenario was Stettin/Szczecin followed by Bydgoszcz and Danzig/Gdańsk. Possible operations for Operation Unthinkable The conclusion of the Joint Planning Staff’s review of the plan (22nd May 1945) was that although it might be possible to shock the USSR into negotiations, it was also impossible to predict the scale of the conflict that might result - including the possibility that the USSR might ally with Japan, as this was before the USSR declared war on Japan on the 9th August 1945. It might, however, be considered, as the result of a political appreciation, that a quick and limited military success would result in Russia accepting our terms… If this appreciation is wrong and the attainment of whatever limited objective we may set ourselves does not cause Russia to submit to our terms, we may, in fact, be committed to a total war… Apart from the chances of revolution in the USSR and the political collapse of the present regime – on which we are not competent to express an opinion – the elimination of Russia could only be achieved as a result of: The occupation of such areas of metropolitan Russia that the war making capacity of the country would be reduced to a point at which further resistance became impossible. Such a decisive defeat of the Russian forces in the field as to render it impossible for the USSR to continue the war. Essentially, the Joint Planning Staff thought that there was no guaranteed way of forcing the Russians to abide by their commitments and a high likelihood of starting an uncontrollable conflict; the scenario was shelved. Joint Planning Staff opinion on Operation Unthinkable Operation Unthinkable was not framed as an aggressive attack on the USSR, as some people suggest, but rather as a means of making Stalin stick to his existing commitments. It should also be noted that such planning scenarios are very common and do not imply that there is any intention of implementing them. For instance War Plan Red was a 1930s US plan for a war with the British Empire, including the invasion of Canada, but there is no suggestion that the US ever intended to implement it. In the event, the January 1947 Polish parliamentary election fell well short of being a free election and Poland had to wait until June 1989 for its first truly free election. The second draft of Operation Unthinkable appears to have been a response to a request by Churchill: Pray have a study made of how then we could defend our island, assuming France and the Low Countries were powerless to resist the Russian advance to the sea. This was a purely defensive scenario and initiated the thinking that led to the formation of NATO and the creation of the British Army of the Rhine (BAOR). It is interesting to note that after seventy-five years of defending Germany, BAOR (British Forces Germany from 1994) was finally phased out in 2020 - just in time for the present unpleasantness. Igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it possible for someone who is not related to royalty or nobility to obtain their own coat of arms? If so, how?
Answer: You will possibly be pleased to know that it is indeed possible to obtain a coat of arms as a commoner. This is also true for our American cousins if they can prove some English ancestry somewhere along the line. The College of Arms, or Heralds' College, is a royal corporation of thirteen officers of arms in ordinary: three kings, six heralds and four pursuivants of arms. These officers are appointed by the Crown and are delegated the authority to act on behalf of the Crown in all matters of heraldry, including the granting of new coats of arms. English Officers of Arms Arms and crests, together with badges and supporters, are granted by letters patent issued by the senior heralds, the Kings of Arms. The applicant must to submit a petition, or memorial, to the Earl Marshal. There are no fixed criteria, but such things as awards or honours from the Crown, civil or military commissions, university degrees, professional qualifications, public and charitable services, and eminence or good standing in national or local life, are taken into account. Basically you need to be (seen as) a good egg. Applicants from citizens of countries where King Charles III is not the Head of State (and where there is no national heraldic authority) must meet the same criteria of eligibility for a grant as subjects of the Crown and, in addition, they must record in the official registers of the College of Arms a pedigree showing their descent from a subject of the British Crown. As of 1 January 2024 the fees payable upon a personal grant of arms and crest are £8,950. If the Earl Marshal approves a petition he will issue his Warrant to the Kings of Arms allowing them to proceed with the design and grant. Grant of coat of arms The Kings of Arms have full discretion over the design but the wishes of the applicant are taken into account as fully as possible. The officer of arms who is acting for the petitioner will discuss with him or her the allusions and references he or she would like made in the design. The design must be correct from an heraldic perspective and be distinct from all previous arms on record at the College. References in the design could be made to the person’s profession, family, interests or place of residence or origin. There is also a long tradition of visual puns in heraldry, some of them obvious, others less so. For example the late Queen Mother Elizabeth née Bowes-Lyon’s arms featured, you guessed it, bows and lions. It is interesting to note that the grant is for the heraldic description, not the artwork, thus: The Royal arms, impaling, quarterly, First and Fourth, Argent, a lion rampant Azure armed and langued Gules within a double tressure flory counter-flory of the second; Second and Third, Ermine, three bows, strings palewise Proper.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you recommend any novels about the US Navy Submarine service during World War II?
Answer: The classic is Run Silent, Run Deep, and its sequel Dust on the Sea, by Edward L. Beach who was himself a decorated WW2 submariner. Also made into a film starring Clark Gable and Burt Lancaster. Although they are about the Royal Navy submarine service rather than the USN, I feel that I would be derelict if I did not also recommend David Black’s excellent Harry Gilmore novels starting with Gone to Sea in a Bucket. Probably the best WW2 fiction I have read - and I’ve read a lot.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why was the B-29 Superfortress only used by the USAAF and USN and not by the RAF?
Answer: Well, firstly the B-29 wasn’t much used by the US Navy either. As far as I am aware, the US Navy only ever acquired four B-29s for evaluation, and that after the war in 1947. They were redesignated the P2B. US Navy P2B 84029, Fertile Myrtle, drops the Douglas D-558-II Skyrocket The B-29 was an astonishing test-bed for new technology, the whole programme costing more than the Manhattan Project. Unfortunately it was also an evolutionary dead end at the dawning of the jet age. The B-29 arrived in May 1944, late in WW2, and its long range simply wasn’t required for the war in Europe. In addition, it suffered a significant number of teething troubles, with fatal engine fires being a particular problem. All in all there was neither time nor a requirement for the RAF to adopt the B-29 in the last year of the war in Europe. However, the RAF did use the B-29, which it renamed the Washington B.1, after the war. The RAF acquired or was loaned 87 surplus B-29s from the USAAF in the 1950 as a stop-gap until the Canberra and the V-Bombers entered service. These B-29s were mostly returned by 1954 although I believe that three were converted for ELINT duties and these weren’t returned until 1958. RAF Washington The Canberra started entering service in 1951, and was so successful that the USAAF licenced the design and built 400 of them as the Martin B-57. The V-Bombers started to enter service with the Vickers Valiant in 1955, the Avro Vulcan in 1956, and the Handley Page Victor in 1958. By this stage the B-29 was a essentially a technological dinosaur despite only having been in service for a decade. English Electric Canberra Vickers Valiant Avro Vulcan Handley Page Victor In fact, the largest user of the B-29 apart from the USAAF was the USSR, which built 847 Tupolev Tu-4s between 1947 and 1952. Tupolev Tu-4 During the war, three B-29s had made forced landings in Soviet territory and been interned whilst a fourth had crashed. Stalin ordered that the plane be copied exactly and mass production started in 1949. However, the Tu-4 was already being phased out of Soviet service in favour of the Tupolev Tu-16 Badger and Tupolev Tu-95 Bear by 1954. The B-29 was retired by the USAAF in 1960, sixteen years after its introduction.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why does the UK have no naval base in the North Sea?
Answer: Because it doesn’t need one. The North Sea is the responsibility of other NATO countries - the ones who have no choice but to be based there - whilst the Royal Navy focusses on the Atlantic. Historically the Royal Navy based its ships on the English Channel coast at Portsmouth or protecting the Thames Estuary at Chatham and Deptford, because the main enemies it anticipated facing were the Netherlands, France, and Spain. Germany wasn’t unified until 1871 and, until 1893 it didn’t have anything bigger than a frigate. However, when the German Navy, the Kaiserliche Marine, started to become a potential threat, the Royal Navy developed a plan to control the exit points of the North Sea and started to develop naval bases at Rosyth on the Firth of Forth and Scapa Flow in the Orkneys (from 1904). With these bases in the North and the existing bases at Chatham, Portsmouth and Plymouth, the Royal Navy was in a position to impose a distant blockade on any ship trying to exit the North Sea. The Grand Fleet During WW1 ships were often based on the North Sea coast at Rosyth, Invergordon, and Harwich. Indeed he base at Rosyth was specifically developed to support ships blockading the German North Sea ports before the decision to move even further north to Scapa Flow. The Grand Fleet at Rosyth The same basic approach was followed in WW2 except that a new Western Approaches command was created based on Liverpool to manage the convoys and their escort groups. Now the Royal Navy is once again concentrated on the Channel ports, except for the submarines, which are based on the West Coast at Faslane on the Clyde.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the reason for not building battleships and carriers anymore?
Answer: Clearly there is still a reason to build carriers because carriers are getting built. However, that does not mean that this will continue for ever, because it won’t. There is a reason for not building battleships anymore and that’s because there simply isn’t a use case for them. There is nothing that a battleship can do that a carrier, or to be more precise a carrier’s airwing cannot do better and at far longer range. The case for building, or not building, carriers is more interesting and more nuanced and I think that it is possible that we may be approaching the end of an era. Weapons become obsolete when other weapons are developed that can overmatch them more cheaply. The era of the battleship came to an end with the development of the torpedo and the mine and their delivery systems, the submarine and the aircraft. These are extremely cheap weapons and delivery systems when compared with the cost of a battleship. We are now clearly entering a new era, heralded by rapid advances in artificial intelligence and drones - in the sense of aircraft and ships as well as the more common sense - with networked behaviours. Taking humans out of the weapon, if not entirely out of the loop, be it a ship or an aircraft or a tank, means that weapons can become cheaper, lighter, faster, and longer ranged. Supporting humans is expensive, and without them you can build more weapons for a given cost and employ them in much more hazardous environments. In addition, the manpower, and thus the cost, required to run your armed forces will also decrease significantly, which frees up even more money for weapons. In the future, weapons may become fully autonomous or they may keep humans in the loop as with, say, the RQ-4 Global Hawk or MQ-9 Reaper. Interesting concepts under development are extenders like the MQ-28 Ghost Bat and even submarine launched drones like SULAS, and there will be many others, some of which will almost certainly have autonomous capabilities. In my opinion what this means is that, over the next decade, we are very likely to see an explosion of drone and swarm based reconnaissance platforms and weapons, including smart mines and naval drones with long range and long-term loitering capabilities. USS George Washington Carrier Strike Group, 2003 Now a US Navy carrier group is an awesome thing, but it is also a very expensive thing. The cost of a Gerald R. Ford-class carrier is around $13 billion and that doesn’t include the aircraft, escort ships, refitting cycle, or running costs. In warfare, it is a bad idea to put too many of your eggs in one basket, and having a few very expensive platforms is risky unless you are absolutely sure that they are close to invulnerable. We simply don’t know how vulnerable carriers are, because they have never been tested in a hot war. A carrier is useful because it can deploy weapons to any location within the range of its aircraft, and because, once it reaches its patrol area, it can be very responsive to rapidly evolving situations. Once the equation starts to shift, either because the carrier becomes vulnerable to new threats, or because weapons come into service that can strike the same targets as the carrier but more cheaply, then the use case for carriers disappears and so will the carriers. At some point this will happen.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the coolest obscure historical fact you know?
Answer: Falkes, or Faux, de Bréauté (died 1226) was an Anglo-Norman soldier, a commoner who was knighted by King John and rose high, first in his service and then in the service of Henry III, before falling into ill-favour and exile. As a reward for his loyalty, John gave Faulkes the hand of Margaret, daughter of Warin Fitzgerald the royal chamberlain. Part of Margaret’s property, inherited from her first husband, Baldwin de Redvers, was a large Manor in South Lambeth. On this property, sometime after 1216, Falkes built a hall, which naturally came to be known as Falke’s Hall. That area of London thus came to be known, and still is known, as Vauxhall. Around 1660, Vauxhall became the site of the New Spring Gardens, also known as the Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens. Patronised by such luminaries as Charles II, Pepys, Evelyn, Fielding, Smollett, and Dickens, for 200 years the gardens drew enormous crowds who were entertained by tightrope walkers, hot-air balloon ascents, concerts and fireworks. Imagine unending avenues, entire woods brightly illuminated with flares; galleries, colonnades, pavilions, alcoves tricked out with murals and busts of famous men; resplendent triumphal arches set in dense greenery, with an orchestra blaring beneath; throngs of people everywhere; banqueting tables everywhere, decorated with flowers and greenery. My dazzled eyes sought out the dark, I entered a narrow covered avenue and was told: “This is Druids’ Delight”! I went on: I could see, by the light of the moon and distant torches, a desert and scattered hillocks representing a Roman encampment; there were cypresses and cedars growing here. On a knoll sat Milton - in marble - listening to the music; further on there was an obelisk, a Chinese garden; finally the path ran out... I returned to the orchestra. If you are quick off the mark, you have realised that I am describing to you the famous English Vauxhall, which other countries attempt in vain to imitate. What a capital evening resort, worthy of a clever and wealthy nation! The orchestra plays mainly favourite popular songs, the singers are actors and actresses off the London stage and the audience keeps throwing them money as a mark of its pleasure… After eleven o’ clock supper was served in the pavilions and horns began to sound in the grove. Never in my life had I seen such a multitude of people at table - the effect was of some magnificent festival. We chose our pavilion, ordered chicken, anchovies, cheese, butter and a bottle of claret and paid six roubles. N M Karamzin, Letters of a Russian Traveller, July 1790 The fame of the Vauxhall gardens spread far and wide and the concept was imitated in many European cities, with the best known surviving example being the Tivoli Gardens in Copenhagen - first named Tivoli & Vauxhall in 1843. In 1780, an English theatre manager, Michael Maddox, created new pleasure grounds within the estate of the Pavlovsk Palace in St. Petersburg, which became known as Vokzal. The first railway in Russia, built in 1837, served Imperial interests, running from Saint Petersburg via Tsarskoye Selo (the Tsar’s Village) to the Pavlovsk Palace. Its terminus near the Pavlovsk Palace pleasure grounds also adopted the name Vokzal, and this soon became the generic term for railway terminii in Russian: Vokzal in the Latin alphabet, and вокзал in Cyrillic. Tashkent railway station Moscow Rizhsky railway station So an obscure commoner born in the 12th Century, ended up being memorialised in the Russian language as the word for a railway station. I wonder what old Falkes would have made of that? As an aside, in 1857, Alexander Wilson founded a manufacturing company which had various premises located in the Vauxhall area. In 1897 the company was rescued from receivership and renamed the Vauxhall Ironworks Company, adopting as its logo the heraldic device of a Griffin (some say a Wyvern) that was said to have been used by Falkes. This device will instantly be familiar to any British reader as the badge still used on Vauxhall cars.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did any of Winston Churchill's grandchildren serve during World War II, specifically on D-Day? If yes, who were they and where did they serve?
Answer: Churchill had five children but one of these, Marigold, died in 1921 at the age of two. The other four were Diana, Randolph, Sarah, and Mary. During the war, Diana was an officer in the WRENs (Women’s Royal Naval Service), Sarah joined the WAAF (Women’s Auxiliary Airforce), and Mary joined the ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service) serving in anti-aircraft batteries in England and Belgium. Randolph joined the 4th Queen’s Own Hussars in 1938, and then served in No. 8 Commando, in Middle East HQ in Cairo, in the SAS (briefly), and then with the Military Mission to Yugoslavia and Croatia. He seems to have been thoroughly disliked by most people who had to work with him, but he was recommended for a Military Cross at one point. Randolph Churchill with Yugoslavian Partisans in Croatia in 1944 Churchill had ten grandchildren, but six of these were born after the war. Of the others, Julian was born in 1936, Edwina in 1938, Winston in 1940, and Celia in 1943. All a little too young to have served in the war - even considering the serious manpower shortage. You may be thinking of Jack Churchill, Fighting Jack Churchill or Mad Jack. Churchill had a younger brother Jack, who served in the Second Boer War and WW1, but this was not he. Mad Jack, latterly in command of No.2 Commando, was a colourful character who carried a broadsword and is reputed to have killed a German with a longbow, but this is probably apocryphal. He also played the bagpipes. Mad Jack was no relative of Churchill and was not present on D-Day as he fought, and was made a POW, in Italy. Lt. Col. Jack Churchill Churchill with broadsword in hand (far right)

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: I have just read an article referring to a kickback to Shapps’ statement. One of the remarks made referred to “irreplaceable talent” in the RAF. Can an Armed Force afford such luxury? Are service personnel, by definition, expendable?
Answer: No, armed forces certainly cannot afford to have irreplaceable talent. It is a fundamental characteristic of any armed force that it must expect to take casualties of any type, at any level, and at any time and keep on functioning effectively without pause. If you have irreplaceable talent then you don’t have an effective armed force. The task of the armed forces is to close with and destroy the enemy as expeditiously as possible. That’s it. It is not a core requirement of the armed forces that they reflect the structure of society. It is a core requirement that they are capable of doing, and can be relied upon to do, the job required of them. That means that, in the Army and Marines, recruits need to be fit, motivated, capable of operating in strenuous and harsh conditions for extended periods, and must have a certain level of aggression. Various sections of society do and do not have these characteristics and recruitment efforts need to be concentrated on those sections that do. Fitness, stamina, and aggression are essential The more chairborne armed forces, the Navy and the RAF can afford slightly more relaxed criteria. The current debate, in the usual febrile environment of over-reaction and escalation, centres around the manifest failure of existing recruitment policies. This either reflects (a) that society has become unwilling or unable to defend itself, (b) that recruitment policy is poorly targeted and needs adjusting, or (c) that poor pay and conditions makes it impossible to recruit in a competitive market. Whatever combination of these factors is the case, this is a serious problem that needs to be addressed quickly, and transparently - and, if such a thing is still possible, in an adult manner.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Do you think the Royal Navy will name another ship Hood?
Answer: Well of course the original Hood was sunk in rather bathetic circumstances in the Battle of the Denmark Strait, which is a bit of a downer as far as these things go. However, the Royal Navy currently has a carrier named Prince of Wales and the last one of those, a King George V-class battleship, was sunk by Japanese torpedo aircraft in 1941. Prince of Wales Previous Prince of Wales sinking An even more apposite comparison would be with Invincible (R05) an aircraft carrier that was stricken from service in 2005. She shared her name with Invincible, a battlecruiser like Hood, launched in 1907 which famously blew up, like Hood, at the Battle of Jutland in 1916 whilst serving as the flagship of the 3rd Battlecruiser Squadron commanded, as it happens, by Admiral Sir Horace Hood. Out of a combined total of nearly 2,500 men there were only six survivors from Invincible and only three from Hood. Invincible Previous Invincible sinking In a strange coincidence, Horace Hood was the great-great-grandson of Admiral Samuel Hood, 1st Viscount Hood, after whom the ill-fated Hood was named. The Royal Navy likes reusing names and actually carries battle-honours from one name to the next - the current Prince of Wales’ first battle honour is St Lucia, 1778. It’s pretty clear that the Royal Navy would be perfectly happy to commission another Hood, the fourth to bear the name. However, we don’t seem to be naming ships after Admirals at the moment.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can someone obtain a British noble title, like "Lord," without being born into a noble family?
Answer: There are two means of becoming a Lord but they are completely different. The proper way is when Letters Patent are issued by the King to create a life peerage. These peerages are appointments for political or other service and are not hereditary. They have to be scrutinised by the House of Lords Appointment Committee and then by the Prime Minister and the King. In 1999, most hereditary peers were removed from the House of Lords except for a rump of ninety who are elected by their peers. The House of Lords is now mostly composed of Life Peers whose title dies with them. Leaving aside the Royal Family, which is a special case, the last hereditary peerages were created in 1984 when Harold Macmillan was created the Earl of Stockton, and William Whitelaw and George Thomas were created Viscounts. As far as I know, there is nothing to stop new hereditary peerages being created but it is not very likely. Peers in the House of Lords The other way is to purchase the Lordship of a Manor - which anyone can do if one is available (no new ones can be created). However, this is not a peerage and not a noble title. The holder of a lordship of the manor can style themselves as Lord or Lady of the manor of [Placename], or Lord or Lady of [Placename]. For example (potentially) I could be Richard Meakin, Lord of [the manor of] Isfield, so long as the "of" is not omitted and the name of the holder is included before so as not to imply a peerage. I couldn’t call myself Lord Isfield as that would imply a peerage. A bit pointless really. If you are desperate, you could always change your name by deed poll as David Edward Sutch did when he changed his name to Screaming Lord Sutch. However, please note that the U.K. Deed Poll Service will not allow you to change your first name to Lord or indeed to anything that would imply you have a title.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Before she was scuttled, what condition was the German battleship Bismarck in?
Answer: She may or may not have been scuttled but , without a shadow of a doubt, she was sinking anyway. There is a peculiar meme going round that the British didn’t manage to sink her and she only sank when the Germans scuttled her. There is actually no conclusive evidence that she was scuttled although it appears that the order was given. But, even if the charges went off it would only have hastened the inevitable so this has always seemed to me a pointless and sterile argument. Obviously some people care but I am at a loss to know why. The Bismarck was not only a mission kill within the first few minutes, with no command control, no steering, and few working guns, but was clearly actually sinking by the end of the battle, well beyond any hope of salvage. Within fifteen minutes of the battle opening at 08:47, Bismarck lost her bridge and main fire control director together with most of her senior officers. Either at that time or very soon afterwards both of her forward turrets, Anton and Bruno, were out of action. By 09:31 all of her main turrets were out of action. According to von Mullenheim-Rechberg’s account, by this time the ship was in chaos with smoke and fumes from multiple fires driving her remaining crew from their stations, ready ammunition exploding, hundreds of men dead or wounded, and damage control efforts having been abandoned. By this time our list to port was heavier than ever and starboard was the lee side. I called to the men to look for a place aft and to starboard on the main deck. Forward, there was too much destruction and the smoke was unbearable. The quarterdeck was out of the question: the sinking ship was too far down by her stern and heavy breakers were rolling over her from her port quarter. In her final battle Bismarck scored no hits on the enemy. A fine ship but a sad and ignominious end for the pride of the Kriegsmarine. KMS Bismarck

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During the Falklands War, was it right for Task Force leader Admiral Sandy Woodward to suggest that ARA Belgrano was part of a pincer movement and therefore represented an imminent threat to Britain’s aircraft carriers?
Answer: Yes, he was right, but it really doesn’t matter, the ARA Belgrano was a warship belonging to a country that had just opened hostilities against the United Kingdom. It is irrelevant whether the Belgrano was advancing or retreating, whether she was inside or outside the exclusion zone, whether she was an imminent threat or not, or what her intentions were. Whatever the case, she was a valid target. HMS Conqueror returns to port after sinking the Belgrano As it happens, the Belgrano certainly was part of an intended pincer movement and she was a credible and imminent threat. In fact, she was in one of four groups of that made up the Argentinian Task Force 79. The carrier group with Veinticinco de Mayo and two Type 42 destroyers was to the north of the Falklands and believed to have been preparing a strike against the British carriers. Also to the north were two other groups one with two Exocet-armed destroyers and one with three Exocet-armed corvettes. The fourth group was the Belgrano and two more destroyers positioned to the south of the Falklands. The final moments of the Belgrano There is plentiful evidence, including that of the Captain of the Belgrano, that she was manoeuvring rather than sailing away, and that she was actively preparing to attack the British Task Force. The story of the Belgrano is tragic but we see this bizarre meme where the aggressor is portrayed as the victim repeated over and over again: the strategic bombing of Germany in WW2, the atom bombs dropped on Japan, the Russian attack on Ukraine, and the Hamas attack on Israel being a few examples. It should be clear to the meanest intelligence, but apparently isn’t, that if you enter into hostilities you really shouldn’t be surprised if your intended victim fights back. You don’t get to complain that is not fair that you then have to suffer the consequences of your own actions.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How is Cleopatra related to Alexander the Great? Are both considered from Macedonian origin despite coming from Egypt and Greece respectively?
Answer: Cleopatra VII was a descendent Ptolemy I Sotor who was the son of Arsinoe of Macedon. Arsinoe was married to Lagus of Eordaia, but she had previously been a concubine of Philip II, the father of Alexander, who gave her to Lagus. The story is that she was pregnant by Philip when she married Lagus, which would make Ptolemy the half-brother of Alexander and Cleopatra VII, the tenth generation of the Ptolemy Dynasty, a very distant half-niece of Alexander. Philip II father of Alexander and possible ancestor of Cleopatra Alexander’s mother was Olympias of Epirus who was a Queen rather than a concubine. She also had a daughter, Cleopatra of Macedonia, who was Alexander’s only full sibling. Obviously Cleopatra was a family name. Cleopatra and Alexander were certainly both of Macedonian origin and both considered themselves Hellenes. Whether they were actually related is unknown. There were certainly advantages for the Ptolemy dynasty in claiming such a prestigious link but, on the other hand, it may well be true.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it true that Cleopatra could NOT have been a Queen of Egypt because she wasn't even an Egyptian but a Macedonian Greek?
Answer: Where did you get the idea that you had to be Egyptian to be the Queen of Egypt? It is not necessary to be a national of the country that you rule. For instance, George I was Hanoverian, but he became the King of Great Britain and Ireland. There were actually several Cleopatras who were queens of Egypt, but I assume that we are talking about the famous one, the Cleopatra associated with Julius Caesar and Marcus Antonius. This Cleopatra, strictly Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator (69 BC to 30 BC), was the Queen of the Hellenistic (Greek) Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, which was a state founded by Ptolemy I Sotor and usually dated from 305 BC. Contemporary Roman bust of Cleopatra VII and possibly Cleopatra in Egyptian style Ptolemy I Sotor was a Macedonian, a General, and one of the Companions of Alexander The Great and also, possibly, Alexander’s half brother and a son of Philip II. Alexander conquered Egypt in 332 BC but died nine years later in 323 BC. As his Empire unravelled, Ptolemy was one of the Diadochi, the successors, and fought against Alexander’s other companions to win control of Egypt and found a dynasty. The Egypt you are probably thinking of, the Egypt of the Pyramids, was the Old Kingdom and already two thousand years in the past by the time of Alexander. The Egypt that Alexander conquered had been ruled by the Persian Achaemenid Empire from 525 BC. It briefly regained its independence in 402 BC, and then fell to the Persians again (Artaxerxes III) in 343 BC. Egypt was no stranger to foreign rulers. Ptolemy based his kingdom in the new capital of Alexandria and was responsible for the creation if the Great Library of Alexandria. His son and heir, Ptolemy II, built the Pharos Lighthouse, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Cleopatra VII was the tenth generation of the Ptolemy Dynasty to rule Egypt. You have to be slightly mad to want to understand the Ptolemy family tree due to their habit of marrying their sisters and assorted dynastic shennanigans. Cleopatra was indeed of Macedonian heritage, with a smattering of Persian heritage, but it was nearly three hundred years since her family had seen Macedonia. She almost certainly saw herself primarily as a Hellene but, as the tenth generation of her dynasty, she was also, without doubt, the Queen of Egypt. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can an old battleship be converted into a modern-day naval vessel?
Answer: Yes, of course it could. The question is whether it would be an effective use of resources, and the answer is that there is no way that it would be cost effective. You could also build a new battleship from scratch which would probably be much cheaper than converting a museum piece but, again, the navies of the world have decided that this is not a sensible option. If they have all reached the same decision then it is quite likely to be correct. Old battleships have old propulsion systems, old sensors and old weapons that would be ineffective in the modern environment. They have also been out of service for a long time and many systems will have been removed or rendered non-functional by the passage of time. To all intents and purposes the ship would have to be gutted and completely refitted, so all you would be getting is an armoured shell; the internal layout being utterly unsuited to modern uses. They also had huge crews which, again, would not be cost effective in today’s environment. Given that the survivability of heavily armoured ships against modern missiles is unproven and that a missile attack is likely to end in a mission kill (destroyed sensors, etc.) even if it doesn’t sink the ship, any such ship would entail a vast expense of resources to produce an operationally fragile package. The same is, of course, true of a carrier, but at least a carrier provides considerable force-projection capabilities. There is also the concept of a large arsenal ship which would have a small crew and as many as 500 VLS cells for missiles. The US Navy investigated this concept, but Congress withdrew funding for the project in 1998. You’d almost certainly be better off building a large number of smaller ships, possibly unmanned drone missile platforms, than investing in what would probably become a white elephant. Delving into the past, in the 1980s, as part of plans to counter the Soviet Kirov-class battlecruisers four Iowa battleships were reactivated and modernized under the 600-ship Navy program. During this reactivation, several concepts entailing removal of the aft 16 inch turret were considered by the US Navy, including a proposal to replace the turret with facilities for 12 AV-8B Harriers, a proposal for replacement of the turret with vertical launch systems for missiles and a flight deck for Marine helicopters and a proposal for a canted flight deck complete with a steam catapult and arrestor wires to operate F/A-18 Hornet fighters. Plans for all of these conversions were dropped in 1984 as uneconomic. Converted Iowa-class to an Interdiction Assault Ship (IAS) concept

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In "Masters of the Air", they claim the USAF did precision bombing by day and the RAF did area bombing by night. Is that true? Didn't the RAF sometimes bomb by day?
Answer: There are actually two different questions being asked here, one about day vs night bombing and one about precision vs area bombing. In the 1920’s the theories of Giulio Douhet were much in favour and his book Il dominio dell'aria (The Command of the Air) was very widely read. Although experience proved Douhet’s theories to be wide of the mark, he had a significant influence over military and political thinking in the pre-war period. In the 1930s, there was a brief period where multi-engine aircraft (bombers) were faster than single-engine aircraft (fighters) and in 1932, this led to Stanley Baldwin giving a speech in Parliament in which he concluded that the bomber will always get through: I think it is well also for the man in the street to realize that there is no power on earth that can protect him from being bombed, whatever people may tell him. The bomber will always get through, and it is very easy to understand that if you realise the area of space. Take any large town you like on this island or on the Continent within reach of an aerodrome. For the defence of that town and its suburbs you have to split up the air into sectors for defence. Calculate that the bombing aeroplanes will be at least 20,000ft. high in the air, and perhaps higher, and it is a matter of mathematical calculation that you will have sectors of from ten to hundreds of cubic miles. Imagine one hundred cubic miles covered with cloud and fog, and you can calculate how many aeroplanes you would have to throw into that to have much chance of catching odd aeroplanes as they fly through it. It cannot be done, and there is no expert in Europe who will say that it can. The only defence is in offence, which means that you have got to kill more women and children more quickly than the enemy if you want to save yourselves. I mention that so that people may realise what is waiting for them when the next war comes. However, technology, including the introduction of radar, marched on and by the time that WW2 broke out the fighters once again had the upper hand. In 1940, the Germans and then the British quickly found that bomber attacks made in daylight resulted in catastrophic losses, a lesson painfully relearned by the USAAF in 1943. As a result, both sides switched to bombing at night. RAF Lancaster over Hamburg However, it would be incorrect to say that the British never bombed during the day, although the vast majority of sorties were certainly made at night. From 1942 onwards, the RAF conducted daylight operations as deemed necessary and, obviously the tempo of daylight operations picked up markedly after D-Day as the Luftwaffe disintegrated and the Allies gained control of the air over Germany. For example: on 27 August 1944, against the Rheinpreussen synthetic oil refinery at Homberg/Meerbeck. Cloud cover over the target was 7/10ths and the attack took place using the same Oboe marking techniques and green target indicators used in night raids… although flak had been reported as “heavy” over the target, no bombers were shot down and the escorting squadrons of Spitfires drove off the Luftwaffe. Some of these daylight raids were of significant size: On 3 September 1944, 675 aircraft participated in daylight raids against six German airfields in Holland, targeting runways and hangars. Only one Halifax bomber was lost to flak over Venlo. RAF Lancasters bomb through cloud during a daylight raid in the summer of 1944 When the USAAF started mounting deep-penetration daylight raids they found, in turn, that their losses were unsustainable. Eighth Air Force losses were so heavy that, statistically, USAAF bomber crews had no chance of surviving a tour. In the first Schweinfurt-Regensburg raid, 60 bombers were lost, and many more damaged beyond repair, out of the 376 participating (16%). After a two month pause to regroup, another deep raid was made on Schweinfurt, this time suffering 77 losses (26%). The shocking scale of these losses led to a four month pause in deep-penetration raids at the end of 1943. Despite the heavy armament of the bombers it was clear that USAAF’s pre-war doctrine of the self-defending bomber formations was deficient and that long-range fighter escort was an essential requirement for deep-penetration daylight raids. USAAF B-17 combat box It is also worth noting in passing that whilst the USAAF bombers claimed 288 German fighters on the first raid, Luftwaffe records show that only 26 were actually downed. That’s a real exchange rate of one fighter downed for every 2.3 bombers lost, rather than the claimed rate of 4.8 fighters downed for every bomber lost. In other words, a 23:1 ratio of crew losses, which is clearly not sustainable. During the pause the Eighth Air Force worked with RAF Bomber Command to experiment with night bombing and flew several missions to see if it was possible to transfer to night bombing. After eight missions, it was determined the B-17s needed further modifications and that the USAAF crews required considerable additional training to perform night bombing raids. The deus-ex-machina event that saved the USAAF’s daylight strategic bombing campaign from disaster was the timely arrival of the new escort fighters. The first P-51 Mustang unit arrived in December 1943, and although the P-38 proved unsuitable for use in Europe, the P-47D also proved its worth as a medium and, later, long-range escort in the late war. The answer to the first part of this question is therefore that the RAF mostly bombed at night because the technology for effective long-range escort fighters did not exist for the first four years of the war and this made daylight raids prohibitively expensive. Conversely, the USAAF was able to bomb by day in the last eighteen months of the war because of the arrival of long-range escort fighters. As to the question of accuracy, I have no interest in discussing the moral issues involved in area bombing, although I am sure that people will emote in the comments in the usual wildly unbalanced way. What I will discuss is whether there was any such thing as precision bombing in today’s commonly accepted sense. We do not regard a fifteen-foot square as being difficult to hit from an altitude of 30,000 feet, provided the new Army M-4 bombsight, together with the Stabilized Bombing Approach Equipment is used. Theodore Barth, Norden In reality, despite the hype, the famous Norden bombsight offered no significant advantages over the British SABS or German Lotfernrohr 7 sights, and, in the event, it turned out that what was possible in ideal conditions was not remotely possible in combat. A word needs to be said on the problem of accuracy in attack. Before the war, the U .S. Army Air Forces had advanced bombing techniques to their highest level of development and had trained a limited number of crews to a high degree of precision in bombing under target range conditions, thus leading to the expressions "pin point" and "pickle barrel" bombing . However, it was not possible to approach such standards of accuracy under battle conditions imposed over Europe . Many limiting factors intervened ; target obscuration by clouds, fog, smoke screens and industrial haze; enemy fighter opposition which necessitated defensive bombing formations, thus restricting freedom of maneuver; antiaircraft artillery defenses, demanding minimum time exposure of the attacking force in order to keep losses down ; and finally, time limitations imposed on combat crew training after the war began . It was considered that enemy opposition made formation flying and formation attack a necessary tactical and technical procedure . Bombing patterns resulted-only a portion of which could fall on small precision targets . The rest spilled over on adjacent plants, or built-up areas, or in open fields… Unfortunately, the major portion of bombing operations over Germany had to be conducted under weather and battle conditions that restricted bombing technique, and accuracy suffered accordingly . Conventionally the air forces designated as "the target area" a circle having a radius of 1000 feet around the aiming point of attack . While accuracy improved during the war, Survey studies show that, in the over-all, only about 20% of the bombs aimed at precision targets fell within this target area. THE UNITED STATES STRATEGIC BOMBING SURVEY USAAF bombers operated in combat boxes sometimes up to a kilometre across and two kilometres deep and dropped their bombs on the command of a lead bomber - who was the only one equipped with a Norden bombsight. It is clear that this practice could not lead to precision bombing as we think of it today. One analysis states that 648 bombs were required to guarantee a 96% chance of two hits on a 400 x 500 ft target, but the other 646 bombs also went somewhere. Precision bombing was emphasised as a sop to US public opinion (except in the case of Japan where it apparently wasn’t an issue). It must always be borne in mind that the bomber war was characterised by the tremendous pace of technological development as measure and countermeasure followed each other with bewildering rapidity. What was possible in 1944 wasn’t remotely feasible in 1940 and this makes a huge difference in the way that the RAF and USAAF strategic bombing campaigns evolved. For instance, throughout the course of the war the British continually invented new navigation and bombing aids such as Gee, Oboe, G-H, and the H2S centimetric ground scanning radar, as well as new tactics such as the Pathfinders, Master Bombers, and Target Indicators. Each of these advances improved accuracy significantly but genuine precision bombing remained in the realm of the low-level Mosquito light bombers, not the four-engined heavies. H2S could see through clouds and smoke screens late in the war Frankly, precision bombing was more of an aspiration than a reality as the technology to support it simply didn’t exist. In addition, the difference between bombing at night and bombing during the day in Europe, where the target was frequently obscured by clouds, fog or smokescreens, was not particularly significant. In conclusion, the RAF bombed predominantly by night between 1940 and 1943 because that was the only way to maintain an acceptable loss rate. However, by the time that the USAAF bombing campaign switched into high gear in 1944, the RAF was also transitioning to large daylight raids because the provision of long range fighter escorts made this possible. So, YES, the RAF did indeed sometimes bomb during the day and NO, the difference between RAF area attacks and USAAF precision attacks is mostly the result of unwarranted hype and the fact that the people of Great Britain, having endured the Blitz, were perhaps less squeamish about calling a spade a spade than their American cousins.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Can you tell me about a heroic act performed by a soldier on D-Day?
Answer: Many heroic acts were performed on D-Day, by soldiers of all the armies involved. However, sadly it is in the nature of things that many of these go unreported and even of those that are reported many go unrecognised. The Victoria Cross is Great Britain’s highest award for conspicuous bravery in the presence of the enemy. A recommendation for the Victoria Cross normally has to be supported by several witnesses of higher rank than the recipient - which is quite a high bar. As an aside, the Victoria Cross can also be awarded by ballot, if a large body of men, a battalion or ship’s crew, performed the act of bravery collectively. Normally, the officers selected one of their number to receive the cross, and in like manner one petty officer or non-commissioned officer and two seamen or private soldiers were selected by their equals. For instance, on the 31st of March 1900, British troops were ambushed on their march to Bloemfontein by Boer commandos. Under heavy fire, 'Q' Battery Royal Horse Artillery, managed to rescue all but one of their guns. As every man in the battery showed considerable bravery four officers and men were nominated by their fellows for the award. Something similar happened to my Uncle Frank who was an officer in an Indian Army cavalry (tank) regiment in WW2 during the fighting at Imphal and Kohima. A Military Cross was awarded to the unit and the commanding officer told my uncle and another officer to toss for it. My uncle lost the toss. Anyway, back to D-Day. There was only one Victoria Cross awarded on D-Day and that was to Company Sergeant Major Stan Hollis of the Green Howards, who landed on Gold Beach. C.S.M. Stan Hollis War Office, 17th August, 1944. The KING has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the VICTORIA CROSS to: No. 4390973 Warrant Officer Class II (Company Sergeant-Major) Stanley Elton Hollis, The Green Howards (Alexandra, Princess of Wales's Own Yorkshire Regiment) (Middlesbrough). In Normandy on 6th June, 1944, during the assault on the beaches and the Mont Fleury Battery, C.S.M. Hollis's Company Commander noticed that two of the pillboxes had been by-passed, and went with C.S.M. Hollis to see that they were clear. When they were 20 yards from the pillbox, a machine-gun opened fire from the slit and C.S.M. Hollis instantly rushed straight at the pillbox, firing his Sten gun. He jumped on top of the pillbox, re-charged his magazine, threw a grenade in through the door and fired his Sten gun into it, killing two Germans and making the remainder prisoner. He then cleared several Germans from a neighbouring trench. By his action, he undoubtedly saved his Company from being fired on heavily from the rear and enabled them to open the main beach exit. Later the same day, in the village of Crepon, the Company encountered a field gun and crew armed with Spandaus at 100 yards range. C.S.M. Hollis was put in command of a party to cover an attack on the gun, but the movement was held up. Seeing this, C.S.M. Hollis pushed right forward to engage the gun with a P.I.A.T. from a house at 50 yards range. He was observed by a sniper who fired and grazed his right cheek, and at the same moment the gun swung round and fired at point-blank range into the house. To avoid the fallen- masonry C.S.M. Hollis moved his party to an alternative position. Two of the enemy gun crew had by this time been killed, and the gun was destroyed shortly afterwards. He later found that two of his men had stayed behind in the house and immediately volunteered to get them out. In full view of, the enemy who were continually firing at him, he went forward alone using a Bren gun to distract their attention from the other men. Under cover of his diversion, the two men were able to get back. Wherever fighting was heaviest, C.S.M. Hollis appeared and in the course of a magnificent day's work, he displayed the utmost gallantry and on two separate occasions his courage and initiative prevented the enemy from holding up the advance at critical stages. It was largely through his heroism and resource that the Company's objectives were gained and casualties were not heavier, and by his own bravery he saved the lives of many of his men.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did the United Kingdom declare war on Finland on December 6, 1941 (one day before the Pearl Harbor attack)?
Answer: Not just Finland. Great Britain declared war on Finland, Hungary, and Romania on the 5th December 1941. One can hardly blame the Finns as they had been attacked by the Soviets in the Winter War between November 1939 and March 1940, which led to the expulsion of the Soviet Union from the League of Nations. After a very poor initial showing in the face of Finnish determination, the Soviets prevailed by sheer force of numbers and the Finns were forced to sue for an armistice in which the Finns lost around 10% of their territory, including their second largest city, and 13% of their industry. During the uneasy peace that followed the armistice in March, the Finns sought alliances and eventually lighted on the Germans on the basis that the enemy of my enemy is my friend. German troops were stationed in Finland and when Operation Barbarossa commenced, on the 22nd of June 1941, the Soviets bombed Finland causing the Finns to declare war on the 25th of June starting what was known as the Continuation War. Finnish Stug IIIs The Finns signed the Anti-Comintern Pact in November 1941 but, unlike Hungary and Romania, never signed the Tripartite Pact. However, Finland joined German troops in attacks on the Soviet Union, including Operation Silver Fox against Murmansk, and this together with Finland’s refusal to discuss territorial concessions offered by Stalin, led the British, who were now allied to the Soviet Union, to declare war on Finland. The British declaration of war was pretty pro forma and the only action taken against the Finns was a token and largely pointless raid against the Finnish port of Petsamo, Operation EF, launched on the 30th of July 1941. Whilst the Finns were technically enemies, one can’t help thinking that most Britons probably sympathised with their predicament.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did Italy surrender in North Africa and not continue fighting against Britain?
Answer: The first major Italian surrender in North Africa took place between the December 1940 and February 1941 when 133,300 Italians surrendered after the British Empire’s Operation Compass. Most of these surrendered at Sidi Barrani, Bardia, Tobruk, or Benghazi. Italian POWs after Compass, Bardia 1941 However, fighting in North Africa didn’t finally cease until May 1943 with the Axis surrender in Tunisia which netted another 200,000 Italian prisoners together with approximately 100,000 Germans. Italian POWs in Tunisia, May 1943 However, Italy didn’t finally surrender in North Africa but after the invasions of Sicily and the Italian mainland. The final Italian surrender came in September 1943 with the Armistice of Cassibile. The point should be made that Italian soldiers were capable of displaying bravery equal to any other army, but they were consistently let down by poor leadership, poor equipment, and poor logistics. This led to poor morale and probably explains why many Italians seem happy to be POWs in the photos. The Italian surrenders in North Africa happened, as with all surrenders, when the Italians found themselves in an untenable situation The final surrender of Italy itself stemmed from the same basis; Italy was no longer capable of pursuing the war. The Allies invaded Sicily and the disastrous military situation caused relations to break down between Mussolini and King Victor Emmanuel III. Mussolini was deposed in a coup on the 25th of July 1943 and channels were opened, through meetings in neutral Lisbon, to discuss peace. The Italians were wanted the Allies to land on the Italian mainland before any surrender, partly as a fig-leaf for their dignity and partly because they were, rightly, concerned about the German reaction to an Italian surrender. The Allies rejected this request and the armistice was signed on the 3rd of September 1943. The Germans, who suspected that this would happen, immediately launched Operation Achse and disarmed the Italian Army whilst occupying the mainland. Fighting in Italy would continue until the end of the war.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If the British Army was attacked by Russia, could they defeat them without assistance from other countries such as France or America?
Answer: The simple answer is no, and it has never been intended that it should do so - hence NATO. The only countries that could withstand a conventional attack by Russia on their own are the United States, China, and possibly India and Turkey. Countries with large populations and considerable military resources. [Edit: I’m getting a lot of repetitive comments. This question is clearly a thought or Gedanken experiment rather than a probable scenario. It does not postulate an invasion of the UK, and any such question would require a lot more information about how we came to that pass. Below, I simply give a comparison of the two forces in a conflict where we are defending (say) the Baltic States - where we currently have a trip-wire battalion stationed.] In raw terms Russia has twice the population of the United Kingdom and although the UK has a larger economy than Russia in dollar terms, it is smaller when compared in PPP terms. Manpower is a major factor in armies and Russia can recruit men far more cheaply that the United Kingdom. The fact is that the average salary in Russia is certainly less than half of that in the UK and probably under a third. With regard to what the two countries spend on defence and the size of their forces, there is no comparison. I believe that Russia is spending about 6% of it GDP on defence whilst the UK is spending 2% - and some of that appears to be the result of creative accounting. The Russian Army has over 3,000,000 men (including paramilitary forces) whilst the United Kingdom has around 250,000 (in all three services), and that number is shrinking quite fast. British Army - a shrinking resource The quality of our men and our equipment is almost certainly superior to that of the Russians on a one-to-one basis, but this can only get you so far. It is a dangerous position to assume that a few high quality, but fragile, platforms will win the day over a significantly larger mass of average equipment. There is also the matter of logistics and most sources seem to agree that the United Kingdom only has the logistics to fight for around two weeks before its war stocks would be exhausted. At that point, its choices would be to surrender or to go nuclear. Effectively, our conventional forces have, for decades, been nothing more than a trip-wire, a small breathing space for diplomacy, before we have to escalate to the use of nuclear weapons. Of course, if we are discussing an attack on the British Isles, the Russians would have to get here which would be a significant problem for them. Then the probabilities depend on whether the Russians have advanced to the Channel Coast or not. We’d need a significantly more detailed scenario to be able to comment on that, and so I am assuming that we are discussing British forces fighting on the Continent - in defence of the Baltic States for instance.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it true that the Waffen-SS was only 40% Germans?
Answer: It’s very difficult to tell because sources disagree significantly. You can find sources that state a total size of 500,000 men in the Waffen-SS and other sources that state a million. A reasonable estimate is that there were probably 500,000 - 600,000 men in the Waffen-SS in 1944. Therefore, we have to list some caveats: As with much to do with Germany in WW2, the SS had a bewilderingly complex structure. If we ignore the police elements (Kripo, Gestapo, etc.) the main components were the paramilitary Allgemeine-SS, which was originally the largest element and certainly recruited foreigners from 1939. Then there was the Leibstandarte, which was Hitler’s personal bodyguard, the Totenkopfverbände (SS-TV), which administered the concentration camps, and finally the Verfügungstruppen (SS-VT) or special use troops. It was this latter organisation that became the Waffen-SS, based on the three Standarten (regiments), Deutschland, Germania, and Der Führer, that made up the original SS division. I count forty-one units that have been considered as Waffen-SS divisions (most sources suggest thirty-eight but there were thirty-nine, and two divisional numbers seem to have been used twice). However, some of these were not real divisions at all, but regimental size units. For instance, 1st SS Panzer (Leibstandarte) had 22,000 men, whilst 24th SS (Karstjäger) had 4,000. It is not, therefore, wise to make deductions about size based on a simple divisional count. It is definitely known that the Waffen-SS recruited foreigners. A quick count suggests that 200,000–300,000 may have served. Of the forty-one named Waffen-SS divisions, fifteen were composed mainly of Germans, three were composed mainly of ethnic Germans, six can perhaps be considered mixed, and seventeen were composed mainly of foreigners. However, it is as well to be careful with these figures. 5th SS Panzer, Wiking, for instance had foreign volunteers from Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Iceland, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Belgium. These contingents were emphasised in wartime propaganda to give the division the reputation of a pan-European force whereas, in reality, the vast majority of the division was made up of German personnel. The primarily foreign divisions included three Hungarian, two Latvian, two Dutch, and one each of Albanians, Belarussians, Estonians, Flemish, French, Italians, Romanians, Russians, Ukrainians, and Walloons (Belgian). There were also lesser numbers of foreign recruits from Bulgaria, Croatia, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, India, Norway, Serbia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom - this latter contributing 54 men who joined the British Free Corps - and the USA. Given the conflicting and missing data, if I had to make a guess, I’d guess that in 1944 approximately 45% of the Waffen-SS were German nationals, a further 6% were ethic Germans, 14% were of mixed ethnicity, probably mostly foreign, and around 35% were foreign recruits. Therefore, including ethnic Germans, you could probably say that 50% of the Waffen-SS in the late war were probably not German nationals.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were enemy submarines in WWII known to run out of ammunition? If so, what were the consequences?
Answer: Yes, submarines did run out of ammunition or, to be more specific, torpedoes. The most common German U-boat, the Type VII had five torpedo tubes (four in the bow and one in the stern) and carried between eleven and fourteen torpedoes. However, to improve the chances of a hit, torpedoes were generally fired in salvoes of two to four. This means that a U-boat could probably only fire on four to six targets on each cruise if not resupplied. This, of course, explains why U-boats preferred to surface and sink their victims with gunfire if at all possible. The Germans did attempt to extend the endurance of their U-boats by resupplying them from pre-positioned supply ships or Type XIV Milchkuh (Milk Cow) submarines, but these latter could only provide four additional torpedoes. When a U-boat had exhausted its torpedoes it had to return to base unless the U-boat command (BdU) needed a boat for spotting or weather reporting. The most interesting incident that I can recall is when U-556 had the Ark Royal in her sights just as the Ark Royal was launching the strike that crippled the Bismarck. U-556 was out of torpedoes. Crash dive. Out of the haze from astern a battleship of the "KING GEORGE" class and an aircraft carrier probably ARK ROYAL come in sight. Bow right target angle 10°. If I only had torpedoes now! ! ! ! I [am] positioned exactly correct for an attack. Without destroyer without zig-zagging courses! ! I could sit down in between and attack both at the same moment. U-556 photographed from the deck of the Bismarck? What makes this poignant is that there was a link between U-556 and Bismarck. Lindemann lent U-556 the Bismarck’s band for her commissioning and in return U-556‘s commander, Kapitänleutnant Herbert Wohlfarth, declared that U-556 would always protect Bismarck. We, U-556 (500 tons), hereby declare before Neptune, , Lord over oceans, seas, lakes, rivers, brooks, ponds, and rivulets, that we will provide any desired assistance to our Big Brother, the battleship Bismarck (42,000 tons), at any place on the water, underwater, on land, or in the air. Hamburg, 28 January 1941 Commander & Crew U556 You can see in the drawing below the U-556’s captain stopping a torpedo that is heading for the Bismarck with his left hand whilst fending off attacking planes with his right. U-556 was sunk on her second war patrol, a month after the Bismarck.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In World War 1, would the capture of Paris by the German Army in 1914 led to the capitulation of the Allied powers?
Answer: No, I don’t think so. After initial successes in August 1914 with the Battle of the Frontiers and the Battle of Mons, the Germans pursued the retreating French and British to the River Marne, only just over twenty miles from Paris. However, at this point the Germans had run out of steam and the Allies counter-attacked driving the Germans back to the River Aisne. If the Allies had not succeeded with the Marne offensive, it is possible that Paris might have fallen. In this event, I can imagine two possible cases. German troops gather for the final attack Requestioned taxis, private cars and buses from Paris rush troops to the Marne In the first case, Paris is captured but the French fight on, much as the Russians did when Moscow was captured in 1812. There’s nothing written in stone that says that you have to surrender when your capital is occupied. It would depend on the will of the French people and government and the strategic position of their remaining forces at that point. In the second case, the French government capitulates (we’ll assume that capitulation is the same as surrender to avoid any potential nit-picking). What the terms of the armistice would have been is unknowable but we do know that after the Franco-Prussian War Germany seized the provinces of Alsace and Lorraine. I would expect that Germany would secure its frontier and hobble the French Army and economy. Belgium would have had no choice but to surrender at the same time as France. Serbia, Montenegro, and Russia would carry on fighting, but the strategic balance would have shifted severely against them and I can’t see either holding out much beyond the middle of 1915. Great Britain on the other hand, was under no immediate threat from the Germans. Providing that whatever remained of the BEF could have been evacuated (and there were plans for that), the Germans would have no hold over the British and the British no means of influencing matters on the continent. Great Britain could still impose a naval blockade on Germany, but with France having fallen I can’t really see that being a realistic option. Germany could seek to exclude British trade from the Continent, but, much like Napoleon’s Continental System (1806–1814) I think that this would have proved to be a very double-edged sword. Therefore the result would be a standoff. The war, at that point, would only have been been running for a couple of months (the First Battle of the Marne took place between the 5th and the 12th of September 1914) and so the situation was more akin to the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 than to the total war of 1914–18. As a result I would suspect that diplomatic niceties would have been maintained and that an armistice would have been agreed between Great Britain and Germany that would have more or less returned to the status quo ante bellum (the situation as it existed before the war). The situation would obviously have continued to evolve with Russia probably being knocked out of the war in late 1914 to mid-1915. The results of this early exit would have been profound. In return for a smug and nationalist, but still civilized Germany, dominating continental affairs, we might not have seen the rise of either Communism or Fascism, and the doddering Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires would have held on for a few more decades. The survival of the Ottoman Empire might, in turn, have stifled the rise of Wahhabism and militant Islam. No Communism, no Fascism, no militant Islam - something to think about.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were amphibious vehicles not used during Operation Overlord (D-Day) by the Allies?
Answer: Amphibious vehicles were used during Operation Overlord, but perhaps not to the extent that they could have been. Firstly, I suppose that the famous DD (Duplex Drive) tanks were amphibious to an extent. Perhaps that’s cheating a bit as they were really a one use vehicle. Then there were the DUWKs (Ducks) which were based on the chassis and running gear of the General Motors CCKW 353 2½ ton (Deuce and a Half) Truck. The DUKWs were genuinely amphibious and over 21,000 of them were built and used in all theatres. Eleven British DUKW Companies belonging to the RASC (Royal Army Service Corps) were involved in Operation Overlord with the strength of each company ranging from sixty to one hundred vehicles. Carrying up to 5,000lbs of cargo, DUKWs carried 18 million tons of supplies ashore over the course of ninety days. A DUKW’s top speed on land peaked around 50 mph, whereas in the water it could only move at about 6.5 mph. Payloads could safely reach 2.5 tons. A rudder and basic three-blade propeller extended out the stern over top of the rear axles. Water getting in was mitigated by “surfboards” on the bow and stern, or expelled by a bilge pump capable of evicting 220 gallons per minute. The driver could inflate or deflate the tyres from within the cab to cater for different terrain types. DUWKs on land US DUKWs heading for the Normandy beaches Whilst most DUWKs spent their time hauling vital cargo to the beaches, some had a more exciting time. In particular, several were assigned to the Rangers for their landing on Pointe du Hoc. Armed with extending ladders taken from London fire engines, these vehicles were intended to help the Rangers scale the cliffs. Assault DUKWs Things didn’t go entirely to plan and the DUKWs either became stuck on a sandbar or couldn’t cross the shell craters on the beach. They were not able to erect their ladders against the cliff but they raised and extended their ladders where they were and Rangers provided covering fire for the men climbing the cliff using the BARs mounted at the top of each ladder. The final vehicle to consider is the LVT (Landing Vehicle Tracked) or Amtrac, a lightly armoured amphibious landing vehicle that was used extensively by the USMC in the Pacific theatre. The LVT-1 could carry 18 fully equipped men or 4,500lbs of cargo whilst the LVT-2 (Buffalo) could carry 24 men or 5950lbs of cargo - more than the DUKW. Although several hundred LVTs were available in the UK, it is not clear whether they were used during the D-Day landings themselves - although some were certainly attached to the 79th Armoured Division, Hobart’s Funnies. Two LVTs were apparently used on D-Day to ferry supplies to Utah beach. Why they didn’t play a greater part in Normandy is unclear as LVTs were certainly used in assault operations in North West Europe later in WW2. One can only assume that they were not extensively used during the landings because they were used mainly by the USMC rather than the US Army and perhaps they were seen as unproved in June 1944?
