Question: Between 1939 and 1942, did the Royal Navy severely underestimate the German Navy's strength, resulting in greater capital ship losses (Hood, Glorious, Ark Royal, Eagle, Barham, Royal Oak etc.), compared to the Kriegsmarine only losing the Bismarck?
Answer: No, the Royal Navy had a very good idea of the strength and capabilities of the Kriegsmarine, the problem was in developing the technology to deal with U-boats effectively. To deal with the last statement first, the Kriegsmarine didn’t only lose the Bismarck. They lost, either to the Royal Navy or the RAF, the battleships Bismarck, Tirpitz, Scharnhorst, and Gnesienau, the pocket battleships Lützow, Admiral Scheer, and Admiral Graf Spee, and the heavy cruiser Admiral Hipper. Of the ships mentioned, only Glorious and the Hood were lost to surface action. In fact, I believe that these two and the light cruisers Charybdis and Sydney were the only ships above destroyer size sunk by Kriegsmarine surface action during the war. The Glorious (an elderly aircraft carrier) was surprised by the battleships Scharnhorst and the Gneisenau with only two destroyer escorts. The circumstances of her loss have never been entirely satisfactorily explained, but complacency seems to be the most likely probability. The Hood, famously, was lost to a lucky shot in the action against the Bismarck. In the final analysis, her loss was a fair exchange for the Bismarck as the Royal Navy was much more capable of absorbing the loss of a capital unit than was the Kriegsmarine. The shock surrounding the loss of the Hood was not so much the loss of the ship, but the speed of her destruction. All the others ships mentioned were sunk by U-boat torpedoes and U-boats were certainly a major hazard in the first years of the war. Barham explodes after being torpedoed by U-331 Ark Royal sinking after being torpedoed by U-81 - she could probably have been saved The fate of the Tirpitz -she lived an invalid's life and died a cripple's death Admiral Graf Spee in Montevideo harbour The Royal Navy and RNAS (Royal Naval Air Service) had become quite proficient in ASW by the end of WW1, but the merger of the RNAS and RFC into the RAF and sharp defence cuts in the inter-war years meant that these skills and capabilities had largely been lost. The evolution of the U-boat required that the Royal Navy, the Royal Canadian Navy, RAF Coastal Command, and their US counterparts, develop new ships, new weapons, and new tactics. Once these came on stream, the U-boats became a nuisance rather than an existential threat. Inter-alia, the Allied response included the deployment of very long range (VLR) aircraft, the development of centimetric airborne radar, improved ASDIC (SONAR), the Leigh Light, intelligence supplied by Huff-Duff and code-breaking, the use of CAM, MAC and Q-ships, the use of escort carriers, improved weapons including forward throwing depth charges (Hedgehog and Squid), the proper organisation of convoys and the deployment of both escorts and hunter-killer (support) groups, as well as new tactics from WATU, some inspired leadership, and rigorous training. In all the Germans deployed 1,162 U-boats and they lost 785 of them.

Question: What are some of the most impressive feats of accuracy via gunfire in naval history?
Answer: From the 1850s to the 1940s, a period of less than one hundred years, there was a tremendous evolution in the size and range of naval guns. In 1855 the British Navy was still using muzzle loading cannon and carronades. Within a generation the new rifled guns would come into service and naval gunnery would become a science rather than an art. Breech-loading, rifled artillery was introduced into the Royal Navy in 1861 in the shape of the Armstrong RBL 7-inch (110-pdr) gun with a range of about two miles. By 1882, the Royal Navy was using the BL 12-inch Mk I with a range of four and a half miles and, by 1918, the BL 18-inch Mk I naval gun with a range of just over twenty-three miles. The Armstrong 7” fired a 109lb shell, the BL 12” a 714lb shell and the BL 18” a 3,320lb shell. The point being that there’s quite a difference between lobbing a 109lb shell two miles in 1861 and a 3,320lb shell twenty-three miles only 57 years later. Naval gunnery is complicated. Both the target and the firing platform are moving and may also be turning. The firing platform is subject to the sea state and will be pitching, rolling, and yawing. Complicating factors include visibility, range, speed, target aspect, the size of target, temperature, air pressure, Coriolis force, and barrel wear – all of which have to be taken into account. It’s fairly amazing that naval gunnery ever hit anything. Warspite Having said that, it wasn’t just the guns that were evolving, fire control systems were evolving at the same time with the introduction of astonishingly complicated, and entirely mechanical, analogue computers, such as the Pollen and Dreyer systems, stereoscopic optical rangefinders and, latterly, of course radar. You can see from the table above that the 12” and 14” guns of the US Navy in WW1 were expected to hit around 10% of the time at ranges of between 10,000 and 17,000 yards, whilst the 16” guns of WW2 were expected to hit something like 40% of the time at those ranges and 10% of the time up to 35,000 yards. All of these figures are optimistic from a historical perspective as they reflect shooting against a non-manoeuvring target, but they are a good indication of the rate of development. Therefore, what constituted an impressive feat in 1860, 1916, or 1945 is completely different. At the Battle of Tsushima in 1905, hits were obtained at 6,500 yards (3.7 miles). Whilst the Russians were scoring around 4.5% of the time, the Japanese were achieving around 19%, which was pretty impressive. As to the longest ranged hits, the most accepted claims are HMS Warspite against the Italian battleship Giulio Cesare at 27,000 yards and Scharnhorst against HMS Glorious at 26,000 yards – both around 15 miles. Scharnhorst There are also less well accepted claims for the Yamato against the White Plains at around 30,000 yards (White Plains suffered a near miss) and the Massachusetts against the battleship Jean Bart at 24,000 yards (a stationary target). Question: Can you explain the medieval English Livery system and how it worked? How were knights compensated for their services, considering they were essentially mercenaries?
Answer: This is either a very specific question indeed or a misunderstanding regarding the differences between livery, heraldry, and feudalism. I think that we can assume that we’re not talking about livery for horses. To take the specific first, an English Livery Company is a descendent of the medieval trade guilds in the City of London. There are currently one hundred and eleven livery companies and they are styled Worshipful Companies. These days the Livery Companies are involved in charitable work and education but they used to be trade associations with monopoly powers. You became a member of the company after completing an indentured apprenticeship in the trade, but now membership is by invitation. As I work in the City of London, I toyed with joining the Worshipful Company of Information Technologists a few years ago but never got around to pursuing it. You can’t say that we don’t keep up with the times in Ye Olde London. The precedence of the original livery companies was set in 1515, with the first twelve becoming known as the Great Twelve: the Mercers, Grocers, Drapers, Fishmongers, Goldsmiths, Skinners, Merchant Taylors, Haberdashers, Salters, Ironmongers, Vintners, and Clothworkers - a good cross section of the essential medieval trades. However, the livery companies have nothing to do with knights or feudalism. The term livery, from the French livrée meaning handed over, is an emblem that identifies the wearer as being affiliated with something. Originally, this was probably something given by a lord to his troops in order that they could be clearly identified in battle. This might be something as simple as a sprig of heather or a piece of cloth. At the Battle of Minden in 1759, English regiments picked roses to put in their headgear and you can see how this sort of thing could be used to identify a body of men who were not uniformly dressed. The units involved, or their successors, still wear a rose on Minden Day (1st August). Minden Day rose In many cases the emblem would be related the the heraldic design that identified the lord himself. Over time livery developed into uniform and might apply to a soldier or to any other servant. You will read about the footmen’s livery worn by servants for example. A very good example is the uniform worn by the Yeomen of the Guard who wear the livery of the monarch. They are not knights, but the servants or soldiers serving a knight - or in this case the monarch - and wear his livery. Yeomen of the Guard In the time of Henry VIII, the Yeomen of the Guard were clothed in: large jackets of damask, white and green, goodly embroidered both on their breasts before and also on their backs behind, with round garlands of vine branches, beset before richly with spangles of silver and gilt, and in the middle a red rose, beaten with goldsmiths' work, with bright halberds in their hands Nowadays they wear the familiar scarlet with gold embroidered emblems on the back and front of the coats consisting of the crowned Tudor Rose, the shamrock and the thistle, the motto Dieu et mon droit, and the royal cypher - clear notification that they serve the monarch. Pro tip: the Yeomen of the Guard wear the cross-belt, whilst the Yeoman Warders of the Tower of London, the Beefeaters, do not. Not many people know that, so now you can amaze your friends with your erudition. Here you can see the change in livery between our late Queen and King Charles III in the undress uniforms of the Yeomen Warders Now, as to the unrelated topic of how were knights compensated for their services. Firstly knights were not necessarily mercenaries unless they served with a foreign army. Secondly knights existed as part of the feudal system. Feudalism is an endlessly complicated topic and we can only scratch the surface in this answer, handwaving away most of the detail. Essentially, everything belonged to the monarch. The nobility held lands from the Crown in exchange for military service, and knights or vassals were, in turn, tenants of the nobles. A knight’s fee or fief, generally consisted of fifteen to thirty peasant families, who were obliged to live on their lord's land and give him homage, labour, and a share of the produce, notionally in exchange for his protection. The fief would support the knight sufficiently that he could arm and mount himself and so provide the military service that he owed his lord. The whole concept of services in return for land was deeply ingrained. Here, in July 1330, William grants Thomas the use of land and, in return, Thomas agrees to feed and clothe William for ten years and to look after his children. The terms are very specific. Note that Thomas has squires and is therefore also a knight and is taking on the education of William’s son as one of his squires. Indenture, whereby, whereas William de Manneby, knight enfeoffed to Thomas de Multon of ffraunkton and Lady Elyzabeth his wife of the Manor of Manneby near Lude, with the appurtenances, the reversion of the wind-mill and two plots of meadow in Salfletby, to hold of the lords by service; Thomas and Elyzabeth grant to William honourable sustenance in eating and drinking at their own table for the term of ten years from the date of the indenture, and clothes suitable to his estate, that is to say, at the new year a double surcoat and a tabard, a fur when Thomas wears one and a bouggee similarly, and at All Saints’ Day a winter robe of two pieces, consisting of a surcoat of bouggee and a chaperon. And Thomas and Elyzabeth will find food and drink for William’s son, Peres, at the table of their esquires, and provide him clothes such as they give their esquires, for William’s life, so long as he behave and serves them honestly. For Agneys, the daughter of William, they promise food and drink at the table of Elyzabeth’s maids, and one mark yearly for her clothes during Williams life-time, so long as she behaves chastely and honestly. For William, the younger son of William, they promise food and drink and clothes during the life-time of William the elder. If William dies before his ten years are up, Thomas and Elyzabeth will give to William his son ten liveries and an esquire’s robe each year until the term is completed. After William’s death, Thomas and Elyzabeth have no more concern with the support of Agneys. And if they cannot get the profits of the manor, mill and meadows, they are discharged from the support of William and his family for ever. After ten years, the manor etc: shall revert to William or his heirs. At Manneby, Saturday after the feast of St John the Baptist, [fourth year in the reign of] Edward III As an aside, I wonder how many of us reading this are descended from Peres, young William, or Agneys? Probably over 50% of those with an English surname or any English ancestry.

Question: Why did Britain choose to use US troops instead of their own in North Africa and Italy, despite their close proximity?
Answer: This is another brain dead question from the Quora Prompt Generator AI. The worrying thing is that it is simply regurgitating something that its training has thrown up as statistically likely. By training, I mean the vast body of text that it was fed with - evidently without the slightest discrimination or fact checking. Relying on the content of the internet as a rational body of knowledge is not a good idea and does not bode well for the future of AI. Of course, even well intentioned sources can get things wrong from time to time, but the internet is full of disinformation and these AIs cannot discriminate. To answer the question, it was a joint effort. Britain didn’t choose to use US troops anywhere, and, indeed, had no control over US troops. Once Allied Force Headquarters (AFHQ) was created to coordinate Torch, the theatre became, and remained, an Allied theatre. As to close proximity, the difference in distances isn’t as great as you might think. It is approximately 4,000 miles from the US to Tunisia and approximately 3,000 miles from the UK to Tunisia - Spain kinda gets in the way. The United Kingdom, together with Empire and Dominions (British Empire) and Allied troops were fighting in North Africa from June 1940. The US joined in November 1942 when the Torch landings commenced. After the final Axis surrender in North Africa in May 1943, the British Empire, United States, and other allies, moved on to the invasion of Sicily (Husky, July 1943), and then to the Italian mainland (Avalanche, Baytown, and Slapstick, September 1943), with fighting in Italy continuing until May 1945. British troops loading for Husky US troops loading for Husky To put all this in perspective, during the North African campaign, the British Empire suffered some 220,000 casualties, the Free French around 16,000 and the United States 20,000. During Husky, the British Empire lost around 15,000 men and the United States around 10,000, and during the campaign on the Italian mainland, the British Empire suffered 148,000 casualties (89,500 from the UK and 58,500 from Canada, India, New Zealand, and South Africa) while the US suffered 119,000 casualties, the other allies 44,000 casualties, mostly Free French and Polish, and the Italians fighting for the Allies around 41,000. Therefore, overall (ignoring the Italians), the British Empire and other allies, principally Poland, suffered around 66% of the casualties, the US 26%, and the Free French 8%. Question: Did the French invent fencing and why is it called "fencing"?
Answer: This is actually quite interesting. Although we tend to associate fencing with the French, probably because we’ve all watched the Three Musketeers, I think that the Spanish may have a prior claim, as may Italy. Fencing involves dueling with épées, sabres, or, most commonly, foils. The foil derives from the small sword or court sword, épée de cour, which itself evolved from the Spanish rapier, the espada ropera, or dress sword. The espada ropera was a light, straight, slender, sharply pointed two-edged long blade wielded in one hand and used for duelling and self-defence - a thrusting sword. The first mention of the espada ropera dates back to the 1450s and carrying a rapier became an essential status symbol for a gentleman from the 16th Century onwards. Fencing with the rapier was simply called la verdadera destreza or the true skill and descended from the older esgrima vulgar or common fencing. As to the origin of the term, the martial art and the archetypal white picket fence both have the same etymological source. Fence and fencing both derive from the word defend. Defend and defence come to English, via French, from the Latin defendere. This is a compound word with the prefix de- (away from) and the suffix fendere (to split or strike). Offend and offense also stem from fendere. In English, defendere became defence and, at some point in the 14th Century, just fence. Fence began its life meaning the same as defence, but then found a more physical form. If you needed to defend an area, you might construct a barrier around it and, by the mid-15th century, that type barrier was called a fence. Also, you might be forced to defend yourself with a sword and by the end of the 16th century, that type of swordplay had come to be known as fencing. This type of reduction can also be seen in the fencibles, a type of defensive militia employed in England and thus in the United States. While some people were fencing their properties and others were fencing on their properties, another group was using secrecy as a defence. The notion that thieves would sell stolen their goods under the defence of secrecy is how, in the 17th century, fencing also became a crime. The verb fend is also a shortening of defend, and defender was shortened to fender, which explains what Americans have on their cars, and also what stops boats and ships rubbing against the dock.

Question: Did Britain stop building large capital ships after completing HMS Vanguard?
Answer: HMS Vanguard was laid down in 1941 but not completed until 1946 due to other wartime priorities. Even then, she was armed with surplus 15″ turrets and guns rather than the 16″ guns intended for the Lion-class battleships, none of which were ever completed. HMS Vanguard Slightly smaller than HMS Hood, she was indeed the last fast battleship built for the Royal Navy and indeed, as far as I know, the last battleship commissioned in any navy - although the never completed Iowa-class USS Kentucky was technically the last to be launched. However, since around 1942 the definition of a capital ship has extended from battleships and battlecruisers to include aircraft carriers. Depending on whether you want to define the Majestic-class, Centaur-class land Invincible-class light fleet carriers as capital units, Britain has built either four or sixteen capital ships since 1945. Majestic-class: Majestic (HMAS Melbourne), Hercules (INS Vikrant), Magnificent, Powerful (HMCS Bonaventure), Terrible (HMAS Sydney). Audacious-class: Eagle, Ark Royal. Centaur-class: Centaur, Albion, Bulwark, Hermes. Invincible-class: Invincible, Illustrious, Ark Royal. Queen Elizabeth-class: Queen Elizabeth, Prince of Wales. Question: Were any UK troops left in France after the evacuation of Dunkirk? Did all of them make it back to England before the Germans captured Paris?
Answer: Yes. Not only were there British troops left in France after the evacuation of Dunkirk but more were landed in France after the evacuation. It is often not properly understood that Dunkirk was a tactical evacuation, not a strategic one. The evacuation of Dunkirk occurred between the 26th of May and the 4th of June 1940 when British, French, and Belgian troops were cut-off after the Germans reached the sea at Abbeyville. Of the troops evacuated from Dunkirk during Operation Dynamo, 198,299 (59%) were British and 139,997 (41%) Allied, mostly French. These men were evacuated by 861 vessels of which 693 (80%) were British and 226 (33%) of the British vessels involved were sunk during the operation. Most of the evacuated French troops were repatriated from the UK to France before the Armistice, but around 3,000 stayed in the UK to form the nucleus of General de Gaulle’s Free French forces. However, the 51st Highland Division, the 1st Armoured Division, and many rear area troops were not bottled in the Dunkirk pocket, perhaps some 100,000 British troops in all. In addition, after Dunkirk, some 60,000 troops were landed in France between the 7th and 13th of June in the form of the 52nd Lowland Division and the 1st Canadian Division (I will use the term British to include any troops from the Empire or Commonwealth). Men of the 7th Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, 51st Highland Division, 6th June 1940 However, it was too late. The renewed German offensive Fall Rot (Case Red) isolated the 51st Highland Division under Major-General Fortune, in a triangular pocket between Dieppe and Le Havre in the north and Rouen in the south. With 5th and 7th Panzer Divisions moving rapidly northwards from Rouen, an improvised evacuation of the British troops was undertaken. The 51st Highland Division was eventually trapped at St Valery and some 7,000 British and 30,000 French troops were forced to surrender on the 12th of June. However, 2,137 British and 1,184 French troops were evacuated from Veules-les-Roses, and a further 11,059 from Cherbourg or Le Havre in the partially successful Operation Cycle. Between the 15th and 25th June (the Armistice was signed on the 22nd of June), 144,171 British, and 47,699 Polish, French, Czech and Belgian troops were evacuated from the French coastal ports of Cherbourg, St Malo, Brest, St Nazaire, Nantes, La Pallice, Le Verdon, Bordeaux, Bayonne and St Jean-de-Luz in Operation Aerial. It was during this operation that the RMS Lancastria was sunk by the Luftwaffe with the loss of between 4,000 and 6,500 servicemen and civilians. Paris fell on the 14th of June and so at least 144,000 British troops were still operational in France at that date, most later evacuated in Operation Aerial.

Question: Royal Navy warships lack firepower to strike Houthi land bases near the Red Sea. Is this a result of Biden’s lackadaisical response to NATO allies not meeting defense spending commitments?
Answer: It is indeed a bit pathetic and sadly typical, but it’s nothing to do with Joe Biden and actually the UK meets its NATO target of spending 2% of GDP on defence - which very few other countries do. The Daring-class Type 45 destroyers are primarily focussed on anti-aircraft operations, although they (should) have limited capability against surface and land targets with missiles. The Darings are designed to provide air defence to the Queen Elizabeth-class carriers, which obviously could strike land targets, but the carriers are nowhere in sight and appear to be undeployable for one reason or another. The obsolete Harpoon Block 1C that equipped the Darings were due to be retired in 2018 and it is the usual incredibly slow and complacent attitude of the MOD that we are now six years on from that retirement date (and at least a decade since they knew they had to replaced) and only just starting to sort out the situation. The Harpoons have been retired and there is currently nothing in their place. An emergency stop-gap, the Norwegian-built Naval Strike Missile (NSM) is apparently supposed to be deployed, prior to a new missile, the Future Cruise and Anti-Ship Weapon (FCASW) supposedly arriving in 2028. One is inclined to think that pigs might fly before the missiles do. Naval Strike Missile Sadly, there comes a point in military procurement when penny-pinching creates a situation where a country, despite spending huge amounts of money on its armed forces, doesn’t have any significant capability. It appears that the Royal Navy is not very far from reaching that point, with its assets either undeployable, insufficient in number, or lacking the capabilities needed to meet current challenges. I really hope that some Navy types will step up and tell me why I am wrong. In any case, how the economics of expending one or two Aster 15s or 30s at around £1-2 million a pop against a drone probably costing less that £20,000 makes sense I don’t know. This new issue of cheap drones emphasises just how important the development of laser weapons is against this new class of threat. The MOD recently announced that it had successfully tested its new DragonFire laser system, which, in theory, should be able to destroy a drone at a cost of about £10 a shot. However, despite considerable razzmatazz around this event, it’s unlikely that the system will be deployable until 2030, and it is also probably pretty short ranged, meaning that the escort ship will need to stay close to potential targets. Dragonfire test It’s a sad situation, but we have to start from where we are. Giving politicians a very hard time - less waffle about trivia and more concentration on the hard stuff like existential threats - and putting a rocket up MOD procurement would be a good first step, although improvements will inevitably come with costs that the public will have to meet in the form of tax rises or cuts in other services.

Question: How was sound used before radar to warn of enemy aircraft approaching Britain?
Answer: It wasn’t. Acoustic or sound mirrors were built, but they were never used to detect aircraft in wartime. During WW1, artillery sound ranging and flash detection was used to locate enemy artillery batteries by triangulation when they fired. The main problem was very difficult to differentiate between the noise of the guns firing and the noise of the shells in the air. The story is that Lieutenant William Lawrence Bragg, still I believe the world’s youngest Nobel science laureate, and Lance Corporal William Sansome Tucker determined how to tell the difference in a series of experiments that involved sitting in their billet’s water closet and some mouseholes. The ‘hot wire’ method that they invented measured how much a heated platinum wire was cooled by passing shock waves. A series of six low frequency ‘Tucker’ microphones using this method were used to record the timings of the sound of guns firing on photographic film using a string galvanometer and, by the end of the war, could be used to locate enemy guns very accurately and tell what size they were and in what direction they were facing. Various other more or less Heath-Robinson style devices were experimented with by different nations with different levels of success during WW1 and the inter-war years. French Perrin telesitemeter, with two myriaphones Japanese mobile sound ranging equipment Fascinatingly there exists a record of the end of World War 1 captured using Tucker’s equipment. You can see the precise moment when the guns fell silent at 11:00 on the 11th of November, 1918. Sound record of the end of World War I Anyway, following the war and well before the advent of radar, it was realised that the technique could potentially be used to detect aircraft outside visual range, and Tucker became the Director of Acoustical Research at the Air Defence Experimental Establishment at Biggin Hill. Initially Tucker experimented with parabolic acoustic mirrors, but the wavelength of aircraft engines was longer than these relatively small mirrors could manage. As a result larger 200′ rectangular mirrors (one still stands at Denge) were planned in a network along the coasts of the United Kingdom. Acoustic mirror at Denge, note the people standing in front for scale A Chain Home station, the radar that replaced the acoustic mirrors In ideal conditions, aircraft could be detected at a range of 25 miles, and bearings from a number of stations could be used to triangulate their position. In the 1920s this was useful technology, but aircraft were rapidly becoming faster and by the late 1930s the aircraft would have been detected too late to allow any useful response. The coincidental development of radar, although early radar also had its its fair share of problems, put paid to plans for a national network of acoustic mirrors. However, Tucker had developed the concept of control centres to correlate information from different mirrors and this concept was taken on, lock, stock, and barrel, by radar. The resulting filter, sector, and group control rooms were pivotal to winning the Battle of Britain, so Tucker’s efforts were by no means wasted.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Which country was the first to invent jet propulsion for aircrafts, Germany or Britain?
Answer: Due to the way that it is phrased, this is not an easy question to answer. The first jet aircraft to fly was undoubtedly the Heinkel He 178 which first flew in August 1939, powered by a Heinkel-Strahltriebwerk 3 (HeS 3) turbojet developed by Hans von Ohain. The rival British Gloster E.28/39 first flew in May, 1941, twenty one months after the Henikel. However, the question is which country was the first to invent jet propulsion for aircraft, not which was the first country to fly a jet aircraft. As with many scientific advances, lots of people were working on similar ideas at the same time. Discarding rocket power, ramjets and pulsejets from consideration, that leaves us with various forms of turbine power. Pre-war researchers in this field included engineers from Norway, Hungary, France, Spain, and, of course, Britain and Germany. The main contenders are Frank Whittle in the UK and the aforementioned Hans von Ohain in Germany. However, before discussing these two, I should mention Alan Arnold Griffith, a very prolific English engineer, who used funding from the British Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (the Aeronautical Research Committee or ARC from 1919) to produce a working axial turbine model in 1929. The funding source makes it clear that the research was specifically with regard to developing an aircraft engine, but Griffiths assumed that this would be a turboprop rather than a pure jet. Frank Whittle was working on the concept of jet propulsion from 1928, and founded Power Jets Ltd in 1936, running test engines from 1937. However, Whittle’s patents date from 1930 whilst Ohain’s date from 1935, as do those of the Spaniard Virgilio Leret Ruiz. It also appears that Ohain had reviewed Whittle’s patents as part of his own design work. Therefore, depending on how you interpret to term invent, you can take your pick. Griffith was one of the first in the aeronautical turbine field but not, initially, concerned with pure jets, Whittle pursued the pure jet idea first with patents in 1930, Whittle and Ohain both started testing engine models in April 1937, but Ohain was the first to a working aircraft in August 1939. The aircraft mentioned above were purely experimental and the first actual combat aircraft were the Me 262 which entered service in April 1944 and the Gloster Meteor which entered service in July 1944. I won’t discuss the relative efficiency of the British and German engine designs in this post, except to say that it was Whittle based designs that powered the majority of the early post-war fighters. Gloster E.28/39 Heinkel He 178

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How could the Norden Bombsight have been kept a secret from the Germans when so many B-17's were shot down? How could B-17's not shoot each other out of the sky while defending themselves against attacking German fighter aircraft?
Answer: It wasn’t. Without wishing to be a killjoy, the first point to make is that the Norden Mk XV sight was not nearly as critical to the US war effort as is often been made out. In fact most of the Norden’s reputation is simply based on marketing hype from the Norden company and the USAAC. B-17s bombing The extreme secrecy, special vaults, not allowing bombardiers to take notes, requiring them to take an oath stating that they would defend the secret with their lives, the pickle barrel myth, can all be seen as marketing ploys. So successful was this marketing that most people have never heard of the, arguably superior, Sperry S-1 sight and A-5 autopilot combination. Norden were not above making impossible claims for their sight: We do not regard a fifteen-foot square as being difficult to hit from an altitude of 30,000 feet, provided the new Army M-4 bombsight, together with the Stabilized Bombing Approach Equipment is used. Theodore Barth, Norden At the time Barth was saying this, the Norden sight was achieving 16% hits on a 1,000 ft square target. It appears that Norden’s accuracy claims were made based on tests carried out at much lower altitudes and speeds than were possible in combat over Europe. Norden Mk XV bombsight In addition, although the Norden was an ingenious piece of kit, it took a significant amount of time to calibrate, and its gyros were prone to tumbling in turbulence from flak or during evasive manoeuvring, rendering it ineffective. When they evaluated the Norden sight in 1942, the RAF decided to adopt their own SABS (Stabilised Automatic Bomb Sight) sight for precision work. A second point is that not every US bomber was equipped with the Norden sight. Eventually, only lead bombers had the sight and the rest of the combat box simply bombed on command. So much for precision. B-17 combat box However, probably the most important point is that the Germans didn’t need to capture a Norden sight. They’d already received full technical drawings in 1938 from Herman Lang, a member of the huge Dusquene spy ring operating in the US. Lang, a German immigrant, was employed as an assembly inspector in the Norden factory and received $1,500 for copying the drawings and passing them to the Germans. Lang received an 18 year sentence and was deported to Germany in 1950. Pretty lenient. The Germans evaluated the Norden drawings and apparently concluded that it wasn’t significantly superior to their own sight, the Lotfernrohr 7, which was based on the same principles. Therefore, shot down B-17s weren’t an issue, the Germans already had all the details. As to the last part of the question, planes in combat boxes did occasionally shoot each other down, but I haven’t seen many reports. The bombers did experiment with formations that stacked planes downward in the direction of the sun to help gunners see their own planes to sunward (Javelin Down formation). One suspects that, in the heat of combat, many incidents went unnoticed, others unreported or suppressed.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it feasible to construct a modernized version of a dreadnought-style battleship that could withstand modern threats such as missiles and torpedoes?
Answer: Why would you want to? Dreadnoughts only had one practical purpose and that was to fight other dreadnoughts. In an evolutionary arms race against themselves, they became bigger, more heavily armed and armoured, and more expensive, until much cheaper and more flexible weapons: mines, submarines, and aircraft rendered them obsolete. Nobody would want to build a ship with big guns theses days. The biggest recent attempt, the 6″ (155m) AGS on the Zumwalt destroyers ended in a shambles. Even these guns, large by modern standards, were tiny in comparison to the 14″-18″ guns found on the later generations of battleships. The longest range naval hit in history was when HMS Warspite hit the Italian the battleship Giulio Cesare at a range of 26,000 yards (just under 15 miles). This is obviously a trivial distance for a missile, the Naval Strike Missile that will equip the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers for instance has a range of 120–160 miles. Warspite’s eight BL 15-inch Mk I naval guns each weighed over 100 tons and they were housed in four massive armoured turrets weighing over 2,000 tons each. Together with all the other gubbins, that meant that Warspite weighed in at around 40,000 tons. A Type 45 can destroy a target at ten times the range of Warspite and only weighs in at 9,500 tons. If you don’t need gigantic guns, you don’t need a gigantic ship. HMS Warspite, a Queen Elizabeth-class dreadnought HMS Diamond, a Type 45 destroyer Warspite is also a good example, because, despite her size, she was vulnerable. In 1916, she was missed by three torpedoes fired by an unknown U-Boat, and another torpedo fired by U-47 missed her in 1940. If any of those had hit, her career might have ended prematurely. She was also badly damaged by German aircraft whilst off Crete and had to sail to the US for repairs, and finally she was hit by a Fritz-X missile (actually a guided bomb) off Salerno and, again, badly damaged. A torpedo, a mine, an aircraft bomb, or a missile, can kill a battleship at a trivial cost, much as we see expensive tanks being destroyed by cheap drones in the Ukraine. The economics and the risk/reward in building them just doesn’t add up. If there is a modern justification for a large ship, it would probably be ana arsenal ship, such as was proposed by the US Navy in the 1990s. These ships need to be large because they are designed to carry hundreds of missiles. However, an even more sensible solution would be to make them submersible and thus only vulnerable to ASW assets. This is the path taken by converting some Ohio-class submarines into SSGNs armed with cruise missiles. There is no viable use case for a modern dreadnought. It couldn’t do anything better than an aircraft carrier can and it would not be proof against modern torpedoes - which are designed to break a ship’s back by exploding under them, rather than by penetrating armour - and, although it might withstand one or two missile hits, it almost certainly couldn’t withstand a determined missile attack without either becoming a mission kill or a total loss. It would also be very expensive to build and man; you’d be better off spending the money on a carrier - although they may also be on the cusp of obsolescence.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the annual defense spending of Britain compared to other NATO countries such as France and Germany? Is this amount considered fair or too high considering the size of Britain's economy and population?
Answer: There are lots of different ways of answering this question. You could look at spending in USD, in terms of PPP (Purchasing Power Parity), or in terms of % of GDP. The latter is probably the fairest comparison as it shows expenditure as a proportion of the economy as a whole. The following figures are from NATO. The NATO estimates for 2023 indicate that the top spending nation is Poland, which is spending 3.9% of GDP, followed closely by the United States at 3.49%. The United Kingdom spends 2.07%, France 1.9% and Germany, lagging somewhat, at 1.57%. In terms of USD expenditure, the United States leads with $860b, followed by Germany with $68b, the UK with $66b, and then France with $57b. Poland is estimated to spend $29b in 2023. In terms of who is trying hardest at the moment, Poland has increased its defence spend by 63.7% over the last year, Finland by 45.7%, Germany by 5%, France by 2%, and the United Kingdom by -4.2%. These figures are in real terms, so an apparent increase can actually be a decrease when inflation is taken into account. Of course, the impact of increases depends on whether you start from a low base or not, so this last figure is only indicative. The UK for instance, has been spending over 2% of GDP since 2014, well ahead of everybody else except the United States and, curiously, Greece. The only other countries to have reached the 2% “target” are Poland, Lithuania, and Estonia, who are evidently taking current affairs seriously. British forces consume 2.07% of GDP, above the NATO average of 1.74% excluding the USA These are just the raw figures. Other major issues are whether a country is getting value for money for its expenditure and also whether purported increases are actually being spent in improving front line strength or whether they are simply creative bookkeeping. This is a subject that I don’t intend to venture into, except to say that it is as well to keep a jaundiced eye on the claims of politicians. In answer to the specific question, the United Kingdom is putting slightly more effort into NATO than France and quite a lot more than Germany. Many NATO countries have been coasting since the end of the Cold War and we are starting to see them waking up to the fact that they have to pull their weight and stop relying on the United States for defence.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why do naval ships no longer have armor? It seems that it would still be useful.
Answer: Armour is heavy and it is expensive. Modern armour plate actually had a relatively short life, first being used on the French ironclad Gloire in 1859 and effectively becoming obsolete by the end of WW2 as a result of developments in naval airpower, mines, torpedoes, and, slightly later, missiles. When a tiny Osa-class missile boat can pack the punch of a battleship with its P-15 Styx missiles, there is no point building the huge ships needed to house, and defend against, 16″ guns. These days, modern warships only have Kevlar or similar splinter protection rather than armour. Osa-class launches a Styx missile I was lucky enough to walk around the USS Iowa in Long Beach just after Christmas and, as well as the belt, the critical parts of the superstructure such as the conning tower are very heavily armoured. There are many different opinions out there about just how resilient a battleship with heavy armour would be against missile attacks. There are lots of arguments about armour piercing (or lack of) capable missiles, top-down attacks, shaped charges, compartmentalisation, reserve buoyancy, ceramic and reactive armours, etc. USS Iowa conning tower armour No battleship has ever been expended in a missile test and so we have no decisive evidence one way or another. However, obviously no battleship would be proof against a tactical nuclear missile and even battleships would be extremely vulnerable to modern torpedo, under keel, attacks. We do know that the Italian battleship Roma was sunk, and that the Italian Battleship Italia (ex-Littorio) and the British battleship Warspite were badly damaged by Fritz-X guided bombs towards the end of WW2. The Roma had 13.8″ belt and 6″ deck armour, rather more than the Iowa-class battleships. The Fritz-X had a 320kg warhead based on the PC 1400 armour piercing bomb, whilst the Russian Cold War KH-22 Kitchen has either a 1,000kg conventional or a 350–1,000kt thermonuclear warhead. Roma, the only battleship sunk by a missile (guided bomb) The Kitty Hawk-class carrier America was expended in a succession of live fire tests, but the results are (as far as I know) still highly classified and so we have no idea how they turned out. In any case, she was not an armoured ship. We have to assume that, as all the navies of the world seem to have reached the same decision, there is no persuasive economic or tactical case for the development of ships carrying heavy armour. Warships are unlikely to be engaged by gunfire, and incoming missiles are better defeated with active defences such as electronic warfare, decoy systems, defensive missiles, or CIWS, than by armour. Adding armour to the mix would not only cost more but would make the ships bigger and heavier, compromising more highly prized characteristics such as speed, agility, and stealth, whilst still not ensuring survival.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Does NATO stand a chance in a war against Russia?
Answer: I’m going to assume that Russia includes Belarus. I’m also going to assume that we are discussing a conventional war. We’ll also assume that Ukraine is neutral, but that all NATO members answer the call, particularly Turkey which has huge armed forces. Also, if Russia invaded a NATO country that was in the EU, say Estonia, then we’d have to consider the forces of Austria, Cyprus, Ireland, Malta, and Sweden - but we won’t. We can posit two scenarios, one which includes the USA and one that doesn’t (just for fun). (All numbers are taken from Wikipedia) If we look at the size of the economies involved, NATO including the USA has a GDP (nominal) of 26.4 times that of Russia plus Belarus. If we exclude the USA, then the ratio drops to 12.3 times in favour of NATO. However, if we adjust for PPP (purchasing power parity) then the ratios become 11.4:1 if we include the USA, and 6.3:1 if we exclude it. Less favourable to NATO but still a clear advantage. Regarding population sizes, the ration is 6.2:1 in favour of NATO if we include the USA and 4:1 if we exclude it. Regarding the size of armed forces (including reserves and paramilitary forces), then NATO has an advantage of 1.5:1 if we include the USA but is at parity (1:1) if we exclude it. If we were only to look at active forces, then the ratios would be 2.8:1 in NATO’s favour with the USA and 1.7:1 without it. In the medium to long term, NATO would get its act in order and inevitably prevail. In the short term, I would predict complete chaos as NATO’s 31 countries try to sort themselves out. On the other hand, Russia’s notorious corruption and poorly maintained equipment will be causing it problems. Let us hope that we don’t have to find out.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What are the historical reasons behind the decline in army numbers in the UK over the past 30 years?
Answer: For context, when I was born in 1959, the UK armed forces (not just the Army) numbered 566,500 (predominantly) men. In 2023 they number 142,500, a fall of 75% or 424,000 over 65 years. In the public debate on defence, the view is often expressed that the defence budget can be safely cut, with instant savings or other benefits to the economy, and with acceptable consequences for national security. Our examination... has convinced us that this view is largely fallacious... The force reductions resulting from the defence review may over-stretch the Services in the fulfilment of their remaining commitments, and may leave an inadequate margin for dealing with unforeseen tasks. Public Expenditure Committee 1975 The question asks about the decrease in the size of the army since 1993. With the collapse of the Soviet Union around 1990 all major countries were keen to reap a peace dividend so that they could spend more money on other perceived priorities. A restructuring called Options for Change in 1990 called for a total manpower cut of 18%. In the Army this meant a cut from 160,000 to 120,000, a reduction of 40,000 men. There followed defence reviews in 1994 (Front Line First),1998 and 2002 (Strategic Defence Reviews I and II), 2003 (Defence White Paper), 2010 (Strategic Defence and Security Review), 2015 (SDSR II), and 2021 (Integrated Review). As early as 2004, repeated concerns were being raised about overstretch: Despite the reduction in infantry battalions, the Army is left pretty much intact and able to carry out all the tasks required of it according to MOD planning assumptions. The problem is that governments continue to get away with ignoring these assumptions and over-stretching the military. Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), 2004 Assumptions were being made that Russia was no longer a major threat: The biggest gamble taken in the White Paper is that this view of future wars is correct. On this view, the wars that will demand British engagement in the next couple of decades are likely to resemble those of the 1990s – Bosnia, Sierra Leone, Kosovo. Or they will resemble those of this century – Afghanistan and Iraq – and will be fought alongside the US. But they will not be like the Falklands, the Cold War or the Second World War. The Times, 2004 Other, equally dubious assumptions were also being made, none of which look particularly safe now: The SDSR identified five key priorities for international engagement going forward, all of which cut across each of the policy areas under discussion. • The pre-eminent defence and security relationship with the US • New models of practical bilateral defence and security cooperation with a range of allies and partners • An effective and reformed United Nations • NATO as the bedrock of the UK’s defence • An outward-facing European Union that promotes security and prosperity SDSR, 2010 Whatever the general waffle around these reviews, the unmistakable fact is that the Army now stands at 75,710 and is expected to fall to around 73,000 (Future soldier: Transforming the British Army, 2021) and may well fall even further. This is well under half the size it was thirty years ago. The situation is exacerbated by two other factors. Relatively poor pay and conditions, together with societal changes, have made it increasingly difficult to recruit and targets are consistently missed. I read recently that Capita (who are in charge of recruitment) has suggested that people with asthma should be accepted into the Army. In addition to the recruitment problem, the Army is also suffering from a retention problem. Again poor pay and conditions, together with overstretch: too many deployments, too close together, is clearly making the Army an unattractive long-term career. Yesterday, in response to comments made by General Sir Patrick Sanders, the Prime Minister ruled out the possibility of conscription into the armed forces. However, clearly, if push comes to shove, the Army will not be able to contribute much at its current strength, and large scale conscription may be required across NATO and the EU if Russia turns westwards. People are not ready to hear that.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What type of plane did "The Red Baron" fly during World War I? How was he able to maneuver so well with limited technology compared to modern planes?
Answer: As far as I can tell, the Red Baron, Manfred von Richthofen, flew consecutively in the Albatros C.III, Albatros D.II, Albatros D.III, Halberstadt D.II, and Albatros D.V, but you are probably thinking of the aircraft that he is most associated with, the Fokker Dr.I triplane. Fokker Dr.I triplanes The Fokker Dr.I was inspired by a captured British Sopwith Triplane, which itself was based on the Sopwith Pup biplane. The advantage of biplanes over monoplanes, and triplanes over biplanes, is that the extra wing area permits lighter wings, a smaller chord, low wing loading and smaller span for a given area. This generates a lot of additional lift making bi/tri-planes highly manoeuvrable. The disadvantage is that the extra wings and,, in particular, their associated struts create lots of drag and so these aircraft were slower than contemporary biplanes. They also have fairly poor visibility for the pilot. Someone remarked of the Sopwith triplane that it looked like a “drunken flight of steps” when it rolled. The Dr.I also suffered from structural problems (the wings tended to fall off) partly as a result of poor quality control and partly because of aerodynamic issues that were not understood a at the time. These issues prevented the Dr.I from having a long career. The result is a plane that is slow but very agile, which is ideal in some circumstances but a serious problem in others. In the end only around 170 Dr.Is entered service.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did Wellington consider resigning after defeating Napolean at Waterloo due to the high number of casualties?
Answer: No he didn’t and, as far as I know, nobody suggested that he should. I don’t believe that resigning was really a concept in the early 19th Century and, anyway, not many people resign after winning a major victory and huge pubic acclaim. The Observer reported: Every incident relating to the late battle is so interesting and honourable to the national character, and the source of so much commendable pride and exultation to every Englishman, and at the same time so much sought after, that we have been induced to collect them from every conceivable source and present them to our readers. But we cannot refer to these without expressing gratification that our pages are emblazoned with fresh proud records of British valour. Heaven has, indeed, smiled on the good cause of freedom and of loyalty, and victory has twined her brightest wreath to decorate the brows of Wellington. Dreadful has been the struggle, and awful indeed, the sacrifice, and even the splendid results of the 18th June have been dearly purchased at the expense of the rich blood shed on the memorable occasion; but in the successful issue of this arduous contest, we may confidently anticipate the speedy destruction of the cause of all the evils which have desolated the Continent for so many years, and the restoration of peace to Europe and the Universe, whose beams have been so sweet and transient. In any case, an analysis of major Napoleonic battles suggests that the Anglo-Allied casualty rate at Waterloo does not stand out as exceptional. Indeed, if we analyse the casualties (those killed, wounded, missing, and captured) for all sides from Waterloo, Wavre, Ligny, Austerlitz, Borodino, Jena, and Leipzig, we find that the Anglo-Allied Army at Waterloo is right in the middle of the pack suffering approximately 22% casualties which is below the French casualty rate at Waterloo, Ligny, Leipzig, and Borodino or the Allied casualty rate at Austerliz, Jena, or Borodino. Waterloo was an unusually constricted battlefield and this resulted in the appearance of a larger than usual number of casualties. Captain Johnny Kincaid of the Rifles wrote that he: had never yet heard of a battle in which everybody was killed, but this seemed likely to be an exception. Heavy casualties were noticed. In Spain, Wellington was certainly aware of the effect on public opinion at home. After Talavera, he wrote: How I shall be abused [by the government and press] for our loss [of men]…I was hit but not hurt and I had my coat shot through. Almost all the staff officers are wounded or have had their horses shot. Never was there such a murderous battle! and later in the Peninsular he made another reference to public sensibilities: This becomes doubly necessary as I see that notwithstanding the fondness of the British nation for the sport, and their exultation upon our success, they began to cry out the other day upon the loss of 300 or 400 men the unsuccessful storm of San Sebastián. However, Wellington was careful to try to deploy his men in such a way as to minimise casualties, although whether this was out of a particular concern for the men or simply good battle management cannot be discerned. Whichever is true, he was keenly aware of the consequences of battle: Well, thank God, I don’t know what it is to lose a battle; but certainly nothing can be more painful than to gain one with the loss of so many friends. After Waterloo, he is reported as being: much affected. I felt his tears dropping fast on my hands, and looking towards him, saw them chasing one another in furrows over his dusty cheeks. However, I should note that this may be because of the loss of senior officers, friends and aides-de-camp rather than the ordinary troops; it is impossible to tell. When Wellington left the battlefield he was utterly exhausted. It is said that he wept as he was told of the terrible losses and said: I hope to God I have fought my last battle. He had.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Was an invasion of Britain through Pas-de-Calais considered easier than the invasion at Normandy?
Answer: Not at all. No seaborne invasion should be considered easy, but the planned German invasion of the United Kingdom, Operation Seelöwe or Sealion, would have been an extremely risky, practically suicidal venture. If we are talking about the fact that it is a shorter distance across the Channel from the Pas-de-Calais rather than to the Baie de la Seine (Normandy) then it needs to be noted that Seelöwe landing beaches extended from Ramsgate to Portsmouth, a broad frontage at least three times wider than that of the Allies in Normandy and involving both long and short transits. There is no particular advantage in distance. Hitler laid down the following conditions for launching Seelöwe: (1) that the Germans had gained air superiority, (2) that all British minefields were swept and the invasion beaches isolated, (3) that the Royal Navy be unable to intervene. The fact that none of these conditions, which all presupposed victory in the Battle of Britain, were met meant that the operation was stillborn. However, even had they been met, Operation Seelöwe would still have been impossible to execute successfully. Planning for Seelöwe was shoehorned into less than two months, whilst the detailed planning for D-Day took more than a year. The Allies had a vast fleet of some 7,000 specially designed ships and landing craft of various types, whilst the Germans relied mainly on 2,400 river barges most of which were unpowered, were totally unsuitable for crossing the Channel in any kind of rough sea, and were very slow and lacking any kind of defences. German invasion fleet Allied invasion fleet Furthermore, the Germans had no capability whatsoever to supply their invasion force with logistical backup, whilst the Allies had prepared the Mulberry floating harbours, the Pluto (Pipe Line Under The Ocean) fuel pipeline, DUKW amphibious trucks and a huge logistical support operation. There is really no comparison between the two operations. Operation Seelöwe was the very definition of wing-and-a-prayer, whilst Operation Neptune, the naval part of Overlord, was meticulously planned and prepared for.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is there a lot of envy in the United Kingdom for the American way of life?
Answer: I can only speak for myself, but I think that there used to be, but less so now. From the 1940s to the 1960s the United States was in a golden age. The evident affluence of the population, the cars, the sunshine, and the exotic locations seen on TV shows and movies made it look attractive to a British population, most of whom had very limited travel prospects. These days, the golden age is over, more people travel widely, and TV and films often portray the United States as dysfunctional and very violent - more violent than it actually is. I have been visiting the United States for the last forty years at an average rate of a visit every two years, sometimes on business but mostly for pleasure. In that time I have driven round the entire perimeter of the country, and I have visited every State with the possible exceptions of Missouri and Nebraska. I think that I have had a pretty good overview. Crater Lake, Oregon - what’s not to like? My first visit was to New York in 1982 and I was immediately struck by how dirty the city was, the point being that locations used for TV or movies tend to look a lot cleaner than they actually are, which gives a rather skewed impression. Our most recent visit was to spend Christmas this year in Los Angeles and it is impossible not to notice the number of people living in makeshift tents, RVs, and cars. I also noticed this in San Francisco in 2019 which presented very differently to the city I first visited in 1995. I don’t know whether this is a result of the opioid crisis, but something had gone badly out of whack in the last couple of decades. Another side effect of intermittent visits over a longish period of time is to notice how much further north the Spanish language is seen and heard. That’s not a criticism, just an observation. There are parts of the United States that I would be quite happy living in: Santa Barbara, Walnut Creek, San Antonio, Savannah, most of New England, the North West. These areas have distinct personalities that makes them appealing, as opposed to the more cookie-cutter parts where you see the same groups of stores every few miles, Dallas for instance. Bits are also incredibly tacky; when you drive out of the Smoky Mountains and into a Dolly Parton themed town, it comes as a bit of a shock. Overall, I love the United States for the scenery, the variety, and the people, but I don’t think that I envy the American way of life - apart from the weather. Day to day, it’s not all that different, but with (from a British perspective) a lot less vacation, a lot more insecurity, and a somewhat increased tendency towards violence. Although, having said that, I’ve only really felt concerned for my safety twice: once walking around central Washington late in the evening, and once in a Dennys in Fairbanks, Alaska when some guy was muttering to himself and seemed about to go postal (he didn’t). I don’t think that’s a bad record. TLDR: The United States looked great to Brits who saw it on films and on the TV in the grey post-war years and into the 1980s. Now that people are generally more worldly wise and the United States itself is no longer in its golden post-war boom years, the shine has worn off a bit.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is the Royal Navy still the second most powerful navy in the world after the US Navy? Can it destroy the Russian Navy in battle?
Answer: No. I would say that the Chinese Navy is clearly more powerful, and that the French and, possibly, Indian navies could give the Royal Navy a good run for its money. As for the Russians, we have to take into account their notorious levels of corruption and apparent incompetence, but they have a slightly bigger fleet and a lot more submarines. I think that the outcome would be very dependent on the exact circumstances and particularly on the level of participation of Russian aviation, naval and otherwise. The Royal Navy’s fleet is described as a balanced fleet, one with a broad range of assets suitable for many different tasks, rather than a fleet designed around one particular mission. Very few other nations are capable of deploying a credible carrier strike group worldwide - what is often called a blue water navy. However, as the Russians found in 1905, it’s one thing being able to steam to the far side of the world, but a whole other thing to win the battle once you get there. You have to be able to do both for a blue water capability to have any real meaning. Whilst there is no doubt in my mind that, ship for ship, the Royal Navy is probably the equal to any other navy, that, unfortunately, is not the only thing that matters. Number of ships matters, manning matters, logistics matter. The size of the Royal Navy has been reduced drastically over the last few years and, as has recently been in the news, it is having trouble manning even the small number of ships that it has left. Currently the navy has two aircraft carriers, but not sufficient aircraft and escorts for both to engage in operations. It also has seventeen other surface units, and six submarines (excluding the four boomers which are not tactical vessels). However two of the frigates, Argyll and Westminster are apparently being taken out of service due to manning shortages. Manning is a problem because of low pay and other in-service factors which lead to problems in retention. You know that something is wrong when the Royal Navy has less than 30,000 sailors but the Ministry of Defence has more than 60,000 civilian staff. All of this leaves the Royal Navy with six Type 45 destroyers and nine Type 23 frigates. Attempts to boost the size of the surface fleet, as is sometimes done, by counting essentially unarmed patrol boats and mine countermeasures vessels, are simply ridiculous. It should also be noted that one-for-one Royal Navy ships are comparatively under armed. Whilst the US Navy’s Arleigh Burke-class destroyers typically have 90–96 missile cells, the Royal Navy’s latest Type 45 destroyers only have 48. This makes the Type 45s significantly less capable in any extended combat scenario. Royal Navy Type 45 Destroyer, great ships but comparatively under armed and very few in number The other major issue is logistics and I would be very surprised indeed if the Royal Navy was capable of fighting for more than a week or two before its war stocks are exhausted. If history tells us anything, it tells us firstly, that politicians are never prepared to spend the money to build up adequate war stocks and secondly, that ammunition is always expended at a far faster rate than anticipated. As an aside, it is clearly not economic to be shooting down cheap Houthi drones with Sea Viper (PAAMS) missiles costing £1.5 million each, any more than it was sensible taking out Daesh 4x4s with air-launched Brimstones. Modern munitions are complicated. Although largely unprepared, we were able to adapt rapidly in WW2, producing some fifteen thousand aircraft in the first full year of the war. How many Typhoons or Aster or Sea Ceptor missiles could we now produce in a year? If we don’t have adequate stocks of these things at the start of a war, we aren’t going to be able to simply pull more out of a hat. As we are finding in the Ukraine, and as Stalin said many years ago, quantity has a quality of its own. In my opinion, the Royal Navy simply doesn’t have the quantity, and its small numbers mean that, in a major war, it is not going to be able to withstand even fairly minor levels of attrition for very long. In the UK, the politicians have been unwilling, for generations, to fund the armed services, including the Royal Navy, at anything like an adequate level, and in this they are reflecting, presumably, the views of the public. Even with the current conflicts in the Ukraine and elsewhere in the world providing a very clear wakeup call if ever there was one, we are still actually shrinking the size of our forces whilst our politicians claim otherwise. As WW2 indicated, it’s absolutely fine to ignore the problem right up until the point that it isn’t. Then you have to pay the cost for being inadequately prepared. However, if we do grow the Royal Navy, it’s going to take time and its going to cost money, lots of money, which means that hard choices are going to have to be made - and politicians don’t like hard choices.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What was the fate of the destroyers gifted from the US to the UK under the 'Destroyer-for-bases' agreement?
Answer: Well, firstly they weren’t gifted. As stated in the question, it was a destroyers for bases deal that granted the US ninety-nine year leases for air and naval bases in various British owned parts of the Americas. The fifty destroyers became known as Town-class destroyers in the Royal Navy, not to be confused with the Town-class cruisers. The US Navy had built 173 destroyers of the Caldwell, Wickes, and Clemson-classes, often referred to as twelve-hundred tonners or four-pipers, towards the end of WW1. These ships were surplus to requirements and many had been laid up in reserve at the end of the war. An unfortunate side effect of this was that some were in poor condition. Forty-two destroyers were transferred to the Royal Navy, who then passed nine to the Soviet Navy: (ex-USN/adopted name) Fairfax/Zhivuchiy, Twiggs/Zhguchiy, Crowninshield/Derzkiy, Yarnall/Druzhny, Cowell/Zharkiy, Maddox/Doblestny, Foote/Zhostkiy, Thomas/Dostoyny, and Herndon/Deyatelny), and eight were transferred to the the Royal Canadian Navy (Haraden/Columbia, Edwards/Buxton, Thatcher/Niagara, Kalk/Hamilton, Mackenzie/Annapolis, Williams/St. Clair, Bancroft/St. Francis, and McCook/St. Croix). Five of the ships transferred to the Royal Navy were manned by the Royal Norwegian Navy, and one by the Royal Netherlands Navy. Of the fifty destroyers, six (Hopewell/Bath, McCook/St. Croix, Satterlee/Belmont, Mason/Broadwater, Branch/Beverly, and McCalla/Stanley) were lost to U-boats and three to other causes: Swasey/ Rockingham struck a mine and sunk under tow, Welles/Cameron was damaged beyond repair in an air raid whilst docked at Portsmouth, and Herndon/Deyatelny was sunk either by a U-boat or by her depth charges exploding. Thirty-five were broken up between 1944 and 1947, three foundered or were scuttled after the war, and two were sunk as targets. The fiftieth was the most famous of all. The USS Buchanan/HMS Campbeltown was a Wikes-class destroyer transferred in September 1940. After refitting she operated in the Western Approaches with the 17th Flotilla before being transferred to the Royal Netherlands Navy and 7th Escort Group. She reverted to the Royal Navy in September 1941 and covered convoys on the West Africa route. USS Buchanan In January 1942, she was determined to be expendable and selected for special duties. Two funnels were removed and the other two cut down to make her resemble, superficially at least, a German Type 23 Raubvogel-class torpedo boat. In addition, twenty-four depth charges, some four and a half tons of explosive was loaded behind her bows and set in concrete in hidden compartments. HMS Campbeltown being converted German Type 23 torpedo boat On the 26th of March 1942, a flotilla of sixteen motor launches loaded with Commandos and the Campbeltown, escorted by two destroyers, left Falmouth to execute Operation Chariot, the Raid on St. Nazaire. The raid was designed to deny German capital ships, especially the Tirpitz, any access to the giant Normandie dry dock by ramming the dock gates with a specially lightened destroyer packed with explosives. The problem was that the dock gates were five miles up the Loire river estuary and were heavily defended. At 00:30 hours on the 28th of March the ships crossed over the sandbanks at the mouth of the Loire, with Campbeltown scraping the bottom twice but each time pulling free. They came to within eight minutes' travel from the dock gates when, at 01:22, the force was illuminated by searchlights and challenged. The ships responded with captured signals telling the Germans that they were friendly forces, which confused them for another few minutes before they opened fire at 01:28. Commanded by Lt Cdr Stephen Halden Beattie, the Campbeltown increased speed and rammed the dock gates at 19 knots, driving her 30 feet onto the gates and crushing the first 36 feet of her bows - three minutes behind schedule. German photographs of Campbeltown after the ramming The explosives on the Campbeltown detonated at noon, some eight hours later than planned, killing some 360 German soldiers and civilians, including 40 officers who were investigating the wreck of the ship, and putting the dock out of action for the rest of the war. The remains of the dock, containing the wreck of the Campbeltown which was swept into the lock - note the sandbank in place of the destroyed dock gates. Of the 612 men who undertook the raid, 228 returned to Britain, 169 were killed (64 commandos and 105 sailors) and 215 became POWs. For great gallantry and determination in the attack on St. Nazaire in command of HMS Campbeltown. Under intense fire directed at the bridge from point blank range of about 100 yards, and in the face of the blinding glare of many searchlights, he steamed her into the lock-gates and beached and scuttled her in the correct position. This Victoria Cross is awarded to Lieutenant-Commander Beattie in recognition not only of his own valour but also of that of the unnamed officers and men of a very gallant ship's company, many of whom have not returned.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What materials were used to make arrows in medieval times, including the feathers and the arrow itself?
Answer: I happen to live near the Sussex village of Fletching whose name refers to the feathers on an arrow and thus the local medieval industry of making arrows. This was a significant industry nationwide. In 1360, 500,000 arrows were delivered to the Tower of London and in the previous year it had been 850,000. In 1417, six feathers from every goose within the realm had to be delivered to the Tower, and the Counties were mandated to supply a total of 1,190,000 goose feathers in the following year. In 1416, to secure the supply of shafts Henry V banned the use of poplar for any other use. In 1371, the Worshipful Company of Fletchers was founded, splitting from the Guild it had shared with the Bowyers. An arrow consisted a the shaft, a nock (the part that engages with the bowstring), fletching (the feathers) and an arrowhead of some kind. The nearly 3,000 arrows recovered from the wreck of the Mary Rose range in size from 27.5 inches to 32 inches, and are 0.5 of an inch at the head, tapering towards the nock. It is clear that there was obviously a good deal of standardisation being practiced. Anton the Bastard of Burgundy Anton holds an arrow where the shaft tapers towards the carved nock and the fletching consists of three feathers. As mentioned above, the shaft was often made of poplar, ash, aspen, birch, or oak, and the head held on to the shaft with a small rivet or, in many cases, beeswax. Shafts were turned on a type of lathe with sandstone and fish skin used to smooth the final surface. The nock slit was cut into the wood with a small saw, and at some point the nocks started to be reinforced with a sliver of horn. The feather fletchings were attached to the shaft using glue, sometimes mixed with beeswax, verdigris, and other materials (to keep insects away during storage), and further secured with a whipping of silk or linen thread. Only geese and swans produced feathers long and strong enough to be used as fletchings and were available in quantities suitable for mass production. The shaping of the individual feathers and the way that they were arranged on the shaft needs a post all of its own but is too complicated to go into here (plus I don’t fully understand it). The only complete late medieval arrow in Britain was found in the rafters of Westminster Abbey, where it must have been placed before the renovation in 1437 (possibly lost whilst hunting pigeons inside the Abbey). The shaft is 29 inches long, probably made of ash, with a diameter of 10.7 mm beneath the socket and 7.6 mm at the rear end. The widest part of 11.4 mm is at about two-fifths of the total length behind the arrowhead, a shaft design known as ‘breasted’ or ‘chested’. A 4 cm long slit was cut perpendicular to the string groove at the rear end, probably to receive a thin sliver of horn as reinforcement. Reddish-brown remains of a glue covered some 18 cm (7 in.) of the rear end in which three feathers and an increasingly narrow binding have left their marks. The head was a type very popular in late medieval England with narrow, curved blades and barbs, but there were a wide variety of different heads used for different purposes. A replica of the Westminster Abbey arrow

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Is it possible for a Panzerfaust to penetrate the armor plate of a tank?
Answer: Yes, very effectively. There were several different versions of the Panzerfaust. The Faustpatrone 30 or Panzerfaust Klein was a one man, single use weapon that had an effective range of only 30 metres compared with the Allied PIAT and M1 Bazooka which had an effective range of over 100 metres. You had to be a brave man to get close to a tank with a Panzerfaust, but they were ideal ambush weapons. The Panzerfaust warhead contained a shaped charge comprised of a 50/50 mix of TNT and trihexogen explosive. Fitted to the warhead was a wooden dowel adorned with folding sheet steel fins that deployed when fired. The round was shipped attached to a simple steel tube and the propellant was simply 3.5 oz of blackpowder (Panzerfaust 30). The Panzerfaust could penetrate 140mm of armour, a decent amount and certainly enough to take out a Sherman with a good hit, they also caused a great deal of dangerous spalling within the target tank. It appears that in 1944 around 12% of all tank losses can be attributed to Panzerfaust or Panzershreck (the Panzershreck was a two man, reusable weapon more akin to the M1 bazooka - although more effective). The number of tanks destroyed with these weapons was highly variable, rising to over 30% on occasion, although this obviously depended on the situation and the other weapons available. They were deadly in close combat, in urban or confined areas, but less much less useful in open areas where they could more easly be spotted. The German bazooka is better than ours due to the fact it is bigger and packs a heavier punch. It is an 88-mm and ours is a 2.36 inch. It also carries a windshield which makes a face mask unnecessary. There have been instances where our bazooka struck an enemy tank and failed to stop it. The German Panzerfaust is a fine weapon. It is light to carry and has absolutely no flash back which will harm face or hands and will easily make a large hole in four inches of sloping armor. The Panzerfaust is simple to op-crate and seems to be very adaptable to inexpensive large-scale manufacture. Our anti-tank weapons are all fine quality but need to be much heavier and more destructive. Lt. Col. R.W. Jenna, CO 41st Armoured Infantry Regiment Later models of the Panzerfaust, the Panzerfaust 60, 100, and 150 had ranges comparable with the Allied anti-tank weapons and could penetrate around 200mm of armour.
