Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Have you ever heard of RAF pilots in the Battle of Britain who saw what they believed to be a mounted knight in the sky?
Answer: Possibly, but I’ve not heard about it. This sounds either like a reworking of the Angel of Mons story from WW1 or a misunderstanding of the phrase Knights of the Sky. Although I can’t track down the first usage of the latter case, it was during WW1 that journalists riffed on the nature of single combat between pilots to create an image in the minds of the public of a glamorous, chivalrous, type of warfare reminiscent of the knights of old. Anyone who has read much history will be aware that chivalry, although it existed, was mostly sadly lacking from combat either in the Middle Ages or the skies of WW1. In both cases, combat was a murderous affair with the best results obtained by sneaking up on the enemy and shooting him in the back before he knew you were there. Beware of the Hun in the Sun was a common warning to inexperienced Allied pilots. The Angel of Mons was on of several stories that arose in WW1. These probably owe their origin the legend that King Arthur will return when Britain is in its hour of greatest need, which legend dates back to William of Malmesbury in 1125: But Arthur's grave is nowhere seen, whence antiquity of fables still claims that he will return. In WW1, the journalist William Machen wrote a short piece inspired by the critical Battle of Mons, which described, as a literary fancy, phantom bowmen from the Battle of Agincourt, summoned by a soldier calling on St. George, helping destroy the German host. This spawned a whole series of tales about various supernatural forces that provided both spiritual and actual assistance in the task of defeating the beastly Hun. These stories included visions of assorted bowmen, angels, and knights appearing on land or in the sky. There are also a whole slew of RAF based ghost stories that might lead into this, including The Shepherd by Frederick Forsyth, in which a lost pilot (in 1957) is guided home by a phantom Mosquito. A good read.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During WW2, didn't the Australians test a Rotabuggy type (flying Jeep)?
Answer: No, I don’t think that they did. I suspect that there may be some potential for confusion between the British Rotabuggy and the Australian designed DCA Fleep, arising from the fact that the designer of the Rotabuggy, Raoul Hafner, was Austrian. Hafner’s Rotabuggy was tested in flight, but never entered production, whilst the Fleep (Flying Jeep) was prototyped but never flew, the project being cancelled before the trials could begin. The Rotabuggy eventually made a flight lasting for some ten minutes at an altitude of 400′. Both of these contraptions had a rotor of around 40′ in diameter, which is a pretty significant piece of kit and they would have had to be flown for long distances behind a towing aircraft (rather them than me). Both projects were abandoned when cargo carrying gliders such as the Horsa, Hamilcar, and Waco became available. The Rotabuggy in flight The Fleep

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the purpose of the rear turrets on Soviet tanks?
Answer: Not just the Soviets. However, the question probably refers to the Soviet T-35, sometimes known as the land battleship, the only tank ever to have five separate turrets. The T-35 had its main 76.2mm weapon in a central turret and then had four subsidiary turrets, two each front and rear, with one in each pair being armed with a 45mm weapon and the other a 7.62mm machine gun. To answer the question, the rear turrets were to provide arcs of fire to the rear of the vehicle for all-round protection. The Soviet Union produced several other multi-turreted tanks and prototypes including the T-28 and the T-100., as did the British, Germans, and the US. Soviet T-35, 1x76.2mm, 2x45mm, up to 7x7.62mm, 10 crew In WW1, the first tanks had multiple sponsons or gun positions to provide wider arcs of fire as the idea of a turret had not yet evolved - although it came along with the Renault FT light tank in 1917 - and this set the scene for the next developments. British Mk I, 2x6-pdr, 3x303, 8 crew In the immediate post-WW1 years quite a few countries experimented with multi-turreted tanks up to, and including, the US M3 Medium or Lee/Grant tank. From both the engineering and tactical perspectives this was a brand new field and a time of wild experimentation - with many failures - a sort of Cambrian explosion in the tank world if you will. The concept was partly to provide all round spatial awareness and defence but also, in some cases, to provide different weapons for different purposes. The M3 had a 75mm gun for firing HE at infantry and other soft targets and a 37mm gun for anti-tank work as it was problematical to develop an effective HE round for small bore weapons. M3 Medium Lee, 1x75mm, 1x37mm, up to 4x.30, 7 crew One of the primary inspirations was the British Vickers A1E1 Independent prototype (it never entered service) which had five turrets and was designed to breakthrough the enemy’s lines, taking on swarms of infantry whilst still being able to engage enemy tanks. British Vickers A1E1, 1x3-pdr, 4x.303, 8 crew However, most multi-turreted tanks are (usually) large, heavy, mechanically complicated (i.e. very likely to break down), unwieldy, and require a large crew - which was difficult to coordinate, all of which made them both very expensive and tactically inefficient as well as having poor cross-country performance. Multi-turreted tanks were also tall making them highly visible, and the turrets provided lots of shot traps. These factors made them much more vulnerable than a lower, cleaner design. Some multi-turreted tanks were conceived as light tanks but this idea also fizzled out. Imagine trying to coordinate an action in this, talk about push me, pull you… Vickers 6-ton Type A, 2x.303, 3 crew

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In Britain's peerage system, do Dukes outrank Earls or are they equal?
Answer: According to the definitive Debrett’s Guide to the Ranks and Privileges of the Peerage (often just called Debrett’s), the five degrees of the peerage, in descending order of precedence, are: Duke/Duchess, Marquess/Marchioness, Earl/Countess, Viscount/Viscountess, and Baron/Baroness. This obviously excludes the members of the Royal Family itself, which has its own quite complicated orders of precedence. There are also Royal Dukes, such as the Duke of Edinburgh who are entitled to the title of Prince and, indeed, Royal Earls, who outrank ordinary Earls. For instance the Earl of Wessex is Prince Edward, who is also now the Duke of Edinburgh, the Earl of Forfar, and Viscount Severn. Within their rank, precedence generally conforms to the age of the title. I believe that the oldest extant English Peerage is the Earldom of Arundel (created in 1138) which is held by the Duke of Norfolk and used by his heir as a courtesy title. Arundel Castle - worth visiting, nice gardens - you can see the original motte (dating from 1067) in the middle There are obviously lots of variations catering for the differences between English and Scottish peers, hereditary and life peers, office holders (e.g. Lord Chancellor), bishops, the various orders of knighthood, etc., etc. It may surprise some non-natives to learn that 99.9% of British people go through their whole lives without the slightest idea about any of this as it doesn’t impinge on daily life in any way. I live in Sussex, but I am in no way beholden to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, although I’d probably be polite if introduced to them - but then I’m polite when introduced to anybody.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: In WW2, could you take a compass bearing while inside the tank?
Answer: Not using a standard hand held magnetic compass you couldn’t, no. Or to be absolutely correct, you could but it would be wrong. Magnetic compasses are affected by local magnetic fields and a tank is a big chunk of ferromagnetic steel. You’d need to be about 25 metres away from the tank to get a reliable bearing from a standard magnetic compass. Tanks in WW2 were fitted with compasses (originally boat compasses) that could be “swung” regularly to determine and record the variation caused by the tank’s own magnetic field - which could be as much as twenty degrees. Notice the constant deviation corrector on the left In the desert, sun-compasses were used to aid in navigation in areas where high iron ore content distorted magnetic compasses. Bagnold sun compass Some tanks in WW2 were fitted with gyrocompasses which do not rely on the Earth’s magnetic field but instead use precession and the Earth’s axis of rotation to indicate true North (not magnetic North). As a consequence, these instruments are sometimes called direction indicators or setters rather than compasses. Originally quite large with electric motors and flywheels, they evolved into vacuum or compressed air spun devices driven by a pump on the engine. I am not sure when the gyrocompass was introduced in Allied tanks but the following is from an Allied intelligence report dated the 10th of September 1942. A German Mark II tank with an electric gyroscopic compass has made its appearance in Libya. It is possible that all commander's tanks may be equipped with this particular device. The whole equipment is first-class in quality and workmanship. It is not likely that breakdowns will occur to any great extent, and the equipment should give long service without overhaul. The main components of this instrument are the generator and the gyro, connected to each other by a flexible multicore cable. Switches for operation and lighting are fixed to the casing. The motor generator is housed in a separate casing which may be placed in a convenient location in the vehicle. A 12-volt motor drives a three-phase alternator supply to the gyro. The whole arrangement is compact, and appears fully suppressed and screened to avoid radio interference. Fitted to the dashboard in front and to the left of the driver, the gyroscopic instrument consists of a small box with a panel showing two cards rotating in a horizontal plane. A switch and two control knobs, one for each dial, are added features of this equipment (see accompanying sketch). German Electric Directional Gyroscope To march on a certain point, a celluloid disk, marked around the circumference in clock-rays, is centered on the position of the tank on the map with 12 pointing due north. A thread leading from the center of the disk is joined to the point on the map which is the objective, and thus shows, in terms of clock-rays, the bearing of the objective from the tank. This is termed the "march number." The indicator must be set before using. This is done by finding the course of the tank, setting the gyro, and starting the gyro and allowing it to gain speed. The course is set on the course-setting dial and the tank steered until the dial markings on both dials coincide. A special compass is provided to find the tank's course. It has a glass marked with clock-ray divisions. The compass user must not stand nearer than 15 yards from the tank when finding its heading. Setting of the gyro is done by turning the gyro dial with the setting knob until it is the same as the tank's course previously found with hand compass. After setting, the gyro must be started and allowed 3 or 4 minutes to gain speed; it then must be set free by pressing the release button. The course-setting dial is to assist the driver in keeping to his course without constantly remembering what the actual bearing is. Therefore, the dial is set to the desired course (or march number) and the tank then steered to make the top dial figures keep opposite the lower (gyro) dial. Resetting of the indicator may be necessary, either periodically because of deviation, or because exceptional tilt temporarily interferes with the internal mechanism. When this occurs a red warning-light is shown.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Did any soldiers of the first wave of D-day invasion be as old as Tom Hanks was when he played one in "Saving Private Ryan" (44 years)?
Answer: General Theodore Roosevelt Jr. aged 56 was, as far as I know, the oldest man to land with the first wave on D-Day (at Utah). Officers are generally rather older than enlisted, by an average of about six years, and the more senior the officer obviously the older they get. Sadly Roosevelt died on the 12th July 1944 of a heart attack. Roosevelt (left) in 1943 The only summary that I have seen for troops in WW2 was a survey of 10th Light Division in 1943. This revealed that (rounded up) 22% of men were aged 18–19, 31% were aged 20–22, 17% were aged 23–25, 12% were aged 26–28, 8% were aged 29–31, 5% were aged 32–34, 4% were aged 35–37, and only 1% were aged 38 or over. Many sites state that the average age of soldiers on D-Day was 26, but Tom Hanks was playing a Captain and I would suggest that the vast majority of Captains would have been in their mid to late 20s or possibly early 30s. Captain Richard P. Merrill, 2nd Ranger Battalion at Pointe du Hoc, was 25 for instance and General Roosevelt’s son, Captain Quentin Roosevelt II, landed with the first wave on Omaha also at the age of 25. The most senior officers to land on Omaha were probably Colonels, but they didn’t land in the first wave, landing in the follow up waves instead. Colonel George A Taylor, 16th Infantry, was 45 and Colonel George A Smith Jr., 18th Infantry, was 42. I would conclude that very few men who landed in the first wave on Omaha would have been as old as Tom Hanks was when he played the role. At his age he would more likely been a Colonel and landed in a follow up wave. The honourable exception to the rule is General Theodore Roosevelt Jr. aged 56.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: During the Battle of France in 1940, the Brit Army cowardly abandoned the front without informing their allies and ran, leaving the French to cover their retreat. Isn't an apology for this outrageous act of treason long overdue?
Answer: Now you know that’s not true Ian. Just in case anybody doesn’t understand the actual situation, it was the Belgian and French forces to either side that pulled back, leaving the BEF (British Expeditionary Force) with its flanks in the air and no alternative but to withdraw. The Germans then pinned in the BEF and three French armies along the coast where the remaining forces concentrated around Dunkirk. Since the French and the BEF had conducted their own separate retreats and were manning their own sections of the Dunkirk perimeter, the Admiralty assumed that the British would evacuate in Royal Navy ships, while French soldiers would evacuate in French ships. However, the French Navy seems to have believed that the Dunkirk beachhead could be sustained and did not prepare sufficiently for evacuation. Long story short, in total some 360,000 men were evacuated from Dunkirk of whom 139,000 were French. Of these 139,000 French servicemen, 102,250 were evacuated in British ships. British and French troops queue for evacuation Order making it explicit that both British and French troops were to be evacuated

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were there ever any attempts to add lights to night fighters in WW2 to spot bombers in a similar way that lights were added to find submarines?
Answer: Yes there were. This was an idea first tried during WW1 when a searchlight was fitted to a Spad XI nightfighter. Spad XI nightfighter In WW2, various options were tried. The next photo is a Douglas A-20 Havoc NF.II fitted with a 2,700 million candela Turbinlight. This needed a 2,000lb battery to give it 120 seconds of life. This added weight and the position of the light ruled out fitting the aircraft with any armament, so the idea was that the plane would be vectored on to the target by ground radar and then illuminate it for two accompanying parasite fighters - Hurricanes or Defiants - to shoot it down. The concept was called ATI—Air Target Illumination. I note that this aircraft also seems to have been fitted with AI (airborne intercept) radar. Aircraft illuminated by Turbinlights(?) Coordinating the three aircraft required was both difficult and dangerous with the parasite fighters often losing contact. Also, of course, the powerful light would have caused everyone involved to lose their night vision as soon as it came on. The experiment didn’t work out with only a single Heinkel 111 and an unfortunate RAF Sunderland flying boat confirmed as shot down while several Havocs and Hurricanes were lost to accidents. The rapid improvement in AI radar, including the development of centrimetric radar, spelled the end of the Turbinlite system. The next generation of night fighters were the heavily armed, radar equipped, two-seat Beaufighter and Mosquito.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: For how long did Mongols (Mughals) rule India?
Answer: The first Mughal Emperor was Barbur (Zahīr ud-Dīn Muhammad) reigning from 1526 and the last was the twentieth, Bahadur Shah Zafar (Mirza Abu Zafar Siraj-ud-din Muhammad), who was deposed by the British in 1858. Therefore, the Mughals lasted 332 years. Although the term Mughal does stem from the word Mongol, the Mughals were mostly ethnic Turks and not Mongolians, having become assimilated with the wider the Turkic population they ruled over. In practice Barbur is identified culturally with the Turco-Persian tradition. His origin, milieu, training, and culture were steeped in Persian culture and so Babur was largely responsible for the fostering of this culture by his descendants, the Mughals of India, and for the expansion of Persian cultural influence in the Indian subcontinent, with brilliant literary, artistic, and historiographical results. Having said that, Barbur (1483-1530) could indeed trace his blood line back to Ghengis (Chinggis) Khan via Timur the Lame (Tamerlane) and thus the Timurid Empire. His grandfather, Abu Sa'id Mirza, was Timurid emperor in the mid-15th Century and some claim Barbur as an Uzbek. Babur Bahadur Shah Zafar

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Were all British colonies involved in the revolution against Britain, or were there some that remained loyal to Britain after the war ended?
Answer: Following the conclusion of the Seven Years’ War (The French and Indian War) the British Empire gained vast territories on the American continent at the expense of France and Spain. This, of course, explains why they were so keen to take their revenge by assisting the American Revolution. Continental British America The resulting set of territories were known as British America and the British West Indies. As well as the Thirteen Colonies, they included the Province of Quebec, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Rupert’s Land, the North-Western Territories, the British Arctic Territories, the Indian Reserve, East Florida, West Florida, Bermuda, Newfoundland, the Windward Islands, the Leeward Islands, and Jamaica (including parts of Honduras and Nicaragua). All of these territories except, rather obviously, the Thirteen Colonies remained loyal. The two Floridas, which were practically empty, were ceded back to Spain after the war and the Indian Reserve and parts of Quebec were ceded to the United States. The remaining territories became the basis of modern Canada and nations in the Caribbean and South America. British possessions elsewhere in the World were unaffected by the Revolution.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What is the reason behind the Navy's Fighting Squadron number being called a "VFA" instead of an "FNA"?
Answer: The V means heavier than air, the F means fighter and the A means attack. The V dates from 1920 when all heavier than air squadrons were designated v (apparently from the Latin volare to fly) and lighter than air squadrons z (for Zeppelin?). In 1922, the US Navy added a “class” letter with F meaning fighter, these were sometimes called fighting squadrons. A VF Squadron was a US Navy fighter squadron and VMF was a US Marine fighter squadron. There were also class letters for bombing, VB, scouting, VS, and torpedo, VT, squadrons. The VF designation was in use until the F-14 Tomcat was retired in 2006. VFA, the A meaning attack, was introduced in 1980 when the multi-role F/A-18 Hornet came into service. In 1983, the Fighter Attack Squadrons were all redesignated Strike Fighter Squadrons but the acronym was retained. VFA-14, Strike Fighter Squadron 14, known as the Tophatters is a United States Navy fighter attack squadron flying the F/A-18E Super Hornet. They are the Navy's oldest active squadron, having formed in 1919 and were designated VF-1 in 1922. VFA-14 Hornet

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: How would a battle between a Tiger tank and a British Sherman Firefly in WWII play out?
Answer: For those who aren’t experts, the Sherman Firefly was a Sherman armed with the British 17-pounder L/55 (3” or 76.2mm) anti-tank gun, versus the Tiger I with its 3.46” 8.8cm KwK L/56 (KwK means tank gun and L/x is the length of the barrel in calibres) At normal combat ranges, up to 1,000 yards, each can kill the other quite handily and so there’s no real need to get into the minutiae of armour, guns, ammunition, optics, turret traverse, or reliability. The outcome will depend on who sees who first and the skill of the gunner. It will also depend on who is advancing. The advantage will be to the defender. The Firefly was a specialised tank killer operating within a troop of standard 75mm gunned Shermans. Standard tactics were for the Firefly to remain in an overwatch position whilst the rest of the troop advanced. Therefore the Tiger, unless very canny, is likely to open fire on one of the advancing 75mm gunned Shermans in the troop and then find itself engaged by the Firefly on overwatch. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: At what rank did Sir Winston resign from his position as an officer in the British Army during World War I?
Answer: Churchill resigned his commission in April 1899, but I am not sure that he resigned his commission in World War I at all. He relinquished command of the 6th Royal Scots Fusiliers on the 16th of May 1916, and reverted from his temporary rank of Lieutenant Colonel to the rank of Major. Churchill’s military career is far from straightforward to follow. He did not do well enough to win an infantry placement at Sandhurst and entered as a cavalry cadet. However, an infantry placement became vacant and he transferred to the infantry. Churchill did well at Sandhurst and was destined for the 60th Rifles. However, the lure of the cavalry beckoned and he wangled a commission in the 4th Queen’s Own Hussars, a light cavalry regiment, and was commissioned as a cornet (2nd Lieutenant) in that regiment in February 1895. A young Winston in the 4th Queen’s Own Hussars Churchill was promoted to Lieutenant in May 1896 after a spell on leave in Cuba as an observer to the conflict raging there. In September 1896 the regiment sailed for India and Churchill was then based in Bangalore until March 1899. During this time, he had himself attached to the Malakand Field Force as an observer on the North-West Frontier. After a great deal of lobbying, and against Lord Kitchener’s express wishes, he was then attached as a supernumerary Lieutenant to the 21st Lancers for the Sudan campaign. It is understood that you will proceed at your own expense and that in the event of your being killed or wounded in the impending operation or for any other reason no charge of any kind will fall on British Army Funds. It was with the 21st Lancers, on the September 2nd 1898, that Churchill took part in the famous charge at the Battle of Omdurman. On the 5th of May 1899 Churchill resigned his commission in the 4th Queen’s Own Hussars in order to pursue a political and journalistic career. However, in January 1900 during the Second Boer War, General Sir Redvers Buller arranged for Churchill to be commissioned as a Lieutenant (unpaid) in the South African Light Horse, despite the fact that he continued to serve as a war correspondent for The Morning Post. Churchill as a Lieutenant in the South African Light Horse On his return to England, Churchill decided to volunteer for a yeomanry (territorial) regiment, and in January, 1902, joined the Queen’s Own Oxfordshire Hussars (QOOH), as a Captain. In 1905 he was promoted to Major and, until 1913, commanded its Henley-on-Thames squadron. As an aside, the regular army did not hold the QOOH in high regard, nicknaming them the Queer Objects On Horseback or the Agricultural Cavalry. After his resignation from office following the Gallipoli debacle, Churchill was attached (for acclimatisation) to 2nd Battalion, Grenadier Guards in France in November 1915 as a Major. Expecting to be given a brigade, Churchill was instead promoted, in early 1916, to Lieutenant Colonel (temporary) and given command of a rather battered New Army battalion, the 6th Royal Scots Fusiliers, posted at Ploegsteert. He commanded the battalion for 108 days until it was merged with the 7th Battalion to rebuild it. As the Colonel of the 7th Battalion was senior to Churchill, Churchill relinquished command and returned to politics. However, Churchill would carry on serving as a reserve officer until 1924, when he resigned from the Territorial Army. Churchill remained the QOOH’s Honorary Colonel until his death, and left instructions that they be given a place of distinction in the procession at his state funeral, immediately in front of his coffin. The story goes that, as the huge procession was forming up, a brigade major of the Guards stormed up to the officer commanding the QOOH detachment and told him that his men were incorrectly arranged according to accepted protocol. The QOOH’s officer replied: In the Oxfordshire Yeomanry we always do state funerals this way. I think that Churchill would certainly have enjoyed that exchange.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: If Nazi Germany had won the Battle of Britain, would the Royal Navy have tried to interfere with the Operation Sea Lion landings?
Answer: They certainly would have. Apart from some curious off-the-wall operations such as Operation Lucid, the Royal Navy’s anti-invasion preparations were fairly standard, with ships covering both the East coast and the Channel. The Home Fleet was stationed far to the North at Scapa Flow in the Orkneys where it could cover the North Atlantic, Norwegian Sea, and North Sea. It would have taken over twenty-four hours for the Home Fleet to intervene in the Channel, but the Home Fleet was not the only force at hand. At the outbreak of war, the Royal Navy had nine battleships, four aircraft carriers, seventeen cruisers, and ninety-six destroyers in Home Waters. Seven battleships (including Hood), an aircraft carrier, twelve cruisers, and seventeen destroyers were with the Home Fleet at Scapa Flow. The rest of the force was split between Rosyth, Humber, Portland, Dover, Portsmouth and Plymouth . Royal Navy Destroyers at sea By September 1940, there were twelve destroyers and one cruiser were based on the Tyne with the aircraft carrier Argus. Ten destroyers were based at Dover and Portsmouth, a cruiser and three destroyers at Sheerness, three cruisers and seven destroyers at the Humber, nine destroyers at Harwich, and two cruisers at Rosyth. The battleships Rodney, Nelson, and Hood, three cruisers and a destroyer flotilla were moved south to Rosyth and the Revenge was moved to Plymouth. By early September the Royal Navy had between Plymouth and Harwich, 4 light cruisers and 57 destroyers together with around fifty MTBs. Together with the Home Fleet, this was far more naval power than the Germans could possibly commit to any invasion even if they wanted to risk their heavy units. However, in all likelihood, any invasion would have been faced by light units: cruisers, destroyers, motor torpedo boats, and submarines. The invasion areas were simply too constricted and too vulnerable to air power to deploy heavy units, except in extremis. In the famous Operation Sea Lion wargame conducted by the Royal Military Academy (Sandhurst) in 1974, the heavy units of the Home Fleet were ordered to stand by but not actually used. If you are wondering why I am discussing the outcome of this wargame, it is because it is the largest simulation of Sea Lion ever conducted. The scenario was based on the known plans of each side and Admiralty weather records for September 1940. The umpire for the Kriegsmarine was Vizeadmiral Friederich Ruge who commanded the naval escort and support operations for the invasion of Poland and then FdM West (part of the North Sea and Channel operations) from 1940 to 1943. Someone who should know what he was talking about. The following extract covers the naval battles but omit the Heer and Luftwaffe elements. It should be noted that many of the Royal Navy’s losses described below would have been inflicted by the Luftwaffe. 22nd September The first wave hit the beaches at dawn. Elements of 9 divisions were landed between Folkestone and Rottingdean (near Brighton). In addition 7th FJ (parachute) Div landed at Lympne to take the airfield. The invasion fleet suffered minor losses from MTBs (motor torpedo boats) during the night crossing, but the Royal Navy lost one CA (cruiser) and three DDs (destroyers) sunk, with one CA and two DDs damaged, whilst sinking three German DDs. 22nd - 23rd September The U-Boats, Luftwaffe and few surface ships had lost contact with the Royal Navy, but then a cruiser squadron with supporting DDs entered the Channel narrows and had to run the gauntlet of long range coastal guns, E-Boats, and Stukas. Two CAs were sunk and one damaged. A diversionary German naval sortie from Norway was completely destroyed. Sorties by MTBs and DDs inflicted losses on German shipping in the Channel. German shipping losses on the first day amounted to over 25% of their invasion fleet. 23rd Sept 1400 - 1900 hrs The Home Fleet had pulled out of air range however, leaving the fight in the hands of 57 DDs and 17 CAs plus a number of MTBs. The Germans could put very little surface strength against this. Waves of DDs and CAs entered the Channel, and although two were sunk by U-Boats, they sank one U-Boat in return and did not stop. The German flotilla at Le Havre put to sea (3 DDs, 14 E-Boats) and at dusk intercepted the British, but were wiped out, losing all three DDs and 7 E-Boats. Sep 24th dawn - Sep 28th The German second echelon set sail, the weather calmed, and U-Boats, E-Boats and fighters covered them. However at daylight 5th destroyer flotilla found the barges still ten miles off the coast and tore them to shreds. The Germans disabled two CAs and four DDs, but 65% of the barges were sunk. Lacking supplies and reinforcements the Germans conducted a hasty evacuation. Of the 90,000 troops who landed on 22nd September, only 15,400 returned to France, the rest were killed or captured.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why did the Allies decide that Rangers scaling the cliffs at Pointe du Hoc was the best option, versus using paratroopers dropped inland at the time of the invasion, or even glider troops?
Answer: I have visited Pointe du Hoc and I can confirm that the German gun positions are right on the edge of the cliff. Point du Hoc In addition, the positions were defended on the landward side and these defences included several belts of wire, minefields, machine guns, and trenches, as well as a couple of probable anti-aircraft guns that could be used for ground defence. The main problem with a parachute attack is that it is quite likely that many of the men would have landed in the sea and drowned. This was a problem during Operation Husky, where several hundred airborne troops drowned, and during Operation Overlord itself, where an unknown number of paratroopers died after landing in the sea or on marshy ground. Had paratroops landed further inland, they would have had to fight through the defences. During the Bruneval Raid, Operation Biting, in 1942, paratroopers were successfully landed close to the coast, but they were not landed right on top of the objective but some quarter of a mile inland. Operation Biting As a matter of interest, it appears that one or two paratroopers, from a misplaced stick of the US 101st Airborne, did end up at Point du Hoc and assisted in the fighting. Pointe du Hoc defences

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: When did the Anglo-Saxons start using iron swords instead of bronze in Britain? Was it a relatively quick transition or did it take many centuries?
Answer: The term Anglo-Saxon began to be used in the 8th century to distinguish Germanic language-speaking groups in Britain from those on the continent. There may have been some settlement of Saxon foederati, barbarian mercenaries, in Southern England as early as the 4th Century but it is still debated whether the term Saxon Shore (as in the military leader, the Count of the Saxon Shore) refers to a shore that the Saxons were defending (as foederati) or one they were attacking (as pirates). In any case, this is a category error. The Bronze aged had ended nearly a thousand years earlier, around 600–800 BC, and Anglo-Saxon swords would have been of iron, possibly with some bronze decoration. Anyone fighting with a bronze sword would have been at a disadvantage, as bronze is much softer and bends, meaning that bronze swords were typically 18–24″ long as opposed to a typical Anglo-Saxon iron sword of perhaps 36″. In any case, swords were high status weapons and relatively rare. About 12% of Saxon burials that contain weapons are found to contain swords. Most Anglo-Saxons probably armed themselves with a spear and the long (iron) knife called a seax, from which the term Saxon might actually derive. The change from bronze to iron weapons would certainly not have been instant, but it occurred quite a long time before the Anglo-Saxons first appeared in Britain. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: Why is it hidden from us at school that Nazi Germany did the bombing raids on Great Britain because Britain did nighttime air raids on Berlin first?
Answer: It’s not hidden from anyone, because its not true. The Germans, actually first bombed London on 31st May 1915, some twenty five years before the British bombed Berlin, but we’ll give them a pass on that. Heinkel 111 over the Isle of Dogs During WW2, the first British raid on Berlin was on 25th August 1940 and was in response to bombs dropped on London by the Luftwaffe on the 24th August 1940, although some newspaper reports suggest that areas of outer London were bombed as early as the 15th or 16th of August. On the night of the 24th of August 1940, Council records show that the blue circles: East Ham, West Ham, Stepney, Bethnal Green, Hackney, Leyton, Walthamstow, Edmonton, Islington and Bloomsbury all recorded bomb damage between 23:00hrs and 01:30hrs. The half red circles: Stepney, Bethnal Green, Hackney and Finsbury recorded bomb damage between 03:00hrs and 03:40hrs. The green circles: Esher, Kingston, Twickenham, Feltham and Staines, recorded bomb damage between 23:50hrs and 00:30hrs. And slap bang in the middle of London, Fore Street in the City. Memorial in Fore Street Clearly at least three separate raids, none of which are anywhere near the supposed targets of Rochester and Thameshaven. Neither the lone lost bomber myth or the lost raid myth are remotely tenable. Much is made of the bombing of Germany, but during the London Blitz, the Luftwaffe dropped around 12,000 tons of bombs and around 20,000 civilians were killed. One of every six Londoners was made homeless at some point during the Blitz, and at least 1.1 million houses were either damaged or destroyed.

Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What did sailors in the British Royal Navy do with the enemy dead when taking ships as prizes in the 18th century?
Answer: It depends on the situation. During a battle the dead, even of one’s own ship, were generally thrown over the side or through a gunport. A fighting ship is a busy place and having dead bodies underfoot is not only bad for morale but a hazard. The cries of the wounded now rang through all parts of the ship. These were carried to the cockpit as fast as they fell, while those more fortunate men, who were killed outright, were immediately thrown overboard… I was an eyewitness to a sight equally revolting. A man named Aldrich had his hands cut off by a shot, and almost at the same moment he received another shot, which tore open his bowels in a terrible manner. As he fell, two or three men caught him in their arms, and, as he could not live, threw him overboard. Samuel Leech, HMS Macedonian After a battle, the dead were most likely buried at sea, although I have read that the French sometimes temporarily buried their dead in the ship’s ballast. Generally a dead sailor was sewn up in his hammock with a cannonball at his feet and the last stitch made through his nose to confirm he was actually dead. Sunday, 27th. Wind at N. V. at 4 AM Tack'd ship. At same time the man who was bade with the flux was found dead in his hammock, at 8 he was sewed up in it and at 9 AM he was burried in the sea after reading the service of the Dead over him, which was done by the Mate. The service was standardised and brief. We therefore commit his Body to the Deep, to be turned into Corruption, looking for the resurrection of the Body, when the Sea shall give up her dead, and the life of the world to come, through our Lord Jesus Christ; who at his coming shall change our vile Body, that it may be like his glorious Body, according to the mighty working, whereby he is able to subdue all things to himself. As for enemy dead, they would either be thrown unceremoniously over the side or, if circumstances allowed, buried at sea, if Christian with the formalities attended to by their surviving crew mates. As with most things at sea, it all depended on the circumstances. Burial at sea
